Adding in some timed walks or stretches is key to arriving feeling fresh. “Simply changing position, moving your joints and getting up whenever it’s safe to do so can make a massive difference,” says Sayers. Pilates stretches to do on a long-haul flight Deep diaphragmatic breathing Sitting in one place for hours can “compress the diaphragm and restrict your circulation,” explains Seleio. You can combat this by practicing deep diaphragmatic breathing, which will help to “maintain oxygen flow, reduce muscle tension, and keep your nervous system calm”. To do this, “place yourself towards the front of your seat with your spine lengthened. Inhale deeply through your nose for a count of four, allowing your rib cage to expand sideways. Exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of four, gently drawing your navel toward your spine and allowing your ribs to soften inward," instructs Seleio. “Repeat five times.” Shoulder rolls To help release tension in your shoulders and upper back, which can so easily become tense when sitting in a rigid seat, you need to make sure your movements go beyond just adjusting your neck pillow. To do this, Seleio says, “Sit upright with your arms relaxed by your sides. Slowly roll your shoulders up toward your ears, then back and down, encouraging your shoulder blades to glide smoothly across your ribcage." Perform five to eight repetitions, then reverse the direction. Pelvic tilts When instructed to stay in one place, our pelvis, seeking comfort, can tilt itself into an anterior (towards the front of your body) or posterior (towards the back of your body) position. If you allow this and don't consciously maintain a neutral posture, it can cause an achy lower back and, over time, a deformed posture. To help find your even position, do some pelvic tilts between over- and under-extension. Not only will this give your lower back some movement and release, but it will also help you to find your healthy neutral sitting position. “Take a deep breath in and gently arch your lower back, tilting your pelvis backwards,” says Sayers. “As you exhale, round through your lower back and tilt the front of your pelvis up towards your body. Slowly alternate between the two positions to add movement.” Seated knee lifts with ankle movement Simply lifting your knees while in your plane seat can improve your blood circulation and activate your hip flexors and core. Start by “sitting tall with your core gently engaged,” says Seleio. Then, “slowly lift one knee a few inches off the floor without leaning backwards. While keeping the knee lifted, point your toes away from you, then pull them back toward your shin three to five times. Lower the foot in a controlled manner and repeat on the other side. Continue alternating sides for 10 to 20 repetitions.” Isometric palm press We can all be guilty of slumping into our seats or rounding our shoulders as we get lost in a classic film on the in-flight entertainment system. Adding some isometric palm presses can help bring an awareness back to your posture, activate your chest muscles, and release tension in your shoulders. “Bring your palms together in front of your chest with your elbows relaxed,” says Seleio. Then, “press your palms firmly into one another while maintaining an upright posture and engaged core. Hold the contraction for five to 10 seconds, then release. Repeat the movement five to eight times”. Spinal rotations When sitting for over an hour, our spine can become impacted as pressure builds on the discs in our lumbar spine. To keep your thoracic spine (the mid-back) more mobile, you can release tension through gentle twisting movements. “Sit up nice and tall, keeping your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears,” says Sayers. Then “gently rotate your upper body from side to side. You can gradually move a little further into the rotation each time, but keep the movement controlled and never force a deep twist”. Toe taps Regardless of whether you’re wearing compression socks or not, your legs and ankles can often become swollen when sitting for long periods. One of the best things you can do to alleviate this is to “get up and walk around when possible,” explains Sayers. But if the seatbelt sign is firmly switched on, you can make a difference by moving your feet. To keep the blood moving and to give your core a mid-flight activation, toe taps are simple but effective. “Sit tall with your spine lengthened and core gently engaged,” starts Seleio. Next, “Lift one foot a few inches off the floor while reaching the opposite hand to tap the toes. Return to the starting position with control and alternate sides. Continue for 10 to 20 repetitions”. Throughout this exercise, you should maintain an upright posture and “avoid collapsing through the chest as you reach for your foot”. With thanks to Sabrina Aparicio Bellesa, Pilates instructor at Real Pilates. A version of this story originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: A Guide to Vagus Nerve Stimulation, the Secret to Making Travel Easier on Our Nervous Systems
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.63
Scroll far enough on social media, and you'll hit a quick fix promising to calm your nervous system in seconds. Mastering vagus nerve stimulation in particular has become wellness shorthand for “calm on demand,” but there's actual science behind how you do it properly—and it goes far beyond a 15-second clip. So, what is the vagus nerve? Essentially, the longest cranial nerve in the body, traveling from the brainstem down through the neck and chest into the abdomen, brushing past the heart, lungs, and gut. It's the main line of the parasympathetic nervous system—your body's primary mechanism for rest, digestion, repair—as opposed to the sympathetic system that gears you up to handle a threat. “If you think of your body as a car, the autonomic nervous system is the drivetrain and brakes,” says Lou Atkinson, clinical wellbeing lead of Yōjō, a health and wellness platform specializing in vagus nerve stimulation or VNS. “The sympathetic nervous system is the accelerator, while the vagus nerve is your essential braking system, slowing your heart rate, initiating digestion, and lowering inflammation.” Activating the vagus nerve can help us feel calmer, but the issue with quick fixes is that we are treating the symptoms of nervous system dysregulation—like anxiety, insomnia, a need to control everything—rather than the dysregulation itself. “If we treat the symptom without ever getting to the root cause, it becomes a tireless battle managing something that cannot dissipate unless we leave the state we're in,” explains Sarah Baldwin, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner. What happens to our nervous system when we travel? Travel obliterates almost all our comforting routines and habits. “It’s essentially a stress-test for your autonomic nervous system, and vagal tone takes the hit," says Human Potential Coach and Breathwork Practitioner, Rob Rea. “Crossing time zones desynchronizes the body's rest-and-digest rhythm from local day and night—a large part of why jet lag brings poor sleep, a racing heart and low mood, not just tiredness.” Short nights, dry cabin air, dehydration, alcohol, and caffeine all tip the body further towards fight-or-flight, leaving less room for recovery. For some, it goes way deeper than jet lag. Leaving a familiar environment removes our daily safety anchors, and unresolved stress can resurface as anxiety or hypervigilance amid the unpredictability of new places. “Long after we’ve arrived, and the danger has passed, the body can keep replaying that same protective response—that’s why so many of us feel anxious or shut down for reasons we can't quite explain, especially when traveling,” trauma psychotherapist Emmy Brunner says. “Release isn't about forcing it—it happens through small, repeated doses of safety, not pushing through.” In practice, this looks like having a vagus nerve toolkit you can turn to when you need it most. "Splash cold water on the face—cold exposure activates the vagus nerve and can pull you out of a spiral almost instantly,” Brunner advises. Another tip she says is to: “Slowly look around the room and name a few things you can see—it reminds the nervous system it's present and safe." Another surprising method that works is quiet humming. “It stimulates the vagus nerve directly through the vocal cords,” says Atkinson. If you feel too conscious doing this in a public place, longer exhales also help engage it: "Breathe gently through your nose, inhale for four seconds, and exhale for six," says Rea. "Let the breath become quieter rather than bigger, and continue for two to five minutes." Making travel easier on our nervous systems Perhaps the best advice is to think of nervous system work as part of your pre-travel prep, along with your packing and booking. “People often wait until they're deeply dysregulated to start regulating, but the earlier you start, the better,” Baldwin advises. She recommends getting outdoor light at both ends of the day to recalibrate your circadian rhythm before, during, and after your trip. As is having a piece of home with you. “Bringing something familiar, a candle, a journal, a photo, and orienting to a new room by consciously noticing its colors and sounds both help signal safety, too,” she adds. For frequent flyers wanting something more hands-off, wearable vagus nerve stimulators like yōjō deliver gentle electrical pulses to the ear's auricular branch, nudging the body into rest-digest mode without requiring meditation mid-flight—wearable while working, watching a film, or trying to sleep. But ultimately it’s about incorporating vagal nerve work into your daily life. “The goal is not a quick fix; it’s to discharge small amounts of activation to lessen our dysregulation by even five percent,” Baldwin says. Our nervous systems need something called disconfirming experiences. “These are moments where we show, not tell, our nervous systems that the thing it thinks is dangerous is actually safe,” she says. After doing that, our nervous system has enough data points to see that the perceived danger is actually safe, and we no longer experience the anxiety we once did. None of this promises to make flying enjoyable—particularly if you struggle with it. But understood and practiced properly, vagal tone could be the deciding factor in whether a trip leaves you restored or wrung out. That’s worth knowing, next time you're stuck in seat 34C convincing yourself it's turbulence, when it’s actually your nervous system on overdrive. - Emmy Brunner’s residential retreats combine hypnosis and somatic practice. The Compass, a four-week online course, fuses evidence-based clinical tools with belief and identity re-patterning. - Sarah Baldwin’s online programs Navigating Your Nervous System and Nervous System Essentials can be found here. Listen to her podcast, You Make Sense Podcast, on Apple or Spotify. - Rob Rea’s Autumn Equinox Day Retreat will be at 1 Hotel Mayfair, London. Follow him online. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 19 Cheap Places to Travel: Where Your Dollar Will Take You the Furthest Right Now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.38
Whether you're ballin' on a budget or Scrooge McDuck-ing into coffers of gold, there are few things more satisfying than getting the most bang for your buck on vacation. The beauty of hunting for cheap places to travel lies in getting to shorten your bucket list at a bargain. If you dream of swimming alongside the candy-colored panoply of fish swarming the coral reefs of the Indian Ocean, there's no need to balk at Maldives prices when you could head to Madagascar for half the price. Or if it's French lavender fields you yearn for, consider Canada's blooming gardens instead. We've crunched the numbers on current exchange rates, airfare, and hotel deals to find the countries to travel to over the next year where your dollar goes the furthest. Of course, rates can fluctuate at any time, though some destinations have a greater likelihood of staying high-value relative to their price tags. With a variety of picks that span the globe, these are the best cheap places to travel around the world right now—and where to stay once you're there. Estonia 1 USD = 0.86 EUR The cat has long been out of the bag on the island-hopping havens that are the Greek Cyclades, Italy's Aeolian Islands, and the Dalmatian Coast. But there are plenty of other European seascapes to explore, with thinner crowds to boot. Rather than docking on the Mediterranean, cast your eye north to the Baltic Sea where Estonia lays claim to over 2,200 islets that are teeming with bucolic inland views and coastal nature in all its unbridled glory. For a glimpse at medieval life in Estonia sail to Saaremaa, home to the Teutonic Order-built Kuressaare Castle. The basement dungeon of the stunning Gothic monument houses a room now known as “the cellar of the immured knight” which, as legend has it, imprisoned an inquisitor monk who was caught in a clandestine romance. For a taste of contemporary—and considerably less morose—Estonian life, check out Kihnu, an island populated by what the BBC describes as “Europe's last surviving matriarchy.” Inside the UNESCO-recognized community, women are the primary keepers of culture, maintaining the island's rich traditions in song, dance, games, and crafts. Where to stay: Base yourself in the historic capital of Tallinn where homey stays like the Nunne Boutique Hotel lend prime access to the charming Old Town at rates beginning as low as $97 a night. Ghana 1 USD = 11.20 GHS Its reputation as the Gold Coast might leave many surprised that some of the most rewarding cultural experiences at this gateway to Africa go easy on the wallet. Reconnect with the outdoors while suspended 100 feet off the ground by hiking across the wooden catwalks perched along the canopy line at Kakum National Park. From this breathtaking vantage point you can spy the mix of rare wildlife that lives in the forest, from massive Bongo antelopes to acrobatic Diana monkeys—and entrance into the park and the canopy walk totals about $20. Ghana's human-made sites are equally wondrous: For a gilded blast from the past, start at the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, where tickets sell for around $11. The region's history as the heart of the Ashanti kingdom plays out through the museum's impressive collection of elaborate royal artifacts. For even more hustle and bustle, make sure to pay a visit to Accra's joyously chaotic Makola Market. From vibrant local fabrics to fragrant spices, beaded jewelry to even spare car parts, locals and tourists alike peruse the stalls to find just the thing they're looking for, or discover the wild card item they never knew they needed. Where to stay: While some of the best things to do in Ghana can be far-flung from each other, it's never a bad idea to base yourself in Accra where stays like La Palm Royal Beach Hotel boast their own share of the coast. Bolivia 1 USD = 11.78 BOB Often topping lists of the most beautiful countries in the world, Bolivia continues to reap praise for landscapes like its mirror-clear salt flats and ultra-saturated volcanic lagoons. But you need not train to assume the mantle of hardcore backpacker to take full advantage of what the gorgeous Heart of South America has to offer. Take to the countryside by car on an epic road trip to destinations like Torotoro, home to the largest collection of dinosaur tracks in the world (park entry will run you about $14), or Sucre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its ornate double-balconied ivory architecture. Of course, one of the best ways to take in Bolivia's incredible biodiversity and abundant landscapes is by exploring it via fork and knife. Look no further than La Paz, a city that is perfectly triangulated between the Andes, the Amazon rainforest, and both areas' surrounding valleys. Gustu has long been a gastonomic giant in the city, pioneering a locavore movement that spotlights ingredients like mountain greens, Amazonian river fish, and llama dairy. For plates fresh from the fire of the hearth, head to Ancestral, where all the dishes are cooked via wood smoke or hot coals to bring out their natural flavors. Where to stay: Get a taste of Cabo in the middle of La Paz at Baja Club Hotel, a 32-key boutique with a chill pool terrace and swanky rooftop bar. Uzbekistan 1 USD = 11,817.44 UZS Uzbekistan is still on the up-and-up when it comes to foreign travel, which makes it one of the most exciting and affordable destinations in Central Asia. The major cities are filled with both intricate mosques and brutalist monuments—all free to explore—and you’ll be hard-pressed to spend more than about $5 per meal at most restaurants. Where to stay: There aren’t too many name-brand hotels set up yet, but even places like the Hyatt Regency Tashkent have nightly rates below $170. Peru 1 USD = 3.30 PEN While some may only know Peru as a gateway country to adrenaline-pumping adventure, it's a veritable destination in its own right, and its capital city of Lima is one of its best cases in point. it's a seaside city that's soundtracked by salsa echoing from its rooftops and colored by the mountains of fruit sold at its open-air markets. The colonial mansions of yore are now filled by Peruvian designers, boutique hotels, and ultra-chic wine bar-listening rooms. There's also loads of history to brush up against just about everywhere you turn (and we mean that quite literally—in this city, pre-Inca ruins still occupy traffic medians). The charming neighborhood of Pueblo Libre has the city's largest concentration of parks if you fancy yourself more of a leisurely stroller than a hiker. Or if you'd rather explore the great indoors, check out the pre-Columbian art at Museo Larco, before lunching at Antigua Taberna Queirolo, known for homestyle dishes like ají de gallina. Those who have come to Lima to dance should do as the locals do and tear it up at El Bolivariano. Where to stay: Next year will be an especially excellent time to stay at Hotel B, known for its rooftop bar, which will soon add 10 rooms and an on-site spa. Belize 1 USD = 2 BZD The easy two-to-one conversion rate between the Belize dollar (BZD) and our US greenbacks means there's no need to whip out your phone calculator when budgeting for your vacation to the Central American country. In fact, don't bother converting any currency or fret over foreign transaction fees as your US dollars are just as good in Belize as they are stateside. With world-famous archaeological sites, rainforests, reefs, and a culinary scene worth traveling for alone, its easy to see why the tiny country has earned a big reputation. Where to stay: This Caribbean nation charmed visionary Francis Ford Coppola so much that he established three beach hideaways on its secluded shores. Canada 1 USD = 1.39 CAD While some may see Toronto's glittering skyline or the myriad of mouth-watering eats in Montreal and not immediately see an affordable travel destination, the Great White North is a vast expanse with plenty of high-value sights to see. Take Quebec City, the only walled city across the US and Canada. From its past as a former French colony, there's history on every street, whether its Quartier Petit Champlain, one of the oldest shopping corridors in the country, or the steps of the Notre-Dame de Québec Basilica-Cathedral. It's a city where you can sample many firsts, like the first cheese ever cured on the continent, which was made by the still-extant Fromagerie de l'Isle d'Orléans? If you thought it couldn't get anymore French, QC also lays claim to some pretty amazing lavender fields at La Seigneurie de l'île d'Orléans where admission starts around $14.50. Clear some space on your calendar in July, to witness the flowers in peak bloom. Where to stay: Nothing beats walking distance convenience, which Hôtel Sépia has in spades with its proximity to sights like the St. Lawrence River and the family-friendly Aquarium of Quebec. Cambodia 1 USD = 4,058.34 KHR E-visas already allow us to skip much of the bureaucratic hassle of traditional visa applications, and Cambodia's e-visa program just got even sweeter. At the start of 2025, tourist visa fees were slashed from $36 to $30. First-time visitors can't go wrong with landing in Siam Reap, where famed UNESCO World Heritage Site Angkor Wat sits among festive bars, vibrant cultural experiences, and French-style colonial streets. Travel to the city is easier than ever thanks to the recently opened Siem Reap-Angkor International Airport (SAI). Where to stay: Located just a 10-minute drive away from Angkor Wat, the Park Hyatt Siam Reap is an ideal home base to soak in all the local flavor. The property also offers crafting workshops from local artisans, so you can take away a one-of-a-kind souvenir (plus a skill or two) back home. Egypt 1 USD = 50.65 EGP Following in the footsteps of pharaohs in Egypt feels like it should be expensive, but the conversoin rate of the Egyptian pound has recently skyrocketed—and that means touring the Pyramids, cruising the Nile, and exploring Cairo has never been more affordable for foreigners. We’re excited to check out marquee additions to the hotel scene like the St. Regis Cairo. In addition to its awe-inspiring views onto the Nile, the hotel houses the Astor Library on its fifth floor, an intimate reading room with its own artifact display and Swarovski diamond chandelier made for book lovers. Though if you're looking to feel absolutely gob-smacked, the Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) has finally opened to the public after years of anxiously awaiting its debut. As the largest museum in the world dedicated to the study of a single culture, it's just the place to get your fill of all things ancient Egypt. Where to stay: There's no competing with the historic Marriott Mena House's location at the foot of the Giza pyramids and adjacent to the GEM. Once-in-a-lifetime views of the necropolis are guaranteed from many corners of the property. Mexico 1 USD = 17.02 MXN Mexico is consistently one of our favorite places to travel on a budget. In Mexico City, with a street food culture rivaled only by its forward-looking restaurant scene, you’ll be spending most of your money on eats. But make sure to leave some bucks to visit all the cultural wonders the city has to offer, starting with the iconic Museo Jumex. If you’re looking to go a little further afield, head to Jalisco to see tequila being made at the source, or Isla Holbox for a sleepy beach scene. Where to stay: You can never go wrong at one of our Triple Crown-winning properties—a distinction for hotels which have won our readers' hearts in the annual Readers’ Choice Awards; a spot on the Gold List, which features the places to stay our editors consider their all-time favorites; and a feature in our Hot List, a compendium of the year's hottest new openings. Mexico is chock full of these distinguished stays, like the One&Only Palmilla, an escape on the very tip of the Baja Peninsula that feels just like home, just with the odd beach cabana and private butler for good measure. Mongolia 1 USD = 3,597.64 MNT We’ve long been fans of Mongolia for its seemingly limitless expanses and adventure camps—and the fact that travel here can cost as little as $75 per day (including accommodations). Over the pas couple of years, the country has expanded the traveler-friendly initiatives it launched in 2024, such as more direct US flight and visa-free travel for dozens of nationalities. You can also expect all the offbeat cultural experiences that make this Asian nation a popular bucket list contender: local operator Breanna Wilson's tours include a Gobi Desert excursion to see snow leopards, a women-only retreat in Orkhon Valley, and a three-day archery training session. Where to stay: Set along the Terelj River, a 90-minute drive from Ulaanbaatar, the Terelj Hotel was originally built in the 19th century for Russian vacationers. When weather permits, guests can ride horses, trek in the surrounding hills, fish for salmon, or bird-watch for the exotic species that fly overhead—all activities happily arranged by the diligent staff. Vietnam 1 USD = 26,072.50 VND Plenty of countries in Southeast Asia are great deals for dollar carriers right now, but we recommend a trip to Vietnam—in part because of the steadily increasing exchange rate, but mostly for the country’s mind-blowing beauty. Last year, we listed Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City as some of our best places to go for their celebrations commemorating the country's national reunification and buzzier than ever food and design scenes. Hanoi is arguably the most romantic city in the region, but don’t be afraid to venture off the beaten track during your next visit: Places like Ninh Van Bay and Phú Quốc island have pristine beaches and intimate resorts you won’t find in the more touristed areas. Where to stay: For a stalwart in the hospitality scene, the Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi has been a fixture in Hanoi since 1901. Brazil 1 USD = 5.18 BRL Like much of South America, Brazil is a good place to visit if you don’t want to break the bank. But the fact that a dollar gets you a little over five Brazilian reals means you can get even better value than usual. Rio de Janeiro is the most obvious place to spend time and money, with incredible restaurants—like Lasai, a 2023 Hot List winner—just steps away from some of the world’s best beaches. But don't forget to visit São Paulo, too, where a younger generation has introduced hip galleries, museums, and bars to several long-neglected neighborhoods. Where to stay: Take a glimpse at what living may look like in the year 3,000 at the Ruy Ohtake-designed and aptly named Hotel Unique in São Paulo's upscale Jardim Paulista neighborhood. Sri Lanka 1 USD = 328.15 SLR The Sri Lankan rupee has slowly gotten more and more favorable over the past couple of decades, but it completely skyrocketed starting a couple of years ago (a dollar converted to 200 SLR in February 2022, and now look where we are). We’re more excited than ever to explore this incredible island nation, where you can see leafy tea plantations, Buddhist temples, golden beaches, and 200-mile hiking trails in one memorable trip. Where to stay: Triple Crown winner Cape Weligama is a glossy clifftop resort that's the triumphant Relais & Châteaux flagship of Resplendent Ceylon’s stunning quintet of properties. Madagascar 1 USD = 4,306.66 MGA For your next tropical island vacation, skip pricey, popular locations like the Maldives and Bora Bora for inexpensive Madagascar—an Indian Ocean treasure filled with breathtaking rainforests and lemur-filled national parks. Swing by the island nation as part of a cruise itinerary: Luxe cruise lines like Silversea, Lindblad, Swan Hellenic, and Seabourne have all added the country as a port of call on new voyages. Where to stay: Plan your stay at Namoroka Tsingy Exploration Camp, which features seven luxury safari tents inside the essentially unvisited Namoroka National Park. Malaysia 1 USD = 4.03 MYR Your cash will stretch far in Malaysia, especially if you fill up on street food and explore cities like Kuala Lumpur on foot. It’s also inexpensive (or in some cases, free) to visit the country’s pristine beaches, limestone caves, and some of the most beautiful tea plantations. Where to stay: If you’re ready and willing to shell out the big bucks, we highly recommend shacking up at The Datai Langkawi. Set within a dense, beautiful rainforest, this legendary hotel is where modern luxury meets ancient nature in one of the world’s most serene, coveted retreats. India 1 USD = 95.18 INR India has always been a cheap travel destination; now that you can get over 95 rupees to the dollar, however, the country is more affordable than ever. As long as you don’t hole up in your resort the entire time, you can visit plenty of attractions and dine at local restaurants on an extremely tight budget. Where to stay: Hotels run the gamut from $60-per-night bungalows to pricey Oberoi and Six Senses outposts, plus hundreds of options in between. Serbia 1 USD = 112.67 RSD Belgrade continues to emerge as one of Europe’s most exciting cultural epicenters, but it’s massively less expensive than, say, Paris or Berlin (at least for now). It’s relatively easy to find hotels under $100, though accommodations aren’t all that important when you spend all night dancing in clubs around the city. But you will want to get some rest to explore Belgrade’s wealth of museums and contemporary art installations, many of which just opened in the past few years. Additionally, Belgrade will be the site of the World Expo in 2027 with a slate of new hotel openings and an expanded to Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG) really rolling out the red carpet for the global conference. Where to stay: Square Nine at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers offers a dose of modernity in the landmark Studentski Trg plaza. North Macedonia 1 USD = 53.04 MKD Perhaps it’s because the coastal countries get all the attention, but North Macedonia remains one of the most criminally underrated (and therefore affordable) countries in Europe. The landlocked nation is a sleeper hit for those in the know, especially if you head to the charming city of Ohrid. It has all the cobbled streets and quaint churches one would expect from a European town, with the added advantage of being right on the shores of the incredibly gorgeous and biodiverse Lake Ohrid.

item.title: The Triumphant Return of the Airline Seatback Screen
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.25
Airline passengers are all too familiar with onboard perks disappearing from planes, whether it’s free seat selection or in-flight snacks, complimentary checked bags, or simply the ability to recline your seat. Now, however, some of the largest US airlines are bringing back one passenger-beloved amenity: seatback entertainment screens. Thanks to a rising demand for more premium products, airlines are reversing course on the steady elimination of individual entertainment screens and are now adding them back to their fleets across all cabin classes. Just several years ago, the demise of the seatback screen had seemed all but certain as part of airlines’ never-ending quest to cut costs and maximize profits. “These systems are expensive to purchase, expensive to install, and have ongoing costs including repair and programming updates,” says Mike Taylor, senior managing director of travel, hospitality, retail, and customer service at JD Power. Plus, airlines figured that 80% of passengers were flying with their own smartphones, laptops, or tablets, so it would be simpler to nix the screens and offer content for travelers to access on their personal devices, according to Taylor. “But difficulties in connecting, the quality of in-flight Wi-Fi, and the variability of streaming bandwidth among various types of aircraft account for the deficit between seatback and streaming experiences,” he says. One of the most notable about-faces on screens is a new initiative from American Airlines. The Fort Worth-based carrier said it will be adding seatback screens back to every seat in its narrow-body fleet of aircraft, including onboard new planes set to be delivered in 2028 as well as retrofitting its existing jets with screens. “In the race for premium traffic, American felt like they couldn’t compete with Delta and United—which have leaned into screens—without their own,” says Gary Leff, an airline expert and travel advisor. United, for one, has been on a mission since 2022 to add seatback screens to every seat in its fleet as part of its Good Leads the Way campaign to improve its onboard experience. As part of that plan, the carrier unveiled 13-inch TVs in economy, which rank among the largest coach screens in the world, aboard its new Dreamliner 787-9 planes. Likewise, Alaska Airlines has been adding its first-ever seatback screens in the carrier's history to its new Dreamliner fleet that debuted in late 2025 and now flies their long-haul international routes from Seattle. Although Delta never reduced the seatback screens in its fleet, the carrier has been heavily investing in its in-flight entertainment system since 2023 with the launch of Delta Sync, which offers a personalized, smart TV-like experience with benefits like the ability to pause a movie on one flight and resume it on the next one. Experts say that aside from the race to provide premium products, there are a few additional factors pushing airlines to reinstate their own TVs at every seat. For one, screen technology has advanced by leaps and bounds compared to a decade ago, when the elimination strategy became popular. Now, the screens are “far less expensive to install than they used to be, since it no longer requires running wires to each seat to feed content,” Leff explains. “The screens can receive their content wirelessly from a server on the plane.” Not only that, but the latest screens offer perks like 4K display, Bluetooth connectivity for wireless headphones, USB-C charging ports, and personalized content. That last feature could even help carriers actually make money off of the systems, too. “The screens also offer a revenue opportunity to monetize the time and attention of the passenger, a desirable demographic to advertise to, with personalized content. They know who is seated at each seat,” says Leff. At the end of the day, passengers simply prefer a seatback screen as a way to get lost in a movie or show while on a long flight. According to JD Power’s airline satisfaction survey data, seatback screens add between 60 and 90 points of customer satisfaction to an airline’s overall score, which is based on a 1,000 point scale. “That is a significant difference in satisfaction in airline experience,” Taylor says.

item.title: The Whimsical British Country-House Fantasy Is Taking Over Upstate New York
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.02
“Britain is a country of great eccentrics,” muses interior designer Adam Greco, whose own view of ‘British whimsy’ manifests in charming chintz and heirloom curios, filtered through the lens of cultural treasures like Sherlock Holmes and Mary Poppins. It's a highly romanticized spin, something the New York City–based designer, who's worked on properties like London's The Ned and Oslo's Sommerro, felt wanting in the hospitality space, even across many landmark British hotels. “As a foreigner I remember walking into a grand hotel on London’s Regent’s Street and thinking it looked like a function room in Cincinnati inside,” he says. “It was disappointing.” Recently, though, a wave of UK properties have started to embrace the kinds of cultural eccentricities that Greco saw as lacking in those hotels. This updated approach to the whimsical British aesthetic, all vintage bric-a-brac set alongside some serious art collections and sumptuous fabrics, is best expressed in the UK at properties like the Three Horseshoes in Batcombe, about 20 miles south of Bath, and the Fort Road Hotel in Margate along the southeast coast. Lately, the design aesthetic has captured America’s attention, and found a home in upstate New York: Soho Farmhouse is due to open its outpost in Rhinebeck, New York, next year. The team behind the Cotswolds’ Estelle Manor is said to be searching for a property in a similar patch close to the Hudson Valley and the Catskills. These new builds are a bid to lure affluent New Yorkers who have outgrown the Hamptons, and, as former magazine editor turned hotelier Dorian Grinspan puts it, “provide something wilder, that feels genuinely rural rather than relocated.” Grinspan’s own property, Maison Monna, is two and a half hours from the city in Old Chatham, a charming hamlet he discovered when vacationing in the area with his partner. With Monna, he wanted to speak to this new breed of luxury traveler, someone who wants to feel “comfortable, cared-for, but not smothered,”—a natural companion to British whimsy's lived-in, been-here-for-decades sensibility. Maison Monna was a perfect canvas for the expression of this trend, largely because it had sat untouched on the market for so many years. The style of the three-bedroom house is Greek Revival, though records show its bones date back to the Quakers (it makes sense, then, that scenes for Mona Fastvold’s award-winning The Testament of Ann Lee were shot close by). To populate it, Grinspan looked to his personal archive of antiques, yet by the time it all arrived, he explains, the effect was “a bit too monastic.” The fix? “To add a little British whimsy.” That translated into custom upholstery; fabrics sourced from textile sellers Merchant & Mills and Notting Hill’s Cloth Shop; DeVol sconces; and cheery ruffled skirting in the kitchen. It also meant being open to quirks and imperfections—Grinspan wanted the creak in the floorboards. He was even okay with gaps, “so long as no one falls through.” With Maison Monna, the style softens the property’s Shaker roots (it was built in 1796), but at the Six Bells in Hudson Valley’s Rosendale, British whimsy is interwoven with pure American nostalgia. Greco, who designed the three-story 1850s property for entrepreneur Audrey Gelman, explains the distinction is key: “It’s Audrey’s love of late 20th century catalogue Americana, the Vermont Country Store and Lillian Vernon,” with its bold ginghams, Laura Ashley florals, and ruffled baskets, trussed up in a design vernacular that feels unmistakably English. When guests step onto the property, Greco’s aim was to create a sense of “déjà vu, or something uncanny—like, have I been here before? Did I imagine this? Is this where my grandmother had her first kiss?” Of the property’s 11 rooms, it is the Innkeeper’s Suite that is his favorite, with a built-in, hand-painted box bed, a hallmark of so many English country homes. Forty minutes further into the Catskills in Hensonville, 2025 Hot List winner The Henson is a marked example of a softer interpretation. At this 16-room inn, living spaces are flooded with natural light, and touches of bouclé and natural woods create a serene, homey feel. The family portraits that hang in the hotel’s ‘living room’ aren’t purely decorative, either—they are hand-me-downs from co-owner Ely Franko's grandparents, who once hung them in their home in Turkey (Ely and his wife Danielle co-own the property alongside chefs Jeremiah Stone and Fabian von Hauske Valtierra). Ditsy floral quilt toppers add a sentimental anchor to bedrooms, while vintage pieces threaded throughout the rest of the property have been lovingly sourced by the experts at New York’s The Somerset House. It’s the same unfussy, lived-in register that both Grinspan and Greco have also created in their respective projects, but here it is without direct reference to Britain at all. And perhaps that is the point. It’s not that a handful of hoteliers and designers are taking a cut-and-paste approach to decorating these properties but rather that they’re paying homage to the instincts behind it: a resistance to newness, artful curation of clutter, and a veneration of the past through beautiful antiques. It is a design language that’s developed enough that American hotels now speak fluently.

item.title: This Fall, Leaf Peep from a Gondola, Helicopter, or Tree House
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.84
Americans call it “leaf peeping,” while the Japanese call it “momijigari.” Whatever the culture, there’s a term for witnessing the changing colors of leaves, a universal act that spurs awe and wonder and makes one reflect on the passage of time. Fall foliage is worth booking a trip around, but you need not limit yourself to the standard hike or road trip. While we’ll always have these classic leaf-peeping excursions, there’s excitement in reinventing a ritual. Once you start to experience the first chills of the season, consider getting a little whimsical: Mush your way through the Alaskan forest, float away on a hot air balloon in the Finger Lakes, or zipline past the Rockies. You could rent a run-of-the-mill cabin somewhere in the Hudson Valley, or you could go big with a tree house, complete with floor-to-ceiling windows. Ditch that standard New England inn and opt instead for a houseboat in coastal Maine, perfect for riverside scenery. The possibilities are endless, and the experiences on this list will ensure you see the changing colors of fall from all kinds of perspectives. Below, seven alternative ideas for leaf peeping across the US. Hop on a gondola While mountain resorts are best known for skiing in the winter, many keep off-season tourists happy with scenic sky rides. Take the Gondola SkyRide at Stowe Mountain Resort, for instance, which carries visitors up to Mount Mansfield, Vermont’s highest peak. Running until mid-October, the ride is an excellent way to bask in New England’s autumnal glory and drops passengers off right at the resort’s Cliff House Restaurant for a scenic meal. Similarly, the Gondola at Telluride Mountain Village in southwest Colorado allows visitors to take in golden aspens from 10,800 feet above and can be used to access various hiking trails. Over at Lutsen Mountains in Minnesota, leaf peepers can take the Summit Express to get some of the best views in the state, including sightings of the Sawtooth Mountains and Lake Superior. Embark on a scenic train ride Nothing says cozy fall trip quite like an old-fashioned choo choo train, and luckily, the country is teeming with locomotives for every kind of traveler. Wine lovers will enjoy the Napa Valley Wine Train, especially between September and November, when harvest season is in full swing, and the vineyards and trees turn shades of gold, orange, and red (temperatures at this time also hover in the 80s—glorious). Prefer something a bit more outdoorsy? Amtrak’s Pacific Northwest Fall Foliage train takes passengers on sightseeing tours of Mount Rainier and Olympic National Park, which boast vibrant maples (and thinner crowds) from mid-September through October, while the Blue Ridge Railway offers dedicated fall foliage tours for those who’d like to experience the beauty of the Toccoa River. For something even more adventurous, Rail Explorers offers an unconventional approach to the train track with pedal-powered bikes you can use to ride the rails, with scenic locations in New York’s Catskills and West Virginia’s Elk River region. Mush your way through the forest In Fairbanks, Alaska, the leaves start changing as early as mid-to-late August, and you don’t have to wait until the snow falls to have an authentic dog sledding experience. On Last Frontier’s unique mushing ride, you’ll have a four-legged team guiding you through the Alaskan forest on UTVs, “learning all about dog mushing, racing, and Alaskan off-grid living along the way,” the website says. The host, Chase, is a former Yukon Quest racer, and he’ll introduce you to his team of dogs, who will be very excited to run after their long summer hiatus. (Because Last Frontier is a co-op, different mushers run their own dogs and make sure their animals are well taken care of). Glide past the trees on a cruise The foliage surrounding the banks of New York’s Hudson River is so striking, it makes sense why it’s served as the subject for a history of landscape paintings. Circle Line offers two cruises for Hudson Valley leaf peeping—an eight-hour journey up to Bear Mountain State Park past the Palisades, or a shorter four-hour run toward Hook Mountain—each with beer, pretzels, and all kinds of other Oktoberfest fare. Adventurers looking for more of a day trip will enjoy the dock at Bear Mountain State Park, where they’ll have about three hours on land to hike, while those opting for the shorter trip will still get to sail past the George Washington and Mario Cuomo Bridges, looking out for hawks, ospreys, and bald eagles along the way. Each departing from Midtown Manhattan, these cruises offer ideal day trips for New Yorkers itching to explore nature beyond Central Park. Zipline through the mountains Adrenaline seekers, this one’s for you—see the trees in a flash on a zipline tour through the mountains. From mid-September to late October, Idaho Springs, Colorado, becomes flush with golden aspens, and you can spend half a day taking in the beautiful scenery from six different aerial lines along the treetops with Arkansas Valley Adventures. Or, if you’d rather get your views from down south, Saluda, North Carolina, is a sight to behold from mid-October through early November, and this Gorge Zipline Canopy Tour will suspend adventurers above the Green River Gorge for unforgettable views of changing maples and alders. Book a unique, foliage-friendly stay Sometimes, autumnal scenery can be so arresting, you can’t help but spend hours soaking in the views. There’s no shortage of fall-foliage-friendly Airbnbs and vacation rentals across the country, so make the most of your autumnal getaway with an unforgettable stay. Commerce director Madison Flager is a big fan of this tree house in Phoenicia, New York, with its soaring windows and proximity to cult-classic Phoenicia Diner. If you’d rather hole up in coastal Maine, White Barn Inn in Kennebunkport (a consistent Reader’s Choice winner) offers a collection of houseboat stays plopped on the Kennebunk River, where you can enjoy your morning coffee from a private rooftop deck, gazing at the golden landscape. - Check availability for the Treehouse in Phoenicia, New York - Check availability for the White Barn Inn & Spa Get a true bird's-eye view There are gondolas, and then there are more extreme ways to soar above the trees. If you fancy floating away on a hot air balloon, head to New York’s Finger Lakes region for a ride above Letchworth State Park, known as the “Grand Canyon of the East,” for a one-hour journey with Liberty Balloon Company. You’ll see vibrant trees framing a 600-foot gorge and three different waterfalls, all from the comfort of your balloon. Or, go big with a private helicopter tour of the Hudson Valley with Wings Air Helicopters, departing from Midtown Manhattan. In just one hour, you’ll soar over the Sleepy Hollow Lighthouse, Bear Mountain, Lyndhurst Mansion, and Kykuit, the Rockefeller Estate, all while enjoying the patches of color.

item.title: For Starry Waters and Tiny Glowing Squids, Head to These Best Places to See Bioluminescence
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.67
The best places to see bioluminescence around the world sit atop many travelers’ bucket lists. Whether it's through the pages of glossy magazines like ours, glittering on social media feeds, or told through the tales our jet-setting loved ones share on their return from their latest adventure, this natural phenomenon is undeniably captivating. Perhaps it's jellyfish that twinkle at the harbor’s edge or plankton that creates scenes akin to starry skies as toes paddle in the ocean. Either way, bioluminescence is a fascinating natural phenomenon that, once witnessed, is impossible to forget. However, it’s unlikely that you’ll see glittering, rippling waters by chance. Here, from the shores of Oaxaca in Mexico to Maldivian atolls via the British Isles, we reveal the best places to see bioluminescence in all its dazzling forms. It is generally safe to touch and swim in bioluminescent waters, especially in destinations where the sparkling waters are featured as tourist attractions with boat trips and excursions. However, some bioluminescence results from harmful algal blooms that can cause skin rashes and severe illness if ingested. When in doubt, research the area you’re visiting thoroughly and speak to guides on organized trips. 1. The Maldives The picture-perfect islands of the Maldives are some of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world, thanks to an abundance of plankton that illuminates the waves after sunset. While it’s possible to see the phenomenon on islands across the archipelago, one of the most famous spots of them all is on the quietest side of Vaadhoo Island, a minuscule island of the Raa Atoll known for its beachy corner nicknamed the sea of stars. When to go: Between June and October How to get there: Domestic flight and boat transfer from Velana International Airport in Malé Where to stay: Vaadhoo Island lacks the honeymoon-esque stays you may associate with the Maldives—check into InterContinental Maldives Maamunagau Resort and appreciate the glowing waters footsteps away from your beachside abode. 2. Mosquito Bay, Vieques, Puerto Rico You may not have heard of the picturesque island of Vieques. However, you’ve likely seen the spectacle that occurs after sundown, when Mosquito Bay becomes a glossy blue portal thanks to the bioluminescent dinoflagellate Pyrodinium bahamense, which glows blue when agitated. Glide through the waters on a clear-bottomed kayak with a local tour operator for a truly mesmerizing experience. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Direct flight from San Juan (SJU) followed by a ferry to Vieques Where to stay: Go back to nature—albeit with the luxury trimmings—at the cozy Finca Victoria. 3. Luminous Lagoon, Jamaica Home to dinoflagellates aplenty, Jamaica’s Luminous Lagoon is one of the most incredible excursions on the island, and a memorable way to shake up the evening itinerary. Hop on a tour boat at sunset, and, soon enough, the water’s epipelagic zone will come alive with a vibrant blue light. Watch as sea life darts under the boat’s hull, leaving phantasmagoric lines of light in its wake. Should you choose, some tours allow you to hop into the (surprisingly shallow) water and watch as splashes create incredible displays of light. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Drive from Sangster International Airport (MBJ) Where to stay: Kick back a 30-minute drive away from the spectacle with an indulgent all-inclusive stay at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay. 4. Jervis Bay, New South Wales, Australia Considering the length of its coastline and the abundance of wildlife that lies offshore, there are surprisingly few places to spot notable displays of bioluminescence around Australia. That said, places do exist, with Jervis Bay in New South Wales being one of the most famous. As the noctiluca scintillans dinoflagellate species washes ashore, settle into the powdery sand and watch the water’s ripples create an effect akin to the Northern Lights on the shore. When to go: Summer; September to February How to get there: About a 2.5-hour drive south of Sydney Airport Where to stay: Escape the hustle and bustle of everyday life with a glamping trip like no other at Paperbark Camp. 5. Krabi, Thailand There are a few bays and coves in this popular region of Thailand that promise a watery light display on clear nights. Ao Nang Beach is one of the most famous and most accessible, with beachside hostels, restaurants and bars a stone’s throw from the shoreline offering places to hide out in ahead of nightfall. While no less famous, perhaps, Phra Nang Beach is another spot a little further along the coast for a peaceful, intimate bioluminescent session reachable by boat transfers from Ao Nang Beach. When to go: November to May How to get there: 20-minute drive from Krabi International Airport Where to stay: Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve is just a 40-minute drive from the glistening waters. Expect villas, pavilions, sprawling pools, and access to dazzling beaches through the lush landscape. 6. Toyama Bay, Japan While many of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world are so due to an abundance of glowing plankton and algae, the story is a little quirkier in Japan’s Toyama Bay come spring. Here, the bioluminescent performance atop the otherwise pitch-black Japanese waters is caused by a considerably larger creature—the firefly squid. Join a fishing trip and watch as the organisms emit blue light from photophores, creating a wet and wild firework display as they are pulled from the icy depths. When to go: April - May How to get there: Hokuriku Shinkansen bullet train from Tokyo Where to stay: The DoubleTree by Hilton Toyama is a perfectly plush spot to rest in between city exploration and bay visits. 7. Oaxaca, Mexico One of the most popular places to visit for bioluminescence in Mexico is the Laguna de Manialtepec, a coastal lagoon about west of Puerto Escondido. As fish (and people braving the water for a dip) dart through the waters, the twinkling algae that call the lagoon home make the water turn fantastically phosphorescent. A little farther on, similar experiences are available at Lagunas de Chacahua. When to go: July to October (rainy season) How to get there: Fly to Oaxaca Xoxocotlan International Airport (OAX), typically via Mexico City. Where to stay: You’re spoiled for choice along this stretch of Mexican coastline—consider earthen Hotel Escondido Oaxaca or eclectic Grana B&B. 8. Koh Rong, Cambodia By day, the Cambodian island of Koh Rong is a natural playground for families and couples who take to the water armed with snorkeling gear, looking down at the vibrant sea life below. By night, the waters beyond the powder-soft sands take on a life of their own, akin to a starry sky beyond the resorts and lush vegetation. While the bioluminescent plankton isn’t unique to Koh Rong—you can spot it on other Cambodian isles—the lack of light pollution around these shores makes nighttime beach strolls and boat excursions under the new moon unforgettable. When to go: November to May How to get there: Fly to Phnom Penh, then catch a bus to Sihanoukville port and catch a boat transfer to the island Where to stay: The Royal Sands Koh Rong is the plushest address on this gorgeous island. 9. Cornwall, England The waters that surround the British Isles aren’t the first that come to mind when you think of the best places to see bioluminescence. However, come summer, the English Channel throws a few surprises upon Cornwall’s shores. Some of the most notable places to spot starry shores in this corner of the world include Grebe Beach, a hidden gem at the end of the Helford River. On balmy nights, the water can turn a luminescent blue with a splash. Elsewhere, in Penzance, the bioluminescent action is best observed at Pedn Vounder, where, a few times a year, the Channel puts on a display under the constellations. When to go: July and August How to get there: A five or six hour drive from London's Heathrow Airport Where to stay: In Falmouth, The Greenbank Hotel, a charming waterside retreat, gets our vote. In Penzance, hang out with the cool crowd at Artist Residence Cornwall, where unique bedrooms are set within a storied 17th-century property. 10. Cat Ba Island, Vietnam The region around Vietnam’s Halong Bay has long been a hotspot for those seeking glowing waters. However, being one of the stops on most travelers’ bucket lists, crowds and light pollution from boats and cruise ships mean the starry displays are notably more striking in the quieter coves and bays. Enter Cat Ba Island’s beaches, where splashes at sea equate to dazzling scenes. The natural wonder is best experienced on an overnight boat tour, as captains typically anchor in quiet spots under sparkling skies. When to go: June to October How to get there: Bus transfers from Noi Bai International Airport (HAN) in Hanoi Where to stay: Why not take over your own incredible villa while soaking up the island’s tranquil vibe from Valía Villa Cat Ba? 11. Waitomo Glowworm Caves, New Zealand Instead of a swimsuit, pair of flippers, or a kayak, the bioluminescence hiding in one of New Zealand’s most recognizable natural wonders requires visitors to wear comfortable shoes and a warm jacket. The Waitomo Glowworm Caves have been a tourist attraction for more than 130 years, with travelers passing through the awe-inspiring caves in silence, watching as the Arachnocampa luminosa glowworm species—only found in this part of the world—show off their captivating colors. When to go: Year-round How to get there: About 120 miles south of Auckland Airport (AKL) Where to stay: Assuming you’re based in Hamilton, about an hour’s drive north of the caves, for a few days, check into The Narrows Landing Hotel. A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 9 Affordable Miami Hotels That Prove You Can Do Luxury for Less
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.63
Miami has never exactly been shy about excess. Between the pastel Art Deco façades, palm-lined streets, glittering pools, and top-notch restaurants where lunch can easily turn into an all-afternoon affair, this is a city that makes it tempting to spend. But after enough trips here, I’ve learned that you don’t necessarily need to splurge on your hotel to get the tried-and-true Miami experience. Some of the city’s best affordable hotels are characterful little boutiques, historic beach hotels, and design-minded stays where the location does more of the heavy lifting than the room rate. At these value-forward bases, you can wake up a few blocks from the sand, wander down Ocean Drive for a cafecito, or retreat to the pool after a day in the sun—all without handing over your entire vacation budget at check-in. From South Beach to Brickell and beyond, these are the affordable Miami hotels—all with average nightly rates under $250—that I’d recommend booking for a stunning stay that won't break the bank. FAQ: What part of Miami is best to stay in? The best area to stay in Miami, of course, depends on your preferences. South Beach is ideal for beach lovers and nightlife seekers, offering a lively atmosphere with easy access to Little Havana, the beach, and buzzy restaurants. For a more cultural experience, consider Wynwood or the Design District, known for art galleries and trendy spots. Downtown Miami provides a central location, great for business travelers and those who want proximity to museums and shopping. Coconut Grove offers a more relaxed vibe. Where should I stay in Miami for the first time? For first-time visitors, South Beach is often the top choice due to its iconic beaches, vibrant nightlife, and easy access to popular attractions. Staying here puts you close to Ocean Drive, the Art Deco Historic District, and numerous shops and restaurants. It’s perfect for a mix of relaxation and exploration. If you prefer a quieter area, consider Coconut Grove or Brickell, which both offer a more laid-back atmosphere but are still centrally located for sightseeing. What is the average price of a hotel in Miami? The average price of a hotel in Miami varies depending on the season, location, and hotel type. On average, expect to pay between $150 and $350 per night for mid-range accommodations. Prices can spike during peak seasons, such as winter or major events like Art Basel, when rates can exceed $500 per night. Budget options may start around $75 to $100 per night, while luxury hotels can range from $400 to over $1,000 per night. How we choose the best affordable hotels in Miami: Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. item.title: 16 Idyllic Hotels in the Catskills, Where Design Meets the Upstate Wild
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.56
I’ve been going to the Catskills for as long as I can remember, and I still adore the feeling when the drive north begins to feel less like a commute and more like a true escape from the city. As a native New Yorker, I’ve spent years getting to know this upstate mountain region in every season: summer afternoons bouncing between swimming holes and farm stands, brilliant fall drives beneath canopies of red and gold, spring weekends when the woods suddenly turn electric green, and winter stays where a fire and a good dinner can easily constitute the entire itinerary. These feelings of comfort, simplicity, and adventure are part of what makes the region such an enduring weekend escape—and what makes its hotel scene so appealing. The best hotels in the Catskills range from characterful country inns and beautifully restored motels to secluded woodland retreats and sprawling estates, many with fireplaces, pools, standout restaurants, and rooms that invite you to linger just a little longer. Some are destinations in themselves; others put you in just the right spot for hiking, antiquing, swimming, or wandering through the region’s small towns. After a lifetime of returning to the Catskills, these are the hotels I’d book for an upstate New York getaway, no matter the season. Our top picks: - Best for families: Urban Cowboy Lodge - Best for design lovers: Hotel Lilien - Best for spruced-up glamping: Postcard Cabins Eastern Catskills - Best for barnhouse wellness: Inness - Best for an upscale, farm-to-table retreat: Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection FAQ: Where should I stay in the Catskills? From trailhead lodges to art-filled inns, the decision of where to stay depends on the tone you want to set for your getaway. In towns like Phoenicia, Big Indian, and Tannersville, you’ll find restored mountain lodges and design-forward motels surrounded by waterfalls, hiking trails, and swimming holes. Big Indian, in particular, offers a quieter, more secluded slice of the Catskills—dense forest, winding roads, and stays that put you within minutes of Slide Mountain and the Esopus Creek. Around Woodstock and Kingston, expect artsy spots that nod to the region’s bohemian legacy, with galleries, vintage shops, and standout farm-to-table dining. For winter ski escapes on the slopes of Hunter and Windham, look for hotels with mountain views and cozy fireplaces. Come summer, lakefront stays near Catskill and Saugerties trade snow for sun and live music nights. When is the best time to visit the Catskills? The Catskills are basically four destinations in one, each season reshaping the landscape and the mood. Spring, from April to June, brings thawed rivers, waterfalls in full rush, and wildflowers along hiking trails. Summer, from July to late August, hums with lake swims, tubing on the Esopus Creek, and outdoor concerts in Woodstock and Saugerties. Fall, from late September to early November, is peak magic for fiery maples, cider festivals, and mountain drives through Hunter and Windham. Winter, from December to around March, draws skiers and comfy-vibe-seekers to slopeside lodges and fireside dining. Which hotels in the Catskills offer the best views and amenities? The top stays in the Catskills balance mountain views with top-notch modern amenities. Eastwind Oliverea Valley captures Nordic simplicity amid forested peaks—its saunas, hammocks, and riverside setting are ideal after a day on the trails. Nearby, The Bradstan Boutique Hotel at the Eldred Preserve brings waterfront, tree-covered luxury, blending eco-minded design (hello, floor-to-ceiling windows with panoramic forest views) with cozy interiors. For architecture lovers, Piaule Catskill redefines the modern cabin with glass-walled rooms that seem to float amongst the trees, complete with a spa and soaking pools. How we choose the best hotels in the Catskills Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.
