item.title: How to Party Like a Local in Mykonos, According to a Seasoned Veteran
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.53
My first Mykonos trip ran on family time: pool swims at my uncle’s sugar-cube villa, a nap mandated by my mother, then dinner at 10 p.m., which, in our Greek family, qualified as an early-bird booking. At 15, I discovered what those naps had been preparing me for at Sea Satin, the late-night dining room for models and designers beneath the windmills, where one half of Dolce & Gabbana was celebrating a birthday a few tables away. White napkins began circling overhead, and people climbed onto the tables one by one until we were up too, a bottle of vodka sweating in its bucket below. My aunts and uncles had no children of their own and therefore a generous idea of my limits, so my glass kept finding its way back to full. On the switchbacks home, I asked my uncle to pull over and spent several minutes bent over the roadside scrub. When I climbed back in, he handed me a napkin, turned the radio back up, and apparently decided the incident did not merit a report to my mother. An island that had spent decades pairing glamour with license was perhaps the wrong place to entrust an adolescent to unusually permissive relatives. Le Corbusier and Albert Camus came when Mykonos was still a rough stop on the way to Delos. Jacqueline Kennedy’s 1961 visit brought the cameras, and that era’s guest list went on to include Grace Kelly, Brigitte Bardot, Sophia Loren and Maria Callas. Celebrities made the island visible, while gay travelers gave its nights their freedom and much of their character. Pierro’s opened in 1972, when Pierro Aversa and Andreas Koutsoukos began fitting drag queens, fishermen, aristocrats, and designers into 540 square feet. Gaultier and Valentino passed through town, while Grace Jones danced at Remezzo. Now craft beer is brewed on the island, and casual Chora bars pour proper cocktails into paper cups and send revelers off into the night. Greek musicians share the calendar with international DJs, periodically reminding Mykonos of which country it belongs to. The familiar bottle-service caricature leaves out the drag stages of the old port and the smaller rooms where a night can change direction without a reservation. Prices remain high and the roads maddening, but few Mediterranean islands offer so many convincing ways to reach sunrise. After enough summers on both sides of the nap, I have settled on seven rules that every visitor needs to know. 1. Make two plans: one for the day, and one for the night Mykonos operates in two shifts, the day party and the night, punctuated by a return to the hotel to shower and change. Choose one beach club for the day and stay until sunset, a pivotal moment on the Mykonos agenda that everyone does differently. As for your day plans? There are plenty of options. At Nammos, where you'll find polished excess, the sunny days move from beach beds at Psarou into a long fish lunch and dancing. Scorpios gathers force more gradually, reaching its peak around the sunset ritual. Jackie O’ Beach carries a poolside lunch into early-evening drag, while Alemagou justifies the drive north to get their when its calendar promises an open-air set. Afterward, return to the hotel and begin again, before choosing a dinner that can carry you into drinks or dancing and, eventually, after-hours. Just avoid crossing the island during the dinner era—it'll turn your night into one marked by traffic. 2. Confirm what, exactly, it is that you booked A booking confirmation can name the right venue while committing you to the wrong part of it. Scorpios splits its reservations four ways: Restaurant, Beach, Sunset Beach, and the Terrace Music Rituals. A proud dinner booking can seat you at a communal table while the ritual you came for happens two zones over. On the sand, an Oasis cabana comes with only a partial sea view, with “Private Beach” being the waterline category. At Cavo Paradiso, the cliffside open-air club above Paradise Beach that has booked international DJs since 1993, VIP does not mean a table. A ticket admits you to VIP Area 100, an elevated first-come standing section with its own bar and no assigned seats. An actual table requires a separate reservation and a 50 percent deposit two days ahead, then gets released 30 minutes after your slot. Have any concierge forward the venue's own confirmation rather than a summary. Before paying, get the zone and seating type in writing, plus whether the booking extends into the late-night program. 3. Choose your sunset venue by its volume Sunset can be a lowkey drink before dinner or it can be the evening’s main event, so decide which vibe you want before reserving a table—and by vibe, we mean volume. The Garden, on the hillside property that Yehudi Menuhin acquired after visiting in 1962, keeps the music low enough for conversation. Scarpa in Little Venice draws a standing crowd and raises the house music as the light drops. Scorpios is the full commitment, with a terrace program that begins in late afternoon and can carry the night toward dinner. Check the artist calendar before booking, since your friend’s triumphant TikTok posted on Sunday says very little about Wednesday’s fete. 4. Dinner can be your final destination, but it doesn't have to be In Mykonos Town, dinner can likewise contain your whole evening, complete with entertainment, or merely set things into motion. Lío is the full-night choice, building an à la carte meal around modern cabaret before becoming a club at 12:30 a.m. If you intend to move afterward, finish dinner first and keep the rest of the night on foot. A sealed to-go cocktail from TYCO buys time while the group settles on a mood. From there, Skandinavian means a loud courtyard and familiar summer hits. Astra offers a more polished dance floor beneath its ceiling of fiber-optic stars, while Lola keeps jazz and chanson at conversational volume. For drag, Jackie O’ carries the island’s queer nightlife tradition into the early morning. 5. Drink locally, then follow the Greek chorus Though Mykonos imports most of what appears in its ice buckets, the island makes its own wine and beer and it's easy to find time to enjoy both. Mykonos Vioma pours organic estate wines at its farm near Ano Mera, while Mikònu moved its taproom in 2026 to Mathios Taverna in Tourlos, where prickly-pear ale comes with dinner and a sea view. After dark, look for a room that has a Greek accent. Nōema’s Sounds of the Avli brings Greek-rooted live and electronic performance to a reservation crowd. On its Greek-music nights, Thalami offers the less polished version after midnight, when regulars and seasonal staff take over the choruses. If a panigiri is taking place in Ano Mera, ask a local when to arrive and attend as a guest rather than a customer. 6. Make your plans based on the artist, not the venue The venue supplies the setting, but the musical art determines the crowd and the shape of the night. In other words, check the calendar before making reservations anywhere. Scorpios suits melodic sets that gather slowly through sunset, while SantAnna books larger house names for pool-scale productions. Alemagou requires a dedicated trip north, so the lineup should justify the drive. Cavo Paradiso belongs to another hour entirely: It opens at 11 p.m., brings on international headliners around 1:45 a.m., and can continue until dawn. Give Cavo its own night and absolutely leave the following morning, maybe even the afternoon. 7. Book the ride home before the first drink Plotting your ride home is a daytime errand. Before dinner, open a WhatsApp thread with a private-transfer dispatcher and tell them where you're staying and how many seats you need, plus a guess at where the evening ends. There are two dispatcher numbers to save: Transfers in Mykonos covers point-to-point and on-call service, while SZS accepts a live location with 30 minutes' notice and replies with an arrival time and a plate number; whomever you book with, make sure to reference a landmark that a car can actually reach and get the fare in writing, then pad everything by an hour in July and August. An evening that begins with dinner in Chora and finishes at a late club is better served by a driver on demand, though Cavo Paradiso's reception will arrange the ride back with an hour's warning. Uber summons the same taxis everyone else is calling, and the last KTEL bus helps only when its timetable agrees with yours. Obviously, the rental car stays where it is once the drinking starts, and Vespas and quads belong to the sober daylight.

item.title: These Best Museums in Tokyo Showcase the Japanese Capital's Unparalleled Arts Scene
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.01
As anyone who has ever dined, partied, or simply wandered around Tokyo will attest, the Japanese capital marches to its own, singular beat. So it makes sense that the best museums in Tokyo are a far cry from the stodgy mausoleums of yesteryear. In lieu of squat buildings full of dusty dioramas, picture cutting-edge modernist structures by some of the country's top architects. Many of the premier art spaces forgo a permanent collection entirely in favor of a constantly rotating roster of high-profile shows by big names, local and international. Even the smaller collections strive to present their subject matter in clever, often wildly creative ways. Not sure where to go first? Here are our picks for 12 of the best museums in Tokyo. Read our complete Tokyo travel guide here, which includes: How we choose the best museums in Tokyo Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that museum. When choosing museums, our editors consider institutions that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. - Read Full ReviewPrince Asaka Yasuhiko, uncle to Emperor Hirohito, came home from Paris smitten, and the residence he and his wife Princess Nobuko completed in 1933, built by a team led by Yokichi Gondo, is the result: a marvelous blend of Deco and Japanese design set in a meticulously sculpted garden planted with dozens of flowering species. It feels like an Agatha Christie novel set in 1930s Tokyo. A contemporary annex, supervised by Hiroshi Sugimoto, added gallery space and a café. While there’s no permanent collection, the museum’s holdings comprise more than 250 works, most of which are incorporated into the design of the house itself . Henri Rapin's interiors conjure the glamour of the age in dark wood and brass, geometric ornament and sumptuous surfaces. René Lalique supplied the crystal chandeliers and glass front doors (fun fact: his first proposal featured nude female figures; the Japanese side asked him to reconsider), and there's a marble relief by Ivan-Léon Alexandre Blanchot. Outside, modern work is scattered across the grounds, including Kan Yasuda's striking white marble Wind. - Read Full ReviewA quirky little art museum hiding in plain sight, just outside the Marunouchi North ticket gates of the busiest commuter hub on earth. It opened in 1988 and, in 2006, closed for six years while Tokyo Station underwent restoration. The museum was relocated to the North Dome and reopened in 2012. The second-floor galleries put you inside Tatsuno Kingo's 1914 original station—a symbol of Western-style modernization, with brickwork and white-framed windows in the Queen Anne style. From the corridor, you can watch the commuter traffic flowing through the station below while getting an up-close view of the ornate carvings beneath the domed ceiling. The range runs from traditional Japanese painters like Kobayashi Tokusaburo to Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita, the midcentury artist whose wartime work still divides opinion. Past exhibitions have also covered the Finnish designer Tapio Wirkkala and the textile artist Miyawaki Ayako. If there's a throughline, it's a penchant for niche creators over marquee names. - Read Full ReviewIt bills itself as an immersive experience and delivers: Shohei Shigematsu supervised a spatial redesign that begins with a striking approach of 24 torii-like structures and projected imagery easing you backward in time. A delight, spread across the fifth and sixth floors in two halves, the Edo Zone and the Tokyo Zone. A full-scale recreation of Nihonbashi Bridge anchors it; the Nakamura-za kabuki theatre, once admired from outside, can now be entered. New life-size reconstructions include the Hattori Clock Shop, which leads visitors from Edo into modern Tokyo, and a faithful reproduction of the interior from the Dojunkai Daikanyama Apartments from 1927. Tempura and sushi stalls have joined the Edo streets, stocked with fabulously realistic plastic food, and screens project changing skies over the rooftops. Much of the collection is hands-on, too: you can climb into a palanquin or a cycle buggy, or shoulder the pole-and-bucket rig once used to haul fish through the streets. - Read Full ReviewA sumptuous, surreal, camera-baiting museum devoted to multi-sensory digital art. Borderless 2.0 reopened in February 2024 in a purpose-built basement space at the Azabudai Hills complex in central Tokyo. There are no walls between works and no map to follow. Installations of constantly morphing patterns and designs flow seamlessly from room to room across a maze-like space, so a school of digital fish or a cascade of blossoms will simply wander off and reappear somewhere else. Getting lost is the intended experience. Alongside updated versions of Odaiba classics, the Azabudai Hills location debuts several major new installations: Bubble Universe, an interactive infinity room filled with glass spheres that ripple with light as you approach them; Microcosmoses, where glowing spheres run along complex overhead tracks; and an expanded series of atmospheric Light Sculptures that project dynamic 3D geometry using light beams and fog. - Read Full ReviewBy outward appearance, Tokyo's Ōta Memorial Museum of Art is unassuming. Even the inside is relatively small. Still, it never fails to provide an inspiring and edifying experience. The museum focuses solely on ukiyo-e, Japanese woodblock prints and paintings, primarily from the Edo Era (1603-1868). For most of his life, the former president of the Toho Life Insurance Mutual Company Seizo Ota collected such works, and three years after his death at age 83, the Ota Memorial Museum of Art was opened in 1980 to showcase his collection. Today, the museum’s collection numbers around 15,000 works. In order to best represent this collection, the museum puts together thoughtfully curated exhibitions, with works changing frequently and many exhibitions divided into separate rotations. Topics ranging from the prosaic to the fantastic are paired with meticulously researched, Japanese- and English-language explanations that provide fascinating rabbit holes into Japanese history and the so-called "floating world" that ukiyo-e depict. - Read Full ReviewA glass, steel, and concrete behemoth at the north end of Kiba Park, and one of Japan's largest museums devoted to contemporary art. Takahiko Yanagisawa's 1995 building announces itself before you're through the gate: a long steel approach of triangular frames punched through with circles, more industrial than inviting, which turns out to be the right register for what's inside. MOT closed for a three-year renovation and reopened in March 2019, and marks its 14th year in 2026. The collection is around 6,100 works, weighted toward postwar art and shown on rotation as the MOT Collection. Warhol and Lichtenstein are among the international names, with Japanese artists like Atsuko Tanaka and Yoshitomo Nara. The temporary program is the reason to keep checking the calendar. Big solo shows—Kohei Nawa, Ryuichi Sakamoto, David Hockney, Olafur Eliasson—sit alongside well-curated group shows of younger multimedia artists, plus regular forays into fashion, design, and architecture. - Read Full ReviewA small but thoughtful tribute to the works of Japan’s most beloved animation studio, the Ghibli Museum's design is as quirky as its collection. Director Hayao Miyazaki lent his personal touch to the building, which loosely echoes a grand Italian villa. A dense layer of greenery covers the exterior of the mansion and a 16-foot-tall robot soldier from the classic film Castle in the Sky peers morosely down from the rooftop garden. More than a museum, this feels like an immersive world. From the walk-through recreation of a Ghibli artist’s workshop to original sketches, the museum uses all sorts of methods to bring Miyazaki’s vision to life. It would be an Instagram dream, if photos weren’t forbidden inside. Anyone who grew up watching these films will love the details, like the ceiling fresco populated by Nausicaa, Kiki, and other familiar faces. Even the tickets are made of original 35mm film prints, and faucet handles resemble tiny creatures. - Read Full ReviewAt first, the somewhat austere, gray facade of the National Museum of Modern Art feels at odds with the surrounding greenery of Kitanomaru Park. Inside, however, is one of the finest collections of modern Japanese art in the world. Walking through the galleries on the fourth through second floors allows you to see some of the most turbulent periods in the nation’s past through the eyes of its most influential artists. The museum’s former film division is now the independent National Film Archive of Japan, located in Kyobashi. More than 13,000 paintings, prints, drawings, video installations, and sculptures reside within the museum’s vaults and exhibition halls. Although there are a number of significant international works, the permanent collection’s strength lies in Japanese masters from the Meiji Period onward. English-language signs provide crucial historical context for each artist. - Read Full ReviewThe institution itself is a national treasure—it's Japan's oldest museum. It also happens to be in one of Tokyo's oldest public parks, Ueno, which wanders a hundred or so acres and bursts with attractions like ancient shrines, temples, ponds, and over a thousand cherry blossom trees. Housing the world's most comprehensive collection of Japanese art, it only displays the tip of the iceberg, rotating its 110,000 artifacts regularly throughout five distinct exhibition buildings. Items spark curiosity, like samurai swords and fabulous kimonos, while ancient sculptures of Buddha and woodblock prints complete the array. Special exhibitions are frequent, and usually last two months. Two separate exhibitions often open simultaneously, and in the past ranged from delightful meditations on the arts of tea ceremony (ancient tea bowls and such) to surveys of prolific Buddhist sculptors. - Read Full ReviewThe Mori Art Museum, the flashiest member of the Roppongi Art Triangle, sits atop the 53rd floor of the Roppongi Hills Mori Tower. Still, past exhibitions have featured works by the likes of Ai Weiwei and Dinh Q. Lê. Curators here do an exceptional job of creating exhibitions that are as thought-provoking as they are Instagrammable. Exhibitions in both the Mori Art Museum and the Mori Art Center Gallery rotate throughout the year. Anything from all corners of the contemporary art world is fair game here, from intricate paintings by the local avant-garde to large-scale international multimedia installations. Nothing feels haphazard here and each individual work has the space it needs to shine. The museum’s location in a glitzy commercial complex means that it draws a mix of dedicated insiders and casual gawkers. Especially on a clear day, the spectacular view attracts at least as many visitors as the art. - Read Full ReviewDating back to the 1870s, the National Museum of Nature and Science, in Ueno Park, is a boon for parents with curious kids. Butterflies, a fallen meteorite, and all manner of marvels pertaining to the broad field of natural science make this sprawling museum feel like an extended field trip. There’s a special emphasis on the anthropological history, biodiversity, geology, and technological contributions of Japan here. With a modest entry fee for adults and free entry for children under 18, the museum offers hours of family-friendly entertainment without breaking the bank. The breadth of the museum’s permanent collection is staggering. Everything from dinosaur skeletons and in-depth exhibits on space travel to a lifesize model of a blue whale outside makes this place feel like a sprawling Wunderkammer. A few of the highlights include a World War II fighter plane, a Futabasaurus plesiosaur unearthed in Fukushima, and—more disturbingly—the taxidermied body of Hachiko, a famous Japanese dog who waited patiently for his master for years. - Read Full ReviewThis serene museum in Tokyo's Aoyama district, rebuilt by architect Kengo Kuma, is a contemporary temple for traditional art. A long, covered outdoor path alongside bamboo-clad walls serves as a minimalist entrance, but once inside, double-height interiors and glass walls stretch over 40,000 square feet while keeping the experience intimate. And while the museum mixes contemporary design and traditional art on the inside, the outside counts, too: The property is home to a stunning private garden that’s worth the visit all on its own. The bulk of the museum’s art was once the private collection of Nezu Kaichirō, the president of Japan’s Tobu Railway. After his death, the collection—pre-modern Japanese and East Asian art, from calligraphy to sculptures to ceramics—was preserved, and his son (and heir) established the museum on the site of the Nezu family residence to display the many works. Since the midcentury, the collection has grown and now comprises over 7,600 pieces. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Seeking Texas's Sartorial Soul in Forth Worth, an Apex of Cowboy Culture and Craft
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.81
Inside Fort Worth's Cowboy Coliseum, a historic 1908 indoor rodeo venue in the heart of the city's famous Stockyards, the gunpowdery smell of pyrotechnics lingers in the air. It's the first round of the Professional Bull Riders (PBR) World Finals, and the very tan and blond singer Charly Reynolds delivers the national anthem in front of a giant screen showing billowing American flags. The bull riders—including the current champion, 20-year-old John Crimber—stand with their cowboy hat over their heart, boots shuffling nervously in the dirt. More fireworks throw sparks into the air and the crowd cheers. Minutes later the finalists will fight to stay on the back of 2,000-pound animals with names like Man Hater and Buck Nasty for eight excruciating seconds, and then dodge the bull's hooves and horns when they're tossed to the ground. Well-heeled locals—the men in sport coats and starched jeans, the women in dresses with yoked tops and embroidery—fill the narrow metal seats to watch. All of them are in boots; most of them wear hats. Chad Blankenship, a friend of a friend and the general manager of the Ariat Texas Rattlers, the local PBR bull-riding team, reserved a ticket for me, thinking—correctly—that it would be a good opportunity to see Fort Worthians in action and explore the Stockyards scene. Every year about 12 million visitors who want some of the Stockyards' rustic-luxe swagger to rub off on them flock to this district on Fort Worth's North Side, which sat at the end of the Chisholm Trail and where cattle drovers traded livestock by the millions beginning in the late 1800s. By the 1970s the area was derelict and prime for reinvention. Thanks to some savvy local developers who fought to preserve its charm, it now sees nearly double the number of visitors as the Eiffel Tower per year. As I look around the coliseum, there is ample evidence confirming my belief that Texans don't do subtle and they don't want to blend in. Texans have always seemed to relish their otherness, maybe even more so now that, in our age of globalization, so much sameness has infiltrated most American and international cities. I flew to Fort Worth from my hometown of Los Angeles with the hope of seeing some of this bold individualism firsthand and to check out how this North Central Texas city has grown into the epicenter of the haute-rodeo lifestyle and the premier destination for custom high-end Westernwear. “I grew up here, and it's interesting to watch Fort Worth and the Stockyards mature without losing their essence and wild frontier spirit,” says Taylor Sheridan, actor, writer, producer, and the creator of the Yellowstone television drama universe. He has dreamed up a show rooted in Fort Worth's history (1883) and another in its present day (Landman), and is at least partially responsible for the city's renaissance. He lives in nearby Weatherford, where Bella Hadid is a neighbor, and owns the 600-acre Bosque Ranch near town, which he uses for filming and production. Many tourists are drawn to the city because they're hooked on the lifestyle Sheridan embraces in his storytelling. “It was the place where people would come and supply up for the season, and it was the last place to stock up before heading West,” he tells me. “It's always been the center of the ranching world. It's still clinging very firmly to its roots.” No place is ushering that classic Texan spirit into modern life quite like Bowie House, Auberge Collection, owned by Jo Ellard, a cutting horse legend and breeder who was a champion of the Western equestrian event that showcases a horse's ability to work gracefully with cattle. The hotel is my home base for the next few days. It's mastered the rich-ranch aesthetic: A seven-foot-tall leather revolver sculpture stands in the lobby lounge, leather and calfskin hides cover much of the seating, and there's an on-site boutique from designer Lela Rose that looks like an updated version of Dale Evans's closet, replete with vintage turquoise belt buckles and long embroidered skirts. I drop my bags and head out to explore. “If you remember seeing one of these as a kid, then we can guess how old you are,” boot fitter Jeff Stevens says with a wink, walking toward me with a vintage metal Brannock device to measure my feet. I'm at Rod Patrick Bootmakers, a 51-year-old local brand in Arlington Heights, not far from my hotel in the Cultural District. It's known for carrying sizes 4 through 17 with a whopping 13 different widths. The walls are lined with photos of rodeo-star customers, and a classic from the Charlie Daniels Band that I haven't heard since the '80s plays through the speakers. Stevens determines, based on my relatively high arch, that I'm a 9.5. He brings out a $2,000 pair of soft black ostrich-skin boots, warning me that it will be hard to go back to stiffer goat or cow leather once I slip the boots on (with the help of two hooks looped into the pull tabs). He isn't wrong. “A well-fitting boot should feel like a handshake around your ankle,” he explains. Long before a cowboy boot became a fashion statement, its form was rooted in function. A narrow pointy-toe boot slipped easily into stirrups. Round or blunt toes were better suited to long days working the ranch. The tall boot shaft was built for protection, and the stitching helped the leather retain its shape as it softened. I don't walk out with a new pair, but I do have a new appreciation for a well-made boot and the incredibly skilled craftspeople in South Texas and León, Mexico. Next up is a drive down Camp Bowie Boulevard, with its historic red brick pavers and mature trees, to the affluent River Oaks neighborhood to meet Jo Latham at her fine jewelry store inside the larger You Are Here boutique. Latham, a chic 50-something Snow White doppelgänger, knows how to buy for those who understand quality and appreciate a little whimsy, including wealthy locals, visiting Texas Christian University parents, and women from across Texas and Oklahoma who make regular shopping trips to town. She shows me a $50,000 diamond-encrusted horseshoe necklace before sending me down the block to Chieffalo Americana, a Westernwear shop that sells reworked vintage and American-made clothing, Montana Silversmiths belt buckles, and refurbished short-brimmed Shady Oak hats. “People here love to live large and look good while doing it,” says Jackie Chieffalo, a stylist who owns Chieffalo Americana with her husband, Rodger. “They do not want to look like everybody else.” She tells me that The Fort Worth Stock Show & Rodeo, an annual three-week-long event at the Will Rogers Coliseum and the adjacent Dickies Arena beginning in January, is the social and fashion event of the year. “There are people who go every night and want to wear something different every time,” she says. “If you have something custom-made, isn't that the ultimate luxury? It's a mindful purchase, an investment that can be handed down.” As I wander around the Stockyards the following afternoon, there's a polished boomtown energy in the air. Seniors from TCU in purple graduation gowns and cowboy boots pose for photos in front of a longhorn steer tied up on the sidewalk. Outdoor bars and tents are being set up for the crowds expected for the bull-riding event that evening, and couples of all ages hold hands and wander the brick streets. “During the day the Stockyards is like the Paris of the West,” says Sheridan. “At night the North Side bars open up and it's a different story. They're the kind of places where you get into fights at the pool table. There was a time in my youth when that would have been a good night out, but now I want a nice place to take my wife for dinner and a drink.” Sheridan closed that gap by revitalizing the Cattlemen's Steak House, a 1947 classic in the heart of the Stockyards, and adding a lower-level members-only club. When I arrive for an early dinner, the dining room's leather booths are already packed with groups of friends in plaid shirts with mother-of-pearl buttons and dressy denim, and stylish couples in sport coats and silky twilly scarves. My server calls me “darlin',” and I order the best steak salad of my life, washed down with perfectly salted “ranch water,” tequila and sparkling water with lime. The next morning I start my day with a visit to Maverick Fine Western Wear, opened in 1987 by the adorable Gayle Hill. Today, Hill is wearing a royal blue cowboy hat with matching eyeglass frames, and her store is stocked to the rafters with colorful dresses, vests, fringed jackets, hats, and homewares. She sells one-off silver and turquoise jewelry from designers like Texas native Richard Schmidt, and Louis Vuitton handbags revamped with whipstitching by Austin-based Leather and Vodka. Hill's sales team, including James, a skateboarding graphic artist turned hat shaper working behind an antique carved wood bar, knows how to sell the lifestyle. Hill leaves me with James for a custom hat shaping and says, “Holler if you get thirsty.” James, sensing this is my first metaphoric rodeo, offers some selections that “suit my coloring.” I land on a tobacco brown felt hat. After measurements come a few compliments from Gayle about my large but symmetrical head (“You'd be surprised how many people have heads like a cashew”), and some deliberation over whether the curled brim should be flat or have a dip in the front (I chose a slight dip). I feel perfectly normal when I walk out in my new lid, a dramatic feather tucked into the hatband. I head across the street to the Murrin family office to meet Hill's son Philip Murrin and his wife, the painter Sarah Murrin. Philip and his brother Stephen manage the family's commercial real estate business that their father, Steve “Cowboy” Murrin Jr., started in the '70s. The elder Murrin is credited with saving the Stockyards from demolition and transforming it into a historic zone; he also invested in the famous local honky-tonk Billy Bob's. He's still easy to spot with his bushy white moustache and tall hat. When I ask Sarah about Fort Worth's unique creativity and appreciation for craft, she suggests that the city's arts scene plays a part. The Fort Worth Circle, a group of midcentury painters, put the community on the contemporary-art map. The Amon Carter Museum of American Art, designed by Philip Johnson, celebrates masterworks and photography with roots in the West. And, she tells me, the Louis Kahn–designed Kimbell Art Museum houses a world-class collection, including Michelangelo's first painting. When we switch to the topic of fashion, Sarah says that “people dress like they do here because it's a way of life. It's authentic, not for show.” I feel a little sheepish about my new hat. “We've seen the trends come and go,” Philip chimes in, in the tone of a longtime resident dealing with the headaches that growth brings. Old-timers like his dad remember the 1980 frenzy over John Travolta in the movie Urban Cowboy. Sarah adds, “Now we have Landman.” Because, I'm told, no trip to the Stockyards is complete without a visit to retailer M.L. Leddy's, I take a look. It started as a custom saddle and boot shop in the 1920s and opened its handsome Stockyards location in 1941; now it's a favorite among professional horse trainers and well-dressed cowboys. It has its own hat-shaping bar and a line of handmade boots that start at about $1,500 a pair. Upstairs is the saddlery. Also on offer are hand-tooled leather belts that can be stamped with your initials, and silver money clips and buckles by legendary Texas silversmith Clint Orms. There is a team of consultants and master tailors at the ready to design and sew a full custom wardrobe. Feeling buoyed by my boot education, and left out because I still don't have a pair, I walk to Hotel Drover, where I'm staying for my last night, and into the Lucchese Custom Collection off the lobby. Lucchese has been an iconic Texas brand since 1883 and sets the standard for fashion-forward handsewn boots. Its primary location, on Exchange Street, is its top-performing retail outlet in the US, but the smaller Drover location is where the team measures for custom boots in exotic skins and dozens of color combinations. I sit in a leather chair and place my foot on a page of a large paper ledger, while a stylish young fitter with a perfect manicure traces my feet, taking five key measurements. While I'm not ordering boots today, I can start the design process and have the specifications sent to its South Texas factory at any time. People choose emblems, like a star or a flower, for a little flair. If you've seen boots with a tulip design on the shaft, that's brand founder Salvatore “Sam” Lucchese's signature. “The starting price point for custom is about $1,500,” says store manager Nate Hill. “After that we'll make as many modifications as you like. The sky is the limit.” He's not kidding. A $10,000 pair is not out of the ordinary. “We take orders for up to 10 custom pairs per day, and anywhere from 180 to 200 hands touch each boot we make.” Suddenly the $700 off-the-shelf Luccheses feel like a bargain. I land on a dressy black pair with graceful brown stitching and walk out two inches taller. My last stop before the evening's bull riding is The Best Hat store. Owner Susan Maddox, wearing a denim shirt and an Hermès scarf tied around her shoulders, welcomes me. She opened the shop with her late husband, Keith, in 1996, then they bought the American Hat Company factory in Conroe, Texas, in 2003. She has run the business with help from her younger daughter, Mercedes, since Keith's death in 2019. Maddox and her daughters, including Treasure, who works in marketing for Auberge, embody the modern Fort Worth aesthetic: refined, colorful, and unabashed. They post their outfits of the day on social media and wear a high-low mix (Chanel with Zara) and Miron Crosby boots—sometimes with an American Hat adorned with their signature “Positive Times” emblem. But when they are asked to describe what makes the local style unique, it's hard for the matriarch to sum things up: “We love a nice elevated Western look, and I don't think we overdo it. We don't put on airs. People who settled here have a very bold spirit and a kind of grit that was required to make it. You can see that spirit in the people here today.” Sometimes it takes an outsider's perspective to decipher what makes the local panache so compelling. I ask Blankenship, my rodeo-ticket connection, who moved here in 2022 to work with the Rattlers, for his take on the town. “I grew up in Oklahoma,” he says. “We always thought of Texans as being very proud and maybe a little annoying about it. Now that I live here, I get it. It's an authentic place, where a handshake still counts as a contract. Yes, there's a lot of local pride, but it's not bragging. It's like people are saying, ‘Let me show you all of our awesome.’” Where to stay The 106-room Bowie House, Auberge Collection has a luxury-ranch aesthetic with large, spotless rooms, a clubby, cozy lobby bar, and an indoor-outdoor restaurant to create a truly unique stay. For the property, owner Jo Ellard selected 400 paintings, collages, photos, and sculptures sourced from antiques sales, Art Basel shows around the world, and her own private collection. Most of it is available for purchase. If you can't score an invitation to a private ranch, a stay at Hotel Drover, Autograph Collection in the heart of the Stockyards, may be the next best thing. The 200-room property is a short walk from some of the city's historic treasures, but it's surrounded by peaceful gardens, a resort pool, and outdoor terraces for drinking and dining. With its warm minimal interiors and crisp, colorful furnishings, The Crescent Hotel, Fort Worth reflects the city's more restrained side. Bonuses: an on-site Canyon Ranch Wellness Club and the elegant (and beautifully lit) Emilia's restaurant. Where to eat and drink The 1947 classic Cattlemen's Steak House, which was given a new life—along with a members-only club in its basement—by mega-producer Taylor Sheridan, features modern steakhouse go-tos. Order ranch water and a steak salad at the bar, and enjoy the world-class people-watching. No trip to Fort Worth is complete without a visit to bustling family-owned Tex-Mex institution Joe T. Garcia's and its sprawling patio. Join the always festive crowd for strong, salty margaritas and classics like enchiladas and chiles rellenos, and mariachi on Friday and Saturday nights and all day Sunday. A piled-high plate of ribs and brisket and an ice-cold beer is a Texas standard, and no one in Fort Worth does it better than Railhead Smokehouse BBQ, a 40-year-old barbecue joint owned by state representative Charlie Geren. Where to find westernwear Realtor Rodger Chieffalo inherited a short-brimmed beaver felt hat beloved by legendary local businessman Amon G. Carter, then began sourcing and refurbishing similar hats to give as gifts to clients. The passion became Chieffalo Americana which now includes upscale American-made and reworked Western vintage wear. Owned and operated by the Franklin family for three generations, M.L. Leddy's sells its own line of custom boots and hats—and anything else a well-heeled Texan might want. The store's rich, wood-trimmed interior smells like saddle leather and oil money. Packed to the rafters with fashionable Western clothing and accessories, Maverick Fine Western Wear is a must-stop shop in the heart of the Stockyards. Owner Gayle Hill hosts several designer trunk shows a year for her loyal customers, who rely on the Maverick buyer's eye for heirloom-quality pieces. Dallas-born designer Lela Rose has elevated and adapted cowgirl chic to appeal to the Net-a-Porter crowd. Her shop inside Bowie House sells clothing, home accessories, and boots from her Lucchese collaboration. At Crissy Jean Faulconer's appointment-only Proper Supply Co. in Weatherford (a ranch community near Fort Worth), Faulconer sells jeans stitched from rare Texas denim and custom sterling silver belt buckles made using vintage molds from Bohlin Company, a favorite of Western stars like Roy Rogers. Diplo is a customer. Where to peruse jewelry The fine jeweler Jo Latham sources unique pieces for discerning shoppers who appreciate craftsmanship with a wink—like horseshoe pendants from French Lebanese designer Selim Mouzannar or a diamond-encrusted pistol charm. “Chief” Garren Still, who is half Cherokee, crafts and sells a curated selection of sterling and American-mined turquoise jewelry, like ornate cuffs and statement necklaces at Weatherford establishment Chief's Trading Post. Where to try on hats The marquee in front of the Best Hat Store reads “Positive Times,” and the optimistic “+ x” symbol is embroidered onto the store's signature hat patches. Inside, rows of in-house brand American Hat Company (manufactured in Bowie) line the walls, and customers queue up for sessions with its team of experienced shapers. The Mule Alley Flea Style, the most successful of the 10 locations owned by Dallas-based former magazine editor Brittany Cobb, caters to a trendy customer who loves the cowboy lifestyle but spends little time on a ranch. Shoppers choose their hat shape and then browse bins of artfully curated bits and bobs sourced from flea markets to adorn it. Where to strut in boots To the trained eye, a Lucchese boot is as identifiable (and aspirational) as a Louboutin. The Texas-based boot brand founded in 1883 has a reputation as one of the world's finest boot makers for men and women, using lemonwood-peg construction (instead of metal tacks) and soft, sturdy leather that's comfortable straight out of the box. Built to last, well-worn pairs can get a factory refurbishment for a few hundred dollars. Rod Patrick, known for its wide spectrum of available sizes among the 15,000 pairs of in-stock boots, sells premium and bespoke boots to a discerning client who appreciates attentive service. Its relatively rapid custom timeline—delivering boots in 6 to 12 months—is also a plus. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. item.title: Designer Thebe Magugu on Where He Shops and Dances in Cape Town
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.68
“The fashion in Cape Town is so inimitable because it takes from our own culture and heritage,” says South African fashion designer Thebe Magugu. Though he's based in Johannesburg, work frequently brings him to the capital—including for a suite he designed at Mount Nelson, a Belmond Hotel, Cape Town, which he filled with works by local artists. For Magugu, whose current collection “looks at the changing face of African spirituality,” it's the people wearing his clothes who help preserve his vision. Here, the spots he never misses. Art institutions, big and small “The Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa is one of the most beautiful buildings in Cape Town. Inside is the largest collection of contemporary art by Africans and the continent's diaspora. I also love Southern Guild gallery around the corner, and my friend Anelisa Mangcu's space, Under the Aegis.” Trawling for inspiration “I like introducing compelling objects from Longmarket Street into my look books. It's lined with people selling African masks, straw mats, and wood carvings of various animals, both realistic and mythological. I always go without a plan, but I know that someday I'll need the items I find.” Get into the groove “Music is a big part of my life in Cape Town—I associate it with being out in the community. I shop at Roastin' Records and dance with friends at Souk. Gqom Therapy is [dedicated to] a new genre of South African dance music and a must-do party with the best sound system.” Shop and rub shoulders “I always recommend concept shop AKJP Studio, which was started by my friends Keith Henning and Jody Paulsen. It stocks some of the greatest South African fashion designers and, from 6 p.m., turns into a bar frequented by local creatives.” This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. item.title: Planning a Wine Country Bachelorette? Check Out These Napa Valley and Sonoma County Airbnbs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.67
If a boozy bachelorette is what you’re after, there are plenty of great options: Las Vegas, Nashville, Scottsdale. But if your bride-to-be prefers something a little more sophisticated, wine country is the clear choice. It offers a party atmosphere, but in a completely different setting. Dark, packed clubs are replaced by sprawling wineries, sun-drenched vines, design-forward tasting rooms, and Michelin-starred restaurants. This slice of Northern California offers a fun-filled weekend for groups without the chaos and crowds that come with some of the more traditional bachelorette destinations. And wine country has enough variety to please everyone, whether the bride is a vino enthusiast, party animal, foodie, nature lover, or wellness girl. While the hotel scene in Sonoma and Napa is certainly impressive, a rental home gives you something you can’t get from a traditional stay: a private space for your whole group to celebrate. Start the morning around a huge kitchen island, spend the afternoon by the pool, get ready together, and end the night at an outdoor dining table under the stars. And because these homes come with multiple bedrooms and bathrooms, everyone can still retreat to their own space when they need it. The best part is that there’s a house for every kind of bride: an adorable treehouse tucked into the redwoods, a historic mansion steps from downtown Napa, and a sprawling estate surrounded by vines in Healdsburg among them. Does she want a giant pool for lounging all afternoon, a wraparound porch for laid-back dinners, or an Insta-ready patio overlooking the hills? There’s a house for that. I rounded up 11 of the best Airbnbs in wine country to help you plan an unforgettable bachelorette trip. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost or Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

item.title: The Best Airbnbs in Denver Whether You’re After Winter Snow or Summer Sun
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.27
Denver, Colorado, is full of adventure in every season—from winter skiing and summer hiking to rainy-day wanderings through an impressive array of arts and culture offerings. One of my favorite things about living in Denver is the neighborhood diversity: Whether you’re looking for a walkable spot that feels like a welcoming local community, a trendy district with buzzy energy and round-the-clock entertainment, or a quiet, pet-friendly greenspace with a lake path, we’ve got it all. Lucky for visitors, there’s also a wealth of vacation rentals to pick from once you do decide which neighborhood to bunker down in. Whether you prefer a charming and historic house dating back to the Victorian era, a sleek artist's loft, or a modern architectural marvel, there’s no shortage of unique places to stay in the Mile High City. Read on for some of the most iconic home bases for an unforgettable trip. No matter what you're in town to see or do, these Denver Airbnbs deliver. —Molly O'Brien We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, editor stays, ratings, amenities, location, decor, and previous guest reviews. Our top picks: - Best for views: Groovy studio with skyline views - Best for pets: Pet-friendly historic home with a hot tub - Best for couples: Unique tiny home in a shipping container - Best for groups: Magnificent (and massive) South Denver art house FAQ: What are the best neighborhoods in Denver? The best neighborhood to stay in Denver depends on what type of trip you’re looking for. Those who prioritize walkability, buzzy energy, and plenty of trendy bars and restaurants will love LoHi (Lower Highlands). If artsy vibes with fun breweries and dining outposts is what you crave, RiNo (River North) is a great place to set up camp. Those seeking something a bit more upscale and refined with the hottest spots for dining, drinking, and arts and culture will love Cherry Creek (which I affectionately call The Beverly Hills of Denver, due to its wealthy—but still welcoming—atmosphere). LoDo is where Union Station, Coors Field, and Ball Arena live, making it a fantastic entertainment hub. Don’t miss Five Points if you seek authentic soul food, City Park for some of the best urban outdoor spaces, and Washington Park for some of the most historic architecture and a down-to-earth feel. When is the best time to visit Denver? As a Denverite, I’ve found every season offers an abundance of activities. Since the sun is so strong here at 5,280 feet of elevation, the air doesn’t feel as chilly, even on the most brisk winter day. Summertime brings sunny days perfect for strolling around an urban lake or biking along a flowing river. Fall is a fantastic time for leaf peeping and enjoying some of the local seasonal produce in the crisp Mile High air. Wintertime is for snow sports—it’s a season most Denverites actually look forward to due to the breadth of different ski resorts nearby. Spring is when the ground starts to thaw, and barring the occasional random snowstorm (we’re told not to plant anything in our gardens until after Mother’s Day), most days feel mild and pleasant enough for a city stroll. What are the best things to do in Denver? Arts and culture lovers can’t miss a stop in the Arts District on Santa Fe, a show at the Denver Performing Arts Complex, or an experience at Red Rocks Park and Amphitheater—which is free and open to the public to explore, outside ticketed showtimes. Those seeking an educational day out will enjoy the Denver Botanic Gardens (for the flora nerds), the Wings Over the Rockies Air & Space Museum (for the aviation enthusiasts), or the Museum of Contemporary Art with its rotating exhibits and beautiful open-air rooftop space. Refueling is easy, because there’s always somewhere new and interesting to eat between one of the many casual food halls like Denver Central Market or Avanti F&B and the more upscale eateries, including Michelin-rated outposts like Alma Fonda Fina or Margot. Shop till you drop along the 16th Street Mall, which features hundreds of storefronts lining a pedestrian-only promenade, capped by Larimer Square, which was the city’s first block, commercial district, and first designated historic district. And since Denverites work hard and play hard, planning for proper relaxation and recovery is essential, which is easily doable at one of the many local wellness institutions like Sway Wellness Spa, unique spots like the Oakwell Beer Spa, and classics like The Spa at Four Seasons Hotel Denver.

item.title: The Best Airbnbs on the Greek Island of Sifnos, From a Converted Windmill to a Modern Apartment
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.26
The Greek island of Sifnos is petite but perfectly formed. The smaller size means you can get a good sense of the place over a long weekend, but you’ll likely still want to return. Its expanse of sandy white stretches is divine, and a scattering of villages sewn throughout unspoiled landscapes hum with activity during the summer months. Most importantly, the food scene is excellent. Thankfully, there’s no shortage of wonderful Airbnbs in Sifnos to book on every corner of the island. Below, we’ve picked our favorite Sifnos Airbnbs for 2026. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost or Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for couples: Converted windmill, Artemonas - Best for families: Sleepy seaside home, Hersonissos - Best for big groups: Elevated Cycladic rental, Platýs Gialós - Best for interior design fans: Traditional stone apartment, Kamares - Best for a room with a view: Cozy cottage, Artemonas - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Proximity to the beach, panoramic sea views, outdoor spaceThe views here are unmatched—sitting and watching as the space catches the golden afternoon light over Kamares Bay is exactly the reason so many make the pilgrimage to Greece year after year. A stay here ensures a front-row seat to the island’s buzzy marine hub, where all rooms are bright and spacious, opening onto their own balconies showcasing incredible panoramic sea views over glistening waters. Plus, you’re just a three-minute stroll from the soft sands of Sifnos’s popular main beach. This makes for the best of both worlds: easy access to tavernas and sunset-dappled paths to amble down, along with good proximity to the scenic Agia Ekaterini trail, which leads to a secluded turquoise cove perfect for rock diving and snorkeling away from the main summer crowds. Location: Kamares Things to do nearby: Agia Ekaterini, beach, Kamares Bay - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Spacious terrace, coastal views, direct sea accessHistory buffs, here’s one for you: Steeped in local artisan history, this is a local type of stay for truly getting under the skin of the island. Once a heritage pottery, this converted shop offers immediate access to the glittering sea in the sleepy fishing hamlet of Hersonissos—a little-known northern haven largely sheltered from the summer winds that are characteristic of this region. The renovation was carried out with families in mind, with a spacious terrace where children can play and adults can read on a lounger against a sumptuous backdrop of wide, uninterrupted coastal vistas. In a fun twist, you can step right off the lower courtyard into the clear sea via a built-in ladder, and it’s just a few wandering steps to a selection of quiet local tavernas. Location: Hersonissos Things to do nearby: Local tavernas, water access - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Olive trees, original stone walls, pergola, terraceSettled within a vibrant garden bursting with olive trees and a blur of purple bougainvillea, this lovingly restored cottage is yet another pretty Greek Cycladic home, this time just outside the labyrinthine village of Artemonas. There’s plenty of character imbued within the original stone walls—you’ll love the built-in masonry beds—and there’s a sprinkling of ceramic accents throughout that honor Sifnos’ rich pottery heritage. A new modern kitchen and naturally cooling design keep your stay easy and comfortable. Each room opens directly onto a stone-paved courtyard shaded by a pergola, for effortless indoor-outdoor living that flows from morning until night. The showstopper is the sun-warmed terrace—the best spot in the house to enjoy breakfasts as the sun rises and evening drinks while gazing across the glittering Aegean. Look closely and you might spot sister Greek islands Mykonos, Syros, and Antiparos. Location: Artemonas Things to do nearby: Artemonas, Apollonia - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Shared veranda, private balcony off the primary bedroom, shared swimming poolDappled light spills across the gardens where this particularly aesthetic home, surrounded by silver-leafed trees, awaits. The space has all that Greek traditional whitewashed calm outside, matched with sleek contemporary living once you head through the door. It’s a larger home than average for the area, with room for the whole family, incorporating breezy open-plan interiors, three bathrooms, and two airy bedrooms. This is for sleepy, relaxed weekends, with a layout naturally encouraging a relaxed lifestyle. There’s a shared shaded veranda on the ground floor, and the primary bedroom has a private balcony with incredible sweeping views of the glittering Aegean Sea. Cool off in the shared swimming pool after exploring the island; for a sociable bolthole for families seeking an authentic Sifnian escape, this is a great option just slightly away from the main bustle. Location: Platýs Gialós Things to do nearby: Beaches, restaurants, mini-markets, cafés - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Windmill, historic building, air conditioningSifnos has around 60 windmills scattered across its rolling landscapes, and here's the chance to take over one as your own. The hosts have worked hard to ensure the renovations pay homage to the mill’s 157-year history—it was built in 1864 and continued to function until 1965—while squeezing in everything you’ll need. There’s a comfy double bed, TV, air conditioning, a fully-equipped kitchen, and even a separate bathroom. One note: Try to pack light, as there are quite a few steps up a hill to reach the mill, and nobody wants to tackle that while lugging heavy luggage. Location: Artemonas Things to do nearby: Artemonas Square - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Proximity to the beach, shared courtyard, outdoor dining tableNow, this is the epitome of beachy Greek bliss—a huge, one-level, airy apartment right on the sands, with plenty of comfy sun loungers, a chef’s kitchen, convivial dining space, and super-smart interiors tying everything together. With two double bedrooms and a third with two single beds, it’s a good choice for family breaks or, really, anyone who wants to stay as close as possible to the waves and salty sea air. Location: Platis Gialos Things to do nearby: Platis Gialos Beach, hiking trails - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Balcony, mountain views, booksBuilt in the 13th century to form part of a castle’s tower, this little Sifnian house is now better placed to serve as your home away from home in the peaceful village of Kastro, which has some of the prettiest pedestrian streets on the island. A minimal palette of grays, whites, and neutral woods is pepped up with bold flashes of blue on the doors and window frames; peer out for gorgeous views over the mountains beyond. Location: Kastro Things to do nearby: Kastro, Seralia Beach - Number of guests: 5 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Pet-friendly, sound system, outdoor dining areaIt’s impossible not to feel cheery inside this airy apartment. It’s dopamine-dressed to perfection with zippy yellow window frames, a powder blue Smeg fridge, smidges of green on the ceiling beams, and a checkered marble floor. The external space is even better, with a positively idyllic courtyard ripe for sundowners against a backdrop of Greece’s famous blazing sunsets. You’re right by the sights of vibrant Apollonia and just steps away from the start of the traditional paved path to Ano Petali. Take a walk one day before stopping in at one of the clutch of nearby tavernas for a pick-me-up en route home. Location: Apollonia Things to do nearby: Apollonia, Ano Petali, tavernas - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Air conditioning, hammock, dedicated workspacePerched on a hilltop just on the cusp of buzzy Appollonia, this newly renovated apartment sits waiting for you to check in. Sandy hues and natural materials give way to sparkly seascapes, hugged by distant mountains, from the courtyard—sit out with a morning coffee and enjoy. Previous guests have raved about this Airbnb; it’s spotlessly clean, tranquil, and the views across the town are unbeatable. If you’re lucky, you might even return home to a complimentary bottle of wine or cake one day, too. Location: Ano Petali Things to do nearby: Apollonia, Artemonas

item.title: After Six Years, These $35 Travel Pants Are Still My Go-To for Flights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.24
At this point, the airport is my home away from home. I’ve been on 30 flights this past year alone, and my travels have taken me everywhere from business trips to Salt Lake City and Jackson Hole to a six-week sojourn in Europe. But no matter where I’m heading, you better believe I’m wearing my $35 pair of joggers from Amazon. I never thought these pants would become my de facto in-flight ’fit when I bought them back in 2020. Truthfully, I heard a colleague wax poetic about them and thought they’d make an excellent addition to my work-from-home uniform. (Like many, I was adhering to a strict drawstring-only dress code.) It didn’t take long for me to realize that these super-soft, zipper- and button-free joggers are the ultimate travel pants. Why I love them for travel It’s borderline sadistic to wear rigid or tight bottoms on a plane, but I don’t subscribe to treating the airport like its a slumber party either. (Trust me, nobody wants to see your PJs.) I try to keep my airplane outfits equal parts refined and relaxed—comfortable but polished enough that I won’t be humiliated if I bump into a colleague at the gate or need to beeline it to a meeting once I land. Most sweatpants are a little too low-effort for my liking, and my skin-tight leggings look a little dorky with compression socks. The Ajisai joggers are different. Instead of the tapered details that plague most sweatpants, this straight-leg style hits right above the ankle to offer a more sophisticated silhouette. (Don’t worry, shorter jet-setters: These joggers come in petite length too.) I can discreetly slip my knee-high compression socks underneath my pants or, if I’m tundra-bound, tuck them into my snow boots. Though I typically wear them with sneakers to the airport, these ankle-baring bottoms are also cute with flats once I’ve reached my destination. This pair’s nylon-spandex blend offers plenty of stretch and moves as I do: Whether I'm bending down to grab my carry-on, running to catch my flight, or shifting in the middle seat, these pants are like a second skin. And unlike super thick sweats, I never have to worry about overheating. In fact, I recently wore these while having lunch in the 93-degree Cabo heat and felt surprisingly comfortable. I’m also pleasantly surprised by how well they’ve held up over the past six years. They have maintained their shape and don’t have any snags or rips, despite countless rounds in the washing machine. And did I mention they have pockets? Most often, I use them to stash my phone in before I hoist my suitcase into the overhead compartment. How I style them If it wasn’t for the elastic waistband and the accompanying drawstring, these pants could totally pass for a work trouser. I like to trick passersby by wearing an oversized button-down that looks quasi-professional and hides the drawstring. If I want to be cute and cozy while sightseeing, I’ll throw on a denim jacket over a white T-shirt. Ajisai offers nine colorways to choose from, including brown, navy, and maroon, but the black is by the far the most versatile for travel. Best of all, they’re only $35 on Amazon. In plane speak, it’s basically a first-class pair for an economy fare.
