item.title: The latest travel advice after flash floods on Nepal-Tibet border
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.70
This is an evolving news story – the information below is up-to-date as of 12pm BST on Friday 28 August 2026. For the latest updates in the UK, visit BBC News and Gov.uk. On 26 August, a devastating flash flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Tibet border, killing at least 469 people in Nepal, while over 1,500 remain missing, according to the latest figures from Nepali authorities. At least five more people have died on the Chinese side of the border in Tibet. The number of missing includes hundreds of tourists, trekkers and pilgrims, with nationals from more than 30 countries reported unaccounted for. The disaster began after a major glacier and rock collapse near the Nepal-China border sent a surge of water, mud and debris through the Bhote Koshi river system. Earlier reports attributed the flooding to an avalanche, but subsequent assessments have pointed to a glacial collapse and the resulting debris flow as the trigger, rather than an earthquake. Fresh flood threat Nepal has now issued a fresh flood warning on 28 August after water levels rose at the site of the original disaster. "Information has been received that the flow of water mixed with debris and mud has increased again on Friday in the same area of the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa, where a major flood occurred on 26 August," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said in a notice, reports IANS. The new danger is linked to a barrier lake formed near the Nepal-China border after debris blocked a river. Chinese authorities had warned Nepal that around two million cubic metres of water had accumulated in the lake, with another three million cubic metres potentially flowing into it over the following days. Nepal Police also said they had received information that a water dam on the Tibetan side had burst again. The lake subsequently began overflowing, temporarily forcing rescue operations to be suspended in some areas. The risk is particularly serious because a sudden breach could send another large volume of water and debris downstream into areas already devastated by the first flood. Authorities are therefore monitoring the lake closely and have asked residents, rescuers and others in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors to remain on high alert. Which areas in and around Nepal are impacted by the floods? In Nepal, Syapru Besi and Timure in Rasuwa district remain the worst affected areas, while damage has also been reported along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot. On the other side of the border, the Gyirong area of Tibet also recorded fatalities. “At approximately 10:30 am, due to a mudslide occurring on the Nepalese side, major casualties and missing persons were caused at the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Shigatse City, Tibet,” Xinhua reported. Regions lying around and below the Bhote Koshi river, which flows from Tibet to Nepal, remain on high alert with local authorities confirming the main road to Kathmandu — which is an important commercial and passenger corridor connecting the capital city to western Nepal, the southern plains (Terai), and the border with India — is closed. The effects are also being monitored downstream in India, where authorities in Bihar have put six districts along the Kosi, Gandak and Ganga systems on alert over the possibility of rising river levels as floodwaters move south. Travel disruptions Travellers flying to Nepal should distinguish between Kathmandu airport operations and access to the flood-hit north. Passengers with flights to or from the region should check their individual flight status with the airline before leaving for the airport. The main disruption is on the ground, with roads and bridges leading towards Rasuwa, Syabrubesi and the Tibet border damaged by the floods. Authorities have advised against travelling into affected areas while rescue operations continue. Travellers with onward road transfers, trekking itineraries or Kailash Mansarovar plans should contact their operator before setting out and should not assume that a previously arranged vehicle or route remains operational. Those already stranded in affected areas should follow instructions from local authorities rather than attempting to cross damaged roads or river corridors. What are governments advising travellers? The Nepal Tourism Board has issued an urgent advisory asking tourists to avoid flood-affected areas and postpone non-essential travel. It has specifically flagged Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan, as well as the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors, and urged travellers to check road conditions before setting out. The Board has also shared emergency contact numbers on X. Visitors can call the board’s helpline at 1234 (toll-free), 1144 (emergency hotline) or contact the Tourist Police on (+977) 9851289445. The UK government's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) handle on X is advising travellers in the region to follow local guidance and stay alert. UK citizens requiring assistance can call (+977) (0)14237100 from Nepal or +44 (0) 207 008 5000 from the UK. The US Embassy in Kathmandu has triggered a security alert, urging American citizens in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan and Tanahun to avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas, seek higher ground and stay away from flood-affected areas. For urgent assistance, US citizens can call (+977) 1-423-4000 or email KathmanduACS@state.gov. Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry, through its embassy in Kathmandu, issued a note saying they are actively monitoring the situation after losing contact with 11 Malaysian nationals believed to be in Rasuwa. Malaysians in Nepal have been urged to remain vigilant, follow instructions from local authorities and contact the embassy if they need assistance. The Embassy of India in Kathmandu has issued emergency contact numbers for Indian nationals affected by the floods: (+977 985 131 6807), (+977) 970 910 7500, ( +977) 981 032 6117 This article was first published by Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: Where was 'Vigil' filmed? A look at all three series of the thrilling BBC drama ahead of series three
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.37
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Vigil filmed? An average of nine million viewers tuned into the first series of Vigil, as Tom Edge’s police drama captivated audiences with its sharp twists and turns in 2021. The first series saw Suranne Jones star as Detective Chief Inspector Amy Silva, supported by talent including Rose Leslie and Gary Lewis, as the action went from land to sea. The first series was such a success that a second followed, with six episodes that transported viewers to the Persian Gulf in December 2023. Now, we see Amy Silva on a third adventure to the Arctic. “The first series of Vigil was written as a limited series, so in both series two and three we have had to reinvent the show whilst retaining its DNA,” said series creator, writer and executive producer. With this in mind, we’re eager to see how the dynamics and lives of the characters have changed in the two years since we last encountered them. This is the lowdown on where each series of Vigil was filmed. Season 3 When a member of a covert British special forces mission is murdered at a remote Arctic research station, DCI Amy Silva and DI Kirsten Longacre are sent to catch the killer and defuse a potential international confrontation. For the Arctic shoot, production moved between Scotland and Svalbard, the remote Norwegian archipelago midway between mainland Norway and the North Pole. “Svalbard was amazing,” says Suranne Jones on filming. “Rose and I felt like we were just on top of the world because we went to places that tourists don’t normally visit since we were filming in such remote locations. There were reindeer outside the breakfast room every morning, we got to drive the snow buggies, and we really had to layer up – the problem was when we got back to Glasgow we were too hot because we still had to film with all our layers on.” The lead actor recalls how welcoming the crew and people of Svalbard were as she sampled moose stew and reindeer and visited a husky café home to retired sledge dogs. Suranne notes how the cast were kitted out with heated gloves and gilets and would settle down beside the fire of an evening; unsurprising considering Svalbard’s average September temperatures of 1°C to 3°C. When asked about her favourite day of filming, Naomi Yang (who plays Shen Jia) said: “There was one day in Svalbard where a very small team of us went to a glacier. I was hiking in my crampons up this glacier. We were with someone with a rifle, because we had to have a rifle with us all the time in case it was needed to scare off polar bears. The glaciers are very blue, due to the way the light is reflected I just remember all of us just being like ‘wow, we can't believe we're in this’.” Season 2 Following the renewal of Vigil for a second series, filming took place across Scotland and Morocco during spring 2023. The second outing follows Silva’s team to the Al-Shawka Air Base in the Kingdom of Wudyan, a fictional location supposedly located in the oil-rich Persian Gulf. As a Royal Air Force prototype combat drone is compromised and kills several soldiers, the team set about trying to find the perpetrator. In an interview ahead of series two’s release, Romola Garai (who plays Acting Squadron Leader Eliza Russell) said, “We were in Casablanca and then Rabat so there’s a completely different aesthetic to the first series. We’ve got these vast desert landscapes of openness and heat haze, people disappearing into a massive horizon – rather than being locked up in a tiny submarine, as we saw in series one. It’s a totally different experience for the viewer as we explore a different world within the military.” As Silva embarks on a journey to the Kingdom, her partner Longacre stays behind in Scotland to lead the investigation there. According to Uni-Versal Extras, Scotland locations to look out for across the series include Glasgow, Luss, North Ayrshire, Lanark, Blantyre, Cumbernauld and Motherwell. Season 1 We first meet DCI Amy Silva and the team when a crew member of the Trident nuclear submarine HMS Vigil is found dead. The police are granted access to investigate, but there’s a catch – the UK’s nuclear deterrent must remain unbroken, meaning the submarine stays on patrol. Despite the death being written off as an overdose, foul play is suspected, but the confined space of the submarine hides many dark secrets. Due to their classified nature, the production team weren’t granted access to real blueprints for nuclear submarines. Filming inside a real submarine would also have been logistically impossible, or at least extremely challenging, so a full-size replica was constructed in BBC Dumbarton Studios in Scotland. The scale of the set, which took up an entire sound stage, reportedly stunned the actors. “The set just blew my mind,” said Surenne Jones. “The size of the subs in real life are extraordinary – they're like four floors, with a bomb shop and missile room. The details that the designers put in is quite something, especially as they couldn't get blueprints of real submarines to work from, because you're not allowed to have them. So they had to be talked through what was there by people who had first-hand knowledge of submarines, and then come up with their own design off the back of that.”

item.title: Art exhibitions in Paris for September 2026: from Musée du Luxembourg to La Collection at Musée National Picasso
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.30
That back-to-school feeling which September brings is always bittersweet. We’ve kissed the summer coastlines goodbye and dusted off our autumn wardrobes, stepping into crisper days ahead. It is a time for a cultural reset, and the Parisian art scene eagerly obliges. The end of August has seen the curtain call of many blockbuster exhibitions, only for September to usher in an array of exciting new ones. Renaissance titans of art like Tintoretto and Pop Art icon Andy Warhol rub shoulders with niche, yet equally beguiling exhibitions – like Bruce of Los Angeles at Acne Studios’ inaugural gallery and a radical exploration of street art inside the Beaux-Arts splendour of the Petit Palais. We update this column monthly so you can always keep track of the best upcoming exhibitions in Paris. The best exhibitions in September 2026 1. La Galerie Dior The luminous museum La Galerie Dior is described as “a place of art and memory” and celebrates Parisian couture and the heritage of the iconic brand. Monsieur Dior was originally a gallerist and was continually inspired by art and architecture as both a collector and designer. The brand continues to be involved in art. The visionary creative director, Maria Grazia Chiuri, has always ensured that inspiring women are perpetually at the forefront of their leadership and vision at Dior. Experience their history through exquisite archival sketches, photographs and original looks as well as sources of inspiration from the artistic to the botanical. Address: 11 Rue François 1er, 75008 Paris Website: galeriedior.com Price: From €12; concessions available Dates: Closed on Tuesdays 2. Claude Monet’s Water Lilies at Musée de l'Orangerie One of the most beautiful corners of the city is the Musée de l'Orangerie, built alongside the Jeu de Paume in the Jardin des Tuileries. It is synonymous with the hypnotic Water Lilies (Les Nymphéas), a series of eight extended canvases by Claude Monet, which were generously donated to the French state after WWI as a symbol of peace. As with Monet’s studio in Giverny, natural light floods into the galleries and illuminates the paintings. Also on display until 20th July is an exploration of Henri Rousseau’s enigmatic oeuvre. In collaboration with the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia, the l’Orangerie will uncover the painter’s unique style alongside his savvy navigation of the late 19th-century art market. After moving to Paris, he often tailored his works to the whims of the wealthy but this show proves he was far from a shallow name. It builds a rich, three-dimensional picture of an artist who remained singular even while playing the necessary games of the Parisian elite. Address: Jardin des Tuileries, 75001 Paris Website: musee-orangerie.fr Price: From €12.50; concessions available Dates: Closed on Tuesdays 3. La Collection at Musée National Picasso Musée National Picasso-Paris is an opulent museum inside Hôtel Salé, which is devoted to the Spanish artist and the artists with whom he worked. 5,000 works of art are held within their collection, including preparatory sketches as well as his prolific photographic archive and correspondence. Their new exhibition, La Collection, offers a new perspective on the work of Picasso. The museum is located on the picturesque rue de Thorigny in Le Marais, not far from Centre Pompidou. Explore smaller galleries nearby like Perrotin and David Zwirner. Address: 5 rue de Thorigny, 75003 Paris Website: museepicassoparis.fr Price: From €16; concessions available Dates: Until 12 March 2027 4. Musée Rodin Only a short walk from the Eiffel Tower and Grand Palais, Musée Rodin was opened in 1919 and has since been devoted to the work of the prolific French Sculptor Auguste Rodin. Get lost in the classical architecture with exquisite rocaille details. The sculpture garden is also exquisite and offers a quiet escape during the summer months. The museum featured in Midnight in Paris, directed by Woody Allen. Carla Bruni had a cameo as a tour guide. Address: 77 Rue de Varenne, 75007 Paris Website: musee-rodin.fr Price: From €13; concessions available Dates: Closed on Mondays 5. Rodeo: Bruce of Los Angeles In June of last year, Acne Studios opened its first permanent gallery space within the historic arcades of Paris’ Palais-Royal. This September it will showcase a series of 77 vintage photographs by Bruce of Los Angeles, one of 20th-century America’s most prolific chroniclers of the male form. Curator Vince Aletti draws out Bruce’s distinct visual language, which toes the line between the sculptural, the erotic, and the refined. Though best known for his photographs of male performance athletes flexing and posing to the camera, Rodeo turns the lens towards working cowboys across American ranches, captured in relaxed and unforced moments. In an era where cowboy imagery has been thoroughly romanticised, the captivating allure of Bruce’s photographs lies in their unvarnished authenticity. Address: 124 Galerie de Valois, 75001 Paris Website: acnestudios.com Price: Free Dates: Until 7 October 2026; Closed Monday-Wednesday 6. We are [STILL] here The bold and storied street art of Paris has made its way inside the grand walls of the Petit Palais to claim its rightful place within the history of art. Featuring 75 street artists from France and beyond, the exhibition conveys the themes, moods and dynamics of our times through an urban medium which reacts to, and quite literally becomes part of its surroundings. We are [STILL] here showcases various techniques and subjects that, while entirely contemporary and self-sufficient, share a surprisingly deep lineage with classical art movements. Address: Avenue Winston Churchill 75008 Paris Website: petitpalais.paris.fr Price: Free Dates: Until 20 September 2026 7. Timeless Tintoretto From 11 September, Musée Jacquemart-André - one of Paris’ most beautiful mansion-museums – will immerse its visitors into the sumptuous world of Jacopo Tintoretto, a leading figure of 16th-century Italian Mannerism. This will be the artist’s first major French retrospective, whose bold, vibrant, and at times controversial paintings were well ahead of their time. Based in Venice, Tintoretto made a name for himself through large-scale public commissions of the city’s most prestigious buildings. In this exhibition, forty rare paintings and works on paper are brought together from both public and private collections worldwide, with the aim of illuminating Tintoretto’s remarkable and widespread talent, and an oeuvre that firmly defies categorisation. Address: 158 Bd Haussmann, 75008, Paris Website: musee-jacquemart-andre.com Price: €14; Concessions available Dates: Until 24 January 2027 8. Andy Warhol: The Line and the Image Andy Warhol’s cult icon status and instantly recognisable oeuvre is a double-edged sword. While it solidifies his position as one of the most famous artists in modern history, it can make it difficult to find fresh ways to be surprised by his ubiquitous screen prints. Enter the Musée du Luxembourg, who tackle this challenge head-on with an exhibition dedicated to Warhol’s lesser-known yet deeply important works on paper. They have collated nearly 150 line drawings complemented by paintings, photographs and archival documents in order to demonstrate the Pop Artist’s delicate process of draftsmanship, invention and seriality. This is a captivating new perspective on a figure that everyone feels they know, yet few have seen through this lens. Address: 19, rue de Vaugirard, 75006, Paris Website: museeduluxembourg.fr Price: €19; Concessions available Dates: Until 10 January 2027 9. Adya & Otto van Rees, At the Heart of the Avant-Garde Dutch-born, Parisian-based couple Adya and Otto van Rees were major players in the city’s avant-garde art scene but fell undeservedly into obscurity in the years following their death. Now, Musée de Montmartre shines a long-overdue spotlight on this couple’s life, love, and professional careers. Influenced by and influencers of their neighbours and friends, Picasso, Braques, and Mondrian among others, this exhibition brings together more than 100 works showcasing the van Rees’ bold and experimental style which traverses multiple artistic disciplines and schools of thought. Address: 12 Rue Cortot, 75018, Paris Website: museedemontmartre.fr Price: €16; concessions available Dates: Until 13 September 2026

item.title: Is your vagus nerve the real reason travel wrecks you?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.06
Scroll far enough on social media and you'll hit a quick fix promising to calm your nervous system in seconds. The vagus nerve in particular has become wellness shorthand for ‘calm on demand’ but there's actual science behind how you do it properly – and it goes far beyond a 15-second clip. So, what is the vagus nerve? Essentially, the longest cranial nerve in the body, travelling from the brainstem down through the neck and chest into the abdomen, brushing past the heart, lungs and gut. It's the main line of the parasympathetic nervous system – rest, digest, repair – as opposed to the sympathetic system that gears you up to handle a threat. “If you think of your body as a car, the autonomic nervous system is the drivetrain and brakes,” says Lou Atkinson, clinical wellbeing lead of Yōjō, a health and wellness platform specialising in vagus nerve stimulation or VNS. “The sympathetic nervous system is the accelerator, while the vagus nerve is your essential braking system, slowing your heart rate, initiating digestion and lowering inflammation.” Activating the vagus nerve can help us feel calmer, but the issue with quick fixes is that we are treating the symptoms of nervous system dysregulation – like anxiety, insomnia, a need to control everything – rather than the dysregulation itself. “If we treat the symptom without ever getting to the root cause, it becomes a tireless battle managing something that cannot dissipate unless we leave the state we're in,” explains Sarah Baldwin, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner. What happens to our nervous system when we travel? Travel obliterates almost all our comforting routines and habits. “It’s essentially a stress-test for your autonomic nervous system, and vagal tone takes the hit," says Human Potential Coach and Breathwork Practitioner, Rob Rea. “Crossing time zones desynchronises the body's rest-and-digest rhythm from local day and night – a large part of why jet lag brings poor sleep, a racing heart and low mood, not just tiredness.” Short nights, dry cabin air, dehydration, alcohol and caffeine all tip the body further towards fight-or-flight, leaving less room for recovery. For some, it goes way deeper than jet lag. Leaving a familiar environment removes our daily safety anchors, and unresolved stress can resurface as anxiety or hypervigilance amid the unpredictability of new places. “Long after we’ve arrived, and the danger has passed, the body can keep replaying that same protective response – that’s why so many of us feel anxious or shut down for reasons we can't quite explain, especially when travelling,” trauma psychotherapist Emmy Brunner says. “Release isn't about forcing it – it happens through small, repeated doses of safety, not pushing through.” In practice, this looks like having a vagus nerve toolkit you can turn to when you need it most. "Splash cold water on the face – cold exposure activates the vagus nerve and can pull you out of a spiral almost instantly,” Brunner advises. Another tip she says is to: “Slowly look around the room and name a few things you can see – it reminds the nervous system it's present and safe." Another surprising method that works is quiet humming. “It stimulates the vagus nerve directly through the vocal cords,” says Atkinson. If you feel too conscious doing this in a public place, longer exhales also help engage it: "Breathe gently through your nose, inhale for four seconds and exhale for six," says Rea. "Let the breath become quieter rather than bigger, and continue for two to five minutes." Making travel easier on our nervous systems Perhaps the best advice is to think of nervous system work as part of your pre-travel prep, along with your packing and booking. “People often wait until they're deeply dysregulated to start regulating, but the earlier you start, the better,” Baldwin advises. She recommends getting outdoor light at both ends of the day to recalibrate your circadian rhythm, before, during and after your trip. As is having a piece of home with you. “Bringing something familiar, a candle, a journal, a photo and orienting to a new room by consciously noticing its colours and sounds both help signal safety, too,” she adds. For frequent flyers wanting something more hands-off, wearable vagus nerve stimulators like yōjō deliver gentle electrical pulses to the ear's auricular branch, nudging the body into rest-digest mode without requiring meditation mid-flight – wearable while working, watching a film or trying to sleep. But ultimately it’s about incorporating vagal nerve work into your daily life. “The goal is not a quick fix; it’s to discharge small amounts of activation to lessen our dysregulation by even 5 per cent,” Baldwin says. Our nervous systems need something called disconfirming experiences. “These are moments where we show, not tell, our nervous systems that the thing it thinks is dangerous is actually safe,” she says. After doing that, our nervous system has enough data points to see that the perceived danger is actually safe, and we no longer experience the anxiety we once did. None of this promises to make flying enjoyable – particularly if you struggle with it. But understood and practised properly, vagal tone could be the deciding factor in whether a trip leaves you restored or wrung out. That’s worth knowing, next time you're stuck in seat 34C convincing yourself it's turbulence, when it’s actually your nervous system on overdrive. - Emmy Brunner’s residential retreats combine hypnosis and somatic practice. The Compass, a four-week online course, fuses evidence-based clinical tools with belief and identity repatterning. - Sarah Baldwin’s online programs Navigating Your Nervous System and Nervous System Essentials can be found here. Listen to her podcast, You Make Sense Podcast, on Apple or Spotify. - Rob Rea’s Autumn Equinox Day Retreat will be at 1 Hotel Mayfair, London. Follow him online.

item.title: “Our earth is only one polka dot among a million stars in the cosmos”: remembering Yayoi Kusama, the girl who covered the world in polka dots
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.97
In 2016, a day before she was to enrol as a student at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, Sunaina Rajan made a pit stop in Los Angeles for a single day. Word had gone round that one of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms was on view at The Broad, the museum that had opened downtown the year before. She joined the line, and waited in it for seven hours till it was her turn to enter the room, albeit for under a minute, strictly timed by a staff member standing outside, who’d briskly open the door once the seconds ran out. “You really get just a very short glimpse of it,” recalls Rajan, who opened Gallery Maxima in Mumbai’s Fort district earlier this year. “But the physical experience is so unforgettable from the moment you enter, the way you experience it…you’re immersed in it completely.” The legendary Japanese contemporary artist passed away earlier this month on 14 August at a hospital in Tokyo, aged 97. Her studio and her gallery, David Zwirner, announced her death on 26 August. The cause was multiple organ failure. Few artists have altered the physical act of looking at art as completely as she did, and she got there first, in 1965, with Infinity Mirror Room – Phalli’s Field, where hundreds of hand-sewn phallic forms, spotted in red, carpeted the floor of a mirrored room that repeated them into the horizon. “Traditionally, museum-going has been about standing in front of one masterpiece and really taking it in,” Rajan shares. “She inverts that completely. Instead of stepping into the museum to see a work, you’re now stepping into the work.” When Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors opened at the Hirshhorn in Washington, DC, in 2017, it drew nearly 160,000 people, and the museum recorded its highest spring attendance since opening in 1974. The show went on to Seattle, back to The Broad, then to Toronto, Cleveland and Atlanta. In 2023 her work arrived in India for the first time as an Infinity Mirrored Room at the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre (NMACC) in Mumbai, now part of its permanent collection. Two years ago, Rajan made a longer pilgrimage to Naoshima, the island in Japan’s Seto Inland Sea given over almost entirely to contemporary art. “You need three modes of transportation to get there – first by bus, then train, then ferry; and you can walk the whole island in under an hour,” describes Rajan, At the end of a pier sits her yellow Pumpkin, which was installed there in 1994, swept into the sea by a typhoon in August 2021, and remade and returned to the same spot on 4 October 2022. What struck Rajan was that the reverence held there too, with nobody enforcing it. “In contrast, there’s no one attending to it, no security timing you. There’s just this sort of decorum around her work, because there’s so much respect for it.” Elsewhere on the island, Kusama’s mirrored spheres sit in a body of water, near buildings by Tadao Ando. “What’s fascinating to see is how the architecture, the art and nature interact with each other,” Rajan points out. The life and art of Yayoi Kusama Kusama was born in Matsumoto, in Nagano prefecture, on 22 March 1929, into a family who ran a seed nursery: fields of flowers on one side, a violent and unhappy household on the other. In her lifetime, she recalled being a child when the hallucinations started. Sometimes it was benign, the millions of white pebbles in the riverbed at Matsumoto, which she would lie and stare at; and sometimes it was not. The episode she returned to for the rest of her life involved a tablecloth: she looked at its red flower pattern, looked up, and found the same pattern across the ceiling, the windows, the walls, and finally over her own body and the universe beyond it. She described the sensation as beginning to self-obliterate, to dissolve into endless time and space. So, she started drawing them to record each vision, which took some of the terror out of them. She found the dot along the way, smaller and stranger than decoration, and compared the single dot to her own life: one particle among billions. The dots were the symptom; making them, over and over, was the treatment, and nearly 70 years of work came out of that single loop. Her pumpkins came from the same fields. As a schoolgirl, she visited a seed-harvesting ground with her grandfather, where she saw her first pumpkin. What she loved about them, she said later, was their “generous unpretentiousness”. Rejecting her dreams of becoming an artist, her mother wanted her to be a housewife and repeatedly tore up her drawings. Kusama, instead, went on to train in traditional Nihonga painting in Kyoto, and on 15 November 1955 she wrote to American painter Georgia O’Keeffe (a stranger to her, whose work she had found in a second-hand book) to ask how a Japanese girl might make a life as an artist in the United States. O’Keeffe wrote back within three weeks. She told her to get to a city, asked what she wanted for the watercolours, offered to show them to a dealer, and advised her to put her work in front of anyone who would look at it. In 1957 Kusama destroyed most of her work and left, first for Seattle, then New York in the summer of 1958, where she spent the rest of her 20s and 30s, creating her vast, obsessive Infinity Net paintings, which were showcased at the Brata Gallery 1959; the Accumulations, ordinary furniture swallowed by soft phallic forms, which debuted at the Green Gallery in late 1962 alongside the Pop artists Claes Oldenburg and Andy Warhol; and, in November 1965 at the Richard Castellane Gallery, Infinity Mirror Room – Phalli’s Field, the first of the mirrored environments that would eventually take over the internet decades later. In 1966 she turned up at the Venice Biennale without an invitation, laid 1,500 mirrored balls on the grass outside the Italian pavilion and sold them for two dollars each beneath a sign reading “Your Narcissism for Sale”. By the end of that decade she was staging anti-war happenings in Manhattan, painting polka dots onto naked bodies. She went home to Japan in 1973 and, in 1977, voluntarily checked herself into Seiwa Hospital in Tokyo, where she lived for the rest of her life, walking each day to a studio across the road. The entire second half of her career was made from that arrangement. In 1993 she became the first artist given a solo presentation in Japan’s pavilion at Venice; then came two major artistic collaborations with Louis Vuitton in 2012 and 2023, her own museum in Shinjuku in 2017, and a scale of fame that very few living artists have known. “Our earth is only one polka dot among a million stars in the cosmos,” Kusama once mused. For Rajan, that is the inheritance: “She took something as simple as the polka dot or the pumpkin, which is so ordinary to us, and made it a portrait of her… showing us that art can be an environment that you’re entering into, and created that incredible legacy for so many artists to come.” How to follow the dots The best place to discover and take in Kusama’s work is on Naoshima, Japan, where her infamous yellow Pumpkin sits at the end of a pier below Benesse House and a red one waits at Miyanoura Port, free and open at all hours (though much of the island closes for maintenance through stretches of January and February). In Tokyo, the Yayoi Kusama Museum spans five narrow floors in Shinjuku; tickets go on sale online on the first of each month for dates two months ahead. And in Matsumoto, where she was born, the city’s museum of art holds a year-round display, with her Great Gigantic Pumpkin outside. Beyond Japan, the touring shows have wound down, so what’s left is permanent: two rooms at The Broad in Los Angeles, Gleaming Lights of the Souls at Louisiana outside Copenhagen, and (closest to home) the Infinity Mirrored Room at NMACC in Mumbai, acquired after her India debut in 2023. This article was first published by Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: We threw our own phones into the sea to find the best waterproof phone pouches in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.91
There are so many adventures where a waterproof phone pouch is a must: paddleboarding over a Scottish loch, dipping into a hot spring in Iceland, kayaking on one of the many lakes in Montenegro, or just lolling by the beach or pool at a resort. Above and beyond the protection your average phone case offers, a waterproof phone pouch creates a full-on barrier around your device, which (depending on the pouch) can be enough for you to even take underwater photos, let alone withstand the odd splash. Plus, a waterproof phone case will often come with additional design features to make your life easier, like a lanyard or strap so you can go hand-free (and pockets empty). Some can even float. With something like this, which needs to keep expensive equipment safe, it’s important to know that you’re getting a product that really stands up to the task. To save you from having to find out the hard way, Traveller editors have tried out a slew of waterproof phone bags and pouches to find out which will really keep your phone dry. As usual, we have been thorough with our testing. On our first run, we trialled pouches with a tissue inside, to ensure there was no immediate water damage, followed by an old (and small) Apple phone. Finally, we braved it with our current, expensive phones inside to see if they survived. We didn’t tiptoe around this testing – with each round, all of the pouches were tossed into a pool or ocean. Luckily, all phones and tissues came out unscathed, which bodes well for waterproof phone pouches in general, but some pouches outshone others in various ways. These are the ones that have made our list. Below you’ll find the best waterproof phone pouches to bring on your next beach trip, cruise, or rainy-day hike. The best waterproof phone pouches at-a-glance The best waterproof phone pouches, tried-and-tested by our editors Other good options: How we test the best waterproof phone pouches To find the cases truly worthy of protecting expensive tech, our editors put a batch of top-rated universal waterproof pouches through a rigorous multi-stage test. We began in the bathroom sink, submerging each pouch filled with dry tissue paper to check for immediate leaks, before advancing to an old iPhone 6. Once proven watertight, we braved the ultimate test: locking in our current, everyday mobile phones – one Pixel and one iPhone – and plunging them directly into the open sea – evaluating seal strength, touch sensitivity, floating capabilities, and photo clarity along the way. Can you swim with a waterproof phone pouch? If your chosen waterproof bag is high quality (read: one from our list above) yes, you can usually swim with it, but it’s important to check that it has been designed for swimming conditions first. The IP rating will indicate how waterproof or water-resistant the pouch is (IP68 or higher means it has been designed to be safely submerged in water). You should also check the recommendation for how deep it can go, ensuring it’s at least one to two metres. Can you take photos through the best waterproof phone cases? Touchscreen can be used through some waterproof pouches, but not all. And the sensitivity is likely to be impacted if the pouch is in water or wet. The plastic of the pouch can cause some image distortion or glare, but some of the best waterproof phone pouches have dedicated camera lens windows to help avoid this. Can you still use your phone in a waterproof pouch? You can still use your phone in most waterproof pouches to some extent, but the touchscreen may be less responsive, face/touch ID might not work, side buttons are likely to be harder to press and audio will be muffled. How deep can a waterproof phone pouch go? The depth a phone can be safely submerged in a waterproof pouch varies depending on the material and design, so it’s best to check with each product. Some waterproof phone pouches can only go as deep as one metre, while others can reach 10 metres. But remember, the deeper you go, the greater the water pressure and the greater the risk of leakage.

item.title: These are the quietest islands in the world right now – and 3 British gems have made the top 20
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.80
There are times when all we desire is a bit of peace and quiet. Life can be a noisy, overstimulating affair as we juggle multiple plates at once, and aside from a stint in a sleek spa hotel, a little bit of serenity is enough R&R to send us back on our way. Overtourism is a greater issue than ever, as millions of travellers flock to the same cities and coastal hideouts. Crowds equal noise, and it’s easy to return from an adventure feeling more burnt out than before. For those of us seeking a more tranquil holiday destination, BookRetreats.com new index has uncovered the quietest islands in the world – perfect for the ultimate reset. According to the leading retreat booking site, searches for "quiet destinations" are up 1,268 per cent year on year globally, while the site’s latest survey found that 56 per cent of those asked now want to retreat for quiet in nature. With insight from silence researcher and psychology professor Olga V. Lehmann, BookRetreats.com analysed several islands against six criteria: road density, untouched nature, air traffic, uncrowded space, dark skies and natural coastal spots. Islands were then ranked according to the UN Environment Programme's definition of a quiet soundscape. "Islands have always been where we go to get away from it all, but very few are still as quiet as they once were," says Sean Kelly, co-founder of BookRetreats.com. "Our Unspoilt Index maps where the last genuinely quiet ones are, and what's clear from the data is that they're peaceful because people chose to protect their quiet." So, where should we be heading to escape the noise? Not some of our favourite European hideouts, it seems. Malta ranks last on the list of 100 islands with a meagre score of just 5.3 out of 100. Santorini ranks 99th thanks to 64km of major roads packed into 76 square kilometres of land, while Tenerife ranks 93rd and Ibiza 85th. Other destinations that didn’t fare too well include the Thai isle of Phuket in 95th place, Martinique in 90th and the Isle of Wight in 81st. However, Brits needn’t travel too far to find peace. St Martin’s, the third-largest of the Isles of Scilly, ranks fifth in the index. The quietest island in the United Kingdom has no main roads, no airport and just 135 residents. Reachable by ferry or via a short flight from Cornwall to St Mary’s, then a boat, this dreamy isle with its 12 beaches is the ultimate day trip for a reset. It’s not the only British gem in the top 20, either. Scotland’s Isle of Skye ranks 11th, where more than 1,600 square kilometres of moor and mountain is shared by just 10,000 people. There’s one hub and several smaller villages and hamlets scattered along the coast, with an otherworldly landscape popular among nature lovers and hikers during the summer months. However, it’s New Zealand’s third-largest and lesser-known island, Stewart Island, that claims the title of the quietest island in the world. The world’s southernmost International Dark Sky Sanctuary is almost entirely untouched and virtually free of artificial light. The Greek island of Anafi is second, with a tiny population and no airports or main roads. Here, we’ve rounded up the 20 quietest islands in the world right now, so you can plot your next adventure and relax like never before. The quietest islands in the world 2026 20. Palawan, Philippines 19. Vis, Croatia 18. La Digue, Seychelles 17. Mljet, Croatia 16. Salt Spring Island, Canada 15. Boa Vista, Cape Verde 14. Herm, Channel Islands 13. Magnetic Island, Australia 12. Isla Holbox, Mexico 11. Isle of Skye, UK 10. Santa Catalina Island, USA 9. Havelock Island, India 8. Koh Rong, Cambodia 7. Koh Chang, Thailand 6. Tioman Island, Malaysia 5. St Martin's, Isles of Scilly, UK 4. Lord Howe Island, Australia 3. Ilha Grande, Brazil 2. Anafi, Greece 1. Stewart Island, New Zealand

item.title: I’ve spent years tracking Nordic wellness trends, and this low-impact Finnish ritual is about to take over
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.45
I can smell the embers of a Nordic trend in the making from miles away. After all, even before the Swedish ethos of lagom (optimal balance) captured the world a few years ago, I’d been unpacking this Nordic mindset around wellness and lifestyle in my storytelling for years. I would go on to write an international bestseller, Lagom, with over 15 foreign editions. From Swedish massages to Finnish saunas, the region is synonymous with wellbeing. While Denmark gave the world hygge (intentional presence), Norway friluftsliv (open-air living), Finland sisu (grit), and Iceland birthed “Viking wellness” with hot baths and cold dips, the reality is that all Nordic cultures share these values under different names. What makes lifestyle trends from the region particularly appealing globally is the foundations on which they’re built. From sustainability-focused mindsets and a return to simplicity to curb undue stress, to government-sanctioned free access to nature (think Allemansrätten in Sweden), which fosters symbiotic relationships with the outdoors, and overall accessibility for everyone because they are egalitarian countries. The Nordic communal goal is a focus on holistic well-being that can be sustained over the long term by every individual, from professional athletes in their prime to elders. The latest Nordic wellness trend, however, has rather practical origins. Ever wonder how cross-country skiers train when there’s no snow? Introducing Nordic walking; not to be confused with hiking with trekking poles. According to its governing body, the International Nordic Walking Federation (INWA), which was founded in 2000, Nordic walking is now practised in over 40 countries for health, fitness, recreation, social connection and competitive sport. As early as the 1930s, competitive cross-country skiers used poles with running shoes for summer training. But it was physical education (PE) teacher Leena Jääskeläinen who brought the concept to the general public in 1966, making it the first documented use of ski poles outside competitive training. “I started Nordic walking in 1998 because it is a fun, social and efficient form of physical activity,” shares Aki Karihtala, president of INWA. “It takes people back to nature.” At the time, he headed the Sports division at Finnish Sporting goods company Exel, the world's largest cross-country ski pole manufacturer. It was Karihtala himself, alongside his team at Exel, who coined the term Nordic walking, which has been widely adopted “regardless of age, religion and culture, because there are no boundaries,” notes Karihtala, highlighting its accessibility. In 1997, Exel designed the first Nordic Walker® poles specifically for the activity. A year later, over 500,000 Finns, in a population of roughly five million at the time, had tried Nordic walking. It's said to be especially effective because it engages the whole body while reducing pressure on your knees with ergonomically designed poles. The federation developed its progressive INWA 10 Step Method™ to teach people the simple technique safely and effectively. Finnish trend and branding expert Katja Presnal is a newer convert to Nordic walking. “I’ve studied trends for over 20 years,” shares Presnal. Her personal lifestyle digital platform was read by over 100,000 monthly readers and millions annually. The irony of Nordic wellness being the hottest lifestyle trend at the moment isn’t lost on Presnal, who grew up in the Turku archipelago surrounded by bays and lush forests. According to Presnal, after two decades of travelling, she stopped “preaching trends” and started “walking the walk” by purchasing a 100+-year-old former dairy tucked away in the Finnish countryside for a slower, more intentional way of life surrounded by nature, lakes, and walking trails. “It was about making everyday life a wellness regimen and creating my own 365-day retreat,” adds Presnal, noting that these were the type of slow living wellness experiences her family would seek in places like Tuscany while travelling. “So I have, in essence, returned to my Nordic wellness roots, which in hindsight was the richness of my childhood.” The low-threshold accessibility, from a physical and financial standpoint, is what makes Nordic Walking perfect right now for newbies like Presnal. Another benefit Presnal notes is connectivity with people. “People are now discovering Nordic lifestyles,” explains Presnal. “You don't recognise your Nordic way of living as something special that could become a global trend or could be taught and shared with somebody because it's just a part of who you are.” How to try Nordic walking You don’t have to wait for the annual World Nordic Walking Day held every May. You can start by: - Finding a local event hosted by over 13 country associations from the Nordics and Baltics to Croatia, Japan, and Australia and joining a group walk with an INWA instructor. - Choosing your favourite local trail and walking at your own pace. - Trying one of INWA’s 25 Nordic Walking Ideas, from themed walks to charity challenges.

item.description:

As the largest glittering jewel in the Canary Island archipelago, Tenerife is our go-to destination for stunning Spanish beaches, activity-packed family holidays, and wonderful villas to rent. Spread across the diverse terrain of island coastline fused with record-breaking peaks (Tenerife’s Mount Teide is famed for being the largest in Spain), the homes here guarantee a good view whenever they might be. And with glamorous new waves of ultra-modern properties peppering the long-established landscape of traditional fincas, there are plenty of villas in Tenerife to suit all tastes. A villa stay is an indulgence, offering space and privacy in a grand home. It’s no surprise then that almost all the villas on our list have gorgeous swimming pools, while lots more offer amenities such as romantic private balconies or even personal chefs. Start chasing the winter-sun with our hand-picked selection of the most stunning villa rentals in Tenerife, from family-friendly farmstays to innovative eco villas. item.title: The Indonesian island that time forgot is one of travel’s most exciting new destinations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.10
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach – good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote & Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels – a few hundred miles apart – front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance, storytelling and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the firepit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument the sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders – and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” This is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile – on the harbour, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “Selamat Datang” – welcome – or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution: one is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling petrol in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese – a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade – resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles, and the Ti’i Langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats; I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel, and fast-float in the choppy current to spy triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colours of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene: “no drugs, no nightclubs”, as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “Many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet”. Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote”. “Here you feel you can give back; life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s dreamy resort, Bo’a Vida, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Shacks, bungalows, resorts and more NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), this 21-villa property on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travellers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. An on-site training academy allows guests to give back to the community. Bo’a Vida Owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs Indika café in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5.30pm, when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Rote Island Huts Nat and Matt Thistlewaite came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channelled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Sardine Beach Rote Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. Here on Rote they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, panelled walls and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Mick’s Place Rote Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of these three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. The lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Minimum one-week stay. 81 Palms Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas and seafood paella.

item.title: I fly 77,000+ miles a year – this is my non-negotiable long-haul travel uniform in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.86
As a professional travel writer, I cover a lot of ground. This year, I’m hopping on several flights per month ranging from long-hauls to Vietnam, Cape Town, and Hawaii, to slightly shorter jaunts to Paris, Rome, and Greenland – a whopping 77,000+ miles so far and counting. One thing that’s hugely important on any trip? Staying comfortable in transit. With all that time in the air, I've perfected my travel uniform, aka the comfortable airport outfit I always wear for long travel days, no matter where I’m headed. My trusty formula almost never veers from the relaxed clothing staples below, from supportive shoes to the perfect tee and a sleek bomber jacket. Read on for my tried-and-true picks that always keep me looking and feeling my best on every journey. A light jacket Cabin temperatures are notoriously cold, but then you’ll step off the plane and into the Med and overheat immediately. As such, layering on a flight is key, and a lightweight jacket is the cornerstone of the look. Rather than reaching for an oversized hoodie that can quickly look scruffy in a lounge, a cropped or smart bomber style adds a little polish to an otherwise casual outfit. They can also be folded and used as an impromptu pillow in a pinch. Look for crease-resistant fabrics and deep pockets that can house a passport, lip balm, and boarding pass for frictionless airport security screening. The perfect tee A good T-shirt is the unsung hero of long-haul travel. When you’re sitting in the same seat for nine hours, the texture against your skin matters immensely. My golden rule is to completely avoid synthetic blends that trap heat and opt instead for 100 per cent organic cotton or ultra-soft jersey t-shirts with a dense weight. A great travel tee needs to hold its shape after hours of reclining, have a non-restrictive crew neckline, and not sheer out or cling after a few washes. Neutral, versatile shades like creamy oat, charcoal, or classic white makes it easy to style whatever you’re wearing, giving you a breathable base layer that should stay fresh through multiple time zones. Put-together trousers Gone are the days when being comfy in the airport meant sacrificing style for baggy grey tracksuit bottoms. Modern travel trousers offer the stretch and ease of loungewear, with crisp tailored finishes. Wide-leg cuts in soft, flexible fabrics and those with tailored pull-on waistbands are my go-to choice for long travel days. They allow complete freedom of movement – whether you’re folding your legs up on a long-haul flight or sprinting through terminals to catch a tight connection – without digging into your waist. The beauty is in their incredible versatility; paired with trainers and a clean tee, you achieve an effortless look that feels like wearing loungewear while looking entirely intentional. Plus, if you’re headed straight to a meeting upon landing, they can be immediately dressed up by swapping your trainers and jacket for boots and a blazer. Compression socks After a 13-plus-hour flight from Ho Chi Minh City to London left one of my legs swollen and uncomfortable this year, I vowed to always wear compression socks on long flights. High-altitude cabin pressure combined with hours of sitting can severely hamper circulation, leading to fatigued legs and fluid retention. Integrating a dedicated pair of graduated compression socks into my travel routine has been a total game-changer. Designed to gently encourage blood flow back up towards the heart, they significantly cut down on in-flight aches and post-flight ankle swelling. My favourites are those made from breathable bamboo fibres – and aesthetically, there are plenty out there these days that look just like regular crew or knee socks, sliding under trainers without sacrificing comfort or style. Comfortable shoes Navigating huge airport terminals, endless security queues, and European cobblestones all in one day means one thing: your footwear needs to prioritise comfort and support above all else. For long-haul travel days, I find a good pair of trainers to be a complete non-negotiable. I rotate between a few different styles, but no matter the pair, they’re always trainers I can rush around the airport in and wear socks with in case I need to take my shoes off in a security line. Seamless luggage set No travel uniform is complete without the luggage to bring all your gear along with. Navigating terminals with multiple bags quickly turns chaotic if your luggage strategy relies on mismatched totes and awkwardly sliding straps. A clever luggage set allows for effortless mobility and proper integrated organisation, so your essential items remain within arm’s reach while your hands stay free for your coffee. My go-to setup is a smooth-rolling carry-on paired with a dedicated travel tote as an under-seat cabin bag, finished with a sleek sling bag where I keep my cards and passport. Look for luggage with trolley sleeves that slide over case handles, polycarbonate or aluminium exteriors that will withstand turbulence, and bags with internal compartments to reduce stress and keep tech, travel documents, and flight essentials sorted throughout your trip. item.title: 17 of the best hotels in the Cotswolds our editors love for a UK staycation with character for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.71
The Cotswolds is a British favourite for a reason. Nowhere does stylish country pubs, grand manor houses and hip boutique hotels quite like it. Choosing the best hotels in the Cotswolds, then, is a tricky ask. From the quintessential to the contemporary, the foodie-focused to the spa-centric, each has the temptation to move here long-term. There's also the ever-welcome fact that it's equally beautiful in the depths of winter as in fair weather. Here, wellies are part of the uniform, trudging through muddy fields and stepping over stiles are par for the course and hunkering down by an open fire to thaw out somehow feels more romantic in winter, anyway. Bookmark the best things to do, add a visit to a farm shop to your list and swoon over Sunday roast menus to plan the ultimate escape-from-the-city weekend. Editor's Picks of the best hotels in the Cotswolds Best for foodies: Bull, Burford Best for wellness: Dormy House Hotel & Spa Best boutique stay: The Pig, Gloucestershire Best for couples: Cowley Manor Best for families: The Fish Best dog-friendly stay: Lygon Arms - Read Full ReviewDown a suitably grand wide driveway where grazing sheep stretch out in the sprawling grounds near Winchcombe, you’ll find the newly renovated Dumbleton Hall. This 19th-century Cotswold stone estate has entered an ambitious new chapter following a major restoration inside and out. Built on a historic wool fortune – the Cotswolds area is well loved for its wool products, as well as its lavender – the manor house has long been a literary and cultural hub, having hosted the likes of Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell, and John Betjeman, among others. Now, within the old stone exterior, it’s a thoroughly refreshed take on country living, with maximalist Belle Époque-inspired interiors (they’ve somehow made leopard-print rugs work in an olde-worlde country manor) and far-reaching bucolic views across the hotel’s peaceful grounds and lake. It’s a true taste of the good life, made a little more elevated – settle in by a roaring hearth, tuck into a seasonal British plate, then sip slowly on something in the Library Bar, which is lined wall to wall with books. It stands out against neighbouring Cotswolds heavyweights by deftly combining the grandeur and scale of an old estate with an intimate ease that evokes staying at a stylish friend’s country seat over a stuffy old hotel. Charley Ward Address: Dumbleton, Evesham WR11 7TS Prices: From about £300 per night. - Read Full ReviewFrom the front, Dormy House Hotel & Spa is every inch the classic honey-hued manor house, but behind the doors lies a carefully curated world of food, fireside lounging and standout wellness that far exceeds expectations. Step through the reception rooms, where roaring fires, leather armchairs, muddy boots and a refreshingly informal ‘no-front-desk’ welcome set the tone. The House Spa is the undeniable star. Its thermal suite invites hours of gentle drifting between steam rooms, saunas and hot-and-cold experiences, including a bracing snow shower and a forest-mist drench shower infused with essential oils. Outside, a bubbling hot tub awaits, best enjoyed as mist rises into the often-blustery British air. Dining at The Back Garden, the hotel’s fine-dining restaurant, delivers exactly what you’d hope for from a refined country hotel: modern British cooking rooted in superb local produce, with estate-grown vegetables and locally reared meat taking centre stage. After long walks across the surrounding hills and a few blissful hours in the spa, the bedrooms are a welcome reprive. Bright, calm and quietly luxurious with roll-top baths, thick robes make the idea of check-out hard to come to terms with. Breakfast is indulgent, with generous spreads of cheeses, compotes, overnight oats, granola and fresh fruit, alongside classic à la carte favourites like eggs royale and hearty house specials, including the aptly named ‘Fully Dormy’ for those with an appetite for the day ahead. Chloe Laws Address: Willersey Hill, Broadway, Worcestershire, WR12 7LF Prices: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewA 16th-century coaching inn turned boutique hideaway – so far, so classic Cotswolds. But as soon as we clamber from the (branded) Defender and slip into reception, it's clear that Bull Burford is about to challenge our expectations. The first clue? There's a Dalí over the fireplace, and a Basquiat hanging over the chess table. Media mogul Matthew Freud bought this 1536-built inn a few years ago. From the outside, it retains a rather wonky charm, looking every bit the quintessential coaching house. Inside, however, Freud has filled every blank wall and disused corner with such an astonishing array of art from his personal collection that you gaze upon works from more world-famous artists during a stroll about the hotel than you might at many a major gallery or museum. The 18 bedrooms are deeply cossetting, carvenous spaces to tap out from reality for a while – we stayed in the Honeymooner, which had plump armchairs next to an exposed-brick fireplace for sinking into with a book (there was a stash of Penguin Classics on a shelf for forgetful types), a freestanding bath, and a separate dressing room for gussying up for supper. Plus, Freud and his team have added restaurants and drinking dens that are as good as anything you'll find in the UK's bigger cities right now – Wild, an open-fire restaurant under canvas in the hotel's courtyard, is the jewel in the foodie crown. Add to the mix personable staff, a treatment suite for facials or massages, and a plum position on the sloping high street of the cute Cotswolds village of Burford, and you've got a country weekender which swaggers rather than simpers. Sarah James Address: 105 High Street, Burford, Oxfordshire, OX18 4QR Prices: From about £270 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Fish is a playful, woodland hideaway just a stone’s throw from Farncombe Estate’s other properties – Dormy House Hotel & Spa and Foxhill Manor – yet it feels like an entirely different offering. Tucked into the trees above the Vale of Evesham and a brisk stomp from the postcard-pretty village of Broadway, it’s made for weekend escapes that balance fresh air with frivolity. While more affordable and better suited to families and groups than its refined siblings, The Fish still delivers its own brand of luxury. Think sheepskin-draped lounge chairs, crackling open fires, cool Scandinavian-inspired interiors and tongue-in-cheek touches, from Hideaway huts named after A Midsummer Night’s Dream characters to treehouses designed for late-night drinks. What really makes it special is the staff and their “nothing’s too much” approach. Food is a highlight, with seafood taking centre stage in the fine-dining Hook restaurant, alongside relaxed crowd-pleasers served in buzzy communal spaces, perfect after long days spent roaming woodland trails, partaking in one of the many activities on-site (like archery) or sinking into an outdoor hot tub beneath the trees. Accommodation ranges from stylish hotel rooms to sprawling tree-lined Hideaway huts with private terraces, making it easy to tailor your stay, whether you’re planning a romantic retreat or a full-blown girls' getaway. It’s informal, fun and refreshingly unfussy, the kind of place that I could see myself returning to again and again. Chloe Laws Address: Farncombe, Broadway, Worcestershire, WR12 7LH Prices: From about £225 per night. - Read Full ReviewWaking up in Cowley Manor feels like you’ve tumbled down the rabbit hole and into a world of comfort, indulgence and serenity, even if just for a night. It’s owned by the Experimental* and – as expected – it’s designed in the brand’s signature contemporary-cool way. Prepare to start planning how best to replicate its interiors at home. Curious, considering its heritage house shell and historical ties to Lewis Caroll’s Alice In Wonderland inspiration. There are subtle nods to the story throughout: gilded gold door embellishments take the form of the rabbit head, and keys are marked on the hallway carpets. It’s not outlandish, though – this is a hotel that’s all about its guests. The spa and pool are simply heavenly, and many while away the day in the glass box that surrounds the water, glancing up from a book only to spot a bunny hip-hopping along outside. Others choose to set up camp in the bar, which is all roaring fire and chairs you can sink into while sipping on one of the mixologist’s most creative concoctions. Wander the grounds before dinner and discover hidden pathways through the surrounding woods before heading to the deep red dining room, where romance comes as a byproduct of any meal. Sarah Leigh Bannerman Address: Cowley, Cheltenham GL53 9NL Prices: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewAn artist's impression of the Cotswolds would probably look a little something like this: a quaint high street, imposing historical buildings made of classic Cotswold stone, and snow falling gently as you cosy up alongside a crackling fire. If you managed to picture that in your head, you’ve probably accurately imagined The Lygon Arms. Standing proudly on Broadway high street – regularly named one of the prettiest high streets in the UK – The Lygon Arms offers that rare experience of a country getaway with plenty of things to do within walking distance, leaving guests to lean into slow weekends spent strolling or sipping as they wish. A former coaching inn dating back to the 1300s, guests soak up the history of the property from the minute they step inside – from the not-quite-straight stairs leading up to the rooms to the many framed maps and trinkets that point to fascinating anecdotes from the building’s many years of service, the charm of the past is inescapable. The hotel offers a surprising 86 rooms – surprising because the many winding corridors and hidden rooms hide the space of the place incredibly well. Rooms themselves vary, depending on whether you’re in the historical rooms (The King Charles I suite, for example, is where the King and his supporters once assembled, and offers a four-poster bed and coat of arms above the original fireplace, plus original paintings) or Courtyard Suites, which overlook individually landscaped gardens. Guests have plenty to indulge in during their stay – whether it’s a treatment in the spa or a dinner at the Grill hotel, with a menu from James Martin consisting of classic British fare done incredibly well. All this to say: when it comes to check-out, you might find it difficult to leave… Abigail Malbon Address: High Street, Broadway WR12 7DU Prices: From around £150 per night. - Read Full ReviewCows amble by The Pig on the way to the milking parlour, glancing over the wall at the vine-covered facade and crenellated porch of this Georgian rectory; later in the day, guests amble into their own parlours, finding an armchair that suits and peering through mullion windows at the scenes outside. In the cocktail bar – a bucolic space with green stools like grassy knolls and a flower-strewn panel taking up most of one wall – daylight streams in, illuminating the coloured glassware like a stained-glass window while a moustachioed bartender shakes the first of the day’s Martinis. In the garden outside, lovingly shaped box trees line the pathway like oversized berets, moss-coated branches twist towards the sky and Adirondack chairs recline on the lawn – even in winter, this is a garden full of interest and colour. Not all the rooms look out over Rosemary Verey’s garden but, in a sense, all are garden rooms – designed to complement the planting outside with intense floral prints that spread across wallpapers, lamp shades, cushions and bed-end benches, with hazy, green-painted walls that seem to give a burst of chlorophyll and vintage Murano flower chandeliers. This is the 10th in The Pig ‘litter’, and established principles apply: food and drink are central to its concept. In the restaurant, comfort food of the best kind – not trying to be clever but with some original flourishes and strong flavours, from the fallow pithivier and ceviche-like monkfish tail paired with white mooli to a Jerusalem artichoke risotto. The wine list has plenty to like, including several English fizzes and The Pig’s own Tuscan wines. Rick Jordan Address: Barnsley, Cirencester GL7 5EE Price: From about £220 per night - Read Full ReviewWindy country lanes, lined with chocolate-box sandstone houses, lead to teeny-tiny Clanfield – a village in the heart of the Cotswolds and home to The Double Red Duke. It’s a 17th-century coaching inn turned pub/restaurant with rooms. We arrive on a typically soggy Saturday in the midst of the English winter. Luckily, wellies and umbrellas await our arrival, but stepping through the door, it’s obvious why guests are using the weather as an excuse to stay indoors. Families cluster around the log fire wearing jumpers and muddy boots and kids play board games while sipping hot chocolate. Parents, on the other hand, have (rightly, in my opinion) chosen local pints and espresso martinis to fuel their afternoon. In summer, it’s a different story. Green vines cover the exterior, and bright purple lavender trails along the edge of the beer garden, which is filled with wooden tables and cheery, candy-striped parasols. There’s a bunch of different sized rooms to choose from depending on your crew and your (or their) preferences. All come with a deep standalone bath and a selection of deliciously smelling 100 Acres bath salts. In ours, the Marshall radio is playing classical music when we arrive. Next to it sits a jar of fresh cookies that we consume immediately. Lunch and dinner are served in one of three rooms and each has its own character. Steak cuts are scribbled on the chalkboards early doors and crossed out throughout dinner service as hotel guests and outsiders fill claim their own. We enjoyed a T-bone fireside with a bone marrow gravy mash and chunky chips. After, we don the hotel’s walking boots and amble the nearby fields, asking staff for advice on the best local walking routes. Sophie Knight Address: Bourton Rd, Clanfield, Bampton OX18 2RB Prices: From around £150 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Rectory sits in Crudwell, one of the most charming small villages in the Cotswolds.
