The Grade-I listed All Saints' Church is visible from the hotel’s gardens and well worth a visit, whether for religious reflection or a nose at 12th-century features. Alex Payne purchased this Georgian manor house in 2016, and the country folk and burnt-out Londoners soon cottoned on. 18 bedrooms split between the main property and a separate cottage offer all the trappings of a cosy Cotswolds hideout – the latter is favoured by families and groups, with direct access to the manicured gardens. Bocca di Lupo alumni Jake Simpson is in charge of the kitchens, which serve up brunch classics and continental spreads by morning and European-inspired a la carte dishes come evening. Guests who aren’t too exhausted after long days navigating the surrounding walking routes stick around a while in the bar and lounge spaces, sipping espresso margaritas beside a crackling fire and chatting – or playing Scrabble – until it’s time to sink into their goose-down bedding. This is the spot for a charming escape in one of England’s most naturally stunning settings – with a fantastic in-house restaurant and a destination pub on your doorstep. Connor Sturges Address: Crudwell, Malmesbury SN16 9EP Price: From about £170 per night. - Read Full ReviewEngland isn’t short of vast, sumptuous country estates and perfectly fetching manor houses. But Lucknam Park, Emblems Collection peeps over the rest from lofty heights. This Grade II-listed pile – creamy stone dressed with creepers tangling down its tower like Rapunzel’s hair, best glimpsed from the melodramatic beech-lined driveway – has been around since the late 17th century, and operated as a hotel under its current ownership since the end of the 1990s. Staying here is a deeply reassuring reminder that, sometimes, the classics endure for a reason. Plump four-poster beds are covered in rich floral fabrics or set against wallpaper patterned like humbugs. Original sash windows welcome in West Country sunshine that glints off chandeliers; in the cosy bar, martinis are whipped up cheerfully by informal but expert staff; and the bikes and golf carts lined up at the entrance can whizz you around the estate at the drop of a hat. These are just some of the smart touches that elevate Lucknam Park, Emblems Collection from reliably traditional to top-of-its-game. Many come here – and repeatedly – for the restaurant (executive chef Hywel Jones’s team have worked to keep the kitchen’s Michelin star for 20 years and counting). But then there’s the 111Skin facials, the gloriously steamy indoor-outdoor pools, the horse riding, clay pigeon shooting and archery. Whatever their poison, guests all appear at breakfast with the unfakeable air of those who are truly rested. There’s no other weekender in the country that does it quite like this. Sarah James Address: Lucknam Park, Chippenham SN14 8AZ Prices: From about £312 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Painswick opened to great fanfare in 2016 under the Calcot Collection banner – it’s big sister, Calcot Hotel & Spa, is about a half hour drive away in Tetbury – and soon after plaudits followed, making it one of the hottest stays in the south of England. A decade later, it has kept all the stuff that originally attracted rave reviews, and also moved with the times. Not too much though: that gorgeous, 18th-century Cotswold-stone building is still the star, sitting proudly atop a bucolic hill. A dander around the local area will pass an hour, and there are short walks to the nearby Painswick Beacon hilltop, and further along on The Cotswold Way. It is the ideal place to spend a weekend, and many, many people do: we can confirm The Painswick thrums on Saturdays, even in the depths of a dark, wet January. The hotel’s common areas are welcoming but unfussy – there's a sense that you could sit around on the sofas, saying hello to fellow guests and snacking on unctuous Scotch eggs, for an entire, unhurried day, despite the fact you’re likely only there for 48 hours. The George’s Suite is a stunner – bigger than my most recent London flat, it has a fireplace, deliciously gigantic bed, rolltop bath; all the good stuff. At sunrise, golden light pours in from the balcony which looks out onto loungers on the West Country-meets-Tuscany-style lawn. There are cookies to nibble on and a copy of Cotswolds classic Cider with Rosie to dip into while stretched out on the gigantic, comfortable sofa. The other rooms in the hotel, of which there are 16, are no less well-thought-through (even the smallest ‘Cosy’ options feature a kingsize). Radios in each provide ambient company and give the whole affair an unhurried feel. A three-bedroom cottage is also available for family stays, and pets are welcome for a small fee. Suzie McCracken Address: Kemps Lane, Painswick, Gloucestershire, GL6 6YB Price: From about £210 per night. - Read Full ReviewOriginally the village bakery, this 17th-century, red-brick pub reopened in spring 2026 after a complete renovation, as the latest addition to The Potted Goose Group. Now, four rooms and a handful of cabins are ready for booking, too – making this a great option for bedding down on a weekend away in the Cotswolds. There are just four rooms: three above the pub and one at the back, accessed via outside stairs. All are similar in style, featuring leather headboards, patterned wallpapers, velvet cushions on the bed, and blue-and-white ceramic lamps topped with Ikat-pleated shades. I stayed in room one, which has wallpaper on the vaulted ceiling (it really works) and a huge bathroom with a roll-top bath. It’s near the pub’s smaller dining room where I sat at one of the outside tables with a pot of tea and ate the homemade cookie that was waiting for me on arrival. There are also five air-conditioned cabins (including a shepherd’s hut) in a wildflower garden, each with individual outdoor seating areas and a shared firepit. Inside, the aesthetic is more neutral, from the rustic wood and white walls to the terracotta tiles in the bathrooms. For anyone interested in craft, Whichford Pottery, a two-minute walk away, is a must. The family-run company hand-throws terracotta pots for everyone from Daylesford to Kew Gardens, and an open workshop policy means you’re free to wander round and watch the makers at work. Once you're done crafting, head back to and order the bar's twist on a Paloma – it has honey at the bottom while the Eastern Standard No.2 – a take on Soho Farmhouse director Tom Kerr’s original – swaps gin for tequila and mezcal. Emma Love Address: Ascott Road, Whichford, Shipston-on-Stour, Warwickshire, CV36 5PE, England Prices: From about £195 per night. - Read Full ReviewWhen Estelle Manor stomped onto the scene in 2023, there hadn't been a Cotswolds hotel opening like it for a while. A Grade II-listed manor, it's lived many lives over the last three centuries: as a hunting lodge, a World War II maternity ward, a police training academy. In 2018, Sharan Pasricha (founder of Ennismore and the man behind hotels such as the slick Hoxton group and the recent makeover of Scottish grand dame Gleneagles) purchased the hall and set about a five-year renovation that got local tongues wagging. A tip-to-toe renovation draped layers of texture across the manor's excellent bones; 108 bedrooms and suites were dressed in sumptuous fabrics; a smattering of larger cottages and houses were added for those seeking privacy. There's also a gym, a heated-year-round outdoor swimming pool (especially magical during the festive season, when a Christmas tree sparkles at one end), and a 3,000-square-metre Roman-inspired bathhouse and spa. Estelle is part country-house hotel that anyone can book, part members club for clued-up, well-heeled country darlings. At any given time, the public spaces – wood-panelled drawing rooms, a richly textured bar with a roaring fireplace – are humming with activity from weekend-ing families or couples as well as members grabbing lunch or tapping away on laptops. There are a few member-only spaces, but most of the main house is accessible for hotel guests. The restaurants are a major draw: my sister and I grabbed small plates and Champagne in the Brasserie on arrival during our stay, although, it being a Sunday, the staff tried their hardest to suggest a roast. We restrained as we had supper booked that evening in the swish Billiards Room – and thank goodness, as the sheer amount of dim sum, bao and roast duck we consumed left us waddling back to our room. Rooms are supremely comfortable, so we fell into a sleep so deep that I felt fully rested for the first time in my 30s. This is the smart set's favourite Cotswolds hotel for a reason. Sarah James Address: Estelle Manor, Eynsham, North Leigh, Park OX29 6PN Price: From about £850 per night. - Read Full ReviewWith its tangle of honey-dipped farmhouses and tithe barns, gravel paths edged with blousy lavender and olive trees and couples playing pétanque on the immaculate lawns, Thyme – in the chocolate-box pretty, chichi Cotswolds village of Southrop – smacks of Provence. When owners Caryn and Jerry Hibbert moved to Southrop from London over two decades ago, their original plan had been to open a small cookery school with a clutch of rooms. But bit by bit, as the risk of local redevelopment loomed, they snapped up more and more buildings in the village. Today, Thyme is not just a hotel but a perfect little Cotswolds hamlet, with sustainability, a deep-seated love of the land and the idea of nature as one of life’s greatest healers right at its heart. Thyme’s 31 bedrooms are dotted around the estate, with none more than a five-minute walk away from the hotel’s main hub. Individually styled by Caryn, each one is joyously different from the next. In high summer, Thyme’s black slate spring-water swimming pool is a lovely spot to while away an afternoon. Tucked away in the gardens behind the main farmhouse, Thyme’s sage-shuttered, green-and-white-tiled Meadow Spa has been a firm fixture and major draw for some time. Lately the thing everyone’s talking about is the brand-new Botanical Bothy, an exclusive-use, deeply luxurious Hamman-like standalone space, a few footsteps away from the seven main treatment rooms. There’s also a tennis court and yoga studio, and the land around here cries out to be explored: pack your wellies and carve out time for an amble through the kitchen garden or the picturesque Cotswolds countryside. Teddy Wolstenholme Address: Thyme, Southrop, Lechlade GL7 3NX Prices: From about £390 per night. - Read Full ReviewIn the pretty little village of Charlbury, where honey-hued homes radiate a level of quaintness only the Cotswolds can achieve, sits The Bull. Phil Winser and James Gummer, the pair behind The Pelican in Notting Hill, oversaw the restoration here. The result is an impeccable interior ambience; fires are roaring, candles are burning, and plush leather chairs are ready to envelop you for a cosy afternoon. The team have kept things minimalistic and focused on bringing the history of British pubs to life with wooden-beamed ceilings, winding staircases, and perfectly preserved stone floors flowing into the bedrooms, where subtle textures and colours create a cossetting vibe. Room 6 was our home for the weekend. It's a show-stopper. A canopy bed frame with a sloped ceiling gives way to my favourite feature, the freestanding bathtub, which comes equipped with a log fire and a view of Charlbury High Street. If by some miracle you can pull yourself away from your room, I’d recommend heading downstairs for what is destined to be a delicious meal conjured up by head chef George Williams. Take the server’s advice, as everything is local, seasonal and a celebration of British produce. Top off your evening with a tipple by the fireplace for the perfect night cap to your day and weekend getaway. Amber Port Address: Sheep Street, Charlbury, Chipping Norton OX7 3RR Prices: From about £170 per night. - Read Full ReviewThis is the kind of place you check in to and simply don't want to leave. For a weekend reset and a true escape to the countryside, it's perfect, and it puts a signature Soho House spin on Cotswolds country life. The restaurant in the Main Barn is where those familiar with the other properties will feel most at home, but the accommodation here is unique its surroundings, and includes huts, cabins and even an 8-bed cottage for larger groups. The wellness offering is front and centre, and it's been amplified tenfold for 2026. Alongside the cold plunge, heated outdoor pool, Reformer Pilates classes and seriously snazzy TechnoGym, it's also home to two new fitness studios and specialist recovery treatments like Red Light Therapy and Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy. But if your idea of wellness is simply being away from the city, getting from A to by by push-bike and sinking into an armchair with a spicy margarita, there's plenty of opportunity for that, too. Sarah Leigh Bannerman Address: Great Tew, Chipping Norton OX7 4JS Prices: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewThis is one of those ‘if you know, you know’ boltholes with a loyal following of sleep-deprived parents. Calcot Manor & Spa has all the countryside charm and honey-hued good looks of a Cotswolds farmhouse, along with a sprinkling of clever details that makes it magic for families with little ones. Sitting on the bucolic fringes of antiques-heavy Tetbury, the country house hotel includes a wisteria covered farmhouse surrounded by a cluster of tastefully renovated barns and cottages. Further afield is 220 acres of idyllic rewilded countryside, home to orchid meadows, sweet little bunny rabbits and roe deer. Rooms are spread across the manor house, the surrounding cottages and the barn, with all manner of higgeldy piggeldy set ups and design – from snug cosy rooms to sprawling split-level family suites. All overflow with character-filled Cotswold loveliness – original beams, twee floral wallpaper, plush headboards and freestanding tubs. New for 2026 are The Hides – two treehouses with cosy living rooms, private decks and additional loft bedrooms ideal for children. While tinies explore the big, shiny multi-story Playbarn an Ofsted-approved crèche, weary parents make their way to the outdoor fireside hot tub at the spa. All gather together at supper, where children can enjoy a dedicated 5pm teatime before heading off to bed – the hotel's baby-monitors reach the lavender-lined and light-filled Brasserie. The chance to tuck in to elegantly plated, fresh-from-the-farm fare while off-the-clock is worth the trip in itself. Lauren Burvill Address: Calcot Manor, Gloucestershire, Tetbury GL8 8YJ Prices: From about £350 per night. How we choose the best hotels in the Cotswolds Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels. This is our edit of the best hotels in the Cotswolds.

item.title: Where the Chefs Eat: Tamar Adler's favourite restaurants in Madrid
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.66
Where the Chefs Eat asks your favourite chefs for their top restaurants in cities across the world. For this edition, we sit down for coffee with Tamar Adler. Tamar Adler is a woman of many great achievements. She is a James Beard Award-winning author, a mother, and a Vogue contributing editor. Yet, as she opens her latest publication Feast on Your Life, it is evident her battle with depression has been utterly crippling. She describes how the autumn of 2023 left her on the floor, both mentally and physically; “I’d recently taken inventory of my life,” she says. “What I’d turned up felt meagre. Somehow, my mistakes and missed chances dwarfed my accomplishments, haunting and hunting me.” This wasn’t the first time Adler had faced the demon that is depression – she has suffered it her whole life – but, from it, her latest book was born, and the result is a stunning diary of food, day-to-day life and the beauty found in the smallest of things. Feast on Your Life began as a gratitude list of sorts, suggested by her husband as part of his efforts to help her. The list was “predictable,” as she says. “Husband, son; warm bed – that sort of stuff.” And, yet, what grew was a gratitude for everything around her – the smell of coffee, “clouds of challah bread” and the “abrasive tang” of pineapples. The repetition of certain things in the kitchen, the stunning description of food – all become entries in a diary for Adler that helped her to rebuild. They bind together into a stunning book that celebrates life, and food, of course, in the most beautiful of ways. When I speak with Adler from her new home in Madrid, I ask her what it is about food that she feels really pulled her out of the grip of such a dark place. “I think it's a few things,” she muses. “I think obviously the immediacy of it is really important: it's right there, and it's unavoidable. So many of your senses are engaged in cooking and eating. You have to be completely present in it. And I think that amount of presence really does kind of remap your brain, even in tiny ways in the moment, because it sort of changes your attention, moving you from the terrible abstract to the sensory present.” And, for those who have suffered depression, even getting out of bed in the morning can feel like climbing a mountain, so the physical closeness of one’s kitchen itself also helps. “When you finish really being present,” she continues, “you actually do think a little bit differently. And, so, I think it does a really amazing job of diverting you towards a way of experiencing the world that is positive and non-abstract, and that is really grounded in the present moment. And it does it through your senses. I think because food demands so much of our senses, it's almost the perfect tool.” Adler’s book is a beautiful tribute to the smallest of acts – stirring a spoon in a cup of coffee, peeling a juicy, fresh grapefruit – and serves as a reminder that joy can be found in all things great and small. But it isn’t just for those suffering. It is a vessel for anyone seeking respite from their day, and it can be read from front to back or enjoyed in small sections. She explains that it is not only “for people in the midst of a major depression, but for those who want a kind of primer that they could turn to every day for a little bit of a reminder that there is something good and that it's right in the kitchen; that it's super close. It's not like you even have to leave your house for it. You can find it right where you are.” Today, her kitchen is in the Las Letras neighbourhood of Madrid. With her husband and nine-year-old son, Adler moved to the Spanish capital city in August 2025. “We really wanted to spend some time abroad, and my husband and I speak Spanish, so we knew we wanted it to be a Spanish-speaking country,” she tells me. “The city is so beautiful and vibrant, so it was a pretty easy decision.” She continues, “I have felt, since moving here, that my daily experience is sort of like a bath in beauty. And that's really incredible. I can't think of another place that I've been to that has so many fountains. There are fountains all over Madrid, and that is just an incredible thing, to always be in the presence of moving water; to always be hearing and seeing moving water is pretty fantastic.” Adler’s ability to appreciate beauty in all its forms, coupled with her profound knowledge of food, makes her a very reliable source for local Madrileño restaurants, and she shares with us her current five favourites. Dolores Dolores is right on the corner near my house, and we go there for one specific thing: the matrimonio (a tapas dish combining anchovies and a boqueron, which is a white pickled anchovy). The right time to do that is just before dinner. So, we tend to go at about 7pm. It’s always packed. We always get this dish wherever we go, but the best that we’ve ever had is at Dolores. What makes theirs so amazing is they make their own boquerones, so they buy their own anchovies, and then they cure them in vinegar in-house, and then when they give them to you it’s like a big beautiful fillet of the anchovy and a house-made white anchovy. They do it with parsley and, I think, garlic and you eat it on potato chips. I don’t think anyone has come to see us in town and not been taken there for that and not totally loved it. Address: Pl. de Jesús, 4, Centro, 28012 Madrid, Spain Farah A Palestinian woman called Heba Kharouf runs Farah, and she is always there. I love to get the lubina (sea bass), which comes with a tahini sauce, and another sauce – they won’t tell you what’s in that one, though it tastes a bit like mustard. It’s served as a whole fish. It’s just amazing. They also have a salad that is truly great. It’s like a chopped Middle Eastern salad with date syrup and pink peppercorns. Address: C. de los Mancebos, 2, Centro, 28005 Madrid, Spain Website: restaurantefarah.com Restaurant Sasha Enter my favourite restaurant in Madrid. The restaurant reservations open up either six or seven days in advance, but you have to book to go because it’s so popular. It’s small and it’s entirely generous. It is the most seasonal, menu-changing restaurant I have encountered in Madrid. It really is different every time. They only put a price on the menu next to the things that they have at that time. It changes dramatically based on what the kitchen sees and loves and gets in. I love the tortilla there. I think it’s called a ‘lazy’ tortilla, a tortilla vaga. Sometimes it will be made with potato chips, morcilla and pickled peppers or it might be served with a fillet of fish. The last time I got it, it was made with shrimp, finally sliced zucchini and some spring vegetables; it’s super simple but just perfectly done. The fried artichokes are also amazing. Address: Zona ajardinada, C. de Juan Hurtado de Mendoza, 11, Posterior, Chamartín, 28036 Madrid, Spain Website: restaurantesacha.com Ton Ton Ton Ton is super delicious and super chic. It’s dark and romantic and small, but it’s just very special. I love the artichoke and the beef tartare. You share lots of very small things, and it’s the perfect date restaurant or intimate diner spot. Address: Calle de Jordán, 7, Chamberí, 28010 Madrid, Spain Website: tonton.rest O’Pazo The same people who ran the renowned restaurant Desde 1911 are behind O'Pazo. It’s unreal. They cook absolutely perfect seafood; perfect in every way. I ordered everything when I visited. We had percebes (barnacles) – the kids tried that, which was really fun. We also had the pink shrimp from Palamos, which I love, along with oysters and tiny little clams. Oh, and I loved that for the main course they served a bowl of potato chips and a bowl of sprouts as the vegetable sides. You can look at all the fish behind you and just pick out what you want. Address: C. de la Reina Mercedes, 20, Tetuán, 28020 Madrid, Spain Website: opazo.es/movil Feast on Your Life by Tamar Adler (Swift Books); £18.99

item.title: 11 Lanzarote Airbnbs that will make you cancel your hotel reservation in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.64
Lanzarote, the easternmost Canary Island, has long been one of its most beloved. The undulating rugged hillsides give it an almost otherworldly feel, thanks to a mix of over 300 volcanoes that punctuate the horizons, inky lava fields, palm-filled valleys and a pretty jumble of idyllic white villages. For every golden beach, there’s another with jet black sands, and then there’s the dramatic Timanfaya National Park, and the striking La Geria wine region, where typical vineyards are usurped by alienlike vines growing in craters. But for all its eclecticism, the island maintains a calm, collected atmosphere beloved by all that return each year. This is half due to its manageable size, which can be traversed in its entirety in a weekend should you please, but also in no small part down to local artist and architect César Manrique. This influential character has stamped his mark all over the island – it's his influence we have to thank for its blissful lack of overdevelopment. Naturally, there’s no shortage of lovely hotels to check into, but the best Airbnbs in Lanzarote are also doing a sterling job of leaning into the locale’s easy charms – without the inevitable crowds drawn in high season. From bohemian cottages to rural fincas and smart apartments right on the edge of the sands, this clutch of excellent homestays offer a luxuriant simplicity in every corner of Lanzarote, for a perfect weekend slipping onto Spanish island time. Editor’s picks of the best Airbnbs in Lanzarote: - For beach access: Four-bedroom pool villa, Binibeca beach - For big groups: La Florida II, San Bartolomé - For interior design fans: El Rincon de Lanzarote, Tías - For a room with a view: Villa Lucia, Playa Blanca How we choose the best Airbnbs in Lanzarote We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. All listings featured on Condé Nast Traveller are independently selected by our editors. If you book something through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This is our pick of the best Airbnbs in Lanzarote.

item.title: Could this pretty little Georgian market town be North Yorkshire’s answer to the Cotswolds?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.40
Is Helmsley the Cotswolds in microcosm? The small market town in North Yorkshire might be small, but it has some of the characteristics: it has biscuit-toned, chocolate-box cottages, a star-studded culinary scene, an ancient castle with walled gardens, a notable Cistercian abbey and beautiful country and coastal walks nearby. The town is perfectly placed to explore the rugged Yorkshire coastline, as the starting point for The Cleveland Way National Trail and sits at the edge of the North York Moors National Park – it’s a bucolic base for a wild and wonderful weekend in the countryside. In 2024, The Good Food Guide named Helmsley and the Howardian Hills the “most exciting food destination” and the title has been retained in 2026. My mother is from Helmsley and I know how passionate locals are about high-quality homegrown produce – there are some incredible places to eat, some that still feel under-the-radar. There’s no direct train to Helmsley and I would advise travelling by car anyway, because there’s so much to see in the area: Castle Howard and the Howardian Hills are within easy reach (a 20-minute drive), the Kilburn White Horse and its high-up countryscape (a 15-minute drive), Goathland and the purple heather of the moors and the sleepy shores of Sandsend or the higgledy-piggledy streets of Robin Hood’s Bay (both around a 50-minute drive). And if you just want to relax with no big plans, do local walks, eat well and sleep well, you’re onto a winner; I always feel restored after a visit. Here are my tips for Helmsley and beyond. Our favourite things to do in Helmsley See Helmsley Castle and Helmsley Walled Garden Small but mighty Helmsley Castle and Helmsley Walled Garden are a must. Historically, it has been a medieval fortress, an Elizabethan mansion and a Georgian ruin. My tip: make a pit stop at the lovely walled garden, which was once a filming location for The Secret Garden. Grab a table at indie Vine House Café, where seasonal plates from the garden like asparagus and mint frittata are served with love – the formidable homemade cakes and freshly baked scones are things of beauty. Address: Castlegate, Helmsley, York YO62 5AB Website: english-heritage.org.uk; helmsleywalledgarden.org.uk Visit the weekly market and browse the boutiques I’d recommend wandering Helmsley’s pretty cream-stone boutiques set around the market square – do venture into the little side streets as there are some hidden gems. There’s The Helmsley Bookshop to browse, Twig & Twine, a florist and vintage homeware shop, pop into Ryeburn of Helmsley ice-cream parlour or Hunters of Helmsley delicatessen has amazing Yorkshire fare: meats, cheeses, chutneys (and pies). Go to Helmsley Market (every Friday; 8am-4pm), it’s a great place for antique finds, handcrafted gifts, flowers and local farm produce – including Yorkshire cheeses. It’s slap-bang in the centre of town and is served with a side of Yorkshire banter. Address: Market Place, Helmsley Website: yorkshire.com Explore gorgeous countryside and coastal spots Rievaulx Abbey, Kilburn White Horse and The Cleveland Way National Trail are all nearby – I’d recommend the decent (7-mile circular) walk from Helmsley to Rievaulx, especially when the woodlands are carpeted in bluebells. The Cistercian abbey (circa 1132) was the first Cistercian abbey in the north of England. Kilburn White Horse is an iconic stop, a 318ft long mare set into Sutton Bank – with inspiring patchwork views of the countryside – you can actually walk the 10 miles from Helmsley, as it is the start of The Cleveland Way National Trail, a spectacular 109-mile route cusping the coastline and moors. Stargazing in the North York Moors National Park is dreamy. Where to eat and drink in Helmsley Book ahead for a table at The Star Inn at Harome. It’s just a skip-and-a-hop from Helmsley in serene Harome, but my top recommendation for a splash-out meal. Harome is worth a look at any time as it’s an endearing place – all mushroom-topped cottages, duck ponds and country idyll but Andrew Pern’s original Star is a classic, a special place to dine. The menu pays homage to the region's natural larder with an excellent balance of seafood and meat – try the pan-roasted skri cod or herb-roasted pork tenderloin; split the date cake ice cream with salted caramel. Spy the Kilburn Mouseman furniture in the restaurant; it’s a nod to British craftsmanship. These are star-studded parts and Michelin-starred or recommended restaurants nearby include The Black Swan at Oldstead and Mýse for whip-smart tasting menus, plus a plethora of excellent country pubs such as The Abbey Inn and restaurants like Pignut & The Hare that rank highly. You will always eat well here. Where to stay in Helmsley I’d recommend visiting Helmsley for a long weekend or as part of a longer tour of the countryside or coastline – you won’t want to dash through it all. For an iconic sleepover, I would book dinner and stay at The Star at Harome (a five-minute drive), or in Hovingham (a 10-minute drive); my pick is Mýse for a two-person stay – with its cosy-cool, cream-on-cream interiors, original beams and Chapter Organics lotions and potions. For a coastal stay, I love Saltmoore in Sandsend; the hotel has a brilliant brasserie, a glossy spa and is set just near the beach – it caters so well to families. For longer stays and larger groups, Beautiful Escapes has some stylish spaces.

item.title: 9 charming family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds, approved by our parent editors and their children
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.30
There’s a reason Americans travelling to the UK repeatedly stick the Cotswolds at the very top of their Blighty bucket lists. They can’t resist the siren call of its bucolic-and-considered countryside, its honey-hued thatched cottages and pretty villages, torn out of a children’s storybook and soft with the centuries. The region’s undulating landscape, carved by oaks, preened hedges plump with wild blackberries, and postcard country lanes, hosts several boutique hotels that city folk and their broods break for, really, whenever they can. They, along with the wide-eyed American tourists, gawk at its misty hills, its rose gardens and handsome manor houses, never far from a pub whispering tales of Ye Olde England under beery breath. The key here is knowing which ones are genuinely family-friendly – aka not the Cotswold-Notting Hill rendition of rural, where muddy wellies in the house prompt shrieks of horror. No, family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds must master the art of accepting the wild unpredictability of young children, the pain points of their weary parents desperate for a break and a blast of fresh air, all while keeping things chic for those without them (or, crucially, away from them). Which is no easy feat. A few have prevailed. From spa hotels with an Ofsted-registered creche and Play Barn to honey-hued manor house hotels tempting exhausted parents with complimentary babysitting hours, here are the most family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds. Editor's picks of family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds: Best all-rounder: The Fish Best for babies and toddlers: Calcot Manor & Spa Best for families with teens: Estelle Manor Best for three generations: Lucknam Park Best kids' club: Woolley Grange Hotel How we choose the best family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. These are the best family-friendly hotels in the Cotswolds. More inspiration on where to stay in the Cotswolds

item.title: “I hope they feel good, hope they feel happy, I hope they feel safe”: remembering Dolly Parton, hotelier, traveller and Dreamer-in-Chief
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.07
Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on 19 January 1946 in Tennessee to parents Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. Dolly credited her mother with her musical abilities, which saw her sell more than 100 million records worldwide across a roster of 49 studio albums through seven decades, as Avie would keep Dolly and her many siblings entertained with stories and ballads. Dolly’s earliest public performances were in the church, and her Christian faith played a major role in her life, undoubtedly trickling into her countless philanthropic efforts over the decades. By the age of eight, she owned her own guitar, and it seems her record-breaking career was written in the stars very early on. At the time of her death this week, Dolly Parton had composed more than 3,000 songs, had 25 chart-toppers on the Billboard Country Music Charts and 44 country albums in the top 10 – a record for any country artist. Dolly put the business acumen she credited her father for into the creation of Dollywood Parks & Resorts, which Regan Stephens discussed with the icon in the interview below in 2023. A statement on the Dollywood Parks & Resorts website reads: “With heavy hearts, the Dollywood family mourns the death of our beloved Dreamer-in-Chief, Dolly Parton. Everyone at Dollywood shares the sorrow of countless people around the world touched by Dolly's warmth, wisdom and generous spirit. Dolly's heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness – a space where families and friends could honour her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams. “The greatest privilege of my life has been helping Dolly bring her dreams to life at Dollywood,” said Eugene Naughton, Dollywood Parks & Resorts President. “Dolly's heart was as vast as the mountains she cherished, and her compassion knew no bounds. She inspired generations to dream boldly and love deeply. While we grieve her loss, we are honoured and committed to carry her light forward. Her legacy will continue to shine in every melody sung, every smile shared and every dream kindled within these gates.” In a video announcement posted on 25 August 2026, Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced her death, which was later understood to have followed a brief battle with cancer. In the video, he said: “By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history. My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you. She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not… May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you.” Below is an interview originally published in November 2023, where Dolly Parton spoke with Regan Stephens about her vision for Dollywood's HeartSong Lodge & Resort, her deep connection to the Smoky Mountains, and the simple pleasures of life on the road. Dolly Parton opened HeartSong Lodge & Resort in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, a glittering rhinestone in the Dollywood Parks & Resorts empire. Set in the rolling foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains, HeartSong Lodge is an homage to the region where Parton spent her childhood – a place that continued to inspire her throughout her 50-plus-year career. The hotel is the second Dollywood resort, joining nearby DreamMore Resort & Spa, which opened in 2015. “Some people are calling me a hotelier now,” she told a crowd gathered to watch the dedication of the hotel that day. HeartSong’s design weaves in its natural surroundings in both striking and subtle ways. In the heart of the 302-room lodge, a four-story stone fireplace (made with local stones, some still covered in moss) anchors an airy atrium, which faces sweeping floor-to-ceiling windows. Fauna and flora of the region pop up throughout the common areas, too: colourful monarch butterfly-shaped trusses are built into the ceiling beams, and inside the elevators, backlit photos show scenes of the Smokies throughout the seasons. Guest rooms also draw inspiration from the Great Smoky Mountains, from the fireflies that trim the lighted bathroom mirrors and murals of bears, owls, and other woodland creatures in nature splashed on the bedroom walls to the sound machines that play a custom mix of soothing sounds – like a campfire crackling or birds singing. Many rooms have balconies that look out over the outdoor pool complex and the surrounding wooded hills. But while HeartSong is a celebration of the Smokies, guests can find plenty of nods to Parton herself, including her larger-than-life portrait hanging in the entryway, and an array of her guitars, her handwritten songs, and other personal treasures on display inside Acoustic Lobby, a private dining room on the resort’s first floor. Like DreamMore, the lodge is designed to facilitate families spending time together, with activities like Parton’s Imagination Library story time and the outdoor campfire where, each evening, guests can gather around to toast marshmallows for “roasties” (think s’mores, but with a more creative and rotating array of ingredients.) Ahead, read Parton's 2023 interview with Condé Nast Traveller about HeartSong, her go-to room service order, and more. Can you tell us about the concept behind HeartSong, and what was most important to you when it came to the hotel’s design? Well, we're proud of everything we do at Dollywood. And every year, we have huge dreams. And, of course, we were so proud when we opened our DreamMore Resort eight years ago. And people just love that and it stays booked all the time. We thought, well, we need another hotel. So what will it be? It needs to be a lodge right here in the Smoky Mountains, as deep in the hills as we can get it. And it needs to have some balconies where people can step out on the balconies and feel like they're part of nature. In the mornings, they can hear the birds and the squirrels and just go out and have their coffee or a little snack. But we felt like it would be good since I grew up in a cabin in the mountains, and kind of just more deep woods than what the DreamMore resort is. And so we just thought that would be a perfect thing, it fit my personality, it fit my childhood. And so sure enough, we are open now and we're so proud of it. What role does your own life or personal connection to the Great Smoky Mountains play in the hotel? You can see the mountains from the hotel, of course. I grew up at the foothills of the Smokies. But we wanted people to feel like they were part of the Smokies, because we know that the national park is the most beautiful and the most popular in the United States. So I've always been really proud of the fact that I was born and raised up here. And so of course I always try, when we do anything at Dollywood, to keep things close to home, things that I understand, things that are part of my childhood, part of my life. These things come natural to us when we start dreaming: What would be good next for us to do? So we're going to build more hotels. I'm not sure what all the themes will be, but this one will always be really special. Because it's more of a country life, although it's bigger. It has a huge convention center, people are going to be able to come to have conventions and even family reunions. You’ve been everywhere – how have your own travels inspired the hotel? Was there any amenity or design element you had to include? I've been all over the country, I've been all over the world, but there are those great places – like when you go to a lot of the ski resorts, places up in the mountains where they have a lot of lodges. When I would go to those places, I always felt so at home, because it reminded me of my own home in the Great Smoky Mountains, whether it be in Aspen, or any of those great places. I’ve seen similar places to our HeartSong lodge, with big hearths, where you really feel like you're really in a big country home. I'm influenced by everything, I'm like a sponge. I just soak up everything, every memory made. I can usually apply that to something else, when the occasion arises. What are your favourite hotel amenities? I think it's really important that you have a really good, comfortable bed, because I sleep so well, when I come up here, even to the DreamMore resort. And it’s real important to have a great bathroom where you have your shampoos and conditioners, and all those comforts of home. I think feeling that you have the comforts of home in a great hotel – we work real hard for that. We cater to our families as well, our bunk beds, and things for the children. Families love that. And the kids certainly do. And we incorporated that into the HeartSong lodge as well, because it was such a big hit at our DreamMore resort. So I just think, having a place that feels like home. And also, the lighting on the bathroom mirrors is so good here. Yeah, well, it is important to have good lighting and good mirrors. That's a big deal, especially to women. Do you have a go-to room service order? I am so simple. Although they have the best foods ever at all of our restaurants – we are so proud of our chefs – but I'm still one of those burger and fries kind of people. You know, when all else fails, get a cheeseburger, some French fries and a cola, and you can't go wrong. What's one memorable experience you hope guests will have during their stay at your hotel? What do you want guests to take away from a stay? I hope they feel good, hope they feel happy, I hope they feel safe. And I'm pretty sure they're going to feel petted and spoiled just a little bit- stuff they might not get when they're home. Especially a mama who's always having to do everything at home, this way, she can get to be pampered just a little bit too. So I think that it's important that they go away thinking, that was such a great vacation, and I felt special. And I know it's so important for you to have families spend time together, and there seem to be plenty of ways you can do that here at the resort. I'm big on family, you know, I grew up in a big one. And we've always tried at Dollywood to make it a family destination, from the rooms [at the resorts] to the foods, to the outside activities like the marshmallows and the campfire sings. All the things that you can have fun with your friends and family, where it really feels like you're in a safe environment, but you really feel like it could be way out somewhere in the wilderness. There's so much to see and do at the lodge here. You can just stay at the hotel and have a great time. I would love to hear about the new Dolly Parton Experience coming in 2024 – which aspect of the museum are you excited for your fans to see? I am so excited about the new museum. I had my own little museum here for many, many years, and we outgrew the space. So we had to expand. Dollywood has been growing at such a fast rate of speed over the last several years, and the museum was no different. In this new day and age, there are so many wonderful things you can do from the technical end, making things bigger and more colourful, more radiant, and really just having more of an experience for people, more of an adventure, so to speak. So we're really proud of that. They're gonna get to see and know everything that I've done since I started, even before I started: my childhood, my people, my faith, my dreams, and seeing them all come true. So they're gonna get to walk through my whole life.

item.title: My favourite Greek island villa: a clifftop fortress with an infinity pool and unbeatable sunset views
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.01
Where in the world graces the top of passionate sunset seekers’ bucket lists more than Santorini? There are few places on the planet where time stops as our star makes its descent into the distant azure, voices hush as brows furrow and cameras silently capture the moment. The jiving and jostling atop the homes, hotels and restaurants of Fira, Santorini’s capital, ahead of this performance have become as iconic as the show itself. It's a ritual I've longed to be involved in for years, and booking a villa escape to the island felt like the right way to do it. As it turned out, the villa itself was perhaps more spectacular than the skies. Beyond Santorini’s northernmost town, past the telegenic tumble of pristine white properties crowned in royal blue that climb up Oia’s cliffside, a Bond-esque lair awaited me and a group of friends. This is where we'd call home for the next few nights and it's fair to say we were wowed. On entering the property, faced with the well-equipped kitchen and a table adorned with sparkling wine and savoury and sweet welcome treats, we felt at home but after a full inspection, we realised only jetsetters who primarily reside in a clifftop fortress could use the term so freely. But we do feel at home. After our first afternoon arriving in intervals, we’re soon curled up in our preferred shaded or sun-drenched corners like the heat-exhausted felines that roam the harbours beyond, clutching glasses of fizz or orange sodas. From this moment on, just as much of our stay is spent sprawled across the villa’s outdoor spaces as its sleek interiors, if not more. Each of the villa's four king-size bedrooms has direct access to the shared terrace spaces and the interior living areas. Days begin with bouncy exits onto the terrace, iced coffees in hand (coffee pods are among the complimentary cupboard fillers). Mornings fly by into breezy afternoons, SPF liberally reapplied as fruit juices are swapped for local beers sourced from nearby stores as someone’s nominated to put on a spread. As for the spreads, it’s recommended to hire a car for a full fridge-stocking excursion. With breakfast in the nearby hotel included and all but one dinner and a few lunches planned in Oia and Fira, we made do (as a gaggle of exhausted type B travellers) by stocking up from stores nearby – Oia Mini Market is the closest, with slightly larger ones along the main road. The lush villa’s exterior space of 316 square metres includes two Jacuzzis where late-night bubbles are enjoyed once the sweltering afternoon becomes a distant memory, while the fire pit can crackle under the night sky with a little help from the concierge team. The infinity swimming pool becomes the central hub of the sun-soaked action for much of the morning and afternoon, with swimwear drying off before the collective upteenth plunge is taken and a new disc jockey sets the waterside mood for an hour via Bluetooth speakers (portable ones not provided). There’s no fear of disturbing neighbours, and the mood can be set by Spotify playlists or the distant crash of waves. Once the salty residue from the island breeze is scrubbed off in en-suite showers, plates are laid and the outdoor kitchen comes to life as we sizzle meats on the outdoor gas hob. Salads are tossed and side dishes cook in the ovens indoors as we steal moments in the golden hour light, camera timers set to capture moments in front of one of the world’s most iconic sunsets. We clink mismatched shot glasses filled to the brim with ouzo with cries of “Yamas!” into the constellations glittering above us, and commit ourselves to an investigation of Oia’s nightlife. We settle nicely into Hassapiko, sipping cocktails into the small hours while befriending the yacht crews, locals and nocturnal tourists that surround us in the moonlit courtyard. It feels sacrilegious not to take to the water beyond our infinity pool, so we secure coveted spots on one of Sunset Oia’s shared catamaran cruises one afternoon. We’re escorted to and from the boat in plush cars, but the departure from Ammoudi Port – famed for its waterside seafood restaurants – means a journey of mere minutes. Hours drift by plunging into hot springs beside the volcano, snorkelling above glistening sealife just off Red Beach and feasting on Greek specialities before we anchor, securing a new sunset vista before repeating the nights before. In addition to the complimentary return transfers, daily breakfast at Santo Pure for all guests and direct villa check-in, the attentive team are able to tailor and itinerise trips as much, or as little, as you desire. Whether it’s a knock at the door from a sommelier for private wine tastings (the island’s volcanic soil produces some impeccable tipples), yoga sessions on the terrace or in-villa spa treatments, there’d be little reason to leave the property if the island’s secrets weren’t so enticing. Our knock at the door comes not from a sommelier, but from the team as they ready us for our transfer, insisting no one lift a finger as our luggage is loaded into the back of a plush transfer car. As we wind through Santorini’s roads past vineyards and storied properties, we yearn for one more dose of the sunset view from that terrace, after an island initiation none of us will forget in a hurry.

item.title: 27 best hotels in the Caribbean for white sand beaches, top-tier hospitality and an island escape like no other
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.01
Nowhere evokes the images of white sand, turquoise water and genuinely warm hospitality like the Caribbean. There are over 7,000 islands here, but the best hotels in the Caribbean can be found on just a small clutch of them. This is the ultimate place to holiday. The sunsets seem to stretch for hours and are best enjoyed with bare feet, salty sea hair, and a rum punch in hand. When it comes to choosing where to go, it's hard to go wrong, but each spot has its own unique charm, quirks and list of beautiful places to stay. Whether you're looking for a beach hotel more akin to a luxury resort with glossy interiors in the Bahamas, or boutique boltholes run by local families in Barbados, there's something in our list of the top addresses in the region. Consider this your definitive guide to the best hotels in the Caribbean. Editor's top picks: - Best for families: The Sandpiper, Barbados - Best all-inclusive: Jumby Bay, Antigua - Best for couples: Jade Mountain, St Lucia - Best for luxury: COMO Parrot Cay, Turks & Caicos - Best affordable: Rock House Hotel, Jamaica - Best boutique stay: Cobblers Cove, Barbados - Read Full ReviewDescending a steep hillside into a 100-acre estate is a momentous entrance anywhere, let alone one stretched out between the iconic peaks of Petit and Gros Piton, after a winding journey up and up and up the mountainside. It’s worth the climb. This historic plantation-turned-playground feels entirely distinct; a classic Caribbean experience in a smart luxury outfit. In bouncy Soufrière, the resort’s 130 bright white villas gleam between the thick foliage and fan out over the hillsides until they reach Saint Lucia’s prettiest white sand beach. Between the chocolate, the cocktails, the sunsets and the salt in your hair, a stay here is a full sensory experience, which continues in the evenings as the Whistling Frogs’ calls ring out into the balmy night, echoing across the mountaintops. Charley Ward Price: From about £900 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe namesake hillside resort set above Toiny Bay gives ‘wild’ an unexpected new meaning when it comes to sceney St. Barts: On the shrubby southeastern point of the island, this unfussy haven is where an in-the-know social set head to find serenity. The star amenity here is the private beach, accessible via a three-minute Defender ride down switchbacking roads Le Toiny’s stretch of soft sand is considered the sole private hotel beach on all of St. Barts. Plus, some of the oldest traditional English-style cottages on the island, dating back to the 1700s, can be found beside the beach club (one is currently used as treatment areas for the spa). The suites and villas were redesigned in 2024 to create airy living spaces that draw your eye outward to the leafy open-air surroundings and azure water views just beyond your private pool deck. Shannon McMahon Price: From about £950 per night. - Read Full ReviewThis constellation of 30 villa suites, situated on a lush, jungle-covered hillside, features private infinity pools landscaped with pink bougainvillaea, mahogany-trimmed rooms, mosquito-netted beds, rattan ceiling fans, and wraparound terraces with sea views. Guests at the tranquil 14-and-over resort head to the palm-thatched beach bar and white-sand beach. Food at the all-inclusive is a standout (the tarragon lobster is a favourite), not to mention the daily “sunset and sushi” cocktail hour, during which guests can dine on fresh tuna, snapper, and mahi-mahi nigiri made by Nobu-trained chefs. No wonder, considering the property was purchased in 2024 by Daniel Shamoon, co-owner of Luxury Hotel Partners, which boasts Spain's Marbella Club, Puente Romano Marbella, and several Nobu hotels, including one slated to open in the coming years on Antigua's sister island, Barbuda. Adam H. Graham Price: From about £1,470 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Moroccan-style domed white villas, which encircle the place like sugar cubes, satisfy the pilgrim’s sense of arriving at a glamorous landmark conjured from the glossy magazines of her youth. But those impressions of '80s-era flash-glam are dispelled upon entering the open-air lobby, the first sign of the recent renovation which replaced the old Arabian Nights-style décor with creamy linens and natural woven-grass rugs. Just beyond is the marshmallow-white mile-long cove of Maundays Bay, lapped by the bluest water. The villa suites are relaxed: four-poster beds, seagrass armoires, twisted-abaca chairs, linen curtains that balloon when the doors open, soft Beni Ourain carpets, and cool-grey arabesque tiles underfoot, as well as enormous bathrooms that lead onto private solariums. Retreating to one’s room in the middle of the day feels like an indulgence at many places, but here the indoor-outdoor flow transforms a late-afternoon nap into a pleasure without the guilt. Each residence is just steps away from the beach, so close that putting on shoes would be foolish. The new Arawak Spa, named for the local indigenous tribe, occupies a breezy former villa with its own serenity pool, and herbal treatments inspired by the island’s first inhabitants. Alex Postman Price: From about £1,200 per night. - Read Full ReviewOn a hilltop overlooking turquoise Castle Harbour, Rosewood is the epitome of extravagance, from its whitewashed marbled corridors right on down to its powdery beach. When this swank resort first opened as Rosewood Tucker’s Point Hotel in 2009, it ushered in a new level of luxury in Bermuda. Nearly 10 years later the bar was raised yet again, thanks to a $25 million renovation of the guest rooms and public spaces. It's now got a handsome new look, a handful of newly built additions, and a bevy of resort-wide upgrades. Expect all the bells and whistles of a full-service luxury stay: A Robert Rulewich-designed, championshi-caliber golf course; several swimming pools (some for adults only, others just for children); a brand-new state-of-the-art fitness centre; a full-service Sense Spa; tennis courts; a kids' club; and a private beach that will keep you dreaming about long after checkout. David LaHuta Price: From about £600 per night. - Read Full ReviewAnguilla is a small-but-mighty island packed with a handful of luxury properties, dining options, and a wide range of of outstanding beaches. Barnes Bay and Meads Bay surround Four Seasons Resort and Residences on both sides, with waters that are occasionally rough but known to be swimmable at other times of the year. Regardless of the conditions, white beach chairs line the sand in pristine formation each morning, and three large pool areas – two family-friendly, and one adults-only – provide plenty of swimming options when the ocean is unavailable. Make sure you’re up early to reserve chairs though, either by placing an item on a chair or notifying a staff member the day before – spots fill up quickly, especially during high seasons like school holidays. Big families and young couples from the north-eastern United States make up a good chunk of the clientele, and you’ll find New Yorkers hitting the gym for yoga early in the morning; people let their guard down here, though, leaving the New York attitude back home. Families are definitely a key focus at the property, and there are plenty of unique amenities that cater to children – a noteworthy kids' club, snacks each afternoon around 3pm, and stations at select on-property dinners for colouring and crafts, run by a staff member. Additionally, there is a children’s pool near the beach with miniature cabanas for full-family enjoyment. Emily Adler Price: From about £740 per night. - Read Full ReviewThis isn’t a resort, it’s a ‘maison,’ and the grand dame of the West Indies. As the only hotel located on Flamands Bay, a protected spot (no yachts can dock here), it has the feel of a private hideaway while being a 10 minute drive from the island's party scene. Of the 60 rooms, no two are alike, and all are so capacious they’re more akin to bungalows. While some are nestled within the lush tropical garden with private terraces, some spill out onto the beach with private pools and lounges on the sand, while others are squirrelled away up the hill with spectacular views of the beach from above. Interiors are elegant yet unfussy, with the occasional bold print or texture that nods to the island aesthetic – a hallmark of legendary French designer Jacque Grange. Mornings begin with couture-perfect pastries and inventive a-la-carte options – island chakchuka – at La Cabane, where seating spills out onto the beach. At La Case, the mood is distinctly elevated, with fresh-from-the-sea Wahoo gravlax and yellowfin tuna tartare, served on tropical fish printed Dior plates (available to buy at the gift shop if you’re so inclined). On the beach there are no watersports or buzzing jetskis. Instead, experiences are private – baking lessons, rum tasting, guided hikes, yoga, plus a bijoux Guerlain Spa tucked away within the tropical gardens. Be sure to leave room in your suitcase, not just for all of the stellar bathroom products (at very least take the hair mask) and the Dior plates you'll inevitably want to buy from the gift shop, but for the generous gifts left by your butler. Lauren Burvill Price: From about £1,600 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe tiny volcanic island of Grenada is both an unexpected and obvious choice for Six Senses’ foray into the Caribbean. Compared to big-hitting neighbours like St Lucia and Antigua, it has been overlooked by travellers to the region. But this means that it remains largely uncrowded and retains a more rustic version of tourism. Six Senses has done well to anchor itself to that: here, your welcome ritual begins with a sensory spice “tour”; its 56 suites and 15 villas are stylish but designed to sit unobtrusively on the landscape; and its curated excursions – rainforest hikes; Rastafarian farm visits – spotlight the best of Grenada’s natural bounty. In classic Six Senses style, wellness is a key protagonist, and you can seek out everything from aerial yoga to sleep therapy, as well as treatments like the Caribbean Cleansing Ritual that nod to the surroundings. It’s very tempting to stay put, heading to the spa or sipping rum cocktails poolside, but you’d do well to pair off with one of the property’s community hosts and head out: to spice-laden markets in its photogenic capital or for a bit of beachside limin’ (defined locally as “kicking with friends”), a beloved national pastime. Arati Menon Price: from around £500 per night. - Read Full ReviewTravellers who want to feel like they’re summering at a friend’s beachfront estate will thoroughly appreciate the laid-back vibe of the Potlatch Club on the isle of Eleuthera. The lush property has only 11 keys on 12 acres, a seamless service team who’ve worked together for more than 20 years at other hotels, and a cluster of storied structures, some of which date back to 1923. In the 1950s, after the property was purchased by a trio of socialites, it became a private hideaway for celebrities like Paul McCartney, who honeymooned here with Linda in 1969. Current owners Bruce Loshusan and his business partner Hans Febles began work on the resort in 2016; Loshusan recruited Nassau-based interior designer Amanda Lindroth to help produce the dreamy, relaxed atmosphere that encompasses what people find enchanting about island life: white shiplap ceilings, pink coral stone floors that extend to the bathrooms, and cosy wooden porches with rattan daybeds and chairs. Alexandra Sanidad Price: from around £750 per night - Read Full ReviewFrom the moment the resort’s yacht glides into the serene waters of Yacht Harbor in Sprat Bay, the transition from passenger to prized guest is practically instantaneous. Peter Island is the largest private island in the British Virgin Islands, yet the resort has managed to capture an utterly intimate vibe. In 2017, Hurricane Irma tragically destroyed homes and upended lives throughout the Virgin Islands. The resort strives to be as sustainable as possible; it has a reverse osmosis water purification plant and two wind turbines that can generate up to 75 per cent of the island's power. And yet Peter Island still doesn't mess with what works, and leans into a familial flavour of hospitality that feels like you’re at your favourite aunt and uncle’s for the holidays. Kat Chen Price: from around £1,000 per night. - Read Full ReviewImages of the Rockhouse’s thatch-roof stone villas and bright red ladders dropping into the sea have come to represent a certain brand of Jamaican cool. The property, currently celebrating its 50th anniversary, isn’t shy about honouring its place in pop culture history: Bob Marley and the Rolling Stones once jumped off its iconic cliffs, and reggae and dancehall ephemera line the walls. Rooms are simple but still retain an essence of the sleepy 1970s Negril that originally defined the property: four-poster beds are draped with mosquito nets and decorated with locally sourced quilts; in the villa rooms, palm-fringed outdoor showers mean morning routines are accompanied by birdsong; and the cool, simple stone floors keep you feeling in tune with island life. Meanwhile, food here is a primer in Jamaican classics, especially at jerk spot Pushcart, where DJs take over the sound systems for regular dance parties. The Rockhouse crowd knows how to have a good time. Lale Arikoglu Price: from around £200 per night. - Read Full ReviewLuxury can mean different things to different people. For me it’s about privacy, freedom, and an exquisite sense of space, combined with subtle hospitality that makes you feel effortlessly at home. Jade Mountain embodies this and more. Perched high on St. Lucia’s rugged cliffs, this architectural marvel, crafted from local stone and rough concrete, rises organically from the lush forest. Designed by Canadian architect Nick Troubetzkoy, Jade Mountain frames the breathtaking views of the Pitons from each of its 24 open-air residences (known as sanctuaries). The pinnacle of luxury, Galaxy Sanctuary JE1, features uninterrupted 270-degree views and a 900-square-foot infinity pool with jewel-toned tiles. Here, serenity reigns supreme. Karin Mueller Price: from around £1,400 per night. - Read Full ReviewLocated on the southern end of the resort enclave of Cap Cana, St. Regis’s debut in the Dominican Republic is the kind of high-end resort where you're as likely to see newlyweds on their honeymoon as you are well-heeled couples or single travellers relaxing by the pool or heading out early to play few holes of golf, as well as the odd celeb or dignitary. The rooms — decorated in colours that evoke the sand and sea — have all the careful details you’d expect from the brand: smart lights that illuminate your way when they sense movement, Frette sheets and robes, full turn-down service that includes slippers by your bedside. Special ground-floor suites have swim-out areas when you don’t want to join other guests in the larger pools. Options abound for food and drink throughout the premises. Enjoy the breakfast buffet every morning at the main restaurant, Cassava, or order à la carte (make sure to get a side of mofongo). Poolside, get your cocktails from the Carey Bay Seaside Bar and savour a lunch of grilled fish and other bites at Marola (or stay in your cabana and have it brought to you). If you’re at the rooftop pool, you can dine and eat at the modern tiki bar Cielo Mio. Damian Fallon Price: From about £330 per night. - Read Full ReviewYou can become a little numb to beauty in St. Barts, but even after having been on the island for days, I think I squealed when I pulled into Eden Rock. It’s just so perfect – so chic, so glamorous, but in this easy, island-appropriate way. It’s the type of place where just being there makes you feel like the most glam, sun-kissed version of yourself. The hotel is almost entirely surrounded by calm, gin-bottle blue water that’s heavenly for a swim. There’s a diving platform a little ways out, and you can take out rafts and paddle around the point, and there’s a reef if you want to snorkel. The rooms are lovely and elegant, with a subtle Carib-meets-nautical vibe, at once bright and airy. When it comes to the food, rockstar chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten is in charge of the menu at the main restaurant, and the resort’s breakfast spread is insane in scope and quality; don’t miss it. Sure, you could have a delightful breakfast by your private pool, but the people-watching here is too good – you’d be missing an opportunity if you stayed in. It’s a pretty diverse crowd in some ways, but the common denominator, to tell it straight, is money. This place is not cheap, but it’s one of the rare hotels that is absolutely worth it. The setting is unparalleled and the food, service, and design are top of the top. There is no way you’ll go and not dream (maybe nightly) about going back – it’s that special. Rebecca Misner Price: from around £1,400 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe sand at wellness-pioneer Como Parrot Cay might be the whitest in the Caribbean, but the massages at its Shambhala Retreat are so effective that visitors may spend more time in the treatment rooms than on the beach. That’s more or less what your days will consist of— not to mention biking around the island, snorkelling, kayaking, and dawdling over long feasts. The only reason to wear a watch is to make sure you don’t miss yoga. For those who prefer their Caribbean hotels a bit more hedonistic, you can always skip the green juice and slurp a mojito at the bar, which Keith Richards has been known to frequent when he’s in residence. The Rolling Stone is just one of the island’s famous homeowners. Donna Karan has called her Balinese-inspired villa on Parrot Cay “a sanctuary where I go to create awareness.” This is a wide-open, big-hearted place that puts beach life first. Laura Itzkowitz Price: From about £1,500 per night. - Read Full ReviewStep onto the grounds of Coral Reef Club, and you would be forgiven for feeling like you’ve been transported back 50 years to a bygone era of old-school glamour. Families frolic by the ocean on chic sun loungers, while glamorous older couples are served sherries by attentive waiters in immaculately pressed uniforms. Built by the O'Haras in the 1950s (and still run by them), the family has preserved the old-world charm and culture that first won the hotel its loyal following while updating it with a luxury spa, tennis courts, two swimming pools and watersports. The 88 suites and cottages with plunge pools or wraparound balconies are intertwined among 12 acres of lush gardens, rooms merging classic Bajan style (think colourful art and cane furnishings) with English touches such as pretty verandas with wooden balustrading and old-fashioned outdoor lampshades. Breakfast is an elaborate affair with both a large buffet offering everything from Bajan fish cakes to fresh pancakes and bacon, and a made-to-order menu. Those with space left over for lunch can enjoy anything from local roti to fresh seafood (think juicy Cajun shrimp tacos and grilled fillet of mahi-mahi) to views of the crashing waves. But supper is where it really gets glamorous, where stone pillars and the most attentive waiters you may ever come across serve a classic European menu infused with Caribbean touches to the sounds of a live singer. Jessica Rach Price: From about £490 per night. - Read Full ReviewGrenada is just 26 miles long, but it packs a punch: here you will find lush rainforests, nature reserves, spice plantations, the charming town of St. George’s, and beaches so perfect that they look photoshopped. For those seeking a serene island escape, the 28-room Silversands Beach House is the place. Time seems to stop here, a feeling that begins the moment you drive up the entrance and the turquoise waters of Porto Beach come into view. The rooms and suites are so lovely – private terraces, floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the sea, calming shades of cream and light wood – that you may never want to leave, but the dreamy infinity pool and sandy beach just a few steps away make a great case for venturing out. The food at the upscale Mediterranean-inspired Azzuro restaurant is another highlight: pasta is made in-house, seafood is locally sourced, and the roasted vegetable pizza (plus addictive sorrel cocktails) is the perfect finale to a day spent on the water. There’s also plenty to experience nearby, and the staff will gladly guide you through activities, whether it’s touring the beautiful island with Garth or a rum tasting with Shanel and Lester. The vibes are unhurried, gracious, and sweet, and you’ll feel yourself slipping into island time along with everyone else. Pallavi Kumar Price: From about £630 per night. - Read Full ReviewThere are Caribbean beach resorts, and then there is Little Dix Bay, which was completely rebuilt after being decimated by hurricanes in 2017, and this year, celebrating its 60th anniversary feels more significant than ever. It’s undoubtedly got the bells and whistles – a truly transcendent spa, one of the best rum collections in the Caribbean, enviable rooms, and so forth – but what sets Little Dix Bay apart is its staff, some of whom have worked here for over 30 years. It’s the kind of place where guests at checkout will turn to their butler and ask, “Same time next year?” Todd Plummer Price: From about £1,000 per night. - Read Full ReviewIt’s easy to imagine that very little has changed at this 1950s-era resort since John F Kennedy absconded to Cottage 25 to chip away at his inaugural address and Oscar Hammerstein wrote The Sound of Music while taking in the killer ocean views. The green-striped awnings shading vast terraces and the interiors’ cream-coloured panelling offset by dark wood, along with the tea and sandwiches served at four sharp every afternoon, enhance that caught-in-time feeling. That in recent years Ralph Lauren had a major hand in the design is a delightful nonsurprise, with a playful preppiness on display at every turn, like the bar with its deep booth benches upholstered in navy and white stripes and photos of bygone guests, like Warren Beatty, covering the walls. Charlie Hobbs Price: From about £600 per night. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1970 and family-run ever since, The Sandpiper’s original charm remains, and despite being renovated (the suites are particularly modern), a thread of tradition runs through this property and nods to its history. Fifty rooms – some with their own plunge pools – span two-storey pavilion-style houses surrounded by lush vegetation. Four contemporary suites with direct beach access and ocean views sit separately in the hotel’s tropical gardens and offer modern comforts like a complimentary starter bar, White Company amenities and even a personally appointed butler. For dining, casual meals, cocktails and smoothies are served at Harold’s, the pink beach bar, while supper at The Sandpiper Restaurant is more formal. Colourful fish ponds frame the mahogany open-air dining room – there's a fine-dining menu of Bajan, African and European fusion feasts. You can also expect complimentary ice cream served daily on the beach, while the nightly turn-down service includes a beautiful ‘good night’ dish with homemade cookies and a card offering an in-room breakfast at no extra charge. Jessica Rach Price: From about £541 per night. - Read Full ReviewAs one of the world’s most desirable winter destinations, the Caribbean has an abundance of resort options based on a familiar model. These are the expansive beachfront properties with grand entries, cavernous lobbies, and ostentatious styling featuring a plethora of palm trees, pools, and piña coladas. I’m not suggesting this can’t make for a fantastic getaway – but if this is what you desire, Rock House is not for you. Located in tropical Turks and Caicos but taking its inspiration from the Mediterranean, Rock House offers guests something refreshingly different. Elegant yet subdued, this is not a resort that overwhelms; instead, it whispers in your ear and asks you to dance. Opened in 2022, the property is the newest addition to the renowned Grace Bay Resorts brand and synthesises 30 years of luxury resort expertise into a modern European-style experience that satisfies the senses and nourishes the soul. Every detail at Rock House, from the painstaking dedication to preserving the native ecology surrounding it to the in-house phone app that enables you to effortlessly communicate with the guest experience team without leaving the beach or your private infinity pool, has been thoughtfully considered. Families are welcome, but Rock House may appeal most to lovers and those seeking a truly tranquil environment to relax and recharge. Caryn B. Davis Price: From about £1,200 per night. - Read Full ReviewBermuda is generally divided into two parts, east and west, with the capital of Hamilton somewhat in the middle. Most luxury resorts reside in Hamilton or on the east end, but one historic hotel is found on the quieter west end. Cambridge Beaches recently completed a full revamp, thanks to new owners Dovetail + Co (the hospitality group behind the Urban Cowboy and Wayfinder brands). The resort’s iconic pink cottages, four bars and restaurants, two-tiered pool, and expansive grounds that include four private beaches have been brought into the 21st century – no small feat since some architectural details date back to the 1600s. The cottages are chic, with a tropical-inspired coral and seafoam green colour palette, dark wood statement beds, quirky rattan chairs, and boldly patterned textiles. Vintage-inspired pastel-coloured scalloped umbrellas and cushy lounge chairs now populate the refurbished pool area and its accompanying bar and restaurant, which also sports a magnificently detailed shell-encrusted back bar. A highlight is the brand-new Sunken Harbor Club (an outpost of the same-named Brooklyn bar), which is decorated with shipwreck treasures rescued by the late Bermudian diving legend Teddy Tucker. Bermudian-rooted cuisine is on offer, with dishes like miso cod and honey-glazed duck served alongside island cocktails. A revamp of the spa and indoor pool is planned for this year. Devorah Lev Tov Price: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewCombining eco-sensitive best practices with true luxury, this sleek eco-resort is a model for Dominica and the wider Caribbean, demonstrating that you needn’t sacrifice creature comforts to have a sustainable holiday. Coulibri Ridge was built with environmental consciousness at its core – a construction process that took the Canadian-Dominican owners a whopping 15 years (including a five-year delay after the devastating passage of Hurricane Maria in 2017) to complete. Now, what was once a colonial-era citrus plantation has been transformed into an eco-sensitive hillside retreat, which aims to be self-sufficient. The 285-acre property is completely powered by the sun via solar 225 panels and 288 recyclable non-lithium batteries; two communal pools are solar heated and kept clean not with chlorine but by using a copper ioniser to kill algae and fungus. But if you think the resort is more functional than fancy, think again. Guests are treated to modern studios, lofts, and penthouses with sweeping views of the water, tropical and bountiful breakfasts (included in the rate), and a spa with open-air treatment rooms. Caryn Davis Price: From about £800 per night. How we choose the best hotels in the Caribbean Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We're always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels. This is our pick of the best hotels in the Caribbean. item.title: What Do Sex and Gender Even Mean Now?
item.description:
Source: Conor Friedersdorf | The Atlantic Score: 4.09
