Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment. The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release. Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years. Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans. But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence. The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important. Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said. Agriculture can work without pesticides Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved. But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012. Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author. Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically. The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security. What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Tragedy in Nepal: How do flash floods happen?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.64
The disaster in the border region between China and Nepal was as sudden as it was unexpected: Within just 10 minutes, enormous volumes of water and debris swept 20 kilometers (12.5 miles) downstream on Wednesday, with devastating consequences for thousands of people in the region. Flash floods are a frequent occurrence in the Himalayas. "They are more the rule than the exception," said Niels Hovius, head of the Geomorphology Section at the GFZ Helmholtz Center for Geosciences in Potsdam. He has worked in the Himalayas and other mountainous regions for many years and is an expert on early warning systems. What triggered the flash flood? Scientific data indicate that the disaster began with a glacier collapse in the northern part of the Langtang massif, when a large amount of ice broke away and turned into a massive ice avalanche. The Langtang massif is located in central Nepal near the border with China. "This glacier collapse sent huge amounts of ice rapidly downhill," said Hovius. The heat generated by friction melted the ice into water, which then swept up debris and mud. The resulting mudflow moved downhill at speeds "reached by passenger cars on German highways." Seismological instruments recorded an earthquake measuring magnitude 4.4 at the time of the glacier collapse. However, Hovius said, it was not a "classic" or tectonic earthquake. Instead, the instruments measured the force of the falling glacier. Why can flash floods in the Himalayas be so devastating? Flash floods in high mountain regions can be triggered in different ways — by glacier collapses or by so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs, or Glacier Lake Outburst Floods). In such cases, the topography around a glacial lake suddenly changes, for example when a slope collapses into the lake. The large volume of water that suddenly spills over the lake's banks can then turn into torrents rushing downstream. In this particular case, however, it's clear that this was not a GLOF, said Hovius. Landslides can also cause deadly mudflows without any glaciers or glacial lakes being involved. In the Himalayas, all three types of events are possible, and historical data show that all three occur regularly. Compared with the Alps, the valleys of the Himalayas are relatively narrow. The water and mud cannot spread out but are instead forced into a confined space, increasing their depth and speed. In addition to the speed of the water and debris, the extent of the devastation caused by a flash flood depends on how far local populations are from the source. How can people be protected from flash floods? Nepal faces two major challenges. Many people have settled along rivers in the valleys of the Himalayas — in precisely the areas that are vulnerable to flash floods. Secondly, there are very few early warning systems in the country, which is one of the poorest in Asia. Even with a timely warning, the particularly devastating flash flood would have given people only a few minutes to reach safety. Hovius described a flood that occurred in the same region in 2025 — smaller, and therefore less severe. At the time, it took the water an hour to reach a settlement, giving people enough time to escape if they had received a timely warning. "There are initiatives in Nepal to establish local acoustic early warning systems," said Hovius. However, these systems are available only on a very limited scale. At most, they cover only 1% of areas at risk. Hovius added that mobile phones should be used to send people warnings via push notifications, and he is researching how the data needed for such a system could be generated. Checks should also be made on how settlements are planned, Hovius said. At present, the bulk of a community's infrastructure is concentrated along rivers. "People have moved down from the mountains and settled in the valleys over the past few decades. Perhaps it would make sense to move back to higher ground," he said. Are flash floods in mountainous areas more frequent amid climate change? "Attributing individual events to climate change is always difficult," Hovius said. But it's clear that glaciers in high mountain regions become less stable as temperatures rise. Larger volumes of water are also accumulating in glacial lakes, making GLOFs more likely. As for the current flash flood, it's too early to say whether climbing temperatures caused the glacier to collapse. Flash floods have long been a regular occurrence in the Himalayas. "But I think it is likely that we will see more and more of these events," Hovius said, warning that future disasters could be even more serious. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: With multilateralism in decline, what's next for the world?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.54
Donald Trump's visit to UN headquarters in New York in September 2025 was rife with symbolism. As the US president stepped onto the escalator in the lobby ahead of his address, it stopped working. Then, the teleprompter failed during his speech, prompting the former TV star to tell the assembled heads of state and government, half-jokingly: "These are the two things I got from the United Nations: A bad escalator and a bad teleprompter." The United Nations is the central institution of the post-World War II order, shaped in part by the United States and based on multilateralism and the balancing of interests. When the UN was founded in 1945, its goal was to prevent wars. Its mandate later expanded to include countless other areas, such as global health, development and climate protection. Today, more than 80 years later, the UN's institutions, above all the Security Council, are widely considered to be in need of an overhaul, much like the UN headquarters itself. The broken escalator incident was apparently triggered accidentally by Trump's own camera operator, the UN has said, rejecting responsibility for the incident. And beyond this symbolic moment, views are split over whether Trump, with his sometimes isolationist America First ideology, is above all a symptom of the crumbling multilateral world order or a destructive wrecking ball. Far beyond escalators and teleprompters, politicians and analysts around the world are debating the question: Is multilateralism coming to an end — and if so, what comes next? A new world order in five years or continued disorder? Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the few heads of state to hold a doctorate in international relations, argues that the world is currently experiencing a power vacuum from which a new world order will likely emerge over the next five years. Other experts expect a longer period of adjustment. "It is time to acknowledge that the old order really has disappeared and to plot a new approach to geopolitics. This moment does not constitute a short interregnum between a US-led order and a Chinese-led one," Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, recently wrote in an essay in Foreign Affairs magazine. "For some time, the world will be without any order at all, swept by fragmentation, contagion, and strangulation or the temptation to weaponize a wide variety of geographic, economic, and technological chokepoints." An era of reform gridlock "That framework of multilateralism, which is connected with the world after World War II [...] and a golden period of then the United Nations, I would say that it's all over," said Teresa Nogueira Pinto, a globalization expert specializing in Africa at Lusofona University in Lisbon. "It's not working," she added. "We can see that in the peacekeeping and peacebuilding missions, most of them, they have been a failure, and then we see that the UN is desperately in need of a reform." Speaking with DW, Pinto cited the UN Security Council as an example, stressing that it doesn't represent the world in 2026. "But who would join? India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Ethiopia — I mean, it's very, very hard to even imagine a reform." Johannes Thimm, head of the Americas Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, takes a different view. "I do not agree that this era is already completely over," he said. "International law is very diverse and also includes a great deal that you don't even notice in the daily relations between states, diplomatic conventions, treaties and so on. And there is still quite a lot there that you don't really notice because it isn't particularly spectacular." But he added that there is no doubt that international law has increasingly been violated in recent times, for example, through wars of aggression in Ukraine and Iran. Meanwhile, violations of international humanitarian law, as in Gaza, also pose a challenge to the multilateral order. Thimm pointed out US withdrawals from dozens of international organizations and treaties as another factor undermining the stability of multilateralism. These include the World Health Organization, the Paris climate agreement, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). Just recently, the US government further stepped up its pressure on the International Criminal Court, which it has criticized. "If the still most powerful state acts this way," Thimm said, "then that poses a threat to the system as a whole. So, I would say, a greater threat than when Russia, for example, wages a war of aggression." Old alliances fray, new ones emerge Trump frequently invokes the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, which defined the Western Hemisphere as an exclusive sphere of influence for Washington. Applied to the present day, this could mean that the rest of the world is no longer dominated by the United States but by other major and middle powers: that's to say a multipolar world order following the departure of the US as the dominant power. For many countries, this upheaval carries the risk of losing influence. For others, however, it can also be an incentive to reposition themselves and secure their place through alliances of their own in a multipolar world no longer dominated by the West. It is no coincidence, for example, that the BRICS alliance of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa has also gained in importance and taken on new members. It is increasingly seeking to establish a confident counterweight to the Western-dominated international financial architecture. "Many African countries are realizing that the previous models were not so advantageous for them, and especially for growth and sustainable growth," said Pinto. "They are taking advantage of this, and I would say also that this is very connected to the comeback of geopolitics. For a period we thought that geopolitics was history, but it's not." The world is also reorganizing itself in terms of security policy. Within NATO, there are fears of a further US withdrawal or even a military attack from within should Trump continue to pursue hi sclaims to Greenland, which is administered by Denmark. In the Indo-Pacific region, and especially in the Middle East, US allies are questioning the reliability of American security guarantees and looking for new alliances. In early August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan launched the Mecca Defense Pact, with NATO-style mutual defense guarantees. The agreement, as well as the European coalition of the willing to support Ukraine, are seen as examples of the smaller, more agile formats that are sometimes referred to as "minilateralism." In many cases, military and diplomatic efforts are being considered together. "A world without rules only helps the strong," said SWP expert Thimm. "Everyone else, whether they are moderately strong or weak, gets crushed. And that is why Europe, which I would count among the moderately strong, naturally has a strong interest in preserving some kind of order." Alongside military considerations, many states are also looking for new, broader economic and political partnerships. Pinto expects regional alliances to gain importance and potentially produce better results than mechanisms at the global level. The World Trade Organization, for example, achieved a great deal in the 20th century, she said, but has not functioned for some time now. "Now, it may be more useful to think about regional approaches such as the African Continental Free Trade Area." The harmonization of African markets is seen as a promising approach to solving many problems. But further implementation of the free trade area, ratified by almost all African states since 2018, has been rather slow. Whose interests will a future world order serve? Pinto said three factors could influence the future distribution of power in a multipolar world: sovereignty, access to resources and, last but not least, demographics. Young, growing societies in Africa and Asia could make themselves indispensable. "India could become a superpower by the end of the century," she said. Amid the decline of US influence, the growing power of other actors such as China, and other factors including minilateralism and regional alliances — it's still too early to say for sure what kind of world order will emerge from the status quo. At least in the short term, however, Thimm fears that "the world will become more violent. There will be more wars. The wars will become more brutal. It will be more difficult to organize cooperation. So I don't know what will happen when the next pandemic breaks out. I don't know what will happen when the next global financial crisis breaks out." Against this backdrop, he pointed out that we still face the climate crisis, a key challenge that can only be solved through collective action. This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Nepal flood: Death toll crosses 900, thousands still missing
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.93
The unprecedented flash flood in Nepal and Tibet has killed more than 900 people and left nearly 4,800 missing, authorities said Monday, as rescue efforts entered a sixth day. "We are working in search and rescue of the stranded people from hills, settlements and river areas," Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal's army spokesman, said. Nepalese authorities said many bodies have been recovered in southern Nepal, miles away from areas hardest hit by last Wednesday's floods. Local media reported that some victims were being buried in mass graves, sparking controversy in the predominantly Hindu country, where cremation is the customary funeral rite. What are the numbers saying? According to the latest numbers, reported by authorities in Nepal and China: - Deaths in Nepal: 903 - Total missing in Nepal: 4,247 - Citizens: 3,655
- Hydropower projects workers: 933 - Nepali army soldiers: 45 - Police personnel: 38 - Customs and immigration officers: 19 - Foreigners: 592 - Deaths in Tibet: 16 - Total missing in Tibet: 546 Multiple foreign rescue teams are assisting local authorities in reaching workers trapped in hydropower tunnels in Nepal. Officials said at least 90 people remain trapped in multiple tunnels. In India's Uttar Pradesh state, authorities recovered 17 bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal. The bodies are believed to be linked to the floods but have not been included in the official death toll pending identification. What caused the floods? Several scientists believe a glacier collapse in the Himalayas may have triggered last week's disaster, sending huge volumes of water down a river valley. The flood, carrying rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below, swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants. Edited by: Rana Taha Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Inside the sea cucumber smuggling boom
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.53
When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade. Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering. Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory — local biologist Sangamesh Uday said they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks." The 1,500 or so species of sea cucumber around the world are great marine recyclers. They eat organic material including bacteria and microalgae, break it down and excrete clean oxygenated sand. This keeps vital nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorous in circulation and suppresses coral diseases. It also boosts ocean alkalinity levels which helps to slow down acidification, which is becoming a huge issue as rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere cause oceans to warm. In short, it's hard to overstate the environmental importance of these innocuous looking lumps. Why are they being smuggled? To their detriment, sea cucumbers are also considered a delicacy, especially in China and Southeast Asia. Historical records show they were traded between Indonesian fishers and Chinese merchants even 800 years ago. They are used in soups, served as pickled sides or turned into traditional medicine. And though there is some scientific evidence that the omega-3 they contain is a useful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, they're mostly popular because they're quite phallic — and therefore considered an aphrodisiac. Since the 1980s, commercial sea cucumber harvesting has expanded globally, with better access as well as higher incomes and demand in East Asia acting as the main drivers. Though many countries have outlawed the practice, some like Sri Lanka and Madagascar do allow fishing and aquaculture. Of the existing sea cucumber fisheries, 70% have become overexploited globally. The combination of the increasing demand and legal complexities has drawn the attention of minor and major mafias. Some of the largest Mexican cartels and even the Japanese Yakuza have been reported as diversifying their portfolios by using sea cucumbers and other sea creatures to keep the money flowing. These illicit groups enter every aspect of the supply chain — from extorting fishermen to the final smuggling of illegally-caught cucumbers across borders. They exploit weak environmental regulations and a lack of official knowledge around rules and species. Sea cucumbers are sometimes marked as legal fish consignments or smuggled into countries that do allow trade in the species. Teale Phelps Bondaroff, a leading expert on sea cucumber crime, said awareness is critical in dealing with the issue. "While many law enforcement officers may be on the lookout for drugs, weapons or well-known wildlife contraband like ivory, rhino horns or shark fins, sea cucumbers may slip past," he told DW. Poachers from overseas drawn to Andaman Islands The Indian government began regulating sea cucumbers in the 1980s and introduced a blanket ban on fishing them in 2001, when it saw the impact of the illicit trade on local populations. Since then, India has become the country with the strongest protections for the species. Anyone who catches one faces a seven-year jail term — the same sentence handed down for poaching a tiger or elephant. As a result, sea cucumbers close to the Andaman Islands have generally thrived. In the ocean around Myanmar, around 50 kilometers (30 miles) further north, it's a different picture. Civil war in the country has severely impacted local livelihoods and local black-market agents are using the instability to offer comparatively higher sums for a boatload of illegally caught sea cucumbers. And as their numbers in local waters dwindle, poachers head south. It is no easy game, however. They have to dodge the Indian coast guard, navy and police, evade local fishermen and even dense populations of crocodiles. They survive on fish, freediving using hookah pipes to breathe, and spend months rationing their diesel to ensure they have enough to make it back home — evading the Myanmar authorities and pirates looking to try and steal their catch. Many poachers are caught by the regional Andaman and Nicobar police, who are being specifically trained to comb the mangrove islands to find them. At least 50 people have been arrested in the past year, some as young as 16 and some in their 60s. Several have come back for the second or third time — risking being incarcerated again after completing full sentences. Is there a way to stop the illegal trade? Despite the efforts of the Indian authorities, the number of poachers coming in, year after year, has stayed stable. Bondaroff sees a need to sound the alarm at a global level. Other similar trades, like that of shark fins, have been slowed thanks to increased awareness about its cruelty and impact on the ecosystem — making it less socially acceptable. "The solution must include educating consumers about the harms of unsustainable and illegal sea cucumber extraction and tackling seafood fraud." Other suggestions include India opening up small areas of its waters where sea cucumbers can be legally fished, or introducing community-based aquaculture that is easier to regulate and would also benefit local fishers. But Bondaroff thinks that tackling the problem also requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue. "This means liaising and information sharing between governments and law enforcement agencies," he said. "And working together to address the complex financial crimes that enable sea cucumber crime." This report was supported by the Pulitzer Center. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Court says India must uphold Pakistan water treaty
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.25
The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague has ordered India to uphold a water-sharing treaty with Pakistan which has led to a recent increase in tensions between the two neighbors. The PCA said New Delhi must "observe its obligations" under the treaty with on the sharing of the Indus and other rivers, which the Indian government this year sought to suspend. In a statement, the court found unanimously found that "none of the grounds" put forward by India were justified and "concluded that the Treaty [...] remains fully in force." The court noted that India "remains bound by the obligations incumbent upon it," particularly regarding the design and operation of "hydroelectric projects on the western rivers." It said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty. A Pakistani government spokesman said Islamabad "welcomed" the PCA order. However, India said that it categorically rejects the order of the Permanent Court of Arbitration. What is the India-Pakistan water treaty? The 1960 Indus Water Treaty governs the use of water from six rivers which originate in India but flow into Pakistan as part of the Indus basin — a resource relied on by hundreds of millions of people. The Indus river cuts through ultra-sensitive demarcation lines between India and Pakistan in Kashmir, the Himalayan territory both countries claim. India said in May 2025 that it was suspending its membership of the treaty after accusing Islamabad of backing a deadly attack on tourists on the Indian side of Kashmir. India's Water Minister CR Patil said earlier this year that the government would ensure that "not a single drop of water" will flow into Pakistan. Pakistan denies backing the Kashmir attack and has accused India of seeking to "weaponize" the precious water resource. Islamabad has previously said it would consider any attempt to change the flow of cross-border waterways as an "act of war." Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Deceived and deployed: How young Cameroonians end up fighting in Russia's war in Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.18
Cameroon has emerged as one of the leading sources of African recruits for the Russian military, with young men lured to Europe by false promises of jobs and fast-tracked Russian citizenship, only to find themselves on the front lines of the war in Ukraine. As of May this year, Ukrainian officials say that nearly 3,000 citizens from various African countries were known to have fought — or to still be fighting — for Russia : Cameroon, Ghana, Egypt, Kenya and Uganda were identified as significant. In April, the Cameroonian government confirmed that Russia had reported the deaths of 16 Cameroonian nationals, seven of whom had died in military action in Ukraine. Poverty driving youths into Russia's duplicitous schemes The actual death toll is likely higher according to DW correspondent Dorcas Ekupe, reporting from Bamenda in northwestern Cameroon. "When you look at other publications and see what is happening — even seeing families who are grieving their loved ones — the number is really much higher than what the government had earlier said," Ekupe told DW's AfricaLink program. She described two forces causing this worrying phenomenon: economic desperation and deliberate deception. Many recruits, she said, travelled to Russia believing they had secured jobs in construction or as security guards, or that they were participating in study programs. "Once in Russia, they then end up on the battlefield," Ekupe said. Russia's perceived appeal meanwhile is also being amplified by well-organized campaigns. Banjo Herman, a lecturer and political analyst at the University of Bamenda, pointed to the key role of the the Russian paramilitary Wagner Group as well as its successor, the Africa Corps, as Moscow's primary instrument for expanding its presence and reputation across Africa. Military recruitment dressed up as 'cultural' outreach Herman also cited Russian government programs such as the African Initiative and Alabuga, which present themselves as cultural or educational exchange schemes but have been linked to military recruitment. "On the surface, sometimes it looks like cultural outreach," he said. "Sometimes Cameroonians are lured, thinking it is for work, not necessarily knowing what is beneath the surfac.," He added that offers of Russian nationality within six months were a particularly powerful draw. France has previously described the African Initiative as a front administered by Russian intelligence services, designed to spread propaganda. Why young men continue to risk their lives Herman stressed, however, that the economic situation of the men was typically the main motivator. "Imagine that you are a carpenter in Cameroon who cannot even earn 100,000 CFA francs (€150; $175) a month, but somebody is promising you 3 million CFA francs to come and work," he explained. "It is very attractive." He also highlighted the fact that not all Cameroonians in Russia were the victims of deception: Some had lived there for years, had been absorbed into the military over time and were doing reasonably well. But he pointed out that it was the promise of financial reward combined with the prospect of gaining Russian citizenship that explained why even people aware of the risks continued to accept recruitment offers to fight in Ukraine. Ekupe corroborated this, noting a prevailing attitude of fatalism among some youth: "Sometimes people say, 'If I die, I die.'" Those left behind often suffer the most Families left behind, meanwhile, are forced to bear the cost in silence: Ekupe described cases in which mothers only learned of their sons' deaths years after the fact — in one instance, when a fellow soldier called home to report that a 35-year-old Cameroonian had been killed in combat. She added that many families had received no financial compensation from the Cameroonian government and that some of the men who died had left behind pregnant wives as well as children. Contact between recruits and their families is often severed abruptly, Ekupe said. "When they get there and discover it was not as promised, it is really difficult to inform their family," she added. "Sometimes they have to take time to adjust to the new environment and the situation, in which they find themselves." Russia ducking from responsibilty On the question of legal responsibility, Herman noted that international law does not, in principle, prohibit a foreign national from voluntarily enlisting in another state's armed forces. Legal liability arises, however, when recruitment involves fraud, coercion, trafficking or mercenary activity. Herman cited Article 47 of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which defines a mercenary as someone who agrees to take direct part in hostilities with private financial gain as their main motivation. Under current frameworks, the responsibility for the death of a foreign fighter in another country's war rests largely with the individual and their family, not the recruiting state. Cameroon: insufficient campaigns to fight recruitement Cameroon's government has stated publicly that it does not deploy troops abroad outside international mandates, and has warned citizens against joining foreign conflicts. Analysts have nevertheless called on the Cameroonian government, and African governments more broadly, to pursue a three-pronged response to stop more people from risking their lives in Russia. This approach would include economic reforms to create opportunities and reduce the conditions that make deceptive recruitment attractive; direct diplomatic engagement with Russia to hold recruitment networks accountable; and a public awareness campaign that issues clear, proactive public warnings to citizens about the dangers of following such schemes. Ghana has also formally raised the issue with Russia, demanding an end to the recruitment of its nationals. However, in Cameroon's case, the country's longstanding military ties with Russia, which President Paul Biya moved to renew in 2014 and 2015, could prevent a similar move. Herman said that the absence of an official Cameroonian policy response to date reflected, at least in part, the government's awareness that the recruitment is carried out by private actors — limiting the state's formal grounds and opportunities for intervention. "For the government to stop this," he said, "it has to go back to its governance policy and have a policy that is inclusive, transparent, and in which people can find opportunities within the system." This article contains material generated by artificial intelligence (AI) from the AfricaLink podcast. Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

item.title: CDU's Volkmann: Ukraine aid is not charity
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.97
At 29, Johannes Volkmann is one of the youngest members of Germany's parliament — and one of the most dedicated supporters of Ukraine. When he was head of the council of the Lahn-Dill district in the state of Hessen, he launched a municipal partnership with the Ukrainian city of Brovary near the capital Kyiv to deliver supplies to those in need. As a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Foreign Affairs and the United4Ukraine group, an international network of lawmakers, he continues to advocate for Ukraine. During his latest trip to the country, he spoke with DW about why he thinks aid to Ukraine is so important. DW: Mr. Volkmann, you were last in Ukraine exactly a year ago. What has changed since then? Johannes Volkmann: The number of airstrikes — and thus the threat to the civilian population — has increased significantly again. And at the same time, there is a sense that the Ukrainian people still want to stand their ground. I have utmost respect for that. Ukraine is demonstrating that freedom and democracy can defend themselves and fight back. That is a very important message of hope. German support is particularly important for Ukraine's defense capabilities — Germany is the largest bilateral donor to Ukraine in Europe. At the same time, political forces in Germany oppose this support. The voters of these parties share this view and consider aid to Ukraine a waste of money. What would you say to them? Everyone needs to understand that Ukraine today is not only defending itself, but also protecting Europe. Russian imperialism is not only a threat to Ukraine's borders, but also to those of our allies in the Baltic states and in Poland. That is why every euro we invest in Ukraine today is a good investment in our own security. On top of that, Ukraine is able to help us more and more in Europe by sharing its experience on the battlefield with European armies — with regard to modern technologies, drones, the training of soldiers and modern tactics. When it comes to experience, Ukraine has a tremendous lead in these areas. That is why Ukraine is now effectively a provider of security in Europe and no longer merely in need of security. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which currently leads the polls, has called for an end to German support for Ukraine. Many in Ukraine are wondering: What will happen if the AfD performs even better in the next German election and becomes part of the government? I can understand this fear. The Bundestag was elected to serve until 2029. For me personally, as well as for my parliamentary group, the CDU/CSU, it is clear that Ukraine must be supported militarily because it is in our own interest in terms of security. For me, the AfD's position on Ukraine is an important reason why my party has ruled out any cooperation with them. There is also a humanitarian responsibility: If millions of Ukrainians flee their homeland because Russia's war of aggression succeeds — and, of course, they won't want to live under Russian colonial rule — then that will destabilize our countries. That would place a much greater financial burden on us than supporting Ukrainians today in their defense of their homeland. Do you view Russia as a military threat to Europe and Germany? Some are asking: If Russia has struggled so much in Ukraine militarily, what threat can it pose to NATO? It is important to understand that Russia's hybrid attacks on Europe are not primarily aimed at military conquest but rather at achieving certain political objectives. These include the destruction of EU and NATO cohesion. So, it is entirely possible that Russia, perhaps with threats involving nuclear weapons, could attempt to occupy specific areas in the Baltic region to test the significance of NATO's Article 5 — the solidarity clause. This is why it is all the more important that we remain vigilant about this issue and develop the capacity to defend ourselves in order to deter Russia from any such aggression. We can only protect peace through our own strength; weakness will be seen as an invitation to attack. Germany was one of the countries particularly hesitant and cautious regarding Ukraine's possible accession to NATO. At the 2008 NATO summit in the Romanian capital Bucharest, it was against granting Ukraine a Membership Action Plan (MAP). Many in Ukraine believe that their country's rapid admission into NATO — or at least the granting of an MAP — could have prevented Russia's hybrid war in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. Was Germany's policy at the time a mistake? It is clear that the hypothesis put forward by the German government at the time has turned out to have been wrong — the assumption that trade, for example in gas via the Nord Stream pipeline, would create mutual dependencies and thus prevent violence from occurring. The same applies to the assumption that neutrality would protect other countries. It was a big mistake for Germany to not listen to the insights of our neighbors to the east, who, because of their own experiences with Moscow, historically have a much better understanding of what Russia actually wants. Apart from accession to NATO, many Ukrainians view membership of the European Union as the best guarantee of security. But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has ruled out Ukraine's accelerated admission to the bloc. Could Germany be making the same mistake again? NATO membership and EU membership are two very different matters. The EU is a very comprehensive community based on the rule of law. There are 35 negotiating chapters necessary for accession. To rush through the process despite Ukraine not being ready in certain areas would do neither it nor the EU any favors. At the same time — as the chancellor has also made clear — the idea is not to hold Ukraine back. It has to be clear that once certain milestones are met, the process of European integration will move forward. Ukraine is fighting to be a European country. That is why I think it goes without saying that Ukraine, too, can be a full member of the European family with free self-determination. We should do everything in our power to support Ukraine on this path. One issue many in Ukraine are concerned about is corruption and scandals — including those in President Zelenskyy's inner circle. How dangerous are such cases for the international support for Ukraine? Personally, I am very worried about this. It would be even worse if corruption scandals were not exposed. It is good when corruption cases are thoroughly investigated and there are no false compromises when dealing with them. That is why we will be closely following the verdicts and consequences that result. I can only encourage Ukrainian civil society, journalists, the public, members of parliament and the opposition to continue keeping a close eye on the situation and to ensure that Ukrainian and European funds are used properly. Today, there aren't even any serious discussions about peace negotiations with Russia. The Kremlin insists on its maximum demands, which essentially amount to Ukraine's surrender. At the same time, there are forces in Germany, such as the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), that have called for talks with Russia. Do you currently envisage any possibilities for diplomatic initiatives? There have, of course, been numerous attempts by the Ukrainian president and Western states to start peace talks. At the same time, there are no serious signs that the Kremlin has any desire for peace. Such a desire for peace will only emerge when Putin recognizes the futility of his efforts for military conquest. This requires an increase in military, financial and civil support for Ukraine. And above all, it requires a clear message that the Kremlin cannot hope that Europe will stop supporting Ukraine in 2027 or 2028. We stand with Ukraine — today and tomorrow. This interview with Johannes Volkmann was conducted by Mykola Berdnyk.

item.title: Italy extends Schengen suspension with Spain
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.84
The government of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni will extend its suspension of the Schengen free movement agreement with Spain for another 15 days at least, Italian media reported on Monday. Rome had already suspended the arrangement with Madrid for a month beginning on July 31, in response to an influx of migrants who crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta. The incident, in which dozens of migrants died, triggered a massive European Union migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism, including from Italy. What else do we know about Italy's extension? Italy's Interior Ministry said the decision to extend the suspension was taken "due to the persistence of the factors that had led to the reintroduction of the measures on Aug. 1," without clarifying. The ministry added that Italy was aware of "the steps already undertaken by Spain, together with the European Union, to help bring the situation in the area back to normal in the near future." The announcement came despite the fact that nearly all of the some 70,000 people who had broken through the barrier returned to Morocco in the days after the incident. Spain had responded to Italy's suspension by introducing its own border controls for passengers arriving from Italy and on Monday reportedly said it was extending this measure by 15 days, in an apparent tit-for-tat move. Sanchez says Ceuta incident traced to Russian, Israeli agents Socialist Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Monday that an "international far-right movement" with "links to Russia and Israel" had created a disinformation campaign on social media that led to the incident at the border fence in Ceuta. Both Rabat and Madrid had earlier said that the crisis was exacerbated by incorrect information circulating on social media regarding a recent Supreme Court ruling. "What we know so far is that a ruling by the Supreme Court of July 8 was distorted, which was spread on social networks through fake news, disinformation and also by criminal organizations that traffic in people," Sanchez told broadcaster SER on Monday. He said there had been a concerted effort "to attack and divide not only Spain but also Europe," without providing further details. Sanchez added that there was no evidence that Moroccan authorities had been responsible. Some 5,000 migrants remain in Ceuta, Sanchez said, with at least 1,200 being minors. On Friday, Spain asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing the remaining migrants, amid rising protests against their presence by residents of the exclave. Ceuta is bordered by Morocco on one side and the sea on the other, with no direct access to the mainland of the European Union, making it difficult for any asylum seekers to access the bloc from there. Edited by: Rana Taha If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Ex-Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead at 84
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.64
Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic, who was serving a life sentence for war crimes committed during Bosnia and Herzegovina's 1992-95 war has died, a United Nations official said. Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday that he died in a prison hospital in the Hague, after suffering several strokes. A family member of Mladic, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation, confirmed the reports to the Associated Press and said Mladic's son, Darko Mladic, was on the way to the Hague. The International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic of charges including crimes against humanity and genocide in 2017, handing him a life sentence. The verdict was confirmed on appeal in 2021. Commenting on Mladic's death on Thursday, United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres expressed his support for the war criminal's victims. "The secretary-general stands in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladic was found guilty," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
'The butcher of Bosnia' Mladic was held responsible for his role in the 1992 to 1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including July 1995 massacre of some 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica. The slaughter, the worst single atrocity in Europe since World War II, saw him named the "Butcher of Bosnia." Under Mladic's command, Bosnian Serb forces besieged Sarajevo and other towns, operated detention camps for non-Serbs and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners. Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al Hussein described him as "the epitome of evil" after his conviction. "This is all lies, you are all liars," he shouted when he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017. On Monday, Serbia's justice minister, Nenad Vujic, asked for Mladic to be transferred to a Belgrade military hospital, warning that his death "could come at any time." Srebrenica massacre discredited international community Born in Bosnia in 1942, Mladic was a former Yugoslav army officer who rose to command the Bosnian Serb army during the 1992-95 war. A hardline nationalist, he portrayed the conflict as a historic struggle against Ottoman rule and celebrated the 1995 capture of Srebrenica. After the capture of the city, Mladic ordered the evacuation of women, children and the elderly but said all men of fighting age are taken prisoner. In the following days more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys are systematically butchered by the Bosnian Serb forces and their bodies dumped in mass graves. In 2022 The Netherlands apologized for the Dutch peacekeepers' failure to prevent the killings. Mladic himself has never repented. Edited by: Rana Taha Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Germany news: Summer was 2nd hottest of the century — DWD
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.54
What you need to know - Average summer temperature of 19.6 Celsius is second only to 2003 figures, Germany's DWD weather service says - Cologne police investigate early-morning shooting of empty cafe in south of city center - Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Tunisia and Algeria - Hamburg's new, larger Sternbrücke rail bridge opens for business, replacing a predecessor from 1926 - Chancellor Merz warns an AfD government would damage Saxony-Anhalt, with vote on Sunday This blog is now closed. Welcome to our roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Monday, August 31. Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. Thank you for reading Thank you for reading Monday's Germany news blog. We'll be back with more in a fresh Germany blog on Tuesday. Tschüss! G20: German finance minister 'irritated' by Russian invitation German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said on Monday that he was "irritated" by the decision by the United States to invite his Russian counterpart Anton Siluanov to this week's G20 meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. Klingbeil, who as leader of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) is also Germany's vice-chancellor, said he would have preferred the Americans "not to have welcomed [Siluanov] like a normal guest" given Russia's ongoing "brutal war" against Ukraine. "There is no normal situation with Russia at the moment," he said, adding that he told Siluanov "directly to his face that the Russian government must end this war" and that Germany would continue to support Ukraine. "Receiving the Russian finance minister here sends a signal I find troubling." Ahead of the meeting, Klingbeil said he made it clear to other European colleagues that he would not pose for a group photograph with the Russian minister and that he was "grateful" that they agreed. At recent G20 meetings, which bring together 20 leading and developing industrial nations, the Russian finance minister has been represented by under-secretaries. But this time, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sat down with Siluanov for bilateral talks during which Bessent advocated for President Donald Trump's peace plan for Ukraine, according to a US official. Asked about Siluanov's attendance, a White House spokesman told the AFP news agency that the Trump administration has been working with Moscow to push for a deal that "would stop the endless bloodshed that the president has really condemned." "The president and the administration will never shy away from talking with the folks we need to talk to, to further that," he continued. "That's what we're working on here at the G20." Klingbeil said he saw "no normalization or relaxation of the situation." He said Russia alone carries responsibility for ending the war, "not Russia and Ukraine." FDP leader: AfD in Saxony-Anhalt would not be 'collapse of democracy' The leader of Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), the business-focused party which formed part of the previous federal government before falling short of the minimum 5% hurdle at the last federal election, has said he does not think an Alternative for Germany (AfD) state government in Saxony-Anhalt would be a threat to democracy. "It would be bad but not a collapse of democracy were the AfD to govern in Saxony-Anhalt," Wolfgang Kubicki told broadcaster ntv on Monday, insisting that even an AfD government would have to adhere to federal laws. If necessary, he said, the federal government in Berlin could enforce this via "Bundeszwang" — or "federal obligation" — as stipulated by article 37 of the German constitution, or Basic Law. Kubicki said this could be the case for certain aspects of the far-right AfD's election program, such as a promise to remove foreign doctors. "It's not as straightforward under the rule of law as the AfD thinks," he said. "Every court would block them immediately. Nothing to worry about." Kubicki's FDP is currently the junior partner in the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, along with the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democrats (SPD), having won 6.4% of the votes at the last state election in 2021. Ahead of Sunday's vote, however, the FDP is polling consistently below the minimum 5% hurdle and, as it stands, is unlikely to even make it into the state parliament (Landtag). Merz warns against anger experiments in Saxony-Anhalt German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned of the consequences of a far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) state government in Saxony-Anhalt, saying the eastern state "must not become an experiment for enraged citizens." Merz was speaking in the town of Quedlinburg alongside current Saxony-Anhalt state premier Sven Schulze ahead of key state elections on Sunday. Schulze is also a member of Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) but has tried to distance himself from the unpopular chancellor during the election campaign. "Should a far-right populist party have an overall majority by Monday morning, international investors will think twice about investing in Saxony-Anhalt," Merz warned, repeating comments made in an interview on Sunday. "A lot rests on this election." According to current polls, the AfD (40-42%) has a significant lead over the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt (22-23%), but Merz insisted that his conservative party would perform better than the surveys suggest. "I am absolutely convinced that we will see a different result on Sunday than what we currently have in the polls," he said. "I want to win these voters for us. And if we've lost them, I want to win them back." 'Resign!': Chancellor Merz booed on northeastern campaign trail German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was greeted with boos, insults and calls to resign while campaigning in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (MV) on Monday. While speaking at a Christian Democratic Union (CDU) campaign stand on the seafront at the coastal town of Kühlungsborn near the city of Rostock, Merz was labeled a "warmonger" and "Pinocchio" by passers-by, some of whom called for him to "resign!" Other members of the public who were listening to him speak called on the critics to remain civil. Earlier, Merz had eaten a Fischbrötchen (a fish roll, a classic coastal snack in northern Germany) at a local restaurant. The owner's son, himself a fisherman, had complained about the problems faced by the fishing industry, including restrictions and seals eating his catch. He said they were on the way to "abolishing coastal fishing in MV." Merz responded that it was important to understand the roots of the problems and also to protect fish levels. Although the afternoon had begun in sunshine, it ended under dark clouds and the sound of thunder and lightning. Later on Monday, Merz was expected in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt ahead of key regional elections on September 6. Elections back in MV will follow three weeks later. German government plays down calls for increased use of coal-fired power plants The German government has rejected calls to ramp up the use of coal-fired power stations to curb rising electricity prices. "This is not entirely straightforward for technical and economic reasons, as well as for reasons relating to European law," an Economy Ministry spokesman said on Monday. On Friday, a leading member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) had suggested making more extensive use of coal-fired plants. Sepp Müller, deputy leader of the CDU's parliamentary group, said the environmentally unfriendly facilities should remain in operation until gas-fired power stations with a comparable capacity have been built, which is expected to be in 2030 or 2031. "[We're talking about] the coal-fired plants which are currently in reserve for times when wind or solar power isn't available," he told the economics magazine Wirtschaftswoche. "These plans should operate permanently." However, the Economy Ministry spokesman questioned the effectiveness of such a measure, describing the reserve power stations as old and inefficient. "That means we would have to assess whether they could actually have a positive impact on electricity prices," he said. Federal government spokesman Stefan Kornelius put a lid on the debate, saying: "This is not a question at the moment." Trains between Essen, Bochum disrupted by cable theft Railway traffic between Essen and Bochum in the industrial Ruhr region of western Germany has been disrupted after unknown perpetrators stole several copper cables. It's the latest of several sabotage incidents to impact the country's rail network this summer. A spokesman for Deutsche Bahn said that both regional and long-distance services had faced disruptions for several hours. He said the route from Essen to Bochum was closed for security reasons as staff rushed to repair the damage. He said the damaged cables and wires needed to be repaired and reconnected by hand in several places. A spokesman for Germany's federal police, which is responsible for transport network security, said officers were investigating a "particularly severe case" of theft involving some 15 meters of copper cables. He said that for now there were no leads on potential perpetrators. Arson attacks and other acts of sabotage have disrupted the rail network over the summer, most recently when unknown perpetrators cut through several cables on a Stuttgart railway line last week. In July, trains in northern Germany were brought to a halt by a suspected arson attack, just days after a similar incident in the west of the country. Women's Bundesliga: Leverkusen's Carlotta Wamser signs for Manchester City Manchester City have signed German international defender Carlotta Wamser on a four-year contract. The English Women's Super League champions on Monday confirmed the signing. Wamser, 22, joins from Bayer Leverkusen for a reported fee of €650,000 (roughly $750,000), which would be a Bundesliga record. "The English league is the best league in the world and Manchester City are one of the best clubs in the world," Wamser said in a statement on City's website. "I feel like I need the next step for my career and I feel that I can develop as a player here very well. And I like the challenge as well, so I think it's the perfect step for me right now," she added. Wamser, who plays at right back and grew up in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, has 14 Germany caps and made her debut in the women's Bundesliga in 2020, before even turning 17. She was a regular fixture in Germany's youth teams before graduating to the seniors last year. City's director of football, Therese Sjögran, said that Wamser "is a player we've admired for some time and [we] know she will bring energy, passion and a willingness to learn to the team." Two German teammates await her in Manchester, Rebecca Knaak and Sydney Lohmann. Wamser was not in Leverkusen's squad for Sunday's Bundesliga match against Wolfsburg, which had already prompted speculation that a transfer announcement was likely imminent. August inflation rate climbs to 2.9%, driven by 10.5% energy bump linked to Iran war Germany's inflation rate rose slightly in August, reaching 2.9% year-on-year, versus 2.8% in July. That's above the national and eurozone target of 2%, if not by a particularly large margin. The increases were driven almost entirely by rising energy prices, which were 10.5% more expensive on average in August than in the same month last year. That's also a fairly sharp rise compared to July, when the energy inflation rate stood at 8.3%. Inflation for food and drink sank once again, to 0.1% year-on-year. Inflation in the services sector was close to the national average, at 2.8%. At present, the energy inflation stems in very large part from rising prices for oil and and gasoline — up by much more than the 10.5% average for the entire energy sector — amid the delivery problems in the Strait of Hormuz, not for gas and electricity. However, as the Iran war drags on and countries use up their gas reserves, this could be liable to change. Further inflationary pressure is likely in Germany in the coming months as a result of the drought and the hot summer and its impact on transportation, food production and industrial output. PROFILE — Sven Schulze, the politician leading the fight against the far-right in Saxony-Anhalt All political eyes in Germany, and indeed beyond, are turning to the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of Sunday's state election in which the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to perform strongly. But who's currently leading the coalition government in Saxony-Anhalt, Christian Democrat Sven Schulze? And what's his message on polling week, as he tries to stay in his job while facing not just the prospect of losing to radicals on the right of politics, but of perhaps needing support from those he might deem radicals on the left to avoid such a defeat? Woman confesses to pretending son had cancer to raise money A German woman on trial in Giessen, north of Frankfurt in Hesse, has confessed to pretending her young son had cancer to raise money online. Her lawyer said in court that she accepted and admitted to the allegations "without any reservation" and regretted what had happened. She's accused of obtaining a total of €358,000 (roughly $415,000 at current exchange rates) in donations between September 2021 and October 2024. The boy was aged 5 to 8 during this time period. The woman is alleged to have come up with the idea after a dermatological examination revealed an issue that turned out to be benign and require no further treatment. She then allegedly claimed that her son was suffering from malignant melanoma and urgently required expensive specialist treatment in the US, claims she also made to the media and online. Prosecutor Kai Karges said that hundreds of individuals and charities responded to the calls, and said that the child also believed he had cancer. The fraud was uncovered when the boy's pediatrician saw the calls for donations on social media and alerted child protection services. He has since been taken into care. Update: Cologne police issue details on suspect in cafe shooting, nobody hurt Just a quick follow-up on our top headline from the early morning today. Cologne police are still seeking a man believed to have fired shots at a Turkish cafe in the south of the city center. They confirmed that nobody was injured in the shooting. Police described the man as "baldheaded, roughly 1 meter 80 (5 foot 11 inches) tall," wearing "sports shoes, black trousers and a gray hooded jacket" at the time of the shooting. Investigators said residents saw the man fire the shots and flee on foot at around 7:40 a.m. that morning. "Based on preliminary investigations, four projectiles penetrated the cafe's front windows," police said, adding that Cologne's criminal investigation department or Kriminalpolizei had taken over the case. UK fuels 50% year-on-year growth in 2025 German foreign direct investment According to a report from the German Economic Institute (IW) think tank, foreign direct investment (FDI) into Germany rose markedly in 2025, reaching just over €86 billion (just under $100 billion at today's exchange rate). Investments from the UK were the largest driver of growth by far. IW put the level of FDI from the UK at more than €26.3 billion, saying it was a year-on-year increase of 284%. This made the UK the largest external contributor to projects in Germany, overtaking the US, as US investment dipped by 44% to around €11.75 billion. Investment from the other 26 EU member states remained the largest source of input, at just over €44 billion combined, with the annual figure more or less stable compared to 2024. "If you include the UK investments as well, then more than 80% of all foreign direct investments came from Europe. The numbers show: the closest and most reliable trade relations remain those with European neighbors." Investment from China, Saudi Arabia and Chile also rose markedly in 2024, but barely totaled €3 billion combined. The figures followed a below-average 2024, with the think tank saying that overall foreign direct investment had risen by 50% year-on-year. FDI figures can be quite volatile annually, depending on what's been agreed and when, with individual large deals capable of skewing the stats quite markedly. Still, 2025's total was also roughly 11% higher than the multi-year median for the period between 2015 and 2024, the IW said. Weather service: 2026 summer provisionally the 2nd hottest of the century Based on provisional data, with the meterological period only ending this Monday, 2026's summer is the second hottest of the century in Germany. Germany's DWD weather service said that its provisional average round-the-clock temperature for the season lay at 19.6 degrees Celsius (67.8 Fahrenheit). "Based on provisional calculations, only the 'summer of the century' in 2003 appears to have been hotter, at 19.7 Celsius," the DWD said. The average lies some 3.3 Celsius degree points above the reference average for the 1961-1990 period. "What was without compare in 2026 was the frequency of the heat," the DWD wrote. On average, areas in Germany experienced around 22 "hot" days — with temperatures of 30 Celsius or higher — and five very hot days with highs of at least 35 Celsius. This included the provisional German record high temperature of 41.8 Celsius, recorded in Möckern-Drewitz in Saxony-Anhalt on June 27. That same night, not far away in Kubschütz in Saxony, the mercury never dropped below 29.4 Celsius — "the highest overnight minimum temperature ever recorded in Germany." Above all, the DWD said, the summer was too dry, with around 171 liters of rainfall per square meter over the summer. This compares to historical seasonal averages of 239 to 241 liters per square meter in Germany. Unlike the astronomical summer, which ends on September 21, the DWD classifies Germany's meteorological summer as the June 1 - August 31 period. First trains cross Hamburg's new Sternbrücke bridge The new Sternbrücke bridge opened for business on Monday in the west of Hamburg, after the major rail line was closed for several weeks during the installation phase. It replaces a 100-year-old bridge connecting the Sternschanze and Altona-Altstadt districts, linking the Hamburg main station with the Hamburg-Altona station for both local and long distance rail lines in the northern port city. The first trains started crossing before dawn on Monday morning, a local service from Kiel being first in line, just ahead of an early-morning express train headed south to Basel in Switzerland. "Everything has gone according to plan here," the project manager at Deutsche Bahn, Janna Widmaier, told local public radio station NDR 90.3 on Monday morning. Some 900 trains will cross the bridge each day. The new bridge with four tracks weighs 3,700 metric tons and is considerably larger than its predecessor from 1926. The bridge was transported roughly 500 meters from its construction site to its assembly position in July, painstaking precision work that attracted quite a crowd as the vast structure sometimes passed within just a few centimeters of houses and other roadside buildings. The project had suffered a delay of roughly two weeks because of problems with the overhead electrical lines. Some of the streets below the new bridge are still closed off.

item.title: Tim Curry, of 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show,' dies at 80
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.21
Actor Tim Curry died at the age of 80, Variety, TMZ and other celebrity news outlets reported on Wednesday. A cause of death was not immediately given but Curry had been in poor health for some time following a severe stroke that left him confined to a wheelchair and wrote in his memoir "Vagabond" last year that he was still not able to walk. Curry won Laurence Olivier and Tony Award nominations for his work on stage in the UK and the US, as well delivering Emmy-winning TV performances later in his career. Who was Tim Curry? Curry was born in Cheshire into a Navy family in 1946 and spent his life bouncing around an array of different homes in the UK and even Hong Kong. He ultimately went to school in Bath, impressing as a soprano singer, and university in Birmingham. He played in London musicals in the late 60s and early 70s seeking his big break, which came in a 1973 unusual musical ultimately destined to graduate to the silver screen. Curry was given the role of the lingerie-clad sweet singing transvestite Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" in 1975. Despite the very German sounding name and initial rehearsals with a German and American accent, he ultimately played the mad scientist with an exaggerated upper class Belgravia accent, in what a Guardian newspaper 1973 review referred to as a "garishly Bowiesque performance as the ambisextrous doctor." He went on to play an array of other roles that involved elaborate costumes, unusual mannerisms, and often a fairly pronounced dark but also comedic side in his career. These included Gomez Addams in the "Addams Family Reunion" cinema reboot, Long John Silver in "Muppet Treasure Island," the suspicious Plaza Hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Pennywise the Clown in a miniseries based on Stephen King's novel "It," and even as the voice of Chancellor Palpatine in "Star Wars: The Clone Wars." In another Star Wars connection, Curry was even cast as the Joker for "Batman: The Animated Series," having been considered for the role in the 1989 film as well, until Mark Hamill supplanted him. Curry also played some of history's most consequential figures like Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, William Shakespeare, and even King Arthur — albeit in the Monty Python musical stage show "Spamalot." He was also among the first actors to branch out into video game roles, perhaps most notably as the fictional Soviet military officer Anatoly Cherdenko in Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3. He released several solo studio albums and also contributed to various soundtrack records throughout his career, with his musical background apparent in many of his acting roles. Edited by: Rana Taha If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is now on its way to study the 'dark universe'
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 6.80
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is now on its way to study the 'dark universe' Its first images are expected to arrive in early 2027. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has officially launched on its mission to explore dark matter, dark energy and other mysteries of the universe. NASA's new space telescope, which is able to image swaths of the sky 100 times larger than what Hubble could capture, launched this morning from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. The space agency confirmed shortly after launch that Roman had successfully deployed its solar panels and lower instrument sun shade. Over the coming days and weeks, the rest of its instruments will deploy and activate. Once it's all up and running, NASA says Roman will send home 1.4 terabytes of data a day. We can expect to see its first images in early 2027. "Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity's most profound questions about our cosmic history," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA's Science Mission Directorate. "With its large field of view and fast survey speeds, Roman will usher us into a new era of discovery and make the invisible visible, setting the foundation for humanity's search for life beyond our solar system." In addition to helping scientists investigate dark matter and dark energy, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will observe exoplanets and planet-forming discs. NASA says it may measure light from a billion galaxies over the duration of its mission.

item.title: How to improve your audio quality on Android Auto
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 6.19
How to improve your audio quality on Android Auto There are several things you should check. If you already have a perfectly functional cable that supports Android Auto, upgrading to a 5Gbps cable isn't going to make Spotify sound like you rebuilt the stereo. Yes, a broken or poorly built cable can lead to dropouts, disconnects and other frustrations, but additional bandwidth won't improve an intact digital audio stream. Google does recommend trying a high-quality or replacement cable when wired Android Auto is acting up, but that's basic troubleshooting, not some secret hi-fi upgrade. If you already have a stable connection, the best places to look for improvement are in the music, any processing your phone or app is doing and finally the car's audio settings. Don't blame Android Auto first -- Check the music app If your music app switches quality depending on the network, a weak cellular connection can result in poor streaming quality, and pre-downloading your favorite playlists or albums can be one of the easiest ways to eliminate this factor. Spotify's Automatic setting adjusts the streaming quality according to the connection, while YouTube Music gives Premium subscribers the ability to set a separate streaming quality level for downloads. That's worth doing if you frequently pass through areas where five bars drop to one with little notice. Next, choose a higher download-quality setting, but don't necessarily set all the numbers to the highest. Android supports playback sample rates up to 192kHz, but Google doesn't provide a universal Android Auto output rate to confirm that your car is getting 192kHz audio. Bigger numbers here don't necessarily help. You should pay more attention to your EQ and normalization settings. An earbuds-oriented profile with a bass boost can sound pretty weird in a car's completely different speaker configuration, especially if the car is adding its own bass boost, surround processing or EQ. Spotify is a great example (and sometimes an annoying one): On Android phones with a built-in equalizer, changes made through Spotify can also affect the sound of other apps. Spotify's Loud normalization setting also applies a limiter, so temporarily flatten the EQ, set normalization to Normal or turn it off and play a familiar downloaded track. Add your preferred adjustments back one at a time. It's simple troubleshooting, but it's better than changing six things and finding nothing. Use wired and wireless connections to narrow it down Wireless Android Auto uses both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, rather than simply sending music over a standard Bluetooth connection. The initial wireless setup pairs the phone and car over Bluetooth, with Wi-Fi also required for the connection. That makes going into Android's developer options to search for aptX, LDAC or some supposedly better Bluetooth codec a bad place to begin. If playback is choppy, playback stalls or sounds obviously wrong, try the same downloaded song over wired Android Auto. If it sounds good, then you've isolated the connection without touching the music itself. If wired playback fails as well, then the cable is finally a suspect. Always use a known, good cable and never use a hub or extension. What you don't need is a cable that you purchased simply because the packaging says it supports transfer speeds that your music will never even come close to using. The last place to check is the vehicle itself. Turn off bass boost, surround mode or other enhancements, flatten its EQ and compare the same track again. There is no consistent menu path because each infotainment system handles these controls differently (some seem to hide them for sport). If the problem persists, it may also be worthwhile to check whether a firmware update is available for an aftermarket receiver. Wireless Android Auto does require a compatible phone with 5GHz Wi-Fi support.

item.title: How to adjust the audio settings for your AirPods (and why you should)
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.93
How to adjust the audio settings for your AirPods (and why you should) They're pretty great out of the box, but there are tweaks you might want to know about. AirPods are perfectly functional out of the box, but you don't have to settle for their default settings if there are aspects you want to change. What you can customize depends on what model you have, so we will specify which models have the features we discuss in this post. To start with, if you're wondering why your AirPods suddenly sound different, it may be because you've accidentally switched "Listening Modes" without meaning to. How to program Listening Mode On the AirPods 4 and on AirPods Pro models, you can switch between Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency mode, which lets ambient noise in, by pressing and holding the force sensor on the stem of your left or right earbud. If you pinch the stem of your AirPods in the front and back, you'll feel it click. That's when the Listening Mode switches. This mode-switching feature is on by default, but you can change it by going to the Settings app on your iPhone, iPad or Mac computer, then into the section that says [name] AirPods or AirPods Pro. Take note that you must be using your AirPods or at least have their charging case open to be able to access this control center. In the device's settings menu, scroll down to Press and Hold AirPods, where you'll be able to customize Listening Mode for each earbud. You can choose to stick with Transparency and Noise Cancellation, but you can also select Adaptive mode, which automatically changes how much external noise you hear based on your surroundings. There's also the "Off" option, which completely turns off advanced noise control features. If you choose more than two modes, your AirPods will cycle between all of them when you press and hold the stem of your earbud. Having a quick way to change Listening Modes can be very useful if you'd rather not take your iPhone out of your bag when you're out, for instance, and would like to be able to hear your surroundings in public for safety purposes.
