The Korean tech giant described its “ThinkQ Claw” as agentic chatbot designed to comprehend the daily context you feed it, then use all that data as a means to automate certain actions, like getting your ovens prepared for incoming guests or enable your air conditioner or air purifier settings before you get home from work. How this differs from LG’s previous smart home concepts is a little more vague. However, LG says its building off its previous acquisition of AI startup Homey in 2024. If this year’s showcase is as cringe-y as it has been at previous IFAs, we’re in for even more Leave it to Beaver hilarity. —Kyle Barr Damn, I can’t believe I’m already gearing up for another one of these. The dread of trying to navigate the labyrinthine halls of the Messe Berlin convention center is ready to make me choke on a curry wurst. With that in mind, I need to carry a few extra gadgets to keep me going. So I’m keeping it classic with a MacBook Pro, better to help me when editing pictures from my Ricoh GRIIIX and newfangled GoPro Mission 1 ILS that I’m in the middle of testing. I have one of the action camera maker’s Media Mod with its attached mic alongside the company’s other Wireless Mic System. Hopefully, that camera and all its accoutrements doesn’t weigh me down. For extra juice on the go, I have a 10,000mAh Genki Energy Pack and an Anker Nano Power Bank. I have my 2TB Crucial portable SSD and my Lenovo travel dock to keep me company. And for my in-flight entertainment, there’s my Switch 2 now packing Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 that will finally give me the chance to play Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. I’ve also been jonesing to read Ursula K. LeGuin’s The Word for World is Forest. —Kyle Barr

item.title: More Evidence Emerges That Gen-Xers Feel the Most ‘Whatever’ About AI
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.47
Earlier this month, I noticed that a Pew survey hinted that Gen-X respondents might not be all that excited about AI one way or the other. Pew’s report highlighted a freaked out response among younger people, but my eye was drawn to the relative apathy on display from 50- to 64-year-olds. That survey wasn’t divided into tidy generational cohorts, but a new study from Glassdoor is, and its findings hint at the same trend as Pew: 46.1% of Gen-X workers had nice things to say about AI use in their workplaces, while millennial and Gen-Z workers spoke positively only 38.6% and 32.2% of the time respectively. The Glassdoor study was reported by Bloomberg. As was the case with Pew, whose survey measured feelings of excitement against concern, the Glassdoor findings showed that the majority of sentiment around AI was negative across all cohorts. But with nearly half speaking positively about AI, and the others speaking negatively at much more overwhelming rates, Gen-X seems to be the outlier. Instead of feeling intensely positive or negative, the data suggests they just don’t feel anything intensely about AI. “This fear that we had that the inability or the unwillingness of older workers to adopt new technologies is going to make them obsolete in the workforce just hasn’t been the case with this technology, at least not yet,” Glassdoor senior economist Chris Martin told Bloomberg. Economic analysis from Glassdoor is interesting, but is drawn from a self-selected group: people who leave Glassdoor reviews. Reviews are then picked apart by analysts and churned into data. That’s probably not the world’s most rigorous way to gather information about public opinion, but that doesn’t mean it should be completely dismissed.

item.title: How To Plan a Campervan Road Trip Across Europe
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.88
A campervan road trip offers travelers more freedom than a typical city break because they can set their own pace, stop in small towns, sleep closer to nature, and bring daily essentials. However, this kind of trip works best with proper planning. Many travelers focus only on the route and overlook practical details. Parking, campsites, toll roads, battery power, and local driving rules can affect the trip as much as the destinations. A successful campervan trip depends on a realistic route, the right vehicle, safe overnight stops, and a setup that supports daily travel needs. Choose a Route That Fits the Travel Time The first common mistake is trying to cover too much ground. Europe may look compact on a map, but driving times often take longer than expected. Mountain roads, border traffic, toll routes, ferry crossings, and city congestion can all slow the trip. Travelers should choose one region instead of crossing too many countries in a short time. A focused route gives more time outside the vehicle and less time checking maps. Good beginner-friendly route ideas include: - Northern Italy, Austria, and Slovenia - France, Belgium, and the Netherlands - Spain and Portugal - Germany, Switzerland, and Austria - Croatia and Slovenia - Scotland and northern England Decide Between Renting and Using a Personal Campervan The next choice is renting a campervan in Europe or using a personal vehicle. Renting is often easier for travelers flying into Europe or taking a shorter trip. Rental companies may provide insurance options, roadside support, kitchen gear, bedding, and basic camping equipment. Using a personal campervan works well for longer trips. The owner knows the layout, storage, driving feel, and power setup. The downside is arranging ferry transport, international insurance, breakdown cover, and vehicle documents for each country on the route. Before booking a rental, travelers should check what is included. They should not assume every campervan is fully equipped. Important items to ask about include: - Mileage limits - Insurance excess - Bedding and towels - Kitchen equipment - Camping chairs and table - Heating or air conditioning - Fridge size - Toilet and shower setup - Power outlets - Battery and charging system - Rules for cross-border travel Understand Driving Rules Before Crossing Borders Driving rules vary between European countries. Travelers do not need to memorize every rule but should check the basics before each border crossing. Important details include: - Speed limits for campervans - Toll roads and motorway vignettes - Low-emission areas - Parking rules - Headlight requirements - Winter tire rules - Required safety equipment - Wild camping restrictions Plan Campsites, Aires, and Overnight Stops A campervan gives travelers freedom, but travelers should not assume they can park anywhere overnight. Europe has many campsite options, but rules vary by country and region. Some places welcome campervans with dedicated overnight areas; others restrict parking outside official campsites. Common overnight options include: - Full-service campsites - Motorhome aires - Farm stays - Private campervan parking areas - National park campsites - Ferry port parking areas - Approved off-grid parking spots Prepare the Campervan Power Setup Power is one of the most overlooked parts of campervan travel. A campervan needs stored power for lights, phone charging, a fridge, fans, water pumps, cameras, laptops, and small cooking devices. If travelers plan to avoid serviced campsites, the battery setup is important. Before the trip, they should check how the campervan stores and charges power. Some vehicles charge their batteries from the engine while driving; others use solar panels or campsite hook-ups. Travelers should review four key areas: - Battery capacity - Charging method - Daily power use - Backup options A fridge running all day can drain power faster than expected. Cold weather also affects battery performance. Long stops without driving may limit recharging if the vehicle lacks solar charging or shore power. Travelers preparing a vehicle for longer trips can compare RV batteries that fit the campervan's voltage, battery space, charging system, and daily power needs. The best RV battery should meet all your travel needs. It should not be chosen by price alone. It must match the vehicle and travel style. A weekend camper has different needs than someone spending weeks moving between campsites, rural stops, and remote parking areas. Pack for Comfort Without Overloading the Vehicle Campervan space fills quickly. Too much gear could make every stop harder. Travelers should pack for daily use, not rare situations. They need clothes, toiletries, cooking essentials, travel documents, chargers, first-aid supplies, and weather gear. They should avoid bringing extra equipment. Useful items for a European campervan trip include: - Compact clothes for mixed weather - Lightweight rain jacket - Comfortable walking shoes - Travel towel - Reusable water bottle - Basic first aid kit - Phone mount - Charging cables - Power bank - Headlamp or small torch - Laundry bag - Quick-dry clothesline - Basic cooking supplies - Reusable food containers Budget for Fuel, Tolls, Parking, and Campsites A campervan trip can be cost-effective, but it is not always cheap. Fuel costs can be high, especially with larger vehicles. Toll roads, ferry crossings, campsites, parking, and rental insurance also add to the total cost. Common costs include: - Campervan rental - Fuel - Road tolls - Motorway vignettes - Campsite fees - Parking fees - Ferry crossings - Insurance upgrades - Gas for cooking or heating - Food and groceries - Paid attractions Keep Food and Water Planning Simple A campervan kitchen does not need to be complicated. Simple meals work best in a small space. Pasta, rice bowls, sandwiches, soups, salads, eggs, and grilled vegetables are easy to prepare with limited equipment. Travelers can shop every few days instead of carrying too much food. European towns often have bakeries, supermarkets, outdoor markets, and small grocery stores. They should learn how the vehicle's fresh water and grey water systems work before leaving the rental location. It helps to ask where to refill water and properly empty waste. Grey water and toilet waste should never be dumped in random places. Travelers must use official service points at campsites, aires, or motorhome facilities. Keep the Trip Flexible One of the best parts of campervan travel is the ability to change plans. A traveler may want to stay longer in a peaceful village, move inland because of bad weather, or take a scenic road not part of the original plan. Flexibility makes the trip feel less rushed. Extra time should be built into the route. Travelers should leave space between major stops and avoid booking every night unless traveling during peak season or visiting busy areas. A flexible plan helps travelers enjoy the trip instead of rushing through it. Final Thoughts A campervan road trip across Europe can be one of the most rewarding ways to travel. It gives travelers the freedom of the road, the comfort of carrying their own space, and the chance to visit places that are harder to reach by train or plane. The key is practical planning. Travelers should choose a realistic route, understand local driving rules, book suitable overnight stops, manage their power setup, and pack with care. This kind of trip should not be planned around distance alone. It should be planned around comfort, time, and the type of travel experience each day should provide. With that approach, the road becomes part of the trip, not just the space between destinations. This article was published in partnership with LiTime.

item.title: What Future Expats Should Know About Portugal's New Tax Regime
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.33
Contribution and legal review provided by Fresh Legal Group. Portugal has a habit of turning short trips into longer stays. You visit for the beaches, food, weather, and slower pace of life. Before long, you start wondering what it would take to make Portugal home. For anyone considering that move, another question is worth asking early: what happens to your taxes once you become a Portuguese resident? For years, Portugal was attractive to international residents because of the Non-Habitual Resident regime, better known as NHR. The old regime is no longer generally available to new arrivals. Portugal now has a different tax incentive called IFICI, or the Tax Incentive for Scientific Research and Innovation. It is sometimes referred to as NHR 2.0, but the two regimes are quite different. IFICI can deliver significant tax benefits for some people moving to Portugal. The catch is that it is much more selective. Here is what you should know before packing your bags. What Is IFICI? IFICI is a special tax regime designed to attract certain professionals, researchers, entrepreneurs, and other highly qualified workers to Portugal. The biggest difference from the old NHR regime is that moving to Portugal alone no longer makes you eligible. Your profession matters. The type of work you do matters. And, in some cases, the company or organization you work for matters too. This means two people moving to Portugal at the same time can have completely different tax situations. Who Can Qualify? As a starting point, you generally need to become a Portuguese tax resident and must not have been one in Portugal during the previous five years. You then need to qualify through one of the professional or economic activities covered by IFICI. These can include people working in scientific research, university teaching, technology, engineering and certain highly qualified professions, as well as some positions within qualifying companies and certified startups. There are several different routes into the regime, each having its own requirements. This is where IFICI becomes more complicated than it first appears. Having the right job title does not necessarily mean you qualify. Depending on the route, Portugal may also consider your qualifications, professional experience, your employer, and your employer's economic activity. Why Is Everyone Talking About the 20% Tax Rate? The headline benefit of IFICI is a special 20% Portuguese personal income tax rate on qualifying employment or self-employment income earned in Portugal. The regime can apply for up to 10 consecutive years, provided you continue to meet the relevant requirements. For a qualifying professional planning to spend several years in Portugal, that can make a considerable difference. But there is an important detail. The 20% rate does not simply apply to everything you earn. Different types and sources of income can receive different tax treatment. Someone earning a salary in Portugal, for example, can have a very different situation from someone who owns a foreign company, receives dividends, or has rental properties overseas. What If Your Income Comes from Outside Portugal? This is especially relevant for future expats with financial lives spread over different countries. Under IFICI, foreign-source income is generally exempt from Portuguese personal income tax, subject to important exceptions and specific conditions. Pension income, for example, does not benefit from the same general exemption. Special rules can also apply to income coming from jurisdictions Portugal considers to have a clearly more favorable tax regime. So, if you are planning to move while keeping investments, a business, rental properties, or other income sources abroad, it is worth understanding how each will be treated before becoming a Portuguese tax resident. What About Digital Nomads and Remote Workers? This is where there is often confusion. Living in Portugal while working remotely does not automatically make you eligible for IFICI. You might work in technology or another highly qualified profession and still not qualify under the specific rules. Your employment arrangement can matter too. Being an employee, independent contractor, company owner, or director can lead to different considerations depending on the route you use to qualify. If you plan to keep your current job and work from Lisbon, Porto, Madeira, or somewhere along the Portuguese coast, do not assume IFICI will automatically apply to you. Your Employer May Matter Too IFICI is not only about what you do. Under some routes, the company or organization you work for must also meet certain conditions. It may need to operate in an eligible sector, meet economic requirements, or hold a specific certification. That makes the basic IFICI test less about asking "Am I a software engineer?" And more about asking "What exactly do I do, who do I work for, and which IFICI route could apply to my situation?" This small distinction can completely change the answer. Don't Wait Until After the Move Tax is likely not the first thing you want to think about when planning a new life in Portugal. But it is an area where doing some homework before moving can save a lot of confusion later. Becoming a Portuguese tax resident can affect how Portugal taxes income earned in and outside Portugal. You must meet the eligibility criteria for IFICI during your first year as a Portuguese tax resident. The formal application must be submitted by January 15 of the following year for which you intend to benefit from the regime. IFICI Is Not NHR With a New Name This is probably the most important thing future expats should understand. IFICI is often called "NHR 2.0," but thinking about it as a new version of the old NHR regime can be misleading. The former NHR system was available to a much broader group of people moving to Portugal. IFICI is a targeted regime. You need to qualify for it from the moment you arrive in Portugal. There are several routes available. The key is to identify the route that makes the most sense for your circumstances and your current stage of life. Portugal is focusing the incentive on specific professions, industries, research activities, startups, and other areas it wants to attract. For the right person, the benefits can still be significant. For someone outside those categories, IFICI may offer no benefit at all. Before Making Portugal Home There are plenty of reasons to consider making Portugal more than somewhere you visit. If a temporary stay is starting to look permanent, your tax position should be factored into the planning. Before establishing Portuguese tax residency, consider where your income comes from, how you work, whether you own a business or investments abroad, and whether your professional situation could qualify for IFICI. The goal is not to let tax rules dictate where you live. It is simply to understand what your move means before you make it. Portugal may still offer an attractive tax environment for certain new residents, but the rules are now much more specific than they were during the NHR years. A little planning before the move can prevent expensive surprises once Portugal becomes home. This article is for general information only and does not constitute legal or tax advice. Individual circumstances and applicable rules should always be considered before making tax or relocation decisions. About Fresh Legal Group Fresh Legal Group advises international clients moving to, investing in, and building a life in Portugal, with support across tax, immigration, real estate, estate planning, and cross-border legal matters.

item.title: The Paperwork Nobody Warns You About: Certified Translations for Visas, Residency, and Life Abroad
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.12
Nobody starts planning a year abroad by thinking about their birth certificate. You think about flights, routes, maybe travel insurance if you're responsible. Then one day you're in a consulate waiting room in Santiago or Seoul with your working-holiday application, and the officer slides your documents back. "This needs to be translated. Officially." Just like that, your start date moves by three weeks. I've seen this scene play out more times than I can count, and it almost always catches people off guard. The travel itself is the easy part now. Border runs, SIM cards, finding an apartment through a Facebook group at 2 am-we've all figured that out. The paperwork behind long stays is where trips stall. So here's the unglamorous guide I wish someone had handed me years ago. When a Stamp in Your Passport Isn't Enough Short tourist visits rarely require any of this. The trouble starts the moment you want to stay somewhere: a working-holiday visa in Australia or Japan, a digital-nomad visa in Spain or Croatia, a student enrollment in Germany, a residency application in Portugal. Each of these asks for supporting documents, and each authority wants those documents in a language its clerks can clearly read. The usual suspects: birth certificates, university diplomas and transcripts, police clearance certificates (also called criminal record checks), marriage certificates, and sometimes bank statements or proof of income for nomad visas. If your documents were issued in English and you're applying somewhere that accepts English, lucky you. Everyone else needs official translations, and "official" is the word that trips people up. A quick note on getting them done. Many travelers try a bilingual friend or a chatbot first, but immigration offices often reject these because there is no accountability. Travelers needing professional help can use a certified translation service like Protranslate.net, which offers document translation in more than 100 languages. Before ordering, confirm that the translation and certification will satisfy the authority receiving your application. "Certified" Means Different Things in Different Countries This part confuses almost everyone, so let's slow down. For applications submitted to USCIS in the United States, a certified translation generally means a complete English translation accompanied by a signed statement confirming that the translation is accurate and that the translator is competent to do the work. Other immigration offices, universities, and government agencies may apply similar rules, but you still need to check the requirements for your particular application. Several European countries use a more formal system involving sworn or officially authorized translators. Depending on the country and the office reviewing your documents, the translator may need to appear on an approved list, use an official stamp, or have the translation certified by a notary, lawyer, consulate, or another authorized body. Spain, for example, commonly requires foreign documents used in visa and residency applications to be translated into Spanish by a sworn or otherwise officially accepted translator. Portugal allows several routes for certifying translations, and some documents in English, French, or Spanish may not require translation at all. The rules can also change depending on the type of document and the authority receiving it. The practical takeaway: never order a translation before you know which system your destination and the specific office handling your application use. Check the exact wording on the authority's website or ask the office directly. Then send those requirements to the translation provider. Ten minutes of reading can save a hundred euros of redone work. The Apostille Is Not a Translation (And Vice Versa) Second biggest source of confusion. An apostille is a separate certificate issued under the Hague Apostille Convention. It authenticates the signature or seal on a public document and the official capacity of the person who signed it. It does not translate the document or verify that everything in it is true. Many residency processes require both a document bearing an apostille from the appropriate authority in its country of origin and a translation, sometimes with the apostille page translated as well. Before beginning, confirm whether the apostille must be obtained before translation and whether the apostille page itself must be translated. The sequence varies by authority. I've seen a couple in Lisbon lose a month because their marriage-certificate translation did not reflect the apostille added afterward. It's a good reminder to get the exact instructions before starting. And on marriage: a surprising number of backpackers end up staying. You meet someone in a hostel in Medellín, and two years later you're filing marriage paperwork in Colombia. Suddenly, you may need your birth certificate apostilled and translated into Spanish, in accordance with the local authority's rules, with your parents' names spelled exactly as they appear everywhere else-which brings us to the pitfalls. Where Applications Actually Fail Names that don't match the passport. Transliteration is the silent killer for anyone with a name that changes alphabets. If your passport says "Aleksandr" and the translator writes "Alexander," a strict clerk can reject the whole file. Always send translators a scan of your passport photo page and ask them to follow it exactly. Expired police checks. Many applications require police certificates issued within a recent window-often three or six months-but the exact rule depends on the destination and visa. People request the check, wait while gathering everything else, then find it expired before the appointment. Sequence your documents: slow-moving ones (apostilles, university records) first, short-validity ones last. DIY and machine translations. Tempting, cheap, and routinely rejected when submitted without the required certification. Even if the translation is accurate, the lack of a certification statement may make it unacceptable. Some countries also bar applicants from translating their own documents, even if qualified. Wrong document version. Universities may issue several transcript formats, while civil registries offer short-form, long-form, or certified copies of the same record. An immigration office may require a version that includes details omitted from the shorter copy. Confirm the precise document type before paying to translate the wrong one. Notarization mix-ups. A notarized translation and a certified one are not the same, and a notary stamp does not improve a bad translation. Some authorities require notarization in addition to certification, while others do not. Paying for it "just in case" may be unnecessary, so check the exact wording from the receiving office. A Little Prep Before You Fly Scan everything before you leave home: birth certificate, diploma, transcripts, and marriage certificate (if you have one), all at 300 dpi and stored in the cloud. Getting a fresh copy of a birth certificate from another continent is a special kind of misery, and most translation providers work happily from clean scans. Budget time, not just money. Some straightforward certified translations can be completed in 24 to 48 hours. A sworn translation in a country with few appointed translators for your language pair may take a week or two, especially around holidays. Consulate appointment slots in busy cities can also book out weeks ahead. Work backward from your appointment date and allow extra time for every step. Keep both physical and digital copies of every translated document after the process ends. Residency renewals, tax registrations, or even opening a bank account may require some of the same paperwork, and you'll be very glad you don't have to start over. None of this is fun, exactly. But there is real satisfaction the day you walk out of an immigration office with a residence card in your pocket, knowing the boring folder of stamped, sealed, correctly spelled papers got you there. Do the dull part properly once, and the interesting parts of living abroad get a lot smoother. This article was published in partnership with Protranslate.

item.title: Why Weekend Getaways Also Need Basic Travel Protection
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.45
Weekend trips may be brief, but illness, delays, baggage problems, or an unexpected change of plans can still disrupt them. Travel insurance for weekend trips can help limit the financial impact of covered events if the policy is consistent with the destination, bookings, transportation, and planned activities. Travel Delays Can Reduce Most of the Trip A weekend getaway usually follows a tight schedule. Travelers may leave Friday evening and return Sunday night. A delayed flight, train, or connection can consume much of the vacation. Some policies may cover eligible expenses from covered delays, such as extra accommodation, meals, or alternative transport. The exact benefit depends on the reason, duration, and policy terms. Sudden Illness Can Occur During a Short Stay Health problems are not limited to long vacations. A traveler may experience food-related illness, fever, injury, or other medical concerns when away. Reaching a doctor in an unfamiliar place may require quick decisions. Basic travel protection may cover emergency medical expenses during the journey. Travelers should check the geographical scope, benefit limits, and claim procedure before departure. This is especially important when visiting places where known medical facilities are distant. Baggage Delays Can Affect the Entire Break Many people carry only a small bag for a weekend trip. Even a short baggage delay can leave them without clothes, toiletries, medicine, or other essentials. A suitable policy may provide benefits for delayed or lost checked baggage, subject to its conditions. Travelers should keep baggage tags, boarding passes, receipts, and written reports from the transportation provider, as these records may support the claim. Prepaid Bookings May Not Be Recoverable Weekend plans often include advance payments for hotels, transportation, guided activities, or local experiences. When illness, a family emergency, or another covered event prevents travel, some bookings may not be refundable. Trip cancellation benefits may help with eligible prepaid expenses when the reason meets policy conditions. Travelers should read the approved reasons carefully and understand the required documents and notification timeline. Road Journeys Can Face Unforeseen Interruptions Not every weekend getaway involves air travel. Many travelers drive to nearby hill stations, beaches, heritage towns, or nature destinations. Road closures, poor weather, vehicle trouble, or an accident can interrupt the journey. Travelers should consider the complete itinerary, including transportation and planned activities. Coverage for delays, accidents, or emergency assistance depends on the policy, whereas ordinary vehicle breakdowns may require separate roadside assistance coverage. Short Trips Often Have Fixed Budgets Weekend breaks are usually planned within a set budget. An unplanned hotel stay, replacement ticket, or medical bill may affect the entire spending plan. The best travel insurance for a weekend journey isn't necessarily the policy with the longest list of benefits. It is the one that fits the destination, booking value, transport arrangements, and travelers' likely needs. Adventure Activities May Need Extra Attention A brief getaway may include trekking, cycling, water sports, or other outdoor activities. These plans can change the type of protection required. Travelers should check whether the selected activity is included and whether additional conditions apply. The activity provider's safety instructions should be followed. Insurance may offer financial support for covered situations but does not replace careful planning. Assistance Can Help in an Unfamiliar Place An unexpected situation becomes harder to manage when the traveler is unfamiliar with the local area. Finding a nearby hospital, arranging transport, or understanding the next step in a claim may take time. Some policies provide access to assistance services during the insured trip. Keeping the policy number, emergency contact details, and digital documents on the phone can make communication easier when help is needed. Quick access to this information also reduces uncertainty during an urgent situation. Before departure, keep digital and printed copies of your policy and other essential travel insurance documents. Final Thoughts Weekend getaways may be short, but they still involve bookings, transport, health concerns, and personal belongings. A minor disruption can affect a major part of the trip because there is little time to adjust the schedule. Basic travel protection can provide financial support for covered emergencies and travel-related problems. Travelers should review the benefits, limits, documentation requirements, and policy conditions before departure to ensure the selected cover suits the actual journey. This article was published in partnership with HDFC ERGO General Insurance Company Limited.

item.title: What Is a Dahabiya Cruise? A More Authentic Way to Sail the Nile
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 2.88
Most travelers come to Egypt to see the pyramids, temples, tombs, and monuments, but did you know the Nile also flows through Egypt? The Nile, which spans about 4,132 miles (6,650 kilometers), is traditionally regarded as the longest river in the world and serves as the lifeblood of Egyptian civilization. Any trip to Egypt, to gain a better understanding of Pharaonic history, would be incomplete without a sail on the Nile. For thousands of years, the Nile has influenced Egyptian agriculture, settlement locations, transportation, food, and everyday life, and a cruise on the river offers visitors the opportunity to see the country from the water. The vessel you take has a bearing on your experience; large cruise ships are good at linking up the main destinations, whereas a Dahabiya affords a more intimate and leisurely association with the river. A dahabiya is a traditional sailing vessel with two masts that has been linked to leisure travel along the Nile in Egypt since the 19th century, and it can offer travelers a more intimate and quieter alternative to taking a large cruise ship by giving them a nearer connection to the scenery and sailing traditions of the Nile. The slow pace of the journey makes it an important element of the Egyptian experience, and the sections that follow outline what sets a dahabiya cruise apart and what to consider when selecting one. A Dahabiya Brings Back the Feeling of Sailing the Nile The Dahabiya are modern sailing ships on the Nile that have been designed in accordance with ancient golden boats; their notable characteristic is that they have two triangular sails, which give a different sensation from traveling on a large motorized ship. The boat's movement is now obvious rather than just background noise, and the wind, the water, the sails, and the changing view of the river all become part of the experience. Swan Dahabiya is a boutique Nile cruise operator that combines traditional sailing qualities with modern amenities. The fact that something is authentic doesn't imply that it is necessary to reproduce historical travel precisely; rather, it means that travelers should be able to experience the river in a manner that represents its long tradition of sailing. Let's take a closer look at how a Dahabiya Nile cruise from Aswan to Luxor is different and why you should include it in your Egyptian vacation itinerary. | Features | What It Means for Travelers | | What is a Dahabiya? | A traditional-style Nile sailing vessel, redesigned today with modern accommodation and comforts. | | Passenger Capacity | Ideally, the passenger capacity of a Dahabiya is less than that of large cruises; it's around only 8-20 passengers. | | Best Suited For | Couples, families, small groups, honeymooners, photographers, food lovers, and travelers who prefer a quieter cultural journey. | | Itinerary Style | Dahabiya sails on the famous route between Luxor and Aswan; with Swan Dahabiya, you can get 4, 5, or 8-day itineraries. | | Onboard Atmosphere | More private and relaxed, with fewer passengers sharing dining and outdoor spaces. | | Accommodation | Cabins are designed for comfort and privacy, giving travelers a quieter place to rest between sightseeing and sailing. | | Deck Experience | Open decks provide space to sit back, enjoy panoramic views, watch the riverbanks, dine, and experience the changing landscape while sailing. | | Best For | Travelers who value time, privacy, flexibility, and connection with the river over extensive onboard facilities and entertainment. | The Nile Has Two Landscapes-and a Dahabiya Gives You Time to Notice Both The Cultivated Nile While sailing on a Dahabiya, from the deck in a calm atmosphere, you will find yourself exploring green agricultural fields which appear right away alongside the river; date palms and crops form a narrow zone of fertility, showing how the legendary River Nile contributes to the landscape. You will also see farmers working the fields, which rely on the river for irrigation, as well as cultivated areas and villages situated where the fertile strip meets the desert. Sailing on a Dahabiya is better because most large cruise ships travel at a constant speed and have more crowded decks; the small Nile boat, on the other hand, has quiet, shaded decks and moves more slowly, which allows you to get a closer sense of nature and makes the experience soulful and satisfying. Many travelers also favor the Dahabiya for its more intimate way of sailing, a feature that is frequently missing on large cruises. Busy Historic Stops Along the Nile As you sail along the river, you will see the scenery change from peaceful river scenes to busy shores. At that point, you stop to visit historical monuments that recount the rich lives of the Egyptian pharaohs and their religious beliefs. The sites most commonly visited are these. The Edfu Temple is an ancient Egyptian temple on the west bank of the Nile in the town of Edfu, frequently visited by tourists on Nile cruises. It is a well-preserved shrine devoted to the ancient Egyptian god Horus, constructed during the Ptolemaic Kingdom (the Graeco-Roman period), and its carvings depict Egyptian religious beliefs as well as the falcon-headed god. Kom Ombo: It is an unusual double temple in Upper Egypt, consisting of sanctuaries devoted to Sobek, the god with a crocodile's head, and Horus the Elder, the god with a falcon's head; the views of the landscape are worth taking in, and the site is one of the most interesting monuments on the Nile. At Aswan, you may choose to end your trip on a Dahabiya voyage from here, and you can visit the Aswan High Dam, the incomplete obelisk, and the magnificent Philae temple, which is dedicated to the goddess Isis. Luxor is ancient Thebes, usually referred to as the world's largest open-air architectural museum, consisting of the Luxor Temple, the Karnak Temple complex, the Valley of Kings, the Temple of Hatshepsut and the Colossi of Memnon, several of which may be included in a Swan Dahabiya itinerary, depending on the route and cruise length. Luxor can also serve as your starting or ending point on a trip down the Nile. Other less well-known destinations: For certain operators, depending on the sailing timetable, some dahabiya tour routes may include smaller archaeological sites such as El Kab or Gebel el-Silsila. Verify all the stops before making a booking. Frequently Asked Questions What is it like to eat on a Dahabiya? At this stage, we hope that you have become aware of what it is like to be on a Dahabiya. A great advantage of traveling on a boutique ship is the opportunity to dine; as you explore the area's history, you also get to taste Egyptian food on traditionally inspired dahabiyas. While on board, you have the opportunity to taste Egyptian food and gain an understanding of Egypt not just through its history but also through its cuisine and cultural traditions. Depending on the menu, meals may include Egyptian dishes such as koshari and desserts such as Umm Ali. The ship also offers a variety of dining choices from different cuisines. When making a reservation, you should confirm the menus and any dietary requirements. How to find a perfect Dahabiya for yourself? If you prefer a Dahabiya over large Nile cruises, here is a quick guide to help you choose an ideal boutique-style vessel for Nile sailing. In Egypt, there are a great many options when it comes to the Dahabiya Nile cruise, but you should choose one that suits your travel schedule and budget, and it also has to have the following: - Comfortable cabins and suites. - A structured itinerary between Aswan and Luxor. - Must include the transfers from cruises to the shore excursions and vice versa. - Should offer seamless and transparent booking services. - The packages include dining. Among the various factors tourists should consider when choosing a Dahabiya vessel, it is advisable to select only a Dahabiya company that is licensed and insured to ensure a good Nile sailing experience. Before making a booking, it is important to review the operator's qualifications, insurance coverage, cancellation conditions, feedback from recent travelers, and the precise services included in the fare. To assess the operator's reliability, you should review the testimonials and reviews from previous travelers. What should you pack on a cruise aboard a Dahabiya along the Nile? - Clothes that are lightweight and breathable for warm days when on the river. - When visiting temples and local sites, it is appropriate to wear simple clothing. - For cooler mornings and evenings, it is advisable to wear a light jacket or shawl. - Shoes that are comfortable for excursions and temple visits. - For relaxing on board, sandals or some comfortable footwear should be worn. - Sunglasses, sunscreen, and a hat for sun protection. - A small bag containing essentials for use during sightseeing stops. - Personal items, such as medicine, toiletries, and a reusable water bottle. When is the best time for a Dahabiya journey in Egypt? Egypt is a year-round tourist destination, and the same goes for Dahabiyas. October through April generally offers the most comfortable weather for sightseeing in Luxor and Aswan. Cruises may also operate during the hotter months, but travelers should confirm availability with the operator and be prepared for intense daytime heat. If you want to avoid the crowds or get discounts, May through September is the best time. Plan to visit historical sites either early in the morning or late in the evening to avoid the worst of the heat. Why Swan Dahabiya? Swan Dahabiya combines traditional sailing-inspired design with modern cabins, furnished decks, included meals, and guided excursions. The wooden fittings are based on Egyptian culture; the cabins are well furnished, and the decks have comfortable seating so that passengers may enjoy the peaceful riverbanks. If you would like to experience the true authenticity of the Dahabiya, then the Swan should be one of your choices, something that experienced travelers compare it to. Final Thoughts You never actually experience the Nile if you go from one ancient site to another, since it's only during the hours in between that you begin to feel it-when the temples are out of sight, and the river then becomes the story you experience on a Dahabiya. Upgrade your Egyptian holiday with both comfort and exploration by adding a Dahabiya trip. This article was published in partnership with Swan Dahabiya.

item.title: Five Italian Cathedrals That Genuinely Stopped Me in My Tracks
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 2.65
I've walked into many churches in Italy. After a few, you feel cathedral fatigue - another nave, another altar, another queue. But a few made me stop and gasp at the architecture. I remember exactly where I stood in each and the moment my brain gave up trying to process what it saw. Here are five cathedrals and churches in Italy I would recommend to all visitors. Cathedrals vs. Churches: What's the Difference? A quick note on terminology: not every church on this list is technically a cathedral. A cathedral is the principal church of a diocese and contains the bishop's official seat. St. Peter's Basilica and Sant'Ignazio are basilicas or churches rather than cathedrals, and St. Peter's is located in Vatican City. They're included because they belong on any architecture-focused church itinerary through Rome and Italy. Duomo di Milano, Milan This was the first cathedral I visited on my trip to Italy, and I will never forget how breathless I was at the sight of this majestic architecture. The minute I stepped out of the Duomo metro station, it looked like something that grew out of the earth rather than was built. The 135 spires, a forest of pinnacles, and the gilded Madonnina shining at the top are masterpieces. The unique marble rooftop is the real reason Duomo Milan is on this list. I booked a Milan Cathedral tour that included access to the terrace. The minute you climb onto the roof, you walk among the spires, close enough to see the carved faces and details on each. On a clear afternoon, you can see the Alps on the horizon. I recommend you do the tour around 5 pm to watch the marble turn warm pink as the light drops. St Peter's Basilica, Vatican City How can you visit Rome without paying a visit to St Peter's Basilica? The scale of this religious building was something I was not prepared for. Scale is something nobody prepares you for. You will likely walk out with neck pain after your visit. The gorgeously detailed dome, marvelous sculptures, Bernini's Baldachin, and more await inside. You can find Michelangelo's Pietà behind glass, just inside the entrance to the right. Note that this is the original statue by Michelangelo and the only one he signed! The dome climb was the highlight of my visit. I paid extra for the elevator to the terrace, then walked the last stretch. The steps curve inward toward the ddome'sshell, so you lean sideways throughout the climb. Midway, you'll follow a walkway around the inside of the grand dome for an up-close look at its mosaics. The dome rises approximately 448 feet above the ground, although the walkway itself is considerably lower. Then proceed to the top to enjoy the view over St. Peter's Square, which is worth every drop of sweat. One practical note: Entry to St. PPeter'sBasilica is free, but all visitors must pass through security. The Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel are separate, ticketed attractions with their own entrance. I booked my Vatican tickets online about three weeks in advance to bypass the ticket line at the museums. Florence Duomo (Santa Maria del Fiore), Florence The Florence Duomo is my personal favorite on this list. I visited twice: once at night to explore the exterior in peace and again in the morning for a tour. Brunelleschi's dome is a 15th-century engineering marvel that outshines modern techniques. Climbing it is the best hour you'll spend in Florence. There are 463 steps, and the staircase narrows near the top so you squeeze between the outer and inner walls of the dome. Halfway up, there's a walkway around the interior of the dome at the level of Vasari's Last Judgment frescoes. You're an arm's length from faces approximately nine feet tall. Then there's more climbing to the lantern, which reveals the terracotta rooftops of all of Florence. Book a slot for the dome tour in advance. You can't just show up to climb it. If the dome is sold out, head across the square to Giotto's bell tower for city views. Sant'Ignazio di Loyola, Rome This was an accidental find while walking from the Pantheon to the Trevi Fountain. I just wanted to step into a quaint church I was passing, only to find the most beautiful one in Rome. The ceiling fresco of Sant'Ignazio di Loyola is so extensive and detailed that you will want to explore every inch. It is free to enter and usually crowd-free. This is also the church with the mirror where people visit to take the iconic photo of the ceiling. You will find a long queue of mirrors, but otherwise the cathedral is empty. I recommend walking to the altar and exploring rather than waiting for the mirror. By the end of the visit, you will have wrecked your neck. Siena Cathedral, Siena The last one has the most beautiful interior. Siena Cathedral is banded in black-and-white marble and feels more like an adorned jewelry box than a church. The Piccolomini Library off the nave is covered wall-to-ceiling with frescoes by Pinturicchio, with colors that look wet. If you're there in late summer, the inlaid marble floor panels are uncovered for a few weeks; I got lucky and saw them. The cathedral is quietly placed in the heart of Siena. I visited on a day trip from Florence but recommend taking more time to enjoy this region of Tuscany. This article was published in partnership with Milan Duomo Tickets and Vatican Tickets Online.

item.title: How Japan’s Oldest Companies Navigate Uncertainty
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.76
Summary. In the period from 1994 to 2024, Japan’s family businesses matched or exceeded the returns of peers in the United States, Germany, and Canada while taking on far less risk. Their advantage In 1945, an air raid destroyed the main Tokyo factory of Toraya, a leading Japanese confectioner since the 16th century. Despite the ongoing world war, the company began rebuilding almost immediately; later, even when sugar became scarce and Japan’s future uncertain, it kept operating, experimenting, pressing on. The logic was simple: Toraya existed to make sweets and would continue to do so no matter what was happening around it. Today, with three factories and some 80 stores across Japan as well as a boutique in Paris, it still does.
