item.title: How People Without Formal Power Gain Influence
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.55
Share Podcast How People Without Formal Power Gain Influence A conversation with author and entrepreneur Pamela Meyer on five ways executives can indirectly assert themselves. In today’s increasingly decentralized workplaces, leaders often need to get things done without having direct authority over the people they depend on. So how can you influence colleagues, clients, vendors, and even senior executives without simply telling them what to do? Pamela Meyer, founder and CEO of Calibrate, says the answer is learning to read the room—and understanding the informal networks, emotional dynamics, and hidden sources of power that shape decisions. She explains five paths to indirect influence: becoming an influence spotter, a backchanneler, a precision mover, a connector, and a pulse reader. Meyer also explains why the best influencers focus less on how they’re performing and more on what the people around them need. Meyer is the author of How to Read the Room: The Art and Science of Social Observation and the HBR article “Five Ways to Wield Influence When You Lack Authority.” ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. This is the HBR IdeaCast. ALISON BEARD: Adi, I don’t know if you’ve noticed this, but because of the way we work today, a lot of us are often leading people we don’t have direct authority over. That’s true whether you’re working on a cross-functional team with clients or outside vendors when you’re trying to manage up. ADI IGNATIUS: When you’re trying to manage your podcast co-host. ALISON BEARD: Yeah, that too. It is very hard. And so today we’re going to talk about the rising importance of indirect influence to persuade people to buy into your ideas, marshal resources, succeed in your work, and advance in your career. Our guest argues that it’s one of the most important skills to develop. ADI IGNATIUS: All right. Consider me influenced. Tell me what to do. ALISON BEARD: Well, she argues that it starts with listening and observing. It’s about recognizing the informal networks, emotional dynamics, and hidden decision makers that exist inside every organization and among external stakeholders and knowing how to work with them rather than against them. And she’s going to share some of the best ways to go about that. Pamela Meyer is the founder and CEO of Calibrate. She wrote the book, How to Read the Room: The Art and Science of Social Observation, and the HBR article, Five Ways to Wield Influence When You Lack Authority. Here’s our conversation. So why is indirect influence so much more important now than it was in the past? PAMELA MEYER: Well, one of the reasons is that we don’t live in a hierarchical world anymore. In fact, in most organizations, authority is really distributed. And so we need to learn ways to work ourselves around an organization, have influence, but not at the same time cause what we call reactance. So what we find oftentimes is when someone tries to influence someone and they put pressure on them, it almost always threatens their autonomy. And when their autonomy is threatened, they pull back, they have reactance, and they’re not able to be influenced. And so now what we really need to do is teach people a sort of artful way to make their way through much more complicated organizations with much more complicated people with different ages and different generations at different levels of seniority and find ways to match their path to the person that they’re actually trying to influence. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. And we do hear so much about how important it is to be authentic and transparent, but what psychologically is going on that just telling someone what you would like them to do or what you think they should do doesn’t work when you’re not their boss? PAMELA MEYER: It actually goes back to social determination theory, which is a very stable theory of psychology developed in the ’80s. And it’s a theory of motivation. Human beings have three very profound needs that they express in the workplace. One of those needs is for competence. One of those needs is for relatedness. And one of those needs, which is really profound, is for autonomy. We really need to feel that we have agency. And what happens with influence and what happens with reactance is that it takes away our sense of autonomy. So what happens, people start distorting the way they express it in the room. Somebody, for example, who, you’ve probably seen this many times at an organization, you can’t get them to do what you want. You just keep asking them. Oftentimes those people are declared, oh, they have executive function issues. No, that’s not what’s happening usually. It’s usually a bid for autonomy. They just don’t want to be told what to do. And so oftentimes what we need to do is think through psychologically when we’re asking somebody to do something for us or we’re trying to get something done or we’re trying to steer a group. What are the needs that each of these people have? And how can I satisfy that so that I can actually provide them with a sense that they are actually making the decision themselves? ALISON BEARD: So you talk about five paths to indirect influence. And the first is figuring out who might not be at the top of the org chart, but still has hidden power. So how do you get better at spotting those people? PAMELA MEYER: I call these people the influence spotters. The bad influence spotter is the one who looks at job titles and says, “Okay, that person has influence.” The good influence spotter walks in the room. They pause. They look around. They’ve done a lot of research on who’s who ahead of time. And then to figure out who actually has influence, they particularly focus on decisions that are being made, who actually influences a hard decision. So when they can figure that out, who might be influencing the decision, where are the micro alliances, who’s looking at whom when there’s a disagreement. Once they start to spot who has influence, then they do what we call a chain analysis. They actually go back a few chains and they figure out who’s influencing that person. So influence spotters are analytic. There’s an art to it and there’s a science to it. They’re artful observers, but they’re also scientific thinkers. They think through who might be influencing the person who actually has the influence, who’s got their ear. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. So I think you’re beginning to answer my next question is sort of when you figure out those people, and I think we all know who they are, like, oh, that person really seems to have a lot of power. How do you bring them on your side? PAMELA MEYER: Well, you have to do it gently and carefully. You don’t just call up somebody and you don’t just… For example, let’s say you decide that the CEO’s long time confidant is the real power in the room. You’re not going to just call that person up and say, “Hey, let’s have coffee.” You’re probably going to really insult the person who really owns that decision. So you have to be very artful and very careful about it and kind of make it optional to open up a conversation with that person. Make it gentle, make it optional. Maybe just get to know them a little bit. You don’t necessarily want to call somebody up and have a direct conversation with them about the exact concern you might have in the moment. You’ve got to be artful about it and you’ve got to kind of work around it and get to know them and bring something to the table. If you think somebody’s the real influencer in the room and you need something from them, also think what are you going to bring to them that’s going to be helpful to them? ALISON BEARD: And I think one thing that really struck me in working with you on the article and in reading the book is that this advice isn’t just for sort of aspiring leaders who quite obviously don’t have any influence. It’s actually for really senior leaders too, who can’t seem to sort of move the needle in the direction that they want. And so they need to be finding these influence spotters within the C-suite or on the board, right? PAMELA MEYER: Yeah, absolutely. Part of what’s happened is our culture really rewards what we say and not what we see. It rewards speaking instead of watching. So a lot of people that are sitting on boards who have a lot to do and they’re flooded with noise and information and many, many more decisions and they’re distracted, they’re preoccupied, they have a lot of stuff going on in their working memory. They don’t have time to think thoughtfully about this at all. And so instead of sitting back and observing and trying to figure out who really has influence, they’ll blurt out exactly what needs to get done or they’ll miss the timing in the moment. And they’re backfiring completely when that happens. They really should not be doing that. They should be thinking it through much more slowly, much more thoughtfully. And usually if you do that and you have an eye towards when a room is shifting, you can get a sense of what caused that and where that influence might be. ALISON BEARD: So the next approach is becoming a backchanneler. What exactly do you mean by that? PAMELA MEYER: So the backchanneler is the one who takes a meeting that’s really frozen where two factions in a meeting just can’t figure it out and a decision can’t be made. And they pull one of those players or two of those players off to the side. Oftentimes today this happens virtually. It’s not necessarily happening at work. Although it does happen at TGI Fridays, it doesn’t always happen on the telephone. And they have a backchannel conversation. They have a private conversation. They open a backchannel. A backchannel has been a function of diplomatic influence for all of history. And it happens as well at the boardroom level and it happens at the junior level. And backchannelers can be unbelievably, unbelievably talented and they can get a lot done. But sometimes what we see is the wrong person tries to open up a backchannel. If you’re not trusted and you’re new to an organization and you all of a sudden start opening up a backchannel and kind of lurking in the corners and having private conversations with people, people are just going to consider you a political animal. If you want to be a backchanneler, ask yourself if you’ve earned the trust of people to do that before you open that backchannel because it’s not for everybody. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. I mean, again, in this age of transparency, great value placed on being upfront with people, this does seem like a tricky thing to get right. So what advice do you have for people who want to do it without being seen as a manipulative political person? PAMELA MEYER: So the most important piece of advice is to do it temporarily. Opening up permanent backchannels makes you look like a power grabber and it makes you look transactional. But if you have a particular item that you want done, you have a decision that needs to be made, you have a frozen conversation that needs to be unlocked, open the backchannel and then close it. Say thank you, that was great. Bring it back to the meeting and make it public that you all had that conversation or not. You don’t have to necessarily make it public, but bring the finalization, bring the final decision public so that people understand that the whole thing doesn’t happen in the backchannel. The best backchannelers, the ones who are the most talented at it that I’ve seen in organization after organization, are the chiefs of staff. They’re the ones that are, they’re pulling someone aside and they’re saying, “Hey, I noticed you were interrupted in that meeting. You didn’t get to talk. I’m putting the postmortem report together. What is it you wanted to say? Let me get that in.” They’re the ones that are observing the room really carefully and they serve usually a CEO or a COO or a CFO. And so people take them very seriously. Sometimes they’re not trusted because they have the ear of power. But the really talented chiefs of staff use the backchannel in a very flexible and a very talented way. And they’re the best backchannelers that I’ve seen. ALISON BEARD: And so the rest of us can learn from how they do it. PAMELA MEYER: I think so. ALISON BEARD: Okay. Another path is being a precision mover who knows sort of exactly the right time to exert influence. Why is timing so very important? PAMELA MEYER: First of all, I just want to say it’s really hard to be a good precision mover because most of us are not regulated enough. We’re not emotionally regulated enough, nor are we strategic thinkers enough to figure out what’s the right time to bring this decision. What’s the time to release this information? What’s the best time to have the labor negotiation? So the strategic thinker tends to be oftentimes the precision mover. It’s very, very hard to get right. One thing that precision movers do really well that most of us don’t even think to do is instead of thinking in moments, they think about time windows. So they’ll say, “Oh, the next quarter might be a good time. Let me just think about when in that quarter I can bring this information forth.” But precision movers often backfire all the time. It’s really hard to do it well. So let’s say, for example, you have really bad news that you need to release and you’re trying to be a precision mover and you’re being thoughtful about it and you’re like, “I’m just going to hold this back one more week.” Well, someone else is going to release that information. It’s going to completely backfire and you’re going to look evasive. So it’s really easy to be a bad precision mover and it’s really hard to do it well, but I will say that there are CEOs all over this country and all over the world who made their way from being an intern all the way up to the top of the organization by being thoughtful and by being precision movers. So it can deliver absolutely outsized influence, but there are very, very few people that do it extremely well. ALISON BEARD: So definitely approach with caution, but is there a way to build up those skills so you’re better at it? PAMELA MEYER: I think you could consider precision moving a micro skill. You could try it in small ways. Let’s say you have a hire you want to bring to your boss. Well, don’t bring the resume up until the perfect time. Let’s say you need to take an extra week off, or let’s say someone’s told you they want to change to a remote work. Or let’s say you’re about to make a hard decision on firing somebody. These are micro decisions. They aren’t major strategic decisions for an organization. Practice those skills. I think it’s a great idea. Go in and try to figure out the best way to time it. And if it backfires, it’s a little bit negative. It’s probably somewhat uncomfortable for you in terms of how you need to navigate next, but you haven’t lost the whole game. ALISON BEARD: Okay. Let’s move on to being a connector. How does that help the leader themselves gain influence, putting other people together? PAMELA MEYER: So connectors can give you unbelievable influence if you’re thoughtful about it. I mean, what connectors do is they find gaps and they provide something in the gap. Let’s say a form of expertise. Let’s say there’s a project that’s across many, many divisions. They allow a certain form of coordination. They can also just figure out that two people would really get along and work well together and they’re in two different places and put them together. So connectors can be incredibly influential and many of us can be connectors. You don’t need to be a leader to be a connector. Oftentimes you’ll see connectors are people at much lower levels in an organization and they found they have social skills, they love people. This is a way that they can actually get an on-ramp into an important conversation and have some influence in the room. But connectors also, again, you can be a good connector or a bad connector. And we’ve all been on the receiving end of that. I mean, when I was single, people would call me up and they’d be like, “Oh, I have a blind date for you to go on.” And so oftentimes I go on that date and I’m like, “That person wasn’t right for me at all.” Sometimes you’re a favor for the other person. It’s not actually mutually beneficial to both people. And so we see this oftentimes. Oftentimes the traditional advice is send somebody a news article, go for coffee, tell them you were just thinking about them. People sniff that out overnight. It is so easy to sniff out someone who’s transactional, who’s collecting people, who’s kind of a surface connector, who wants to have a huge Rolodex. That’s not going to work in this era because we’re in an era where anybody can call anybody. It’s not the way it used to be. You can use LinkedIn, you can use any other platform, and you can find your way through any connection to connecting with anybody you want. So I tell people, dial it back. Be much more thoughtful about it. If you want to be a valid connector, somebody that people really listen to and you don’t want to waste their time, only connect people when you know that both sides are going to benefit from it. Because if you don’t, they’re not going to take you seriously and they’re going to sense that you’re doing it for yourself rather than for them. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. I’m laughing because I just got an email from a college friend who said, “Oh, I have someone in Boston who you might want to interview.” And I’m like, “No, I don’t want to interview that person. Why would you think I want to interview that person?” PAMELA MEYER: I mean, informational interviews are out, sending around news articles that might be interesting, out. Would you meet my daughter’s friend? Out. Yeah. ALISON BEARD: Exactly. PAMELA MEYER: Don’t do favors. Only be someone who’s known for really thinking through what people need and you’ll have incredible influence from it. ALISON BEARD: The final path to influence is being a pulse reader. So explain a little bit more about what you mean by that. PAMELA MEYER: So the pulse reader is the person who reads the vibe of the room. They’re the person who understands what people need from a kind of heart perspective. Indra Nooyi, the former head of PepsiCo, she ran a $64 billion company, 260,000 employees. And she was famous for writing letters to 400 of her best employees’ parents every year to tell them in a paragraph what they accomplished as essentially sending a message, “You raised a successful person and I’ve noticed it.” She got at the heart of what mattered in that culture. And that’s incredibly, incredibly influential. And the pulse readers are able to do that. They’re able to kind of observe what the room needs, but the really good ones also have the ability to articulate what it needs. So if you’re someone who figures out, “Oh, everybody’s really stressed out because AI is coming in and it’s going to take everybody’s jobs. There’s ambient dread all over the organization. I need to really help with this.” It’s not going to work unless they can actually name in the moment in a way that people resonate with what’s actually happening. So that’s the art and science of it. Again, you can be a great pulse reader, but if you don’t have the ability to actually talk in an articulate way about what’s going on, nobody’s going to pay attention to you. ALISON BEARD: So again, how do you develop those skills if they don’t come naturally to you? PAMELA MEYER: So there are a couple ways that you can do that. As a pulse reader, the most important skill you can take on is pausing. Walking in the room, pausing, trying to think through what will make this room better. Getting out of your own self-monitoring, getting out of your own self-consciousness and thinking through who in this room needs something? What do they need? Do they need a sense of relatedness? Do they need to be given more agency? Are they somebody where they’re making bids for competence and they actually need me to acknowledge that they are competent? Start with pausing, observing the room, and trying to figure out what it is people need. And if that’s too complex for you and it’s a really busy day and it’s an incredibly busy meeting and you don’t have time to figure all that out, step back and ask yourself, you know what? As you look at each person in the room, are they a visionary or are they a detailed person? Just make it that binary. If you start to do that and you start to think about people that way, you’ll just get out of your own way and you’ll start to read the pulse. People do this with kids when they’re teaching them how to identify their emotions. You can make a list of all the possible emotions you might see in a room. You might actually ask, are people nervous? Are they anxious? Are they dreading something? Are they warm? What’s actually happening in the room? And use that vocabulary to start naming it. And you’d be amazed if you actually walk into a room with that list of vocabulary words and you start to throw them out there. You’ll know. It’s like a fishing expedition. You throw it out there, you’ll know, people will start nodding. They’ll start looking at you. You’ll get a sense when you throw out what you think is happening, they’ll give you the positive feedback that what you said is actually the real case. I’ve often had a situation where I’ll walk in a room and I’ll say, “You know what? I think the problem is we’ve got a trust issue here. We really don’t trust that this outside vendor that we’re working with is going to deliver. Let’s just be clear about it. Do we need to back up and re-license or do we need to confront them directly? What do we need to do?” The minute you say there’s a trust issue, the heads start nodding. All of a sudden you’ve kind of named what’s at the core of it. ALISON BEARD: And this seems like something that everyone can get better at because it really involves staying quiet, listening, looking. It doesn’t require those sort of timing skills or political skills. It’s much more about being empathetic. PAMELA MEYER: I think so, but I think it also involves understanding that there’s an element of timing to this as well. A pulse reader can read the pulse, run away and write the right memo, not necessarily name it in the moment. So if you’re in a room and the room is, this is going to sound a bit metaphysical, but you’ll be able to feel it if you actually walk in the room and you try to practice this. If you ask yourself, is this room expansive or is it contracting? Are people still frictionless? Are the jokes not landing? Are people blurting out kind of a bad laugh at a bad joke? Do you have a sense that people are kind of withdrawing? In that kind of contracted environment, you don’t necessarily, even if you know what the problem is and even if you know you could name exactly what’s at the pulse of that. It’s not necessarily the right time to do that because there’s already an incredible amount of tension in the room. Maybe you just wait. If you’ve got a room that’s expansive and there’s like a frothy, happy, almost like a, I wouldn’t say happy, but let’s say there’s a room that’s expansive and there’s a big argument going on, but there’s trust in the room and you kind of feel the friction and the room feels like people are willing to kind of get into the muddy middle of it. That’s a time when you really can be a pulse reader. You can have an incredible impact. ALISON BEARD: In the executives that you counsel and coach, are you trying to get them to build all of these skills in tandem or do you tend to encourage them to focus on particular ones? PAMELA MEYER: So I spend a lot of time coaching people not only to develop these skills, because you certainly need room reading skills and you certainly need to be able to walk into a room and understand and intuit where the power alliances are, who’s got influence, who’s withdrawn, who’s actually taking up too much space and shouldn’t be. All of that I can teach them to do. But I also spend an enormous amount of time with executives retraining them on how to prepare to walk into the room because there’s a lot you need to do before you even walk in the room to be effective. I teach them what I call the triple B method. We actually profile people. We look at their background, their behavior, their beliefs. We figure everything out we can about them before you walk in the room. For example, I know you and I went to high school right down the street from each other. ALISON BEARD: Oh, I didn’t realize that. PAMELA MEYER: Yes. I went to Sidwell, you went to Walt Whitman. ALISON BEARD: Yep. Okay. PAMELA MEYER: I know you were a star athlete in college. Still hold the record for best assists in volleyball. ALISON BEARD: Wow. You’ve done a deep dive. PAMELA MEYER: Yeah, of course. I know you care about your local community. I know a lot about you before I walk in the room. And we train executives to do that and to try to understand as much as they possibly can about somebody. Not just their background, but also what are their belief systems? What kind of behavioral, we call it behavioral residue, they may leave in the room. Really, who are they as a whole person? Why? Because if you want influence downstream, you’re going to need some way to connect with them. You need rapport. You need to understand them in a much more deep way. And certainly you can, I mean, you can use AI to kind of speed read somebody in the bathroom right before you meet them if you don’t have a chance to do that. But what we do is much deeper and it’s much more thoughtful. And we actually spend a lot of time retraining professionals on how to invest the time to do that well because that is where they get their edge. There are a lot of people that can walk in and kind of wing it in a meeting, but managers tell me over and over again when I consult to them, please tell my staff to prepare because I know who’s prepared and who’s not when they walk in the room. ALISON BEARD: And tell listeners about your own unique background that’s prepared you to teach executives on these skills, these reading the room skills? PAMELA MEYER: Well, so I spent over a decade teaching people how to detect deception and how to elicit information from people. We use this on inside threat detection and on figuring out when people might be deceptive and certainly in negotiation. And I did that for a very, very long time and I still do that. I still train people all the time on lie spotting and deception detection, but the environment’s changed. We’re in the middle of a trust epidemic now. And so what used to be kind of a quaint polarization, people are in different silos, it’s much more embittered. People really feel it. And the reason I wrote this book, How to Read the Room, is because I really want to get people back to a much more reasonable and thoughtful conversation into that middle ground and learning how to kind of be brokers of trust because we’ve got a real problem. Everybody, every single person, every single audience that I talk to, every single organization I work with will tell me, yes, people are way too polarized and we’ve got to do something about it because we’re all going to have to get along. The more positive the environment you’re in, the better work you’re going to get from people. If you push them down and you take autonomy and agency away from them, they’re going to withdraw and they’re going to become embittered and you’re not going to get their best work. So you can have a room full of absolutely brilliant people and if they can’t read each other, it’s very emotionally expensive for the organization and for them. So I teach people to read each other, to read the power dynamics, and also to really focus on how to develop trust in teams because that ends up being much, much more important downstream than just having a collection of geniuses in the room. ALISON BEARD: So is the idea that leaders can either do all of these things themselves or if they’re more senior in the organization, make sure that they have people on their teams to play each one of these indirect influencing roles? PAMELA MEYER: I think every leader needs a panoply of talented, diverse, skilled people around them. I don’t think it makes sense to say, “Okay, I need one backchanneler, one influencer, one precision timer.” What I do think you can do with leaders though is to attune them to these skills. So when they’re interviewing people and when they’re developing people to kind of note, does this person have the emotional intelligence to be a pulse reader? Does this person have the strategic long-term thinking skill to be a precision timer? Does this person have enough personal sway if they were an influence spotter to actually be able to have a conversation with the person who’s the most influential in the room? So I think it’s a matter of not finding somebody who can go on every path, but on thinking through a new set of skills that will help people read the room and be more influential long term. But I think it would be very dangerous to select just for somebody who’s good on these skills. The bottom line is that it’s a great idea to have diversity across your team, but you shouldn’t take every path literally. These are skills, they’re composite skills. So it’s worth understanding what the paths are so you can really select for those skills here and there. So if somebody walks in the door and they have emotional intelligence, that’s great, but you might want to ask yourself, do they have the ability to be kind of regulated enough to be a precision mover as well? Would they be able to withhold information for two weeks if you ask them to do that? Does somebody have the pulse reading skill? Well, you don’t necessarily want to ask yourself, do I need a pulse reader in the room? But you might want somebody who’s articulate enough about how they describe what happened in a room that the emotional resonance of it was able to be understood. So you don’t want to create a phantom cabinet of every single path taker, but you do want to focus on the skills and see if you can start to select for them a bit. ALISON BEARD: So let’s say our listeners have heard this podcast, they’re bought into the idea of exerting indirect influence more effectively. What is something or a few things that they should do in the next week or the next month to start building these muscles? PAMELA MEYER: The first thing you want to do is you want to just think of the room as not one audience. When you walk into the room, pause, get a sense of the vibe, look around, be prepared, know as much as you can before you walk in the room, but realize this is a collection of individuals with very different needs. So it’s not one audience. Do not focus on how you’re going to sound, what people are going to think about you, your performance. Focus on how you can make that room better. Once you do that, you’ll be able to pick a path to influence. The second thing I think is that you probably want to think through, like if you’re trying to figure out what’s happening with influence in the room, where are the influencers? Where can I make a difference? You probably want to watch the room and take particular note of when there’s a challenge to authority, when there’s an inflection point, when there’s a battle, when a joke lands badly, when something happens in the room that kind of shifts the energy. One thing that you can do that you probably didn’t do before, instead of watching the action and getting the popcorn out and saying, “Whoa, those two are really having a fight,” look around the room. Who’s glancing at who? Who’s already landed on a Slack channel? Who’s leaning towards someone else? Where are those micro alliances starting to form? Once you start to look past the action in the room and instead at the patterns that occur after something important has happened, after there’s been a major shift, once you start to focus on that and really build that muscle, you’ll start to see paths to influence everywhere. ALISON BEARD: Wonderful. Well, thank you for teaching me and our listeners how to build more influence in our organizations. Thanks so much for being on the show. PAMELA MEYER: Goodbye. It’s been great to be with you. Thanks for having me. ALISON BEARD: That’s Pamela Meyer, founder and CEO of Calibrate and author of the book, How to Read the Room: The Art and Science of Social Observation, and the HBR article, Five Ways to Wield Influence When You Lack Authority. Next week, Adi speaks with Jared Diamond about some of history’s great leaders and how much of what they accomplished was due to chance. If you found this episode helpful, please share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to our team, senior producer, Mary Dooe, and senior production editor, Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Alison Beard.

item.title: 4 Steps to Transform the “Middle Office” with AI
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.11
Summary. Companies are spending heavily on AI, but many are still struggling to turn that investment into measurable business results. One reason is that they’re overlooking the middle office, where Recent evidence on AI adoption has revealed a sobering paradox. Economists who linked large-scale adoption surveys to administrative payroll records found that although most employers had rolled out AI tools in areas where AI should have the highest probability of impact, the effect on earnings and hours two years on was statistically indistinguishable from zero. Despite capable technology and workers reporting productivity gains, the promised benefits failed to materialize on the bottom line.

item.title: What Separates AI Agents That Ship to Production from Those That Don’t
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.07
The enterprise AI conversation has quietly shifted. Two years ago, executives asked whether their organization could build an AI agent. Today they are asking whether their organization can trust an AI agent. The question of trust runs on two fronts: the agents they have built that now run in production and the coding agents their developers rely on daily to build software. Most organizations can’t trust their agents in either case. Working demos of AI agents are common, but agents customers depend on day after day that improve over time and hold up to real-world edge cases are rare. Closing the gap is not a modeling problem. It is a verification problem. Organizations can build software at agent speed, but they cannot yet verify software at agent speed. Traditional software testing is a solved problem: Engineers write unit tests, continuous integration blocks regressions, and deployments are gated. But AI agents break every assumption behind that playbook. They are nondeterministic. The same input can produce different outputs. Small changes to a system prompt or tool description can cascade into failures that only appear in multi-step workflows. A model upgrade meant to improve performance can introduce silent regressions no one notices until customers report them. Five Components of the Feedback Loop Many engineering teams still operate their agents the way they first tested them: manually, in a spreadsheet, iterating on prompts, and hoping a fix does not quietly break three other workflows. The business consequences add up quickly. Projects that reach a working demo stall for months, sometimes indefinitely, because the team cannot demonstrate the agent is safe to release at scale. Engineering time drains into whack-a-mole debugging. Release cycles slow down. Anticipated return on investment (ROI) does not materialize because the agent never reaches the customer-facing scale the business case required. Cost visibility becomes its own problem, as fleets of agents, including the coding agents that developers are running on their laptops all day, can quietly drive up spend that no finance team can attribute. The gap between organizations that have institutionalized this discipline and those still improvising compounds every week. The teams closing the gap treat AI agents like a software product, with a real feedback loop built on observability. Five components define the foundation: - Production traces flow continuously into an observability layer using open standards, so every agent decision, model call, tool invocation, retrieval, and response is inspectable. - Evaluation moves from brittle string matching to layered evaluators, including large language model (LLM) judges scoped narrowly to specific behavioral checks and deterministic code-based tests where they apply. - Real production traces, including failures, become the golden data sets teams evaluate against, not synthetic happy-path examples. - Experiments compare prompt, model, and configuration changes against those data sets before anything ships. - Continuous integration pipelines gate merges on evaluation pass rates. Because the underlying instrumentation follows OpenTelemetry-based open standards, the same discipline works across cloud-native runtimes without locking teams into any single vendor’s stack. What is new, and where the industry is heading, is that the loop itself is starting to run without humans driving every step. Long-running agents now surface what to investigate, propose fixes as pull requests, and grade their own work with engineers supervising and approving rather than executing every task. An Advanced Testing Framework One AI-native engineering team has spent more than two years building and operating a production agent that helps developers debug and improve other agents. The team’s earliest testing framework was a spreadsheet. What changed everything was the shift to treating real production traces, measured in trillions of spans and evaluated across tens of millions of evaluation runs, as the foundation of engineering. Today the team runs continuous evaluations in production, gates every prompt and tool change behind continuous integration (CI-integrated) evaluation suites, and increasingly uses long-running agents to triage, categorize, and prioritize the team’s own production failures. What used to take hours of engineer debugging now takes minutes. The team ships faster, catches regressions before customers do, and continues to improve the agent even as usage scales. The durable advantage in agentic AI will not come from the underlying model. Foundation models will keep getting better and cheaper for everyone. Code is being commoditized by coding agents. Models are being commoditized by the menu of foundation models available on every hyperscaler. What is left and what compounds is context: the observability, the evaluations, the release discipline, and the feedback loop that makes every deployment safer than the last. Enterprises accelerating agentic AI on AWS are increasingly relying on partners that have already built this discipline into their own platforms. To see how AWS and Arize are helping teams operationalize agentic AI in production (agents running in your applications and the coding agents building them), visit Arize on AWS Marketplace or explore the resources at arize.com/partners/aws.

item.title: The Right Way to Deliver Bad Earnings News
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.43
Summary. Leaders often assume that delaying bad financial news until an earnings announcement will soften the market’s reaction. Early disclosure won’t eliminate the harm entirely, but how On July 14, Arvind Krishna did something CEOs spend their entire tenure hoping to avoid. Eight days before IBM was scheduled to report second-quarter earnings, he published an open letter to investors warning that the results would fall well short of expectations. By the closing bell, IBM’s stock had fallen roughly 25%—the worst single day in the company’s 115-year history. Within days, Wall Street was debating whether activist investors might try to break up Big Blue.

item.title: The Store Isn’t Dead—but the Merchant Model Is
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.41
Summary. The decline of many retailers reflects not the death of the physical store but the failure of the traditional merchant model, which requires retailers to forecast demand, own inventory, and absorb Walk through a department store at the end of a season and the signs tell a familiar story: 40% off! 60% off! Clearance! Retailers often treat these markdowns as a tactical problem, the result of the wrong product, the wrong promotion, or bad weather effects. But they are better understood as confessions. They reveal the downsides of the traditional retailing model. The retailer acted as a merchant, committed to inventory before demand was known, absorbed the risk of being wrong, and then paid for that error in margin erosion and brand equity dilution. Under this merchant model, retailers routinely take on more risk than they can handle.

item.title: Do Your B2B Customers See the Value You Deliver?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.12
Summary. Many B2B companies suffer from a “value gap”: Customers benefit from their products but cannot clearly measure, articulate, or defend that value to stakeholders within their companies. Most B2B companies have long harbored a costly blind spot: a gap between the value they create for customers and the value those customers can see, measure, and defend. For many, early strong growth masks the problem until sales slow or competitive alternatives drag down margins. Closing that gap is an executive decision—and one most leadership teams have never explicitly made.

item.title: How Fiserv Turned Payment Data into a Growth Engine
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.02
By Prasanna Dhore and Praveen Arivazhagan Companies looking to grow revenue and profits can overlook opportunities they are already sitting on. They may pursue extensions of business as usual rather than trying to develop new business lines with the assets they already have. They may also focus on their core market rather than looking to entirely different products, markets, or industries. Fiserv was sitting on a deep pool of real-time spending data. To unlock its untapped value, it needed to explore markets beyond its core financial services customers and work with a partner that has forged deep relationships in those new markets. The resulting corporate venture empowered the financial services company to turn its data into an intelligence platform that helps consumer product and retail (CP&R) businesses get ahead of their competition by understanding how their consumers are spending and where new opportunities lie based on that behavior. This approach became a solution that can help retailers, restaurants, and consumer products companies better meet their customers’ desires. Attacking Information Asymmetry Fiserv already had real-time transaction data with a broad geographic footprint based on the trillions of dollars in payments it processes through its systems annually and the millions of small businesses running on its point-of-sale systems. Incorporating AI helped synthesize the data at scale so the company could use it to develop signals for future consumer spending while maintaining the privacy and anonymity of customers and consumers. Lacking key relationships in the CP&R industry, Fiserv collaborated with EY-Parthenon to access insights on what these customers needed from its data. The Corporate Venture Building team found a gap between the information consumer companies have and what they need to know to make optimal decisions about pricing, location strategy, product innovation, mergers and acquisitions, and marketing. Building Together with Customers The team had the deep sector experience to understand how the financial data could fill gaps for CP&R companies. It also had relationships with key decision makers such as strategy, marketing, consumer insights, and data analytics leaders in the industry. These factors helped identify the drawbacks CP&R companies saw in other data sources, such as long latency, relatively small panel sizes, and the lack of coverage of customer behavior at small businesses, including convenience stores and mom-and-pop restaurants. After developing prototypes and conducting testing with industry users, the team worked with a few proof-of-concept customers to join in product development and provide their input on market willingness to pay. The team conducted benchmarking against data sources that were already in the market to help determine both the pricing and the commercial model. It also built the business case and three-year venture-based financial model. Working closely with Fiserv data scientists to design the technical architecture, the team built AI into the offering to aggregate and turn the data into decision-grade insights in a more actionable way than typical informational dashboards. AI helped connect data pools and allowed users to ask questions about consumer behavior using conversational language. EY-Parthenon also embedded an AI-powered pricing workflow, supported by EY professionals’ commercial excellence methodologies and experiences. The resulting data products help Fiserv customers track granular market share movements, make better pricing decisions, identify and monitor new brand introductions, and assess early-stage companies as potential acquisition targets. By turning its data into intelligence on how consumers are spending, Fiserv developed a potential revenue stream outside its core business that it’s now testing and scaling with customers in the retail and consumer packaged goods (CPG) industries. Bringing It to Life The corporate venture-building approach is a method CEOs and other growth leaders can adopt to quickly achieve meaningful revenue growth. To make it work, companies need to: - Look at assets and their potential customer base in a different way. Languishing intellectual property, customer relationships, supply chains, and technology can all be the building blocks of a new business. - Use AI to compress the capacity, capabilities, and capital required to build, launch, and scale. - Treat the new venture as a startup outside the regular profit and loss statement to help give the venture time to develop without the pressures of the quarterly reporting cycle. - Conduct small experiments and set specific success metrics for additional funding. Don’t be afraid of failure. To the contrary, companies can build compensation metrics around the willingness to experiment. - Communicate, communicate, communicate. Starting from the top, spread the message throughout the organization that employees have the freedom to create new ventures within the company. Celebrate successes, break down silos, and allow more people to think like venture builders. - Find the right partners. The company may not have all the expertise or relationships it needs internally to make the connections it needs and fill in any capability gaps. This story shows how to turn underutilized assets into a new revenue stream that can support company growth for years. The next growth engine may already exist inside your business, waiting for forward-thinking leaders to see it and then team with an experienced partner to help test it, scale it, and bring the venture to life. Prasanna Dhore is President and Chief Data Officer of Data Commerce Solutions at Fiserv. Praveen Arivazhagan is the EY-Parthenon Americas Corporate Venture Building Leader, Ernst & Young LLP. Lauren Schmeer, EY-Parthenon, Executive Director and Venture Builder, Ernst & Young LLP, also contributed to this article. Learn more about how the EY-Parthenon Corporate Venture Building team helps companies originate, build, and scale new businesses and reimagine their core business for growth. The views reflected in this article are the views of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of Ernst & Young LLP or other members of the global EY organization.

item.title: Garmin inReach Subscription Cost: Which Plan Is Cheapest
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 6.43
Garmin inReach Subscription Cost Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Jump to a section A Garmin inReach subscription is required to use your device, and there’s a lot of variation in what you’ll pay. There are even inReach plans that Garmin doesn’t sell. Here’s how to figure out the best plan for you. | Plan | Best For | Price | |---|---|---| | Enabled | Pay only for what you use | $7.99/mo | | Standard | Sharing your live position with family on every hike | $29.99/mo | | ProteGear | Power users who want maximum flexibility | Pay per day | | Suspended | The cheapest way to keep 24/7 SOS (compatible devices) | ~$8/yr | Info I’ve paid for my own inReach device and subscription since 2014, when I got my first one. I buy all my own gear and don’t take sponsorships, so I’m free to use and recommend what works best. What You Get A Garmin inReach subscription is a monthly service plan, just like a cell phone plan. Two things have to be in place to get connected: an active subscription (these plans) and an inReach device to run it on. No plan means no SOS or messaging, even if you own the hardware. Here’s what a subscription unlocks: - Emergency SOS to the 24/7 Garmin Response center, who coordinate (but don’t perform) the rescue. Included on every plan, and still works when suspended on compatible devices - Two-way text messaging using satellite when you’re beyond cell range - Location tracking that shares a breadcrumb trail over satellite that others can follow on a map - Weather forecasts with hourly and multi-day outlooks, including a marine option - Photo and voice messages over satellite on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus and Mini 3 Plus - Check-in messages, three preset “I’m OK” type messages you can send for less than a normal message Pricing Levels Pricing on each plan is purely based on how much you use it. The more expensive the plan, the more usage you essentially prepay for. | Plan | Price/mo | Annual | Texts/Weather | Photo/Voice | Live Tracking | Check-ins | Text Overage | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Enabled | $7.99 | $95.88 | $0.50 ea | $1.00 ea | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | $0.10 ea | $0.50/msg | | Essential | $14.99 | $179.88 | 50 | 25 | $0.10/pt (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Standard | $29.99 | $359.88 | 150 | 50 | Unlimited (10 min+) | Unlimited | $0.50/msg | | Premium | $49.99 | $599.88 | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited (2 min+) | Unlimited | N/A | - There’s a one-time $39.99 activation fee on all plans, charged on every device, including inReach smartwatches like the Fenix 8 Pro. - A weather forecast counts as one satellite text message. - Incoming messages count too, including replies to your check-ins. - Emoji reactions (tapbacks) to messages in the Garmin Messenger app are billed the same as check-ins: free/unlimited on Essential, Standard, and Premium, and $0.10 each on Enabled. - Messages sent over Wi-Fi or cell through the Garmin Messenger app don’t count against your plan. Only satellite messages do. - Live tracking points always go out over satellite, so they’re always charged, even if your phone has signal. - A group message counts as a single message, but each reply costs a message. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices like the Messenger Plus, GPSMAP H1i Plus, and Mini 3 Plus. - You can switch between plans at any time for free. You can also keep more than one device active on a single account (a new option since the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro), but each one needs its own activation fee and subscription. - Every plan includes Emergency SOS messaging through Garmin Response. - The plan prices are identical whether you carry a Mini 2, Mini 3, Messenger, or a GPSMAP. Garmin charges for the plan, not the device, so the “Garmin inReach Mini 2 subscription cost” is the same as the Mini 3 or Messenger. - Photo and voice messages only work on inReach Plus-enabled devices, so on an older unit like the Mini 2 those rows simply don’t apply. - Smartwatches with inReach (like the Fenix 8 Pro) add unlimited LTE messaging and calling when you have cell service. Cost Calculator Enter your estimated monthly usage and how many months a year you use the device, and this shows the monthly and annual cost for each plan. Click “Edit Charges” to adjust pricing for your local currency or region. Edit Charges Simply change the numbers here based on your currency. Overages | Plan | Monthly | Annual | |---|---|---| | Enabled | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Essential | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Standard | $0.00 | $0.00 | | Premium | $0.00 | $0.00 | Annual is your monthly cost times the months you use it, assuming you suspend for $0 the rest of the year. Year one adds a one-time $39.99 activation fee on every plan. - Most people: Enabled, about $146 a year. Full SOS, and you only pay for the tracking and messages you actually use. - Track every hike? Standard. Unlimited tracking beats Enabled once you pass about 36 tracking hours a month. - Essential rarely wins. It only makes sense for steady messaging with almost no tracking. Any real tracking, around 25 hours a month, pushes you to Standard. - Premium is niche. It’s only worth it above about 190 messages a month, or if you need 2-minute tracking, like guiding a team or sailing. - Seasonal user? Suspend. Keep SOS on a compatible device for about $8 a year instead of paying all year. Suspending You can suspend your plan for $0 for up to 12 consecutive months, with no reactivation fee. This is the move for seasonal users, and it beats canceling, which wipes your data and charges a fresh $39.99 activation fee to come back. The big deal is SOS. On compatible devices, Emergency SOS keeps working while your plan is suspended, even though messaging, tracking, and weather are off. That means you can carry a working SOS beacon in the off-season for almost nothing. To qualify, it has to be a compatible device, on the latest firmware, and previously on an active plan before you suspend. Not every device supports it, and the list keeps growing, so check Garmin’s current compatible-device list before you count on it. Older units like the original Mini and Explorer don’t qualify. After 12 consecutive months suspended, Garmin automatically moves the device onto the Enabled plan ($7.99/mo) to keep SOS alive. So the real cost of free suspended SOS is one paid month every 13: twelve months free, then the single auto-Enabled month before you suspend again. Call it about $8 a year. Third Party Plans A few partners resell the same Iridium connection with different pricing. ProteGear is the one worth knowing, and its whole angle is pay-per-day instead of per-month. - Pay-per-day. A €49 yearly base, then only the days you’re active, from about €1.50/day (safety) to €6/day (expedition). Flip it on and off yourself for free. - Same safety net. SOS still routes to Garmin Response, and you keep the Garmin Explore account and apps. - Extras Garmin dropped or lacks. Editable preset messages, a dedicated two-way email address, tracking down to 30 seconds, better weather reports, and Wikipedia or Google News over satellite. - The catches. The dashboard and setup are power-user territory and can be confusing, but human support is excellent and responsive. If you’re in Australia or New Zealand, TrackMeNZ is another third party option. inReach Rentals If you only go off-grid occasionally, renting can beat buying a device and paying for a plan. Outfitters will mail you a unit for your trip, usually around $10 to $15 per day with a few-day minimum. The typical flow: - Order online and choose a data plan and insurance. - The device ships to your home or a pickup location. - You get setup instructions by email. - Use it, then mail it back. I don’t have any specific company I recommend. Google “Garmin inReach rentals” and compare options. inReach Professional Garmin’s Professional plans are built for teams, organizations, and families that want one account across multiple devices. - Central management. Run multiple devices under one login, assign them to users, and monitor everyone from a single dashboard. - Best for. Guides, SAR teams, land managers, and anyone coordinating a group in the field. - Pricing. Tiered by how much messaging and tracking your team needs, billed monthly. See Garmin’s Professional plans for current rates. - Off-season. You can suspend Pro devices and still keep SOS on compatible units, so a fleet doesn’t lose emergency coverage when it’s stood down. Rescue Costs Your subscription pays for the SOS service, not the rescue itself. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can cost thousands, which is what rescue insurance covers.

item.title: Garmin inReach SOS: How It Works & When to Use It
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 5.22
Garmin inReach SOS Guide Updated & Reviewed July 2026 The SOS button is the most important feature on a satellite communicator, and the one people understand the least. It’s not the same as calling 911. An inReach SOS routes to Garmin Response, a 24/7 center that coordinates with local rescue teams and messages with you the whole time. Here’s when to hit it and what to actually expect if you do. When to SOS - Unsure of a safe outcome? Hit it. The best advice I’ve heard, from an LA County search and rescue veteran: if you’re not sure you’ll be okay, press SOS. It’s two-way, so you can describe the situation, lost, stranded, chest pain, and Garmin Response helps you figure out what to do. - Not just for the backcountry. Garmin’s own SOS data is full of vehicle use: cars, boats, motorcycles. Carry it when you drive out of cell range, because a flat or a breakdown can just mean a tow, not a helicopter. - Medical issues and injuries are the top reasons people hit it. A pre-existing condition doesn’t disqualify you. If something feels wrong, ask. - More than half of SOS calls are for someone else. Like calling 911 as a Good Samaritan, hitting SOS for another person doesn’t make you liable. Just know that rescue insurance only covers you, not them. - Don’t abuse it. Being tired or having a sore stomach isn’t an emergency. Use common sense, same as you would with 911. Hitting the Button - There’s a countdown. Once you trigger it, the device counts down before the message goes out, and you can cancel during that window. - Sent one by mistake? Cancel it, don’t power off. Cancel the SOS on the device and reply to Garmin Response so they know you’re okay. Powering off leaves them assuming the worst, and a search may start anyway. - False alarms don’t cost you. Garmin doesn’t charge for an accidental activation you cancel. Cancelling isn’t an embarrassment, it’s the system working. - SOS can stay active on a suspended plan. On compatible devices you keep a working SOS button even with messaging suspended. Details on the subscription page. What Happens When You Hit SOS - A helicopter is not the default. Garmin’s data shows most rescues aren’t helicopters. They’re usually local volunteers organized by a sheriff’s department or park service. - It takes hours to mobilize. Even a helicopter rescue usually takes several hours. Be ready to wait, and carry enough to spend the night: an emergency bivy, extra layers, and food. - Rescue comes in many forms. It might be self-evacuation with guidance, a ground team, a cliff extraction, or just a ranger walking you down. I’ve seen that on Mount Whitney for altitude sickness. About 10% of people handle it themselves. - You stay in contact the whole time. Unlike a one-way PLB, Garmin Response keeps messaging you updates until help arrives. Rescue Costs Triggering SOS is included in every inReach plan, so there’s no charge to hit the button. The rescue itself is a separate question. Most rescues are free, but if a private helicopter or air ambulance gets involved it can run well over $20,000. That’s what rescue insurance is for, and I break down the options on that page.

item.title: RECCO Reflector Review: What It Is & Does It Work
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com Score: 4.55
RECCO Reflector Review Updated & Reviewed August 2026 Cheap, weightless insurance for being found, but only where rescue teams have detectors, and never instead of a satellite communicator. A RECCO reflector is a battery-free radar tag that makes you searchable to equipped rescue teams when you can’t call for help. After two years with one on my pack and talking to the SAR professionals who train with the detectors: if teams in your area carry them, it’s worth the $40. If they don’t, skip it. Either way, your primary is a satellite communicator; this is the passive backup that answers when every battery is dead. How I Earn I buy gear with my own money. It's the only way I can be 100% honest about what works. No sponsors, no free gear. Use the links below to buy, and you support these ad-free, independent reviews at no extra cost. Video What I learned in the two years since recommending the RECCO: what SAR teams told me, the documented rescues, and where it falls short. How It Works Crack one open and you’d find two foil antennas connected by a diode. No battery, no electronics, no registration. It’s a harmonic reflector, not an RFID tag. - The detector does the work. Rescuers carry a handheld detector, or fly a helicopter-mounted one, that broadcasts a specific radar frequency (917 MHz). - The reflector answers. When the signal hits the reflector, the diode doubles the frequency and bounces it back (1834 MHz). The detector hears that answer as a distinct chirp, so rescuers know it’s a RECCO and not a random piece of metal. - Closer means louder. The stronger the chirp, the closer the searcher is to you. The helicopter detector sweeps about a 300-foot swath and can clear roughly a square kilometer every six minutes. - False hits happen. Detectors sometimes get weak reflections off phones, radios, and other electronics, even powered off. A real reflector returns a much stronger, cleaner signal, and any ping still gives searchers a clue. Rescue Record Has RECCO found anyone? The question that matters, in three parts. - Documented live saves exist, all in avalanches. A skier in Spain was located alive under the snow in 2015, the first case published in medical literature. Another was found alive under 3.2 meters of snow in Switzerland in 2019. RECCO’s own count is 17 live saves through 2019, mostly in Europe, none in the US. - Recoveries are more common. Most confirmed finds are body recoveries, including climber Marc-André Leclerc (from the film The Alpinist) in Alaska in 2018, where rescuers who worked the search say RECCO was essential to locating him. That’s worth something on its own: it ends a search and gives a family an answer. - No documented live save of a lost hiker yet. The technology doesn’t care whether you’re alive, a reflector answers either way. The record is thin on summer rescues because few hikers carry reflectors and detector coverage is still growing. Every SAR professional I’ve talked to says the same thing: the tool works, the bottleneck is people carrying it. Coverage A reflector is only useful where someone has a detector. Check before you buy. - Check the coverage map. RECCO publishes a map of every team and resort with detectors that you can filter by handheld and helicopter units. If nobody near your trails has one, skip it. - US helicopter coverage is small but growing. Eleven US agencies fly the SAR helicopter detector as of mid-2026, including LA County Sheriff (the only one in California) and a new unit covering the Sierra out of Reno. Hundreds of ski patrols and SAR teams carry handhelds. - One reflector works everywhere. Detector frequencies vary slightly by country, but the same reflector answers all of them, US and Europe alike. Carrying It - You might already own one. RECCO has been sewn into ski jackets, pants, and helmets for over a decade, and it’s now showing up in backpacks and even trail runners. Check your gear for the logo before buying anything. - Old reflectors don’t expire. There’s no battery to die and nothing to wear out. A reflector in a 2012 jacket works like a new one. - Placement matters. Anything between the reflector and the detector weakens the signal, including your body, which is mostly water. High on your pack keeps it clear if you’re face down. The other school of thought puts it on your person (a belt loop) in case you’re separated from your pack. Or carry one in each spot. Be Searchable The reflector is one layer in a system. If you can’t hit SOS (heart attack, stroke, rockfall), these are the layers that get you found: - Leave a plan. Send someone your route link and a turnaround time. Searchers start where your plan says, not from the whole mountain. - Note your RECCO in your emergency details. Add “carrying RECCO reflector” to your inReach or PLB emergency notes and tell whoever holds your trip plan. SAR can only deploy a detector if they know to look for one. - Turn on tracking. inReach breadcrumbs give rescuers a trail to your last known point. - The RECCO is the last line of defense. A PLB’s homing beacon and your phone are useless after a few days of battery drain. The reflector still answers. From the comments: if everyone carries one, how do rescuers know who’s lost? They don’t scan the whole planet. They grid a defined search area for a missing person, and any return in that area gets checked. More reflectors make the tool stronger, not weaker. Worth $40? The materials inside are worth maybe $2, and yes, you could technically build one. What you’re paying for is a tested, sealed unit that’s part of a system rescue teams train on, and RECCO reinvests a portion of reflector sales into putting detectors in SAR hands, which is the only way coverage grows. For me the math is simple: a few grams and $40 for a chance of being found when nothing else on my pack works, and at worst, a faster answer for my family. I’m still carrying mine. If you hike where teams have detectors, it’s cheap insurance. If you don’t, spend the money elsewhere, and check the full gear list for where I’d put it instead.

item.title: 4 creative ways people use Android Auto outside of their cars
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.07
Android Auto is strongly associated with cars and driving. I mean, it is right there in the name. But while navigation gets most of the attention in its interface, Android Auto is really a simple interface with large buttons, voice controls, and easy access to a few essential apps, which makes it surprisingly useful beyond the driver's seat. With a third-party app like Open Headunit, you can turn an Android phone or tablet into an Android Auto display. It lets you run standalone Android Auto, but the best part is that it connects to your main phone, allowing you to use the interface on a second screen. Once you set the app up, there are plenty of creative ways to put it to work outside the car. Android Auto makes a ton of sense on a desk A dedicated desk display can be surprisingly handy I turned my old phone into an Android Auto display for my desk a couple of months ago, just to see how it would work, and it ended up being way more useful than I could've imagined. Many people repurpose their old phones by giving them a single task: they turn them into a Home Assistant dashboard, dedicated Spotify controller, or Gemini device. But with Android Auto, I don't have to choose—I get to have those big, easy-to-tap buttons for all my apps. My favorite part of this setup is that I can see messages from my phone at a glance when it's connected, and I don't have to pick up my phone if I want to respond immediately. And if I miss a message because I was focusing on my work, I can check what I missed in just a few quick taps. It's essentially like having my phone always propped up in front of me, but thanks to Android Auto, it's limited to a few essential apps, which really shows that it was designed to supplement driving as the primary activity. I'm not tempted to pick up my phone and start doomscrolling after every quick chat. Android Auto makes a great dashboard for two-wheeled vehicles Give your bike a smart dashboard Android Auto gets a lot of praise for how it revolutionized navigation and entertainment while driving, but a very similar activity—riding a motorcycle—barely gets any mention. And if there's a vehicle where you could make good use of navigation and, to a limited extent, other features, it's a motorcycle. Unfortunately, Android Auto support is limited to a handful of luxury touring bikes. But the good news is that there's no shortage of small, water-resistant aftermarket displays that clamp directly onto the handlebars, unlocking next-level navigation that you can put to excellent use on a fast two-wheeler. But motorcycles aren't the only two-wheelers where you can take advantage of Android Auto. Bicycles and electric scooters are another great place to repurpose an old phone for Android Auto. This way, you don't have to worry about cracking your primary phone or exposing it to the elements, and you get incredibly convenient access to navigation and music controls. A boat can make use of an Android Auto dashboard, too Take Android Auto out on the water Land vehicles have it easy with road navigation in Android Auto through apps like Waze and Google Maps, but all the things that make it great are surprisingly fitting for maritime navigation and entertainment as well—and MasterCraft Boat Holdings has finally announced that it's officially coming to some of its boats. But if you've got a boat, you don't have to wait to start using it right away. If you're willing to do some DIY, you can probably get a portable Android Auto head unit to work pretty easily. If that sounds like too much work, you can always repurpose an old phone or laptop instead. In any case, Android Auto on a boat makes a ton of sense. Apart from the usual Spotify and podcast apps, there's even a dedicated marine navigation app called Savvy Navvy. The app lets users discover optimal routes to places, check nearby boat traffic, get estimated times of arrival, and a lot more. A workshop is the perfect place to place a dedicated Android Auto dashboard Greasy hands and phones don't mix If you've got a workshop or perhaps just like to work on your car in the garage know how annoying it can be to deal with a phone while working on something. You have to take off your gloves, take the phone out of your pocket, and by the time you swipe to answer that call, the person on the other end has already hung up. But if you've got a dedicated Android Auto phone on your workbench or cart, it becomes way easier to keep track of messages and calls and respond to them hands-free. It's also a cool place to run your entertainment, and every time your phone rings, the music playing in the background automatically pauses, resuming after you're done with the call. Android Auto's big buttons make it surprisingly versatile Although Android Auto is primarily designed for driving, its simple, glanceable interface and the way it transforms your phone into a little dashboard actually make it a surprisingly versatile addition to a wide range of scenarios. You don't need to sit behind the wheel to benefit from having your favorite music apps, messages, and calls all accessible through a streamlined interface that prioritizes simplicity and minimal distractions above everything else.

item.title: The 5 times you really should use solid infill on your 3D printer
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.07
When you slice a 3D model to print, you have to make a decision about what the inside of that model will look like. Unless the designer created a custom internal structure, any open volume inside the model will be filled somehow. Most of the time, you'll want to use a type of "infill" that saves on material while still offering the right degree of strength. You can find plenty of arguments online about which patterns are best for what job, but most of the time no one will advise using 100% or "solid" infill because it's unnecessary and wasteful. However, the option exists for a reason, and these are a few of the times when you'll want to move that infill density slider all the way to the right. Small parts where infill barely has room to work What is this? Infill for ants? This issue is simple enough to understand. When you're printing objects that are very small, like gears, spacers, clips, pins, brackets, and the like, they have so little internal volume that the algorithm for generating infill has nothing to work with. It will still attempt it, but the results can be strange, and even result in part that will break too easily or fail. Your slicer might automatically mitigate this, but with solid infill, it's just a straightforward print, and since these parts are so small anyway, you wouldn't have saved much in materials anyway. Parts you plan to drill, tap, or machine afterward What this needs is more holes There are cases where you'll want to modify a 3D-printed part after making it, and if that involved drilling holes in it, tapping threads, or trimming parts to get a perfect fit, then hollow infill can be an issue. Screws need solid internal material to grip. Trimming the end of a model and exposing the infill might not look right, or cause issues with strength and durability as one wall is weakened. By using solid infill, you're putting more material inside the print to work with. You can, of course, change your model so that it already has screw thread or holes in the right places. You also don't have to use solid infill across the entire model. Areas around screws, inserts, bearings, and press fits Heavy metal needs heavy materials Since you might only want solid infill specifically around screw holes, press-fit parts, fasteners, or any bit of the model that's likely to experience high loads, you may feel like you're stuck between all-solid models or sparse infill, but that's not true! In programs like Orca Slicer, you can use "modifier meshes" to alter the print settings for specific parts of the print. So, you might have 90% of your print use regular square or honeycomb infill, but then have specific parts that need it using solid infill. The infill pattern isn't the only thing you can change. You can alter all sorts of settings that influence print quality and strength. That lets you strike a good balance between material saving, weight, and model strength. Prints that actually need the extra weight Gaining weight is hard when you're hollow inside One of the reasons to use sparse infill is to make the models lighter, but sometimes you want your model to weigh more. The reasons for this can vary, but tall bases and stands benefit from having a lower center of gravity. You can use the aforementioned modifier meshes to make only some parts solid to transfer the weight where you need it, but this is the simplest way to make a model heavier. That said, most filaments aren't particularly dense anyway, compared to materials like metals. So if you really need weight, the more complex method is to leave cavities inside the model, stop the print, and then place your metal weights before letting the printer complete the job, sealing the weights in. You can also do this with magnets, which opens up all sorts of other cool possibilities. My colleague Joe Fedewa has even used Plaster of Paris to add weight to 3D models, by pouring it into cavities. You can see here how he created a design specifically for this, and since the plaster sets so quickly, it's not even necessary to encapsulate it in the model. Parts that will be heavily sanded, cut, or reshaped When you're not quite sure if it's going to be right One of the main selling points of 3D printing is rapid prototyping, and sometimes in that process you'll be physically modifying a part to make it fit or alter its purpose. In that case, you'll want it to be solid, so that you can cut and send it as you need to. Then, you can measure the dimensions of the modified part and alter your model file to match. Another use case is if you're printing cosplay parts that are going to fit for someone, sanded, cut, shaped, and painted. In that case, you probably also want things like armor pieces or masks to be printed with solid infill. Experienced cosplayers may instead use tools to leave the deep interior of the piece with sparse infill, and then beef up the outer wall thickness to withstand sanding and heavier modification, but each project has different needs.

item.title: A $25 power bank is all you need to stay online during a power outage
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.77
As a general rule, it makes good sense to plug your networking gear into an uninterruptible power supply (UPS). But does that mean that every single home and every single router requires that additional expense? Nope. In fact, certain router owners can get by with a dirt-cheap power bank and nothing else, and their connection will still be secured during a blackout. Here's how it works. Your router uses surprisingly little power Keeping Wi-Fi alive doesn't take that much battery Look, I firmly believe that plugging your network gear into a UPS is great, especially if you're running a home server. But the reason isn't that your router consumes some crazy amount of power, because it really doesn't. At least most of them don't. Compared to most electronics in your home, routers are surprisingly low-key. Take Amazon's eero brand as an example. The eero 6+ averages around 4.5W, while the eero 7 and eero 7 Pro average about 7W. That's nothing compared to most of the stuff that's plugged into any of your outlets at any given time. These modest requirements make it so that during a blackout, you don't have to scramble and wish you'd bought that expensive UPS. All you need is a power bank. A battery designed to charge a phone or a tablet at 30-45W has plenty of output headroom for a router, so that shouldn't be a problem. Well, it can still be a problem if your router is one of those intense $600 gaming beasts. Of course, the power bank still has to support the voltage and current profile your particular router expects, so this isn't a blanket promise, but it is worth checking out. It's especially easy and convenient to do with routers that already use USB-C for power, such as several eero models, which is why I mentioned them in the first place. Without that USB-C power, you'll probably have to mess around with USB-C PD to DC barrel jack trigger cable. A $25 power bank already has more than enough output You don't need anything super fancy You really don't need anything fancy for this to work. Many power banks will do the trick. For the sake of this article, I picked out the INIU 45W power bank, which fits the under $25 bracket. It can deliver up to 45W over USB-C, and that's comfortably above something like an eero 6+ or eero 7 might ask for. From a raw power perspective, it'll get you what you need to keep the router going during a blackout.
