In addition, this card earns 10% back in Disney Rewards Dollars on purchases with the three Disney-owned streaming services, so not only will cardholders get reimbursed for the subscription, but they'll also earn some rewards that they can redeem for theme park tickets, resort stays, cruise line packages, Disney Store purchases and more. Bonus: Disney+, ESPN or Hulu through the American Express Blue Cash Cards Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express cardmembers receive up to $7 monthly in statement credit (up to an $84 annual value). Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express cardmembers can get up to $10 per month in statement credit toward their Disney digital entertainment (up to a $120 annual value). Terms apply. Keep in mind. Neither of these cards will cover the cost of a streaming service subscription completely. The cheapest monthly subscription to Disney+ or Hulu, for example, costs $11.99 — and that's with ads. All information about the Bank of America® Premium Rewards Elite credit card has been collected independently by NerdWallet. To view rates and fees of the American Express Platinum Card®, see this page. To view rates and fees of the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express, see this page. To view rates and fees of the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express, see this page. How to maximize your rewards

item.title: No Trail Shoes? Here’s How to Hike Safely in Sneakers and Not Wreck Your Feet, According to Podiatrists.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.42
(Photo: Canva) This article has been medically reviewed by Peter Mason, PT, DPT, OCS, a board-certified orthopedic physical therapist. Very few decisions can ruin a scenic hike, but choosing the wrong footwear is one of them. Podiatrists agree that for moderate to advanced hiking on rocky, uneven terrain (think: a surface that could roll an ankle), you need hiking boots or hiking shoes. But if you’re headed up a gradual incline on a well-maintained trail constructed with packed dirt, you can likely still have a smooth, comfortable outing in your gym or running sneakers. Whether you’re on vacation and didn’t pack your hiking boots, or you’re a city-dwelling runner or cyclist seeking active recovery in nature, here’s how to know when it’s OK to hit the trails in sneakers—and tips for doing so safely. If you’re looking to hike in sneakers, Anne Sharkey, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist based in Austin, Texas, said that it’s important to research the terrain before embarking on your hike. Trails with lots of loose rocks and tree roots can cause your foot to roll if your shoe isn’t supportive enough, while creeks or streams and slick surfaces can lead to falls if you don’t have enough traction on your outsoles. “You can see this wide spectrum of problems or pathologies that can occur just from not being in the right shoes,” Sharkey told Outside. Since hiking boots and shoes tend to feature thicker soles and deeper treads—the pattern of divots on the bottom of the shoe—they provide more traction and stability on loose surfaces. High-cut boots will also hold your ankles in place to help prevent sprains—one of the most common hiking injuries, board-certified podiatrist Elynor Giannin Perez, DPM, told Outside. “As soon as there’s going to be any amount of loose gravel where you’re off of paved trails or hitting more uneven surfaces, that’s where I would say, ‘I’m going to wear a trail shoe instead of a running shoe for this,’” Sharkey said. When in doubt, opt for a short hike on a well-maintained trail if sneakers are all you have access to, and save the scree fields and bouldering for another day. Still, be careful with very high-cushion sneakers because they add extra height, which can create ankle instability. Every distance runner knows the importance of keeping toenails short to prevent bruising and nail loss. Hiking, especially downhill, also puts repeated pressure on your nails, so it’s important to trim them before you head out. And since sneakers tend to have thin mesh uppers with little-to-no toe protection, you’ll want to take extra care to avoid kicking or jamming your feet into anything when hiking in them. Hiking can increase blood flow to the feet and cause swelling, Perez said, so even if your shoes feel good at the start of a hike, they may be too tight by the end of it. Ill-fitting footwear can lead to ingrown toenails and calluses—even over the course of a short trek. To leave yourself some room, she recommends wiggling all your toes when you put your sneakers on: you should be able to do so without restriction. Another good test is to ensure there’s at least a thumb’s width of distance between your longest toe and the end of your shoe, Sharkey added. To check, put a thumb in the back of your shoe, just behind your heel. If you can fit your thumb in there without much force, you’re good to go. If you can’t pass those two tests, you’ll need to choose a pair of sneakers that has a wider toe box and is one size (or more) larger than your usual, depending on the shoe and the shape of your foot. Opting for roomier shoes can help prevent blisters as well—as long as you pair them with a good pair of thick, cushioned socks. Make sure to lace them properly, too; sloppily tied shoes can wreck stability and put you at risk for injury. No matter your footwear, warming up your feet, ankles, and Achilles before a hike can help prevent injuries, Perez said. At the start of the hike, do a few rounds of standing calf stretches, calf raises, and “good morning” stretches to prepare the lower body for movement. To do a good morning, stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and then place your hands behind your head. Lower your hips back and down as if you were trying to press your butt against an imaginary wall. Keep lowering your hips back until your chest is parallel to the floor. You should feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings. Then slowly return to standing. (This hips-back-and-down movement is the same method you use in a Romanian deadlift.) As you climb unfamiliar terrain, especially in sneakers, it’s important to watch your step. If that means slowing down the pace a bit, that’s fine—all the more time to take in the landscape. “If you hit an uneven surface, you’re more prone to an ankle sprain in a running shoe versus a trail shoe,” Sharkey said. If you know you’re prone to ankle injuries, you might want to wear a light ankle sleeve or brace “as a kind of substitute for a shoe that doesn’t have as much stability,” she said. Hiking in a mesh running shoe is a recipe for wet feet, which can breed fungus and create blisters. Perez says to pack an extra pair of socks, just in case your feet get sweaty or you hit an unexpected water crossing. And keep some band-aids or medical tape on hand so that if a blister does develop, you can address it quickly and keep it covered until you can do a more complete triage at home. As always, staying hydrated and fueled will help you feel and perform your best, so be sure to bring along some snacks (here are a few of Outside‘s favorites) and enough water. “Usually, people who do a lot of exercise and are athletic assume pain will just go away, and they can keep going,” Perez said. But it’s important to note any pain or discomfort. The trick is knowing when to push forward and when to stop. For instance, slight discomfort can be normal and may be attributed to fatigue. However, if, on a scale of one to ten, you’d rate your pain at three or higher, that’s past mild ache territory and time to end the hike. If any pain alters your natural gait, it’s best to stop, rest your feet for a bit, or see a doctor if the pain is intense. If you feel determined to push through, do so with caution and keep the following in mind: Perez said even a dull ache could be the start of something more serious, like a stress fracture or strain, and according to Sharkey, when pain takes over, it’s natural for your body to compensate in other ways. This may put you at a greater risk for slipping, falling, or injury, especially if your shoes are on the flimsier side. But if you’re ever in doubt—you can always hike another day. Even a short hike can make your body move in ways it usually doesn’t—especially if you’re new to it. So show your feet some TLC when you get home by stretching them out, sticking them in an ice bath, or running them over a small foam roller to release tension. Perez said that, for those with plantar fasciitis or heel pain, rolling your feet over a frozen water bottle might be a nice follow-up to a day on the trails. Another option is to take rest days between your hiking treks; intermittent breaks can prevent overuse injuries. After you chill for a day or two, it’s time to refuel, sleep, and dream of the hiking shoes you’re going to put on your birthday wishlist. About the medical reviewer: Peter Mason, PT, DPT, OCS is a board-certified orthopedic physical therapist based in Wyoming. His clinical work centers on the evaluation and rehabilitation of active and athletic populations, with a particular focus on runners, cyclists, CrossFit athletes, and mountain sport athletes, including hunters, climbers, and backcountry recreationalists. His approach integrates evidence-based orthopedic rehabilitation, load management, and detailed movement analysis, with an emphasis on helping athletes return to performance in complex, real-world environments. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: A Climber Dropped His Backpack in a Crevasse in 1963. The Ice Just Gave It Back.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.75
A photo taken during the 1963 summit attempt (Photo: Courtesy of Tyrol State Police) In August 1963, German climber Alfred Rothfischer, then 23, was returning from summiting Schrankogel—Austria’s second-highest peak in the Stubai Alps—when he fell into a crevasse. He was crossing a glacier, and it could have been a mountaineering disaster save for his quick thinking. He hucked his heavy backpack, lightening his load and steadying his feet. He was safe; only his backpack was lost. That is, until 63 years later. On July 16, 2026, a mountain guide leading a group across Sulztalferner Glacier discovered the backpack and its contents partially revealed in melting ice, Austrian officials with the Tyrol State Police said in a statement. The weathered bag sat at an elevation of roughly 9,695 feet. Inside were an ice axe, a camera, a whistle, and a damaged folder with papers dating to the 1950s and 1960s. Police said they initially investigated whether the pack could be tied to an unreported accident from decades ago, but a closer inspection of the papers in the sack showed Rothfischer’s name faintly written, according to Austrian newspaper Kronen Zeitung. “When I entered the name into the search engine, a landline number in Bavaria appeared. I called it,” investigating police officer Gregor Gatt from the Neustift police station told Kronen Zeitung. Now 86, Rothfischer recounted his harrowing tale over a phone call with Gatt. He was hiking with two climbing partners at the time of his accident, a three-man rope team, when he slipped and fell. He dangled about 24 feet above the crevasse before his friends helped him out. Rothfischer survived the fall with minimal injuries and reported the missing backpack with identification documents to local police, according to Kronen Zeitung. On August 25, police returned the recovered equipment to Rothfischer’s son. Sulztalferner, where Rothfischer dropped the pack, lost about 67 feet between 2024 and 2025 and has retreated 4,970 feet since 1923, the Austrian Alpine Club estimates. Those trends are consistent across Europe, too. A 2025 study published in the science journal Nature found that glaciers in the continent’s central part, including the Alps and the nearby Pyrenees, lost about 39 percent of their ice between 2000 and 2023. The backpack is among the latest slew of weird items recovered from melting glaciers. In July 2026, a hiker encountered human remains on Switzerland’s Trift Glacier that DNA testing later identified as two Belgian alpinists who disappeared in 1992, The Associated Press reported. In October 2025, hikers found a body that melted out of a glacier on Ober Gabelhorn, Switzerland. Authorities later determined it belonged to a climber who went missing in November 1994. And in July 2023, hikers came across the body of a climber uncovered in melting ice near the Matterhorn, also in Switzerland. Melting ice has revealed more than just bodies, too. In August 2026, the wreckage of a 1968 crash melted out of the Aletsch Glacier in Switzerland, and a retreating glacier in Italy’s Stelvio National Park exposed a complete shelter built by WWI-era soldiers. Here, archaeologists later found beds, coins, clothing, and furnishings. Since 2010, search teams in Alaska have also found the remains of several plane crashes in melting glaciers, including the remnants of an aircraft with 52 people on board.

item.title: How Reju Is Turning Polyester Textile Waste Into New Materials
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.29
Former sportswear executive Patrik Frisk, now CEO of Reju, stands among mounds of textile waste that his company plans to turn back into new outerwear materials. (Photo: Reju) Patrik Frisk has spent his entire career selling polyester. At companies like Under Armour, The North Face, and Gore-Tex, he oversaw the production of synthetic base layers and fleeces, technical shells and packs—all made, at least in part, with the petroleum-derived material. But looking back on three decades in the sportswear industry, Frisk has been left with the uncomfortable realization that much of what he helped put into the world will eventually be thrown into the mountainous pile of textile waste, ending up in landfills or incinerators. In a way, he’s now cleaning up his mess. As CEO of Reju, Frisk is working to develop technology that can turn discarded polyester textiles back into new materials. “If we don’t do it, you and I are going to be swimming together in the waste,” Frisk says. The problem is so much bigger than just those outdoor brands Frisk once led. Plastic in fabric form, polyester is the most ubiquitous synthetic fiber in the world, with more than 124 million tons produced each year. It is a workhorse in outdoor gear, prized for its durability, low cost, versatility, and performance, and it’s in everything from midlayer fleece and running shirts to backpacks, tents, and sleeping bags. Polyester is simply too useful to stop producing. Yet less than one percent of textile waste is recycled back into new fibers for clothing. That means most polyester has a one-way trip: from fossil fuels to fibers to goods and garments, many of which are inevitably tossed after only a few years in somebody’s closet. Through Reju, Frisk is trying to disrupt that cycle, intercepting polyester on its way to the dump. Founded in 2023, Reju is backed by the French engineering and technology company Technip Energies. Reju’s corporate offices are in Paris, where Frisk lives, and its pilot textile-to-textile recycling plant is in Frankfurt, Germany. There, at what Reju calls the Regeneration Hub, engineers and chemists have been testing different processes. To start, post-consumer polyester garments, no longer wearable, are stripped of zippers, buttons, and other trimmings, then shredded or cut into tiny little pieces. Herein lies the challenge that has long stumped textile recyclers: Polyester is rarely the only fiber content. A typical garment might combine it with cotton, nylon, or elastane, and separating those fibers has long been one of the thorniest problems in the world of circularity. Reju’s process, however, uses chemistry to tease apart those materials, isolating the polyester and breaking the polymer down into a monomer. What’s left behind is a powder of pure polyester that is turned into polyester pellets, which can then be extruded into fiber and yarn, and finally made back into a fabric of high quality. The long-term goal is to eventually partner with brands—perhaps Under Armour or The North Face?—that will buy and use the fabric for new garments. “The end game here should be that we take whatever is produced, and put it back into the value chain of the brands,” Frisk says. A point of resistance: The Reju process is quite pricey. But Frisk argues that for years, brands have already been paying to turn plastic waste back into polyester, using PET water bottles and even fishing nets. Those bottles are mechanically shredded into flakes, melted, and spun into fiber—a process that, Frisk says, degrades the polyester each time it’s recycled, gradually reducing the quality of the material and limiting how many times it can be recycled. Frisk, who was an early advocate of the system, sees this as a significant limitation of mechanical recycling. Why, then, turn an apple into an orange when you could make a better apple? Reju’s process, he says, introduces something new and better, using the material world’s finite resources as the solution. But before Reju can even consider selling its material, first it has to build the infrastructure. This year, Reju announced its initial two U.S. facilities. A Regeneration Hub in Rochester, New York, is expected to begin operations in 2029, and a Research & Development Center in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, will focus on developing new recycling technologies. By no coincidence, Rochester is also home to Goodwill of the Finger Lakes headquarters. Reju has spent the past three years working with the organization, as well as Waste Management, to figure out how to “minimize the waste and maximize the value”—and, Frisk says, not “resort to bailing that up and shipping it into some foreign country.” Goodwill of the Finger Lakes CEO and President Jennifer Lake has a front row seat to what’s being hand-sorted, and therefore what items still have value and what items don’t end up on shelves. Over the last five years, the number of low-value items that end up at Goodwill has increased, says Lake, who chairs the company’s circularity committee. “When you think of things that are beyond the point of repair, is there a way for them to be turned into, in textile’s case, the textiles of tomorrow?” Lake says. For gear users who are increasingly conscious of repairing their gear and wondering where it goes when it finally wears out, Reju offers a reason for optimism. By the time its New York hub is operational, in about three years, the company hopes to regenerate the equivalent of 300 million garments annually. And polyester is just the start.

item.title: The Grand Canyon Was Rocked by a Flash Flood. One Person Is Dead and More than 20 Hikers Are Still Missing.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.19
A debris flow in front of the Phantom Ranch Ranger Station sign (Photo: NPS) This is a developing story. We will continue to update this article as more information becomes available. At least two people have died, and another 15 are missing after a flash flood tore through Grand Canyon National Park, causing significant damage to hiking areas. On August 29, floodwaters pummeled Bright Angel Canyon, a ravine that feeds into the Grand Canyon, and Phantom Ranch, the lodge at the canyon’s base, destroying historic bridges, trails, and structures. In a multi-agency news briefing, NPS Incident Commander David Black said authorities have accounted for all but one missing person in Grand Canyon National Park, per the permit system. Initially, the NPS received reports of at least 30 missing hikers. Black added that some day hikers in the area were not required to register a hiking permit, and the NPS does not know how many hikers entered the canyon without one. People with information about any hikers in the canyon should call the ISB tip line at 1-888-653-0009. Brian Drapeaux, deputy superintendent of Grand Canyon National Park, added that older sections of the Trans-Canyon Waterline are “battered, bruised and decimated” in certain areas. More responders are being sent to the park on September 1. Both the North and South Rims of the Grand Canyon are open to the public, Drapeaux said. In response to the flash floods, authorities closed the Colorado River for the first time in known history. The NPS has since reopened the river to private and commercial river trips. In an email to Outside, Phantom Ranch concessionaire Xanterra Travel Collection reported no known damage to buildings at this time. Andy Stiles, Xanterra general manager at the Grand Canyon South Rim, said that his team has been supporting evacuations in coordination with the NPS and Arizona Department of Public Safety. “Phantom Ranch will remain closed until it is safe for guests and employees to return,” Stiles said. “In addition, South Rim lodges cannot accommodate overnight guests through September 6.” Affected guests are being contacted directly. Stiles added that visitors with existing reservations that cannot be rebooked are receiving refunds. NPS has recovered two bodies. In a statement on August 30, NPS wrote that the agency recovered a 46-year-old male near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. An estimated 15 people are still missing. Authorities have estimated that at least 40 percent of the Transcanyon Waterline was damaged or destroyed. Visitors are asked to remain out of the closure area while search and recovery operations continue. The following areas remain closed until further notice: The NPS says it may close additional areas as the full extent of the damage becomes known. For more information on trail closures, Backpacker is updating this interactive map. At least 62 people have been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail, a 14-mile hiking route from the canyon’s North Rim. More evacuations are scheduled for August 30 from Cottonwood Campground and Phantom Ranch, authorities said. “If you know of hikers or backpackers who were in the Bright Angel Creek corridor on August 29, or if you had a campground reservation in the affected area, please contact the NPS Investigative Services Branch (ISB),” NPS wrote in a statement. People with information about hikers in the following areas should email ISB at nps_isb@nps.gov or call the ISB tip line at 1-888-653-0009: “Please provide any information you have, including a person’s name, approximate location, travel plans, group size, clothing or backpack description, or when they were last known to be in the area. You do not have to provide your name,” NPS wrote. In an update sent to Outside, the NPS said all overnight lodgings in the park are closed to guests beginning Monday, August 31. This includes hotel facilities operated by Xanterra, such as El Tovar, Bright Angel Lodge, Maswik Lodge, and Phantom Ranch, as well as Delaware North’s Yavapai Lodge and Trailer Village. Officials closed the Colorado River to boaters, citing concerns over metal structures and debris entering the river. Isabell Holt, a spokesperson for Arizona Raft Adventures, told Outside that their commercial trips are currently permitted to launch. NPS is advising anyone with plans to visit the canyon to contact their outfitters or the River Permit office for more information. “Grand Canyon National Park staff, in coordination with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, are continuing evacuation and response efforts and working to account for individuals who may have been in the affected area,” the National Park Service said in a statement sent to Outside. “Evacuees are being transported to the Maswik Lodge Cafeteria on the South Rim, where the American Red Cross is coordinating assistance, NPS wrote. “No injuries have been reported as of the latest available information.” Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek, a fast-flowing tributary that flows into the Colorado River, have been destroyed. Hikers no longer have access to the area, which includes the historic Phantom Ranch landmark. “Park staff is continuing to assess damage to trails, bridges, utilities, facilities and other infrastructure,” NPS wrote. Authorities warn that additional rainfall is expected on August 31, which the NPS says could lead to more flash floods, debris flows, rockfall, and changing trail and river conditions. Hikers and boaters should contact their commercial outfitter or the NPS River Permits Office for more information about any upcoming trips.

item.title: Microsoft Finally Lets You Dismiss the OneDrive Prompts for Good
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.74
If you don't use OneDrive, you can finally dismiss prompts for Microsoft's cloud backup service in Windows 11 25H2. The next time a OneDrive pop-up appears asking you to protect your files, you can simply opt out of further suggestions, Windows Latest reports. With Windows 11, Microsoft integrated several of its first-party services more deeply than before. OneDrive was a big part of that, and every time you installed Windows 11, you'd be prompted to install it. Often, the only way to avoid it was to select "skip for now" or "remind me in 3 days," so a pop-up was always looming. Now, however, when the "Protect your files" reminder appears in Windows 11, it includes a new Opt out of backup selection. Click it, and the notice will no longer appear. Microsoft tries to upsell you on the idea beforehand, promising to effectively backup your PC's files and folders, retain memories, and sync across your devices. If you don't want it, though, you can now say so, and Microsoft will seemingly respect that choice. OneDrive is a capable backup solution; it earned our Editors' Choice award for its overall completeness, reliability, and polish. But if you already have a cloud backup service of choice, the pop-ups could get annoying. Microsoft offers several methods to pause OneDrive syncing with Windows or unlink it from your main account. But that's a lot of hoops to jump through. This change doesn't kill off OneDrive; Microsoft recently trialed a OneDrive Photos app that's seemingly designed to replace the existing Windows Photos app with a cloud-connected one. It implements some AI features like facial detection, but its automated rollout to users who weren't expecting it didn't set it up well for its initial launch. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Asus Zenbook A16 Review: A Featherweight 16-Inch OLED Powerhouse
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.53
Luxury pricing for laptops often comes down to two things: performance and panache. This year's Asus Zenbook A16 (starting at $1,699.99) aims for both, combining high-end processing power with a distinctively rich, tactile build. The result is a lightweight and premium ultraportable laptop in a desktop-replacement size, complete with Copilot+ PC features. With a 16-inch OLED display, Qualcomm's top-tier Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme processor, and a staggering amount of memory, the Zenbook A16 makes a compelling case for the modern flagship, earning an Editors' Choice award for big-screen ultraportables, a rare breed. Going in, you need to know two big things about the Zenbook A16: configuration options are limited, and the pricing options are puzzling. The model we tested—briefly listed at Best Buy for $1,699—comes equipped with the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme (X2E-94-100) processor, part of Qualcomm's flagship line of laptop CPUs. Our test unit also sported a 2,880-by-1,800-pixel OLED touch screen. However, at press time, this configuration was no longer being sold. For buyers seeking peak headroom, Asus also sells a version with the slightly higher-spec Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme X2E-96-100, along with a more expensive Windows 11 Pro license, for $2,199 in the Asus Store. This Asus model has a similar 3K OLED display, but no touch-screen capability. Both of these options come with 1TB SSD and 48GB of dual-channel, 128-bit LPDDR5X memory. That is a deeply impressive hardware combination aimed at heavy AI users, providing plenty of on-device capability through a powerful NPU, and qualifying the Zenbook A16 as a Microsoft Copilot+ PC. Pairing that with such a massive memory allotment is frankly a tad extravagant given current memory prices. However, it's also the only RAM configuration currently sold in North America. Before you start dreaming up ways to strip those memory modules for resale, know that they are soldered directly to the motherboard—upgrading or removing the DRAM is out of the question. Just to make things more confusing, retail costs are inconsistent across sellers. Best Buy lists a version featuring the same X2E-94-100 processor and 48GB of RAM for $1,899.99 despite pairing it with a smaller 512GB SSD. Meanwhile, online retailer ExcaliberPC offers that exact same 512GB configuration at a promotional price of $1,699.99, making it all the more important to shop around for the best price, regardless of the configuration. Asus dresses up the Zenbook in a magnesium-alloy chassis that would be impressively lightweight all on its own. But the machine also comes with Asus' Ceraluminum coating, which uses impressive material science to achieve a ceramic-like finish, boosting the rigidity and durability of the build while keeping the weight down to just 2.87 pounds. The finish genuinely feels like real ceramic, closer to tile or stone than an all-metal laptop chassis. It comes in two color options: Zabriskie Beige and Iceland Gray. The finish doesn't just look good, though: It is highly resistant to wear, scratches, smudges, and even minor drops or shocks. A rigid build means you don't get the keyboard flex common on ultra-thin 16-inch laptops, though you may notice a slight flex in the lid if you open it by a single corner. And the total package is half a pound lighter than direct competitors, such as the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro (3.5 pounds) and Acer Swift 16 AI (2026, 3.4 pounds), without feeling flimsy. As for size, this 16-inch laptop measures roughly 14 by 10 inches, giving it an impressively compact footprint for the screen size. It also measures just 0.65 inch thick, slim enough to easily carry by hand or in a laptop bag. The Zenbook's display also gets the premium treatment, serving up a 16-inch Asus Lumina OLED panel with 16:10 aspect ratio and ultra-thin bezels for 90% screen-to-body ratio. With a 3K native resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate, the panel proves sharp and fluid, delivering the vibrant color and deep contrast expected from OLED technology. It's also well-suited for HDR content, receiving a VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1000 rating and producing a peak HDR brightness of 1,100 nits. My review model has a touch screen with a glossy glass surface, which offers intuitive touch controls, but it was prone to noticeable reflections from overhead lights and smudged easily. Note that the laptop doesn't come with a stylus, but the touch screen fully supports active digitizers, including the Asus Pen 2.0, the Microsoft Surface Pen, and other models. Appropriately enough, using the Zenbook A16 is a luxurious hands-on experience. Matching the Ceraluminum chassis, the keycaps feature their own specialized ceramic-like coating rated to resist fingerprints and oil smudges across 50,000 of what Asus calls "rubbing cycles," essentially a lifetime of use and physical wear. With 1.3mm of travel, each keystroke provides satisfying depth and snappy tactile feedback. The backlit keys give you clean visibility in dim rooms, and stay legible in bright daytime environments. (On the downside, you don't get a numeric keypad on this model, and the arrow cluster uses half-height cursor keys.) The top-right corner houses a chamfered power button, though US models do not include an integrated fingerprint reader. The laptop sports a huge glass touchpad, one of the biggest we've seen on any machine, at 5.9 by 3.7 inches. The surface extends down to the front lip of the palm rest, providing smooth gliding and swiping, though the mechanical click mechanism felt a bit stiff during testing. Then there's a bigger issue (so to speak): The oversize surface left the pad prone to accidental palm touches and cursor jumps. It’s a minor shame, as standard touchpads have mostly solved this issue with palm-rejection software. Above the display sits a full HD front-facing webcam with infrared support for Windows Hello facial recognition. The chassis, though, lacks a physical privacy shutter. While not strictly required, a physical cover always provides extra peace of mind when connected. Asus does include a pleasingly compact 130-watt power adapter that keeps total carry weight low. The company also throws in a protective sleeve, which is a welcome touch. On the software side, Windows 11 Home comes bundled with several preinstalled Asus utilities: Asus GlideX, ScreenXpert, MyAsus, StoryCube, and Asus Recovery. The most useful is MyAsus, which allows fine-tuning for adaptive screen dimming, AI noise cancellation, and fan-cooling profiles. Security features include an integrated Microsoft Pluton security processor alongside firmware-level TPM 2.0 protection. On the left edge, the Zenbook features two USB 4.0 Type-C ports supporting up to 40Gbps transfer speeds, DisplayPort video output, and charging. An HDMI port allows easy connection to external monitors, accompanied by a 3.5mm audio jack. The right side houses a single USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A port (10Gbps) and a full-size SD-card reader. Having both USB-C ports on the left side can get awkward when routing cables or managing multiple peripherals, but the legacy port reduces the need for adapters and dongles. The laptop's wireless connectivity runs on Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. For this review, we evaluated the Zenbook A16 against several high-end competitors in the large-screen ultraportable category. Some, like the Asus Vivobook S 15 ($1,399.99), come close to the Zenbook's lightweight portability. However, most are heavier by several ounces, like the Acer Swift 16 AI ($1,799.99), Apple's 2025 M5 MacBook Pro 14-Inch ($2,349), and the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro ($2,649.99). Beyond mere physical footprint, this group's internal hardware spans a broad spectrum of power, memory, and platform architecture. The budget-friendly Vivobook S 15 keeps its price down by relying on a previous-generation Snapdragon X Elite chip paired with a modest 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD. Meanwhile, the Intel-powered Acer Swift 16 AI and Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro—alongside Apple’s M5 MacBook Pro—all standardize on 32GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. What truly sets the Zenbook A16 apart in this premium field is its hardware allocation: It packs a massive 48GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s flagship Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme processor, delivering heavy-workload headroom and next-gen Arm efficiency in a chassis that remains lighter than smaller 14-inch competitors. Our primary tests for Arm-based laptops are CPU-centric or processor-intensive. Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the freeware video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Other tests we usually use on Windows systems, namely UL's PCMark 10, aren't available for Arm-based CPUs, so they're excluded from this comparison. Windows on Arm has far better app compatibility than before, but it can't run everything that x86-based PCs can. In the benchmarks we have for Arm-based systems, the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme performed exceptionally well. Its single-core Cinebench 2024 score of 151 points put it right alongside rival Intel and Apple hardware. In multi-core rendering, it dominated this field, scoring nearly 1,500 points where competing systems struggled to break 1,000. In the HandBrake video-transcoding test, performance was slightly slower than average, finishing in 4 minutes and 40 seconds (4:40), compared with the 4:29, or faster, that competitors delivered. For casual use, that's a minor margin, but the seconds really add up if you're doing heavy video editing with longer exports. The Zenbook regained its lead in Geekbench Pro, topping 22,000 points where competing laptops failed to cross 18,000. Overall, Qualcomm’s flagship chip delivers outstanding computing power, provided your primary apps run natively or emulate well. We challenge each reviewed system’s graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next two, Steel Nomad's regular (4K) and Light (1440p) subtests, focus on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. A fifth test, Solar Bay, measures ray-tracing performance. Because the Zenbook A16 relies on integrated graphics rather than a discrete GPU, it isn't designed for heavy AAA gaming. Nevertheless, it posted impressive scores across our synthetic 3DMark suite. It landed near the top of its class in several subtests, trailed primarily by the Apple MacBook Pro M5. Apple's unified architecture gives it a unique advantage in GPU-heavy workloads, but the Zenbook holds its own remarkably well for an ultra-thin integrated system. We test laptops' battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. We also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor-calibration sensor and software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). While competing systems pulled ahead in total battery endurance, the Zenbook’s results were far from disappointing. Where machines like the MacBook Pro and Galaxy Book6 Pro stretched past the 24-hour mark, the Zenbook A16 logged 18.5 hours—more than enough power to survive a full workday away from an outlet. It speaks to the efficiency of modern hardware that an 18-hour result can look average. Finally, the 3K OLED panel posted top-tier color-gamut coverage and high brightness metrics in testing. The combination of rich color saturation and high luminance successfully offset the dimness sometimes seen in OLED screens, delivering one of the most vivid visual experiences in this price bracket. Getting this level of display quality and overall horsepower inside a 16-inch chassis weighing well less than 3 pounds remains the Zenbook A16's standout achievement. Final Thoughts Asus Zenbook A16 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Asus Zenbook A16 successfully delivers a large-screen ultraportable that's a smart buy for mobile professionals, executives, and content creators who want maximum screen real estate without hauling a heavy five-pound brick. By pairing Qualcomm’s top-tier Snapdragon chip with a durable, ceramic-like Ceraluminum chassis, Asus gives you an unbeatable mix of lightweight luxury, class-leading multi-core power, and genuine all-day battery life. To reap those rewards, you will need to accept a few core trade-offs—namely, an oversized, finicky trackpad and the occasional software-compatibility quirk inherent to Windows on Arm—but the stunning 3K OLED display and whisper-quiet efficiency make those compromises easy to live with. Where the Zenbook A16 truly cements its appeal is in its value proposition. At $1,699, bundling 48GB of fast memory alongside flagship silicon is a steal, especially when configuring a MacBook Pro or competing x86 laptop with 32GB to 48GB of RAM easily pushes total prices well beyond $2,200 to $2,500. You should buy the Zenbook A16 if you prioritize display quality, massive multi-core headroom, and all-day endurance for modern productivity and AI-driven workflows. Skip it only if you require a discrete GPU for heavy 3D gaming, prefer a traditional metal finish, or rely on legacy x86 software that struggles under Arm emulation. It's not as powerful as, say, the Framework Laptop 16, but it earns its own Editors' Choice award as the best 16-inch ultraportable system. About Our Expert From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: I Test AI Every Day, and I Still Have No Idea What I'm Paying For
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.23
As PCMag's resident AI expert, I test everything from AI chatbots to AI music video generators daily. But no matter what I'm doing, I never really know how much usage I can get out of a given service before it cuts me off. How many images can I generate? How much coding can I do? The answers are just totally unclear. Below, I take you through the many ways AI companies obfuscate usage limits and what needs to change. With AI Services, You Pay for Usage, Not Features When you subscribe to any AI service, you're essentially paying for temporary access to a data center with the hardware necessary to enable a given capability. AI usage, as a concept, simply refers to how much access you have to an AI product before you hit a specified limit. To continue using a service after you expend your allotment, you have to wait for a limit reset or spend more money to unlock more usage. AI companies use all kinds of terms to define AI usage, whether it's credits, subscriptions, tokens, five-hour limits, weekly limits, and more. For example, I pay for a Google Drive storage plan, which includes access to Gemini AI Pro. As an AI Pro subscriber, I get 1,000 Google Flow credits to use each month with Gemini’s excellent AI video generation models, Omni and Veo, among other things. This is a common way companies sell AI usage, but it’s far from the only one. The only time you don’t have to pay for some form of access with an AI service is if you run it locally on your computer. Realistically, though, that’s often not an option. Most AI apps don’t let you run anything locally, and even if they did, you might not have the hardware necessary to ensure a good experience. The 'More' Trap: Paying for Vague Tiers I enjoy vibe coding apps to help me improve at video games, such as Magic: The Gathering Arena and Warframe. My favorite tool for those projects at the moment is ChatGPT, and I have a ChatGPT Pro 5x subscription that costs $100 per month. What is a Pro 5x subscription, you might ask? It’s one of ChatGPT Pro’s two flavors: 5x or 10x, and it refers to how much more usage you get than with ChatGPT Plus. How much usage do you get with ChatGPT Plus? Well, for starters, you get more than you do with ChatGPT Free or ChatGPT Go. Confused yet? OpenAI advertises Plus with nebulous descriptors, such as “expanded Codex usage” or “expanded messages and uploads,” but doesn't attach concrete numbers to these claims. So, from the very beginning, you’re paying for the abstract idea of 'more' usage, not a certain amount. This makes it impossible to determine which of ChatGPT’s plans is right for you. This kind of setup also means OpenAI never has to raise prices. Netflix makes headlines every time it hikes rates, but imagine if your Netflix subscription let you watch only an unknowable amount of programming each month, depending on the things you choose to watch. If you hit your limit in the middle of your favorite show, you would have to upgrade your subscription or pay for continued access. Then Netflix could just quietly change the monthly limits on each plan and subtly push you to spend more money without ever raising its prices. That's how AI services currently work. Moving the Goalposts With Random Resets and Hidden Caps The situation goes from bad to worse once you actually start using an AI service, thanks to arbitrary rate resets. For example, since the launch of GPT-5.6, OpenAI reset weekly usage a bunch of times, letting you get another full week’s worth of access even if you had none left. This makes it really difficult to determine which ChatGPT plan will provide enough usage for your needs. Beyond this, OpenAI is reportedly now testing paid usage resets. If that sounds a lot like the first hit being free and the rest costing you a pretty penny, well… Aside from usage resets, OpenAI obscures limits in other ways, too. For example, ChatGPT used to have both five-hour and weekly usage limits. OpenAI recently did away with the former, which makes it more convenient to use than Claude (which still has them). However, the new system still encourages you to quickly blow through your usage and then spend money to unlock more, upgrade to a more expensive plan, or wait for (or buy) a potential usage reset. Discounts That Disguise the Real Cost Promotions also add to the confusion. For example, as of this writing, Claude is running a temporary promotion in which you get 50% extra usage in Claude Code. OpenAI has run similar promotions, too. On a fun note, this promotion is for weekly limits only, not five-hour limits. In other words, you won't be able to get more out of a single session. Instead, you need to use Claude for as many five-hour periods as possible during a week to take advantage. Considering how few five-hour periods you are likely able to sit at your computer and vibe code during a given week, it's entirely possible that you might not benefit at all. At face value, promotions are a win for consumers. But if you dig deeper, they end up being clever ways to hide how much usage you really need to complete a project. And if you have to upgrade eventually, that can mean a jump from $20 per month to $100 per month, or from $100 per month to $200 per month, depending on the plan. Also, when I say temporary promotion, I don’t mean something that lasts just a few weeks. Claude’s current promotion has been running since May 13, which is more than enough time to forget what you're actually paying for. Upgraded Models Mean Downgraded Value The unending onslaught of new models and pricing adjustments further complicates this already puzzling situation. Setting aside whether you actually need the latest AI models (you don’t), fresh releases often mean higher usage rates. For example, when Claude launched Fable 5, its most powerful model ever at the time, it burned through usage significantly faster than Anthropic's previous top model. It’s one thing if, for example, you’re a gamer and you have to buy a new console every seven or so years. It’s another thing altogether if you pay for a subscription to a service to use its top-tier tech, but then the top-tier tech changes several times a year and the value of your subscription plummets. Now, you might think that you just don’t have to use new models, and that’s sometimes true, like with Fable 5. However, that's not always an option. For example, the oldest model available to me on ChatGPT’s web interface is GPT-5.5, which OpenAI calls a legacy model. Mind you, this “legacy” model launched in April 2026, just under four months ago. So, if you really like the blend of performance and usage you get out of a particular model, you can only use it for so long. New models sometimes have additional restrictions, too. Fable 5, for example, is available only to certain tiers of Claude subscribers. And even if you can use it, you can only do so with 50% of the weekly usage allocation of your plan. I have a Claude Max 5x plan, which costs $100 per month. How much can I use Fable 5? Well, I can use it for 50% of 5x the usage of Claude Pro, which gives me “at least 5x more usage per 5-hour session than [Claude] Free.” Even if you don’t pay for AI model usage with a subscription and stick with the same model, you’re still not safe. DeepSeek, for instance, is well known not only for funneling foreign data directly to the Chinese Communist Party, but also for its low API access costs. API access for AI models is a pay-as-you-go system in which each prompt you send incurs processing costs, and DeepSeek charges you based on the number of tokens you use. Recently, DeepSeek massively hiked the cost of tokens for existing models. So, now you can either spend a lot more money or use DeepSeek a lot less than before. How to Fix AI Pricing: Just Give Us the Raw Numbers With some technology, variability is baked into the cake, and understandably so. For example, when you pay for internet access, the speeds associated with your plan are estimates because they can vary based on several factors. With AI, it’s inevitable that new models will come with different value propositions from older models, and that’s OK. What’s not OK is how AI companies continue to rely on sketchy monetization practices. Instead, they could simply allocate a clearly defined number of tokens to each plan per month. And, there’s no reason why older models have to disappear so quickly, either, especially if they’re popular or more efficient. Yes, token allocations might need to change from time to time to accommodate new models and features, but every other company has to deal with that, too. Why should AI companies get a pass here? I’m not asking to get more for less here, just to know what I’m actually paying for. I’m more willing to spend extra money on something when I don’t feel like it's a form of gambling. As it stands, I’d rather downgrade to a cheaper plan (or temporarily sign up for one) to make the most of promotional periods and usage resets than spend on a more expensive plan. Stay Subscribed, But Vote With Your Wallet You shouldn't stop using AI just because the pricing is a mess. After all, I still use streaming services even though I hate how many I have to pay for to watch the content I want to see. Instead, vote with your wallet by downgrading when tiers get vague, cycling plans, and refusing to pay for overpriced top-tier black boxes. You don't have to quit the tech entirely, but more than ever, you need to be diligent about staying on top of what you actually need—and what you're willing to pay for. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 Wishlist: 5 Upgrades Standing Between Meh and Must-Have
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.20
At its 'Surprise and Shine' event on Sept.9, Apple will all but certainly announce a Series 12 smartwatch. I don’t expect Apple to throw out the playbook here, despite new leadership. If history is any indication, its next Apple Watch will have accurate health and fitness tracking, a square face, and tons of apps. Apple has a history of taking small but meaningful steps forward with its smartwatches. Last year, the Apple Watch Series 11 introduced the first significant bump in battery life for the company’s watches since the very first model. The year before, the Series 10 introduced a thinner case with a larger screen visible from a wider viewing angle. This year’s watch will almost certainly focus on AI capabilities, given the new Siri AI app at the center of watchOS 27. Besides that, here are five upgrades I'd like to see that would keep the upcoming Apple Watch at the forefront of the increasingly competitive smartwatch field. 1. Price: Hold the $399 Line Apple has kept the starting price of its flagship Series watch consistent since the Series 4 in 2018. At $399, Apple's past models have always been more expensive than competing flagships from Google and Samsung, but its pricing consistency over more than half a decade is commendable. As for the Series 12, my hope is simple: I want the starting price to remain at $399. The reason I question this, despite Apple’s track record, is those same competitors. Both Google and Samsung raised the prices of their flagship smartwatches this year. The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 starts at $379.99, a $30 increase over its predecessor. Google bumped the base price of the Pixel Watch 5 by $50 over last year's model, matching the Apple Watch Series 11 at $399. Apple is as affected by the rising costs of memory and storage chips as its competitors are. Amid the global AI-related memory shortage, the company has already raised prices across several product categories this year, but not its smartwatches. Even so, I’m hoping Apple bucks the trend. If it remains at $399, the Apple Watch Series 12 will seem more value-rich than ever. Likelihood: Medium 2. Performance: Give Us a New Chip The Apple Watch Series 11 has the same S10 processor as its predecessor, so a new chip for the Series 12 just makes sense. Given the importance of Siri AI to the upcoming watchOS 27 software, a new, faster chip will help make sure the digital assistant can process complex tasks with relative efficiency. Before the Series 11, Apple’s previous flagships had a long track record of debuting with a new chip. Apple obviously felt the S10 was still up to the task in the Series 11, and my testing verifies that. It handles all health-tracking and lifestyle tasks without lag and is highly responsive when switching between apps. Still, I want to see what a new chip can do, and I’m pretty sure we'll be getting that chance. Likelihood: High 3. Battery Life: Break the 2-Day Barrier For the Series 11, Apple offers an official battery life estimate of 24 hours, up from 18 hours for all earlier Series models. Moreover, Apple tends to underpromise and overdeliver on battery life. In my real-world testing, the Series 11 lasted 43 hours with typical use and the always-on display enabled. The Series 10 also beat its official 18-hour estimate, powering through 36 hours in testing. Just a small increase could push the Series 12's real-world battery life over two days. For comparison, the Pixel Watch 5 lasted 56.5 hours in testing, the best battery life result I've seen from a name-brand flagship smartwatch yet. While Apple almost certainly won’t raise its official estimate for the Series 12 from last year, improved software efficiency or a potential new chip could lead to a tangible improvement. Likelihood: Medium 4. Fitness: Build a Better AI Coach I've been testing the public preview of watchOS 27 on my Apple Watch Ultra 3, so I already know that Siri AI can offer detailed answers to complex questions, build on previous responses, and find information from across the apps on the watch. WatchOS 27 also comes with an improvement to Workout Buddy. Apple’s AI-powered guide provides a friendly voice during certain exercises. The cheerful Workout Buddy offers words of encouragement and provides updates on your weekly activity stats and how your current workout compares to your past ones. The latest update provides even more context and specific stat details. While I like Apple's Workout Buddy, Google has a more all-encompassing AI wellness assistant on its latest wearables, including the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air, called Health Coach. Available with a Google Health Premium subscription ($9.99 per month), the Gemini-powered Health Coach takes all of your data into account to create a personalized fitness plan based on your goals, and can even adapt it to your changing needs and schedule. Thanks to its personalized advice and adaptability, the Google Health Coach is my favorite AI-based fitness planner. In theory, Apple has the tools to do something similar. The company partnered with Google while developing Siri AI. However, Apple has generally offered descriptive, rather than prescriptive, wellness insights. Even Workout Buddy avoids giving any advice. It can tell you if you’re falling short of a pace goal, but only if it’s a goal you’ve set. An overarching coach similar to Google’s would go against this trend. Even so, Apple could find its own unique way to structure a plan for you, especially if it integrates workouts from its premium Fitness+ service. Plus, Apple captures all kinds of interesting health data on its watches and last year introduced the holistic Sleep Score metric to help you quickly gauge your slumber. An AI-based coach would be a big step, but one built on a solid foundation. Likelihood: Minimal 5. Health: Unlock On-Demand Blood Pressure Tracking Blood pressure measurements are a growing trend in smartwatches. It’s potentially the next big frontier in terms of the health and fitness data wearables can provide, but no model has perfected it yet. Last year, Apple brought hypertension (high blood pressure) notifications to its watch lineup. The feature runs in the background, collecting data on your heart rate patterns for 30 days, and then alerts you if it detects any signs of trouble. While a handy way to potentially alert you to a hidden condition, you can't actively check your data during the 30-day collection period. You also can’t see any of the collected numbers or even get confirmation that it didn’t find anything. Once you turn the feature on, you either get an alert that the watch detected a problem, or you see no further sign of it in action. While Apple’s version is painless, it’s entirely passive and has no way to take an active reading. Samsung lets you take an active blood pressure reading, but this requires tedious setup with a separate cuff. Google’s upcoming blood pressure feature doesn’t require the same calibration as Samsung's, and you can’t take an active reading, but it will provide a monthly report for more consistent feedback than Apple’s current version. Apple could get ahead of the crowd on this with a watch that can take an active blood pressure reading without calibration with a separate cuff. Even aside from active readings, Apple could improve hypertension notifications just by adding regular feedback on its passive readings. While I’d call the chances of active blood pressure readings quite low, small improvements to Apple’s existing feature seem like a reasonable bet. Likelihood: Medium Bonus Round: What About the Apple Watch Ultra 4? In addition to the Series 12, we could get an update to the Ultra line this year. Reliable reports say that an Ultra 4 launch is likely. If so, I want even better durability stats, given that Samsung’s Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 just caught up to Apple’s Ultra line with certifications for diving and high-velocity water sports. We’ll know all of the details about Apple's latest watches soon. I plan to put any new Apple Watch to the test as soon as I can to see how it performs in the real world, so stay tuned. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Razer Iskur V2 NewGen Review: Finally, a Gaming Chair That Actually Breathes
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.08
The $649.99 Razer Iskur V2 NewGen is exactly what I needed during the oppressive heat wave that recently hit New York. I've had gaming chairs that provided lumbar support, but felt too stiff and unforgiving. Conversely, I've sat in gaming chairs that were soft and plush but lacked proper breathability, turning my under thighs into a swampy nightmare. The Iskur V2 NewGen, the successor to the original Razer Iskur V2, strikes a balance between the two design philosophies. After testing it for a month, I appreciate that the well-design chair supports my lower back, uses sweat-resistant cooling leather, and has a ventilated cushion that stops my legs from overheating. However, despite being a few years old, the $579 Secretlab Titan EVO (our Editors' Choice winner for gaming chairs) offers a similar experience at a lower price. The Iskur V2 NewGen gaming chair I tested comes in that familiar black-and-green color scheme that recalls the company's gaming laptops. It has that electric green, three-headed snake logo on the black, memory-foam head cushion strapped to the chair's top. You can find more of that neon green in the stitching that runs along the contoured edges of the backrest and seat. The Iskur V2 NewGen also comes in black, light gray, and quartz, but the black-and-green model is the most visually striking option. The SecretLab Titan EVO, one of NewGen's rivals, has a massive selection of colors, including Black, Mint Green, Plush Pink, Pure White, and Soda Purple. There are even special-edition models for fans of Harry Potter, Pokémon, Star Wars, and other notable pop culture brands. In fact, I counted an incredible 86 finishes on the Titan EVO's product page. Likewise, the Herman Miller x Logitech G Vantum offers more design options than the Iskur V2 NewGen (Black/Mystic, Black/Nightfall, Black/Helio, Black/Abyss, Black/Obsidian, Black/Polar, and Black/Flare), but far fewer than the Titan EVO. The Iskur V2 NewGen is available in a single universal size that accommodates heights from 5'3" to 6'6" and supports a maximum weight of 299 pounds. The G Vantum also comes in one size, but supports up to 350 pounds (the company doesn't publicize a recommended user height range). The Titan EVO, on the other hand, comes in three sizes. Small is recommended for folks between 4'11" and 5'6" (up to 200 pounds); Regular is recommended for people between 5'7" and 6'2" (up to 220 pounds); XL is best for those between 5'11" and 6'9" (up to 395 pounds). As a result, you can find a more personalized fit with the Titan EVO than with the Iskur V2 NewGen. Unless you're The Hulk, you’re going to need assistance putting this chair together. And that starts with getting the box inside your home, since the shipment is a hefty 70 pounds. I enlisted my dad to help me haul the box through the front door. I started by snapping the wheels into the star-shaped base and sliding the gas cylinder into the middle hole. Next, I screwed the metal tilting mechanism onto the bottom of the seat cushion and mounted the seat onto that gas cylinder. Because the chair parts are heavy and awkward, it was easiest for me to flip the seat on its side to attach the armrests. Then, I slid each armrest into its designated slot and screwed it down tightly. Doing it this way kept the screw holes aligned. Next, I used that same sideways approach to attach the backrest to the side brackets. Once the arms and back were bolted in place, the chair was ready to flip upright. Don't worry about fetching your toolbox for this chair installation. The Iskur V2 NewGen comes with handy tools to put everything together. Plus, you'll find a QR code inside the box that leads you to an extremely helpful YouTube video that made the setup a breeze. I timed myself to see how long it would take my father and me to put this together: The chair was ready to go in 25 minutes, which is about average for a gaming chair. As mentioned, the NewGen is the successor to the 2024 Iskur V2, so the question is, what's new? For one, the chair's wrapped in a new proprietary synthetic leather that's designed to keep your entire body cool. But Razer didn't stop at the upholstery. The seat cushion also features what Razer calls "dual-density cold-cured foam." The marketing speak simply means that the seat cushion features a soft foam layer on top of a firm base, with tiny perforations that let heat escape. Lucky for you (because it benefits this review), and unfortunately for me (because heat waves are awful), I've had the displeasure of surviving several high-temperature days in New York. Despite suffering through 100-degree heat, I was surprised to see that my thighs, as well as my body overall, remained sweat-free. That's particularly impressive because my office is located in the hottest area of the house. Razer states that the Iskur V2 NewGen features a proprietary "HyperFlex Lumbar Support System" that provides posture support no matter how you sit. I was eager to test this. Before leaning back, you can use the dual knobs on the lower backrest's sides to help the chair match your spinal curve. Whether you’re sitting upright, leaning forward, or reclining, the Iskur V2 NewGen's lumbar support moves with you. This tech consists of a 360-degree swivel mechanism that Razer calls the "first of its kind" in lumbar engineering. In other words, the chair features a multidirectional support structure that moves both vertically and horizontally, adapting to your body as you shift around in the chair. Here's how it works: Let's say I need to reach to my right to charge my phone at a wireless charging station or to my left to grab a cup of coffee. The bottom area of the backrest moves with me to support my spine. Razer claims the chair also adapts to both forward and backward motion. However, I found it more supportive during side-to-side reaches. Although the front-to-back tracking is more subtle, it’s a minor quirk rather than a deal-breaker for an otherwise responsive chair. The Titan EVO has a similar design, the "4-way L-ADAPT Lumbar Support System." Unlike the Iskur V2 NewGen and Titan EVO, the G Vantum lacks multidirectional lumbar support. Herman Miller claims that it reinforces users' pelvis and lower back by supporting the "sacral-lumbar region," which is just a fancy term for the lower part of your back. As someone who sometimes loves sitting cross-legged, I appreciate that the Iskur V2 NewGen lets me sit like a pretzel when I want to get my feet off the ground. That comes courtesy of the Iskur V2 NewGen's spacious seat, which is close to 21 inches wide. In comparison, the G Vantum’s seat base is 20 inches wide, while the Titan EVO's seat base is somewhere between 18 and 19 inches wide, depending on the size you get. The Iskur V2 NewGen has 4D armrests, which means they can be adjusted in four directions: up and down, side-to-side, forward and backward, and angled inward or outward. I appreciate this flexibility, but I don't use it much. You can tweak the armrests' height, depth, width, and rotation using release buttons and latches. The Titan EVO has 4D armrests, too, but the G Vantum features 3D armrests instead. In other words, the G Vantum has the same range as the Iskur V2 NewGen and Titan EVO except for inward and outward movements. Other Iskur V2 NewGen adjustments include the seat height, which is controlled by a lever under the seat base's right side, a tilt lock managed via a lever on the left, and a customizable tilt tension adjusted by a knob tucked underneath the middle of the seat—all standard controls that you'll find on the Titan EVO and G Vantum, too. The Iskur V2 NewGen has a 152-degree recline function. I'm not sure why I would need to bend that far back, but I guess it's nice that the option is there. I've tested leaning back to the absolute limit, and for a split second, I got that heart-drop feeling that I was about to go head over heels. However, the Iskur V2 NewGen had my back, literally, and kept me stable without dropping me like a hot potato. Triggered via the recline lever tucked on the right side of the seat base, it lets you kick all the way back safely. The Titan EVO features a massive 165-degree backrest decline, so much so that you could lie flat if you wanted to. The G Vantum has a limited recline range between 98.1 and 117.1 degrees. The Iskur V2 NewGen strikes a balance between firm, supportive, and comfortable, without feeling too soft. This seat isn't sink-in soft, which has never been my preference for gaming chairs. But it doesn't feel like you're sitting on concrete either. My main purpose in seeking a new gaming chair was to find something that could withstand sweltering New York summers while supporting a healthy posture—the Iskur V2 NewGen hits both marks in comfortable fashion. I've only had the NewGen gaming chair for a month, so I haven't seen any signs of wear and tear. However, Razer claims that the synthetic leather upholstery is engineered to be 13 times more durable than standard PU leather. As a result, it should be more resistant to peeling and cracking. As for the seat cushion, Razer says it was designed with a uniform cell structure, which should prevent the foam from collapsing out of its supportive shape. Plus, the chair features a steel frame and a reported "heavy-duty" aluminum alloy wheel base. The Titan EVO has similar materials, including a steel frame, an aluminum alloy wheelbase, leather-like upholstery, and foam cushioning. The G Vantum's chair consists of a glass-reinforced nylon frame and base, a proprietary elastomer-and-polyester suspension backrest, and a polyurethane foam seat cushion. However, keep in mind that the G Vantum has a 12-year warranty. This long window speaks to Herman Miller's confidence in the chair's durability. Razer covers the Iskur V2 NewGen gaming chair with a three-year warranty, which is pretty standard. It covers mechanisms and moving parts, but not normal wear and tear. For no additional cost, you can extend this coverage to five years by participating in Razer's Extended Warranty Program. However, that's only available to people who purchase their chairs directly from Razer.com. Titan EVO's warranty window matches the Iskur V2 NewGen, but the G Vantum is the winner here, featuring a lengthy 12-year warranty. Final Thoughts Razer Iskur V2 NewGen - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Razer Iskur V2 NewGen is supportive without being punishingly firm, comfortable without being overly soft, and it keeps the sweat at bay during brutally hot summer days. The 360-degree lumbar support moves with me when I shift around, while the roomy seat and flexible adjustments make it easy to sit in a pretzel when I'm feeling froggy. However, putting it together is a two-person job (though that's par for the course for most gaming chairs). Plus, at $650, it's not cheap. As good as the Iskur V2 NewGen is, our Editors' Choice remains the $579 Secretlab Titan EVO, which offers a similar experience to the Iskur V2 NewGen and even more colorway options for less cash. SHOULD I UPGRADE? If you have the 2024 Razer Iskur V2, it’s only worth upgrading to the Iskur V2 NewGen if you live in a climate that gets unbearably warm and would benefit from the new, more breathable materials, including the sweat-resistant cooling leather and the ventilated foam cushion. Otherwise, nearly everything else, from the steel frame and 4D armrests to the 360-degree pivoting lumbar support system, remains virtually identical to the original model. In that case, you can safely skip this one. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: Windows 10 and 11 users are seeing a Defender warning that isn’t real
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.90
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Windows 10 and 11 users are seeing false warning messages claiming Microsoft Defender has been turned off, despite the security software remaining fully active. - The issue stems from a recent antivirus update bug, causing incorrect notifications across multiple Windows versions. - Microsoft is aware of the problem and is working on a fix expected in an upcoming update, so users should not panic. Over the past few days, some Windows 11 users have been getting incorrect warning messages about Microsoft Defender—the operating system’s built-in security solution—being disabled. According to Microsoft in this Windows Health post, the warnings are caused by a bug that was introduced in the latest Defender updates: After installing the latest updates for Microsoft Defender Antivirus, notifications might appear stating that “Microsoft Defender Antivirus is turned off,” even though the antivirus is functioning correctly and all settings show it as active. These notifications can appear when Windows starts and intermittently afterward. They persist even if notification settings are turned off. Per Microsoft, this bug currently affects Windows 10 (versions 22H2, 21H2, Enterprise LTSC 2019, Enterprise LTSC 2016), Windows 11 (versions 26H1, 25H2, 24H2, and 23H2), and Windows Server (versions 2025, 2022, 2019, 2016, 2012 R2, and 2012). The bug is scheduled to be fixed in the next Defender update, which currently has no release date: Next steps: We are working to release a resolution in a future Microsoft Defender Antivirus update and will provide more information when it is available. Further reading: 5 Microsoft Defender settings I always change ASAP

item.title: The Google Docs backup trick everybody should know
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.53
Anyone who frequently writes documents has had that moment where a big edit goes sideways. So what do you do when you’ve deleted a paragraph you needed, rewrote half a document only to regret the whole thing, or opened a shared file and scratched your head, wondering who changed what? There’s no need to freak out. Google Docs has a safety net called “version history” that remembers every version of your work. To find it, open your document and go to File > Version history > See version history. You’ll see older drafts listed by date and time on the right side of the screen. You can click on any of them to preview how the document looked at that point. Google also shows who made changes, with different colors tied to different editors, which I find really helpful when several people are working in the same file as me. If you find the draft you want, click Restore this version, and Google Docs will replace your current document with that older draft. You can also make a separate copy of an older version if you only want to recover a section without replacing your current work. One habit I highly recommend is naming important versions before you make any major changes. Go to File > Version history > Name current version and give it a useful label such as “First draft” or “Final draft before edits.” Named versions are much easier to spot later, and Google even says naming a version also keeps it from being merged with other revisions later. It only takes a few seconds, but it can save you from the headaches of trying to remember your earlier brilliant idea before someone accidentally deleted it. For more fun and helpful tips, tricks, website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: Windows 11’s latest optional update finally fixes search clutter
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.59
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft’s Windows 11 optional update KB5120981 cleans up Windows Search by removing cluttered Bing and MSN results, prioritizing more relevant local results instead. - The update also improves typo handling, file categorization, and introduces gradual features like taskbar repositioning, making it a meaningful quality-of-life improvement. - However, users should be aware of potential cursor and wallpaper bugs post-installation, so waiting may be wise if stability is a priority. A few days ago, Microsoft rolled out KB5120998, an optional update for Windows 11 that introduces several new features and improvements (like the taskbar being repositionable again). Another noteworthy improvement is that the built-in Windows Search has been tidied up, meaning you’ll no longer see results from Bing, Copilot, and MSN mixed in. Other search-related changes include: web searches no longer prioritizing ads and product suggestions, instead now always showing the most relevant result first; more clarity as to whether a search result is an app, a setting, a file, a web page, or a Microsoft Store recommendation; and the ability to cleanly handle typos and incomplete terms. Since KB5120998 is an optional update, you’ll have to install it manually if you want to take advantage of its benefits. Otherwise, you can wait for it to release as part of September’s big update.
