To install now, go to Settings → Windows Update → Advanced options → Optional updates. If you’re still seeing old functionality even after installing KB5120998, it’s because you haven’t gotten the new features yet. Microsoft is rolling out the features gradually over the next week or two. (Or, at your own risk, you can unlock features early with a free tool called ViVeTool.) Note that you may want to skip KB5120998 for other reasons, namely because it’s causing cursor and wallpaper issues for some users, and the direct causes of those issues haven’t been identified yet. If you want to be on the safe side, you should wait until September’s update.

item.title: Building a new PC from old parts? Don’t reuse these components
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.58
When building a new desktop computer, it makes sense to reuse as many components as possible from your old machine. That very flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a self-built system! Nevertheless, it is worth exercising caution here: some components age without you realizing it, or are no longer technically compatible with modern hardware. Anyone putting together a new PC should carefully check which parts should really be reused. The power supply is particularly critical. Whilst many users continue to use a high-quality model across several generations of computers, electronic components do age. Capacitors lose performance over time, and new graphics cards or processors may have higher or different power requirements. Newegg You should therefore check the age, power rating and condition of the power supply unit before installation. If the unit is already many years old or offers only a small power reserve, replacing it is usually the safer option. A common and potentially dangerous mistake concerns modular power supply cables. Even if the plugs look identical, the pin configurations often differ between different power supply models. Connecting old cables to a new power supply can lead to short circuits. Therefore, when replacing the power supply, always use only the cables supplied with the specific model. Older hard drives and SSDs should also be assessed carefully. Kingston Mechanical hard drives are subject to wear and tear due to their moving parts, whilst early SSD models often have significantly lower write endurance than current flash memory drives. Such storage devices can still serve as a secondary drive or for less important data, but should, where possible, no longer be used as the system drive. The same applies to mixed or very old RAM modules. Although different memory modules often work together, stability and speed are always determined by the weakest module. For a new PC, a uniform RAM kit is therefore usually recommended. Foundry Old all-in-one water-cooling systems also warrant attention. The integrated pump has a limited lifespan and may lose performance or even fail over the years. Modern air coolers now also achieve very good results and are often the more reliable choice in the long term. As a rule of thumb: please only carry over components if their condition, age and performance are still suitable for the new system. You should check the power supply, cables, storage drives, and cooling system particularly carefully to avoid subsequent problems or damage to new hardware.

item.title: These 8 clever PC desk upgrades free up more space than you’d expect
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.23
I write about cables, docks, peripherals, laptops, and all sorts of PC gadgets. Every day, random items wash up onto my desk, like a shipwreck after a storm. De-cluttering my desk is a priority…if only! Part of my problem is my setup. My father owned an antique rolltop desk, and I decided I wanted one too, full of nooks and crannies and drawers to store cables and pens and all sort of little geeky knickknacks. The problem is that those desks don’t really work with what I’d like to do: Organize my desk space using the accessories below. My plan right now is to possibly invest in a new workspace for my office, including the stylish, functional desk at the end of my list. But I’ll need to build it out with the necessary accessories to neaten, straighten, and de-clutter. This is my potential shopping list. Hopefully, it benefits you, too. (One theme you’ll see here: think vertical! Put stuff above or below your sightlines to reduce clutter.) Xpatee Under Desk Cable Management Tray: $15.99 Cable clutter comes in two forms: I/O cables like HDMI and Ethernet that can snake across your desk, and power cords to connect and power all of your gadgets. I’ve been considering a cable tray for a while now, and my colleague Alaina Yee owns and recommends this cable tray, by Xpatee. The point here is that it all lives underneath your desk, out of the way. Amazon This rather spacious (15.7 x 6.1 x 7.3 inches) wire mesh cable tray also includes four cable clips and six cable ties. It’s a clamping model which means that it might work for the lip that surrounds my rolltop, but it’s just the thing for a flat, traditional desk. Your desktop just has to be between 0.4 inches and 2.4 inches thick. It looks like it works best if your power cables can either go through a built-in cable port on your desk, or if your desk is pulled out slightly from the wall so that they can reach. CCCEI Mount Surge Protector: $35.99 A side- or under-mounted surge protector is another option; instead of placing a traditional surge protector in a bin like Xpatee does, this surge protector clamps onto your desk. This power strip has six outlets — not as many as some do, but arrayed on the top and side to allow for different types of plug arrangements. There’s always that odd plug (like a Google Home device, or a smartphone charger) that can throw the whole arrangement off. Also, there have been no complaints about the clamp strength, which can be an issue if you’re plugging or unplugging a cord or simply dealing with the weight of the assorted cables. There are USB-A ports and a USB-C port for charging, too. Amazon Note that I chose the version of this surge protector that pushes out 65W through the USB-C port, giving you an additional power option, as well as the 10-foot cord. Just be warned: The vast majority of clamping power strips do not carry UL certification, which means that they haven’t endured UL’s safety inspection. If that worries you, use a traditional UL-certified power strip with the cable-management tray, above, or Cable Matters’ 6-outlet desk-mounted power strip, for $41.99. The only thing about the Cable Matters power strip, which I haven’t tried, is the mounting option. It’s a fixed shell of plastic with an adjustable flip-up latching mechanism? It’s definitely a little odd, and only supports up to 24W of USB charging. But it appears to be designed with safety in mind. MSI MAG MT201 Single-Monitor Desk Mount: $69.99 Clutter can include the monitor itself! A monitor mount allows you to raise and lower the display as you like, and move it around your desk to accommodate your position and ergonomics — or just get it out of the way. Our list of the best monitor arms highlights the MSI MAG MT201 for its combination of features and affordability. MSI This arm will need some assembly and setup, which differentiates it from the more expensive models. Still, it’ll support up to 44 pounds (way more than necessary), with an easy-release VESA screw to quickly add or replace and existing display. Ugreen Vertical Laptop Stand Holder: $19.98 If you own a laptop, you have a few options for how it sits on desk: on your desktop itself, up and out of the way on a laptop riser, or a third option: a vertical laptop stand. This Ugreen laptop stand holds the laptop vertically, and closed; the idea is that you’re using the laptop as a sort of a mini PC, with an external keyboard and display. Amazon Some of you might like to use that built-in display, especially if it’s an OLED or a high-refresh-rate display. But laid flat, any laptop takes up desk space. Placed on its edge, your desk space increases dramatically. This holder fits any laptop that’s between 0.47 and 1 inch think (from gaming to productivity devices), with a nice bit of cushy rubber to hold and protect your laptop. Ignore that Apple logo; it works with Windows laptops, too. SVNNELP Under Desk Drawer: $29.44 You’re always going to end up with little bits of stuff on your desk: staples, push pins, pens, cables, and more. How you deal with it is up to you, but one way is with an under-desk drawer. Amazon SVNNELP offers a trio of small, medium, and large desk drawers that you can pick and choose from. The kicker here is that they’re held on by strong adhesive, rather than screws. You can always opt for a more permanent screw-in model, but these sticky drawers work as long as you don’t store anything too heavy in them. OPNICE Desk Organizer: $21.99 One important point for desk organization that I mentioned earlier is to go vertical: A display that can be aligned vertical in portrait mode can improve a desk’s usable space. In this case, the OPNICE Desk Organizer is actually a monitor riser and a collection of bins to hold all of your extra stuff. Amazon If you’re like me, you raise your monitor up a bit via its stand or a riser. In this case, you’re using the extra space (20.5 x 9.5 x 6.3 inches) to good use. It’s all made of metal, and can support up to 44 pounds, which is way more than a traditional external display weighs. JAKO Headphone Stand: $6.95 I personally don’t have a need for a headphone stand or hook — but many people do, just to clear the last bit of gear off their desk. Amazon Jako’s headphone stand doesn’t do anything unique, but it clamps on to your desk and provides a home for your headphones. It’s available in three colors: black, white, and aluminum. Tribesigns 78.7-inch Computer Desk: $179.99 Now I do love my rolltop, but if I wanted to fully implement my de-cluttering plan, I’d need a new desk. I’m seriously considering this Tribesigns computer desk as an alternative for my home office, perhaps even two of them. Why two? I like being able to pivot between tasks, and an L-shaped desk is pretty ideal for my needs. My second choice, SEDETA’s $109 66-inch L-shaped desk, might even be too small. Sure, I’d lose a little space putting two Tribesigns in an L-shape, but the tradeoff is a generous amount of desktop, sufficient for an office setup as well as after-hours play space. Amazon The Tribesigns desk measures 78 inches wide, and 27 inches deep, and about 30 inches high. It’s made of 0.59 inch MDF wood, with metal legs. It’s sturdy and supports up to 200 pounds; the desk itself weighs about 60 pounds. Also, it ships in a variety of finishes, from a neutral walnut finish to coffee and an oak-like stain. Aside from a new desk, however, most of these improvements don’t cost all that much. With PC prices through the roof, maybe it’s time to save on the other stuff!

item.title: Best USB-C hubs and dongles: Add ports to your laptop or tablet
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.08
The best USB-C hubs add ports to your PC, providing connections to legacy peripherals like mice, keyboards, printers, or more. If you follow my advice, you shouldn’t pay that much for a hub, either. Most users will probably be happy with any of my standard hub recommendations. But if you want to go further, I have additional options for more specialized purposes. Those include USB-C docking stations that sit on your desk, plus some higher-end alternatives: DisplayLink docks, as well as the best Thunderbolt docks. They cost more, but provide more functionality. (A FAQ at the end of this roundup can help you decide.) At a glance | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | Check on Amazon | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | Check on Amazon | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | I keep at least one of these lightweight little USB-C hubs in my backpack at all times. You should too! Why you should trust PCWorld for USB-C hub reviews and buying advice: PCWorld has been supplying news, reviews, and recommendations for the best computing products since our first magazines hit newsstand shelves in 1983. We maintain a rigorous testing process, and our reviews are not influenced by advertisers or other considerations. Most of these products were purchased directly by PCWorld reviewers, but in certain cases review units have been provided by the manufacturers. Anker 555 8-in-1 USB-C Hub – Best overall USB-C hub Pros - Excellent build quality - Supplies 85W of power - Good mix of ports Cons - 4K output is just 30Hz Who should buy the Anker 555 8-in-1 USB-C Hub? I’d recommend this USB-C hub to just about anyone. Most users will be able to take advantage of the USB-A ports for legacy mice and keyboards, the HDMI port, a USB-C port, and Ethernet. These are the ports I’d expect on a device like this. If you’re looking for more display ports or more USB-C connections, however, you’ll need to buy a more premium device. Anker 555 8-in-1 USB-C Hub: Further considerations Can a USB-C hub feel elegant? This one does. Anker’s 8-in-1 USB-C hub feels surprisingly weighty (4.5 ounces), with a premium metallic (aluminum and polycarbonate) sheen that keeps the hub cool. Overall, Anker’s hub is well designed, with adequate spacing between the two 5Gbps USB-A ports. There’s also a 5Gbps USB-C connection for data, plus a second USB-C port for power input at up to a rated 85W. (The charger allows up to 100W in, but supplies 85W.) There’s both an SD card slot and a microSD card slot, too. I had previously recommended Anker’s 7-in-1 Hub instead. Both hubs are similar, but this upgrade adds two things: an Ethernet port, and an HDMI port capable of 60Hz. The earlier pick output just 30Hz, and that capability was getting a bit outdated. The hub offers an 18-month warranty, and it even ships with a carrying pouch. I think this hub includes the right mix of ports for the right price. Hiearcool USB-C Hub – Best budget USB-C hub Pros - Just the basics - Solid price - 100W pass-through charging Cons - No Ethernet Who should buy the Hiearcool USB-C Hub? This is a hub for basic expansion, especially if you own an older laptop. It has one HDMI port that’s only capable of 4K resolution at a fatiguing 30Hz. However, it will work just fine for a single external 1080 display or even a 1440p monitor, if you own one. The two USB-A ports are designed for a mouse and keyboard, or a printer. If you need something cheap and capable, this hub will work just fine. Hiearcool USB-C Hub: Further considerations Let’s face it: If you’ve ever browsed Amazon’s inventory of USB-C hubs, it’s easy to be overwhelmed. I can tell you that I factor in price heavily on some of these picks, and this is a USB-C hub that I’ve personally used. It works, it offers a myriad of ports, and it does so at a very, very good price. It even ships in multiple colors, which is handy when peering into the depths of a travel bag or briefcase. This hub includes a pair of USB-A ports, microSD and SD card slots, and an HDMI port, and that’s all. It accepts up to a rated 100W of USB-C input charging, too. OWC USB-C Travel Dock – Best budget USB-C hub runner-up Pros - Compact - A good mix of ports Cons - A little on the slow side - USB-C cable feels a little short for comfort Who should buy the OWC USB-C Travel Dock? I’ve reviewed USB-C hubs and dongles that forego the traditional long, rectangular “dongle” form factor into something that’s a bit more stable. Dongles do have a tendency to flop all over your desk, and the OWC Travel Dock feels like a cross between a traditional docking station and a dongle. And it’s cheap, too! Dongles are usually reserved as travel gear, and I think this would work well for an executive or someone who likes a tidier desk. OWC USB-C Travel Dock: Further considerations The “hidden” USB-C cable is a nice touch, though extended it’s a bit short. This was also a 5-in-1 hub, so while it provides the essentials (two USB-A ports for mouse and keyboard, Ethernet, and HDMI, plus USB-C charging input) there’s not much else. (Editor’s Note: OWC updated this dock with an additional SD card slot, increasing the price slightly.) Read our full OWC USB-C Travel Dock review Monoprice 13-in-1 Dual-HDMI + DP MST Dock – Best premium USB-C hub Pros - Multiple display possibilities - Tons of ports Cons - Confusing documentation - Slow SD card slot - High-speed ports can get clogged by the main 10Gbps USB-C connection Who should buy the Monoprice 13-in-1 Dual-HDMI + DP MST Dock? If you own a modern laptop and want access to a ton of legacy ports for a reasonable price, this Monoprice hub/dock should be your choice. You need to own a modern laptop, though; a Microsoft Surface Book 2 with an 8th-gen Core chip inside didn’t produce any output over its USB-C port; several Samsung and Surface laptops with 12th-gen and 13th-gen Core chips from 2022 onward worked well, though. More recent laptops from 2024 on through 2026 should also work fine. Monoprice 13-in-1 Dual-HDMI + DP MST Dock: Further considerations If it looks like a hub or dongle, but is priced like a dock, is it a dock? You might not care, but it’s certainly on the pricey side. This 13-in-1 USB-C hub does it all, including connecting to two 4K displays (one at 60Hz, one at 30Hz). It does so by using support for built-in compression techniques within modern laptops to squeeze more effective throughput over the 10Gbps USB-C port. There are absolutely gobs of ports, including five USB-A ports (two at 480Mbps for mice and keyboards), two HDMI 1.2 connections, and even a DisplayPort port. There’s even a power input jack, so you can use your laptop’s charger and feed up to a tested 87W into the laptop. There aren’t any USB-C ports, but the assumption is that you can use your laptop for that. Read our full Monoprice 13-in-1 Dual-HDMI + DP MST Dock review Dockcase Smart USB-C Hub 10-in-1 Explorer Edition – Best premium USB-C hub runner-up Pros - Detailed, informative LCD display - Excellent information and controls - Top-notch performance Cons - No manual?! - Some instability - More charging power needed - Demands an up-to-date laptop for best results Who should buy the Dockcase Smart USB-C Hub 10-in-1 Explorer Edition? Nerds. Yep, this is one of the nerdiest products I’ve ever used, and I like and loathe how it just lets you sort of discover what it can do. But it tells you what your laptop is connecting to and how it’s working! It even reports glitches! I love that. Are you the type of person who owns an OBD scanner to diagnose any issues with your car? If you are, this is the USB-C hub for you. The Dockcase Smart USB-C Hub 10-in-1 Explorer Edition: Further considerations Part of me loves the sheer nerdiness of the Dockcase 10-in-1 Dock, if only because I’ve never seen anything like it in terms of the information it offers. Note that Dockcase offers alternatives: There’s a $69.99 6-in-1 dock, and a newer Dockcase “Visual Smart” 10-in-1 dock that eliminates some of the labeled ports in favor of a jet-black aesthetic. I prefer the nerdier version with lots of ports. Not only is the metal hub larger than most, with multiple external connectors that designate a premium hub, but there’s an actual display: A small LCD screen provides a detailed look at what devices are connected to each port and what their capabilities are. Put another way, the Dockcase Smart USB-C Hub 10-in-1 feels more like an OBD2 diagnostic device for your car, or a USB multimeter. As a dock, it’s excellent. As a tool, it can use some improvement: The interface is extremely clunky, and Dockcase really doesn’t even have a manual that explains it all. But this device is also small enough that it fulfills the requirements of a docking station without it being ungainly. Read our full Dockcase Smart USB-C Hub 10-in-1 Explorer Edition review Mokin 160W GaN All in One Docking Station – Best full-sized USB-C docking station Pros - Informative LCD screen - Excellent performance - Nice mix of USB-A, USB-C ports - Charging power easily exceeds smartphone needs Cons - Odd mix of powered and unpowered data-only ports Who should buy the Mokin 160W GaN All in One Docking Station? For those of you who want to know what’s going on under the hood of your USB-C docking station, this dock is for you. This dock always reports how much power it’s supplying, but when you insert or detach a monitor cable, it will alert you to what’s going on there, too. This might be a little too much information for some users, but if you’re the type of person who has a CPU widget floating on their desktop, this might be the dock for you. Mokin 160W GaN All in One Docking Station: Further considerations The split between data-only and charging ports is a little weird, especially if you’re using a mouse, keyboard, and webcam — and that extra USB-A port just isn’t available. (Really, who needs a power-only USB-A port?) But this dock pretty much nails your basic needs, offers a compact form factor, and is priced right, too. Read our full Mokin 160W GaN All in One Docking Station review Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615 – Best full-sized USB-C DisplayLink dock Pros - Terrific price and value - Excellent stability - Great display port flexibility - Support for two 4K60 displays Cons - Have to provide your own power supply - Can get quite warm - Mandatory software driver Who should buy the Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615? DisplayLink docks fit between a USB-C dongle and a Thunderbolt dock, and I always think of a DisplayLink buyer as a small business owner or home worker who is focused on productivity and lots of high-end displays. DisplayLink docks excel for office work, but struggle in handling high frame rates for games. This is our top pick for an upgraded DisplayLink dock, which has its own pros and cons — slightly more expensive than a USB-C docking station, but more features, too. Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615: Further considerations Ugreen’s 9-in-1 USB-C docking station is typical of the brand: quality design and manufacture, obtuse naming, and pricing that seems to vary from one vendor to the next. But this DisplayLink dock offers an excellent mix of port flexibility at a solid price. There is one catch: It lacks any power input at all, and you’ll need to use your laptop’s USB-C power supply (or buy one) to charge both this dock and the laptop itself. Like most DisplayLink docks, this dock was unusually stable, with no flickering between displays — one of the reasons I like DisplayLink docks. The price nails that sweet spot, too. Just remember to bring your smartphone charger. Read our full Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615 review Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ) – Best full-sized USB-C DisplayLink dock runner-up Pros - Support for three 4K60 displays - Six USB-A ports - 60W of power Cons - Great, stable image quality breaks down slightly with video - No USB-C or fast-charging ports Who should buy the Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ)? As noted in the best pick above, DisplayLink docks work best for a home office, with an emphasis on productivity. You’ll want to avoid gaming. Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ): Further considerations Plugable’s dock means that you can connect to three 4K displays, even if you don’t absolutely have to. Most docks ask you to choose between DisplayPort and HDMI, or even use a direct Thunderbolt connection. Plugable offers both. The performance of this dock was up to par, though keep in mind that DisplayLink uses compressed data running over a 10Gbps connection. Press it too hard, and you will see some degradation in video and storage performance. Read our full Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI and DisplayPort Display Horizontal Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ) review Other USB-C hub/dock reviews and features - Anker Nano 13-in-1 USB-C dock review: This combo USB-C dock/hub doesn’t deliver the amount of charging power I’d hope for, though the two-for-one special is unique. - Mokin 160W GaN All-in-One Station: With great power comes great…performance. - Ugreen’s $5 cable deal: Deals come and go, but check back for an attractive price. - USB-C buying guide: Our friends at PCWelt have some advice on how to differentiate USB from Thunderbolt. How we test USB-C hubs We test USB-C hubs/dongles slightly differently than docking stations. A separate article offers a detailed explanation on how we test USB-C hubs, but here’s a short summary: First we test the physical configuration, and how ports are spaced and whether filling one port impedes use of the port next to it. We also run performance tests to make sure ports function as advertised. Finally, we consider price and weight it against functionality and build quality. More complex hubs usually command more money, but that’s not always the case! Who curated this article? My name is Mark Hachman, and I’ve been working as a technology reporter and reviewer for 30 years. I review USB-C hubs/dongles, Thunderbolt docking stations, and DisplayLink docks, so I have a good handle on the different types of I/O technologies being used and what will be best for you. I’ve been reviewing these devices since work-from-home became popular in 2020, realizing pretty quickly that home users wanted a mix of displays and legacy peripherals. How to choose the best USB-C hub You’ll want to do a careful of assessment of your work equipment and your needs in order to find the right hub or dock for yourself. First, take stock of your peripherals Here’s where to start: Take a look at the peripherals you own, or plan to buy. Do you have an old external hard drive that uses a traditional USB-A cable? Do you manually back up photos from an SLR camera via its SD card? Or is your Wi-Fi connection unreliable enough that you’d prefer Ethernet? Figure out what ports you’ll need. This advice is for Windows users; Macs have their own limitations on USB-C connections. Keep in mind that you may want to use both a mouse and keyboard, and possibly connect a printer, too. You can disconnect a keyboard to print, but it’s kind of a pain. Even if you own a modern 2026 laptop, you may still have hardware from several years ago. A hub bridges your laptop to its peripherals, but can serve as a bridge to the past, too. Next, check out what ports your laptop already has It’s also important to take stock of your laptop or tablet’s ports: Does it have one USB-C port or two? If your device only has one port, is there a separate charging connection? If your laptop or tablet has a USB-C port and uses it exclusively for charging, you’ll want to buy a USB-C hub with a dedicated charging input port. Note how much input power the port allows, and confirm that it will be sufficient for your laptop. Otherwise, you’ll be forced to choose between charging your laptop and accessing other devices, which makes little sense. Most laptops will pop up a warning about a “slow charger” if your laptop’s not getting enough juice. Matt Smith/IDG Video adds another wrinkle. Older laptops often included dedicated video ports, often HDMI; modern laptops in 2026 may include a dedicated video port as well. But video can also run over the USB-C port through a technology called DP Alt Mode which enables certain USB-C ports to send video signals to external monitors using the DisplayPort protocol, via the USB-C cable. The problem, even as manufacturers like BenQ admit, is that these cables aren’t often properly labeled. There’s no way for us to tell you whether your USB-C port can support video passing over it. You’ll need to consult your laptop’s manual to tell. If the port does support video, you can either use a USB-C hub to connect to an external monitor. Alternatively, you can run the USB-C cable to a display with a USB-C cable input. These USB-C displays have only been available for a few years, but they provide an alternate way of routing video out of your laptop. Assess your laptop and peripheral power needs Desktop hubs will often take power in from an external charger like the one you plug into your phone, and use it to power your laptop. On these hubs or dongles, there will be a dedicated USB-C input port to accept power, but not data. A powered laptop docking station, on the other hand, ships with its own charger — which may be hardwired into the docking station and take will power in and also push it out to peripherals. As I noted above, the input power to your laptop needs to be sufficient to power it. But if you’re investing in a powered USB-C docking station, check our reviews to see how much power the hub or docking station can push out to peripherals. The 2026 iPhone 17 Max consumes 40W of charging power to fast-charge the phone; most docking stations won’t get near that. But an older phone, such as an Apple iPhone 14, only needed 30W of charging power. Older phones need even less power to fast-charge them. You certainly don’t have to buy a USB-C docking station or hub to charge a phone; most hubs weren’t built with them in mind. It’s useful to know, however, what your hub or docking station will be able to do or not do. Making sense of the USB-C technologies A USB-C port on your laptop can either run at 5Gbps or 10Gbps, with the latter being almost ubiquitous these days. That’s plenty of bandwidth for a printer, a mouse, a keyboard, or a hard drive, even all at once. Products like displays, Ethernet, and high-speed SSDs gobble up that bandwidth, however. Display technologies tend to have the most influence over what you should buy. If you simply want to connect to an external 1080p display — or two — a USB-C dongle should work fine, provided that the dongle has the available ports. It’s certainly the cheapest option. If you want to connect more displays with higher resolution, you may have to examine other choices. Traditionally, the only other alternative was a Thunderbolt dock. Provided your laptop had a Thunderbolt port, Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps bandwidth allows for two 4K displays, running at 60Hz, plus various peripherals. (You can use a 10Gbps USB-C dock even if you have a 40Gbps Thunderbolt port, but only 10Gbps of that throughput will be available to the 10Gbps dock.) Thunderbolt is usually associated with laptops which use Intel processors; laptops with AMD Ryzen or Qualcomm Snapdragon chips inside use the “generic” equivalent, also called USB4. There are also two intermediary technologies to choose from: a DisplayLink USB-C dock, and a USB-C dock that takes advantage of something called HBR3 and DSC. DisplayLink, owned by Synaptics, uses software compression between your laptop and the dock to approximate a Thunderbolt experience over a generic USB-C connection. It requires a software driver, but our experience is that it’s an excellent choice for office work, but not gaming. Here are the best DisplayLink docks and why to buy them. HBR3 with Display Compression (HBR3 with DSC) is essentially an industry standard version of DisplayLink. The problem? The technology hasn’t been widely publicized, let alone supported. Our experience has been that docks that support HBR3 work well with laptops using 12th-gen Core processors on up. Laptops with a 10th-gen Core chip inside them aren’t supported, and 11th-gen Core laptops are iffy. If you own a laptop chip with a 12th-gen Core chip or one that’s even more recent, you stand a good chance of success. Otherwise, don’t bother. Finally, don’t worry about platform branding Because USB-C is common among Macs, Windows PCs, and phones, some hubs align their branding with a particular platform. Go ahead and use that USB-C that’s billed as being “for MacBook Pro, Chromebook, and XPS” with any Windows PC — we did, and it works just fine. You won’t need any special software or drivers. After testing our USB-C hubs, we can confirm that some no-names perform just as well as their more well-known counterparts, and for less money, too. One thing to keep in mind: Because price is so critical to our recommendations, know that some of the prices may change as manufacturers offer sales. Therefore some hubs we didn’t recommend primarily based on price could become more purchase-worthy. FAQ Why buy a USB-C hub or dongle? Remember when laptops used to contain all sorts of ports: USB-A, HDMI, SD card slots, and more? And do you remember how svelte the early Macintosh laptops looked, especially when Apple began removing all of the ports in favor of USB-C and Thunderbolt? PC makers did, and decided that was the approach that they would take, too. Unfortunately, that left laptop owners like you with the problem of legacy hardware: printers, keyboards, SD card, micro SD cards, and so on — and with no ports to plug them into. Enter the USB-C hub, an inexpensive product that helps solve that problem. Just pay attention to what ports the USB-C hub offers, to make sure it meets your needs. I don’t understand what the difference is between a USB-C hub, a DisplayLink dock, and a Thunderbolt docking station. What do I need? Here’s the short answer: If you want to connect your laptop to a printer, an SD card or microSD card, mouse, keyboard, or legacy 1080p monitor, stick with a basic 10Gbps USB-C hub/dongle. If you want to add a pair of additional displays (especially 4K), or high-speed SSD drives, we’d recommend you look at our list of 40Gbps Thunderbolt docking stations. Generally, the larger, powered docks offer more features. It is confusing, since they all use the “same” USB-C port. Generally, most modern laptops have a small Thunderbolt “lightning bolt” logo to help distinguish the faster port. What’s the difference between a USB-C hub, USB-C dongle, and a USB-C docking station? A USB-C hub or dongle (we use the terms interchangeably) is a small, portable device that you can slide into a bag or backpack. A USB-C docking station tends to be heavy and bulky enough that you’ll want to keep it on your desk. It’s not true that a USB-C docking station will have more features than a USB-C hub, as some compact USB-C hubs pack in a surprising number of ports. Docking stations tend to be bigger and bulkier, and are designed to live on your desk. If there’s anything that docking stations tend to have that dongles sometimes don’t, it’s a USB-C port designed only to accept power from your laptop’s USB-C charger. That allows you to gain additional ports as well as charging capabilities from the same dock. How much does a USB-C hub or dongle cost? Expect to pay between $30 and $40 for a good USB-C hub, even in 2026 — maybe a bit more with tariffs. USB-C docking stations are bigger and bulkier but add even more capabilities. We’d expect you to pay over $100 for these. How much does price matter when buying a USB-C hub or dongle? Honestly, not much. Pay attention to our reviews and those from other shoppers, but buy according to what the hub or dongle offers. You can absolutely find solid USB-C hubs and dongles for an inexpensive price. USB-C docking stations, though, can feel a bit overpriced. In part, that’s because Thunderbolt docks were wildly expensive during the 2020 to 2021 pandemic years. USB-C docking stations are an alternative, but their prices were nudged upward, too. Fortunately, prices have come down, as the supply chain regained a semblance of normalcy. What is the difference between USB-C and Thunderbolt? Both USB-C and Thunderbolt use the same USB-C connection. The difference is that a “generic” USB-C connection typically provides 10Gbps of bandwidth, and Thunderbolt provides 40Gbps, or 120Gbps with Thunderbolt 5. Thunderbolt ports are becoming much more common, so it’s possible that your laptop won’t have any “USB-C” ports; they’ll be Thunderbolt-enabled instead. (To tell the difference, consult your laptop’s manual or look for a small “lightning bolt” logo over the port itself. That’s usually a sign that it’s a Thunderbolt port.) A USB-C dongle and a Thunderbolt dock are similar, in that they both provide a number of additional ports. There’s a key difference, though. The rule of thumb is that a USB-C dongle provides enough bandwidth for two 1080p displays at 60Hz, or a single 4K display at 30Hz. (Staring at any 30Hz display for a length of time can tire out your eyes, so I don’t recommend it.) A Thunderbolt dock, however, allows enough bandwidth to connect two 4K displays at 60Hz, plus all the peripherals you wish to attach. If you don’t need big, high-resolution displays, don’t buy a Thunderbolt dock and purchase a USB-C hub instead. What’s a DisplayLink USB-C dock? A DisplayLink USB-C dock is what you might call a “tweener” device: something between USB-C and Thunderbolt. DisplayLink docks embed a small chip from Synaptics in the docking station, and require use of a software driver that you’ll need to download. (USB-C and Thunderbolt are essentially plug and play.) The Synaptics chip compresses the data, and gives you the ability to connect (no joke) up to three or sometimes four 4K display all over a 10Gbps USB-C cable. It feels a bit like black magic. They’re not foolproof; DisplayLink docks are best for office work (email, Word, Excel, and so on that don’t require a whole lot of bandwidth, because the images are largely static) and web browsing. Transfer a lot of data (or play back a lot of high-bitrate video) and you’ll see some stuttering. We used to break out DisplayLink docks into their own page, but we now include recommendations on this list of the best USB-C hubs, as well as our list of the best Thunderbolt docks. If you shop smart, you can get the capabilities of a Thunderbolt dock, for less. Can you connect a USB-C dongle to a Thunderbolt dock? Or to another USB-C hub? You can absolutely connect a USB-C hub to a Thunderbolt dock. You probably won’t be able to connect a USB-C dongle to another USB-C dongle/hub, but if your laptop has more than one USB-C port, you can connect a USB-C hub to each. Thunderbolt offers the ability to “daisy-chain” devices, however, so you can connect one Thunderbolt dock to another. USB-C, however, does not. Why do USB-C hubs get so hot? USB-C hubs can get warm or even hot while using them to transfer data or charge devices. This is because the electronic components and circuitry within hubs build up heat during use. Depending upon the hub’s material, heat can become trapped inside the hub leading it to become hot to the touch. If you are concerned about your hub becoming too hot during use, you may consider purchasing a hub made from metallic parts, such as aluminum, so that heat can more easily dissipate as it builds up. We’ve given you a lot of detail on what makes a good USB-C hub or dongle and what to consider when buying one. In general, however, these are fairly inexpensive, flexible ways to upgrade your laptop, and I’d recommend always carrying one in your laptop bag!

item.title: My robot vacuum can map a house. My car broke its brain
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.80
So let me set the scene here. It’s Friday afternoon, and I’m picking up a few friends for a Taylor Swift-themed hangout later on. But the backseat of my car is covered in dog hair, and I’m in no mood to wrestle one of those long-hosed vacuums at my local car wash. The suction on those things sucks anyway. Literally. And then it dawned on me. I’ve got two robot vacuums upstairs. What would happen if I just stuck one of them in the back? Just to give you a visual here, my car is a hatchback, so it’s shorter than a sedan. I’ve also got a giant greyhound, so I tend to drive with the back seats folded flat (he needs a lot of room!). In other words, it’s a (mostly) flat area. Surely a robot could handle that? Or so I thought. First, I plopped the budget robot vacuum in the back of my car. It’s got a suction power of 20,000 Pa, which is pretty good for a budget model. (In case you’re curious, it was the Dreame D20 Air Plus). Next, I programmed it to run in Standard mode. After it created a small map of the back of my car, it ran for about… five minutes. When the Dreame app told me it was finished cleaning, I scoffed. No way. So, I ran the robot vacuum again. But this time I turned up the suction level to maximum power. Sigh. Again, it finished in five minutes. I understand it’s a small space, but I expected the robot to spend more time cleaning the area. It’s definitely more thorough when it’s zooming about the house. I don’t think it sucked up a single strand of dog hair, either. My next plan? Trying a more advanced model with 35,000 Pa of suction. Maybe the trick here is more suction power. Uh, nope. It did worse than the budget model. First, it got stuck on a weird ledge and wouldn’t move because the wheels were lifted. It did manage to successfully map the back of my car (hilariously enough, the app labeled this area “Kitchen”), but when I tried to run it again, it got stuck on the same exact ledge. (It’s the Roborock Saros 20, by the way). Why suction power isn’t the issue So why didn’t this work? Well, it turns out that a car is a much weirder environment for a robot vacuum than you might think. Foundry / Ashley Biancuzzo Even with the back seats folded down, my car doesn’t have one big, continuous expanse of flooring. The folded seats actually create a small hill in the middle. There’s also a few ledges at the corners where the surface drops down to the floor. This was enough to trip up the more expensive robot (the Saros 20). When one of the wheels lost contact with the ground, it stopped. That’s when I had to step in and physically move it. Unfortunately, it wasn’t able to finish a single cleaning cycle. These machines are designed to navigate predictable environments. Give them hardwood floors, furniture, a few walls, and they’re pretty good at figuring out where they can and can’t go. A car is a totally different story. I don’t think the robot vacuum can tell the difference between a raised ledge it can theoretically climb over and a step it absolutely cannot. It just sees a floor it thinks it can navigate. And when it gets that wrong, all the suction power in the world doesn’t matter. It’s also worth noting that the carpet in your car is very different from the carpet in your house. Automotive carpeting is usually flatter and more tightly constructed. It’s supposed to be more durable, able to withstand the constant friction from shoes. House carpets have more variation in terms of pile and texture–they can be softer and more flexible. That’s more of a robot vacuum’s bread and butter. That’s the lesson I took away from this ridiculous experiment. I went into this thinking suction power was the key here. It isn’t. A robot can have 20,000 Pa or 35,000 Pa, but suction is only useful if it’s cleaning an area it knows how to handle.

item.title: Kensington Triple 4K TB5 dock review: Killer speeds, but a few glitches
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.46
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Affordable for a Thunderbolt 5 dock - Fastest performance in some tests - Two HDMI ports saves on cable cost - Ports are clearly labeled - 140W laptop charging - Lock options Cons - Stable on a TB5 laptop; varied significantly on TB4 - Ports spaced a bit close together Our Verdict Kensington’s Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station (SD5010T5) is an attractively priced 13-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 dock, with excellent performance but questionable stability. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $299.99 Best Prices Today: Kensington SD5010T5 EQ Thunderbolt 5 Dock Kensington’s Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station (SD5010T5, sometimes referred to as the SD5010T5 EQ) feels like a 13-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 dock for the PC, rather than the Mac, with multiple HDMI ports rather than a host of Thunderbolt upstream connections. Performance is stellar; stability, less so. In 2026, a Thunderbolt 5 dock probably shouldn’t be your first choice, precisely because Thunderbolt 5 host support is limited to a few gaming laptops like the Asus ROG Strix, which served as my testbed for this review. Nevertheless, my list of the best Thunderbolt docks includes both Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 5 offerings, precisely because of the willingness of manufacturers to keep pricing in check. At about $300, Kensington’s dock is priced roughly in line with where I’d expect a TB5 dock to be. A Thunderbolt 5 dock is designed for up to three 4K displays, at 144Hz apiece, up from the two 4K60 displays that Thunderbolt 4 supports. Alternatively, you can connect a pair of 6K displays, or one running at 8K resolution. Through last year, TB5 was more of a performance play, for gaming. At CES 2026, however, we saw mass-market 6K displays enter the market, adding a new productivity wrinkle. Kensington Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station: Construction and ports The dock’s design is straightforward, with a small but thorough instruction sheet and small icons on the dock itself which spell out the capabilities of most of the ports themselves. Case in point: On the front, underneath the power button, a small icon notes that the 10Gbps USB-C port charges at up to 30W, enough for most of the latest smartphones to fast-charge. The 10Gbps USB-C port next to it is a bit more vague, with a battery icon. It too provides power, but just 7.5W. The USB-A port to the right also provides 10Gbps of throughput, but just 4.5W, which is normal. This dock includes what Kensington calls KonstantCharge, which will keep the peripheral ports active and charging even when there’s no laptop connected. That function worked as advertised. Mark Hachman / Foundry There are also two Thunderbolt ports on the rear of the dock. The first, which serves as an additional display port, only supplies 15W, somewhat surprisingly low for a Thunderbolt 5 port. Next to it are a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports. Above are a pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports, a 2.5Gbps Ethernet connection, and a pair of Kensington locking ports, nano and standard. I rarely complain about the port spacing on a powered desktop dock, but here I feel that the spacing between the two Thunderbolt ports on the rear of the dock — the connection to the laptop, and then the additional Thunderbolt 5 connection — are too close together. It’s not impossible to manage, but with those and the Ethernet cable in close proximity, inserting and withdrawing a cable has to be fiddled with. A wider, rectangular dock usually doesn’t have this problem. The second Thunderbolt 5 port supplies 140W to the attached laptop. That’s a problem — and will always be a problem, since gaming laptops with Thunderbolt 5 connections generally require 200W or so under load, including gaming. On the other hand, while my test laptop did complain of a “slow charger,” the laptop only lost about 4 percent of its battery while connected over the course of an afternoon’s worth of work. Put another way, the power that most TB5 docks provide will be insufficient for the Windows laptops which can connect to them, but not dramatically so. Dock makers have told me that placing wireless charging into the top of the dock can cause crosstalk and noise that can interfere with signaling. Still, there’s a lot of unused surface space, which mounting the dock can get around. Otherwise, the top of the dock became what I would call hot to the touch. There’s no active cooling, so that surface area is used to dissipate heat. Mark Hachman / Foundry I tend to favor vertical docks, because they can provide additional space savings on a crowded desk. However, Kensington’s 13-in-1 TB5 aluminum dock is incredibly sturdy and secure, with a rubberized surface that covers the entirety of the underside and prevents it from being moved or dragged by the weight of the attached cables. It can even be mounted via a pair of screw holes on the bottom, too. (For a Mac-specific perspective on the Kensington SD501T5, see Macworld’s review.) Kensington Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station: Performance I usually test docks over a period of several days, using our methodology for testing Thunderbolt docks, to assess how stable they are. Does the dock light up the displays when it comes back from sleep? Are there issues with it disconnecting? My test laptop produced a BSOD on one occasion following a graphical glitch on one display when it resumed from sleep, which may have been due to the laptop rather than the docking station itself. After a reboot, one of the displays failed to light up until after I reconnected it. My stability testing varied dramatically. On my Thunderbolt 5 test bed, the dock was extremely stable. On a laptop with Thunderbolt 4 ports, however, I noticed that one of two displays didn’t resume after bringing the laptop back from sleep. A reboot solved this. More annoyingly, one of the displays would flip off for a second or two, every few minutes. I tried six different Thunderbolt 4 laptops; three demonstrated this problem, while the other three did not. Otherwise, two displays lit up at 4K/144Hz, as they should, and the dock powered a third display that I connected with a USB-C cable. (It’s worth noting that the Kensington Dockworks software can be downloaded and installed, though it’s more for management rather than stability — quicker switching from Ethernet to Wi-Fi if the connection shifts, for example.) In my tests using a USB voltage meter, I found that the dock supplied 26W out of the front charging port, versus the rated 30W, but 8.1W out of the second USB-C port, versus the rated 7.5W. The other front USB-A port delivered 2.4W. Mark Hachman / Foundry As a Thunderbolt 5 dock, however, paired with capable hardware, this dock simply flies. As per my testing methodology mentioned above, I stream a 4K/60Hz video and note any frame drops. There were none! (I usually see a few frames drop.) Ditto for two displays. I then connect a Thunderbolt 5-capable external SSD to the dock and run PCMark’s external storage drive test. The only odd thing I noticed here is that the drive wouldn’t function on either of the two front-facing 10Gbps ports. It should have, just at slower speeds. On the rear Thunderbolt 5 port, it performed normally. Well, not totally normally. Using PCMark and the TB5 SSD, the dock achieved 444 megabytes per second, sneaking past the Plugable TBT-UD3 (432MB/s) as the fastest dock in that particular test. Running in the background while I was streaming the 4K video reduced the performance slightly to 439MB/s. My next test is to copy a folder full of multimedia files from the drive, through the dock, and on to my PC’s desktop. Last year’s Sonnet Echo 13 holds the crown at 13.9 seconds to complete the task. This took a few seconds longer, at 18.7 seconds, a 30 percent difference. I can remember the days when I would get a cup of coffee while my PC booted; five seconds or so isn’t a huge difference, but it is significant. While streaming and copying, the process took 20.2 seconds. Should you buy the Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station? Great performance, iffy stability — at least on my tests of Thunderbolt 4 hardware. I’m always a fan of display ports, as it means that you won’t need to buy adapter cables. That’s a not-so-hidden gotcha of docks like the Plugable TBT-UD3, which simply includes Thunderbolt ports instead. Tack on a couple of cables to the Plugable’s $250 price, and you’re inside the $300 price of the Kensington SD5010T5. I’m going to have to do a bit of thinking on whether I include this dock among my recommended best picks for Thunderbolt docking stations, which already include some Kensington docks. Kensington’s Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station is a solid dock if you already own a Thunderbolt 5 laptop; otherwise, the possible stability issues on a Thunderbolt 4 laptop might prove annoying.

item.title: 10 underrated national parks that are easier to get into than the famous ones
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.36
10 underrated national parks that are easier to get into than the famous ones These underrated national parks skip the permit lotteries and timed entry windows that now shape trips to Zion, Rocky Mountain and Acadia A trip to Zion National Park now starts with a lottery. Every hiker who wants to reach the chains on Angels Landing has to win a permit through Recreation.gov. That means entering a seasonal lottery months in advance, then often a second, day-before lottery for latecomers. Rocky Mountain National Park runs on timed entry from late May through mid-October. Visitors have to book a two-hour arrival window before they know what the weather or traffic will look like. Acadia requires its own separate reservation just to drive up Cadillac Mountain for sunrise. None of this makes those parks less worth visiting. It does mean that planning a national park trip increasingly happens on a screen, weeks in advance, competing against thousands of other travelers for a handful of slots. The 10 parks on this list operate by different rules. None of them require a lottery, a timed entry reservation, or a shuttle ticket just to get through the gate. Several charge no entrance fee at all. All of them see a fraction of the visitors that pass through Zion, Yellowstone, or Great Smoky Mountains each year, based on the Park Service's own visitation data. That makes them easier to plan around and easier to enjoy once you arrive. Parking lots fill up more slowly, and popular trails rarely demand the kind of pre-dawn arrival that famous parks now require. These underrated national parks were chosen for one reason. Each delivers a legitimate national park experience, cliffs, caves, ancient trees, volcanic terrain, river canyons, without the reservation systems that have become standard at America's most photographed parks. Some sit an easy drive from a major city, while others require more effort to reach, which is exactly why they stay quiet. What follows is a state-by-state look at 10 parks where a person can show up, pay at the gate or walk in free, and start hiking within the hour. Congaree National Park skips permits, fees and lottery systems entirely Credit: Leslie Cross / Unsplash Congaree National Park in South Carolina charges no entrance fee, requires no permit for day hiking, and has no shuttle or reservation system of any kind. A visitor can drive to the Harry Hampton Visitor Center outside Columbia, South Carolina, park, and start walking within minutes. The park protects the largest intact expanse of old growth bottomland hardwood forest left in North America. Loblolly pines and bald cypress trees tower overhead, some reaching more than 130 feet, making this one of the tallest deciduous forest canopies on the planet. The signature 2.6-mile Boardwalk Loop Trail lifts visitors above the floodplain on an elevated wooden walkway. Even after heavy rain, when much of the forest floor floods, the trail itself usually stays dry and open. Congaree draws only a small fraction of the crowds that visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park. That holds true despite sitting within a few hours of several major Southeastern cities, including Charlotte, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina. There is no timed entry window to plan around and no competitive permit lottery for the main trails. A weekend trip can be booked with a few days' notice instead of months. Paddling is where Congaree sets itself apart from most other underrated national parks on this list. Cedar Creek runs through the heart of the floodplain, and canoe or kayak trips let visitors glide beneath the same old growth canopy that towers over the boardwalk. Paddlers often pass turtles, wading birds, and, in warmer months, water snakes sunning on fallen logs. Canoe rentals are available in nearby towns, and the park itself does not require a permit to paddle Cedar Creek during the day. Congaree is also known for a synchronous firefly event that draws crowds for roughly two weeks each late spring, when a native firefly species flashes in unison after dark. This is the one exception to the park's otherwise permit-free approach. Evening access during the firefly event requires a separate parking pass distributed through a lottery, because the trail and parking area cannot safely hold unlimited visitors after dark. Outside of that narrow window, Congaree remains one of the simplest national parks in the country to visit on short notice. There is no fee at the gate and no reservation required to walk the boardwalk or paddle the creek. Great Basin National Park is free to enter and rarely crowded Credit: Canva Images Great Basin National Park in eastern Nevada charges no entrance fee and rarely requires more than a same-day reservation for its most popular attraction, Lehman Caves. The park sits roughly 300 miles north of Las Vegas. That is far enough from a major airport that it never developed the crowds found at Utah's national parks a few hours to its east. Wheeler Peak rises to 13,063 feet at the center of the park, and a scenic drive climbs to roughly 10,000 feet. That puts alpine terrain within reach of anyone with a car and a few hours to spare. Near the summit grow groves of Great Basin bristlecone pine, among the oldest living trees on Earth, with some individual trees estimated at more than 4,000 years old. A short interpretive trail near the Wheeler Peak parking area passes through one of these bristlecone groves without requiring a permit or a lengthy hike. Below ground, Lehman Caves offers guided tours through a marble cavern filled with rare shield formations, a type of cave decoration found in only a small number of caves worldwide. Tours run throughout the day and can typically be booked a day or two in advance through the park's own reservation system. That is a far simpler process than the seasonal lotteries required for popular hikes at busier parks. Great Basin also holds a designation as an International Dark Sky Park. Its remote location means the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye on clear, moonless nights. There is no competing for a spot with other stargazers, the way visitors often do at more accessible dark sky sites. The park hosts an annual astronomy festival each September that draws amateur and professional astronomers with telescopes set up for public viewing. Because Great Basin draws only a small share of the visitors that pass through nearby Utah parks each year, trailheads rarely fill. Campgrounds often have same-day availability outside of peak summer weekends, and rangers have time to answer questions in detail. The remoteness that keeps visitor numbers low is the same quality that makes a trip here feel unhurried once you arrive. Capitol Reef is the quietest of Utah's Mighty Five parks Credit: Martin Podsiad / Unsplash Capitol Reef National Park has no timed entry system, no shuttle requirement, and no permit lottery. That makes it the most straightforward of Utah's five national parks to visit on short notice. Zion, Arches, Bryce Canyon, and Canyonlands each carry some combination of shuttle mandates, permit systems, or seasonal congestion that Capitol Reef has largely avoided. The park protects the Waterpocket Fold, a nearly 100-mile wrinkle in the earth's crust where rock layers tilt and buckle into cliffs, domes, and narrow canyons. Highway 24 cuts directly through the park, so travelers driving between southern Utah's other national parks pass right through Capitol Reef whether they planned to stop or not. Many who do stop end up staying longer than expected. At the center of the park sits Fruita, a former Mormon pioneer settlement where the National Park Service still maintains historic orchards of apple, peach, cherry, and apricot trees. During harvest season, visitors are welcome to pick and eat fruit for free within the orchards, or pay by the pound to take some home. It is a rare hands-on activity inside a national park. The paved Scenic Drive and short trails near Fruita are open to any vehicle and require no advance booking. That includes the popular hike to Hickman Bridge, a natural sandstone arch that frames the canyon behind it. Cathedral Valley and the park's remote southern districts sit at the end of long unpaved roads that demand a high clearance or four wheel drive vehicle. Flash floods can make these roads impassable without warning, so reaching them requires checking current road conditions and planning around weather, not around a reservation system. Because Capitol Reef sees far fewer visitors than Zion or Arches despite similarly dramatic scenery, parking at trailheads near Fruita is rarely a problem outside of major holiday weekends. Backcountry campers need a free permit, self-issued at the visitor center, but day hikers exploring the main corridor of the park can simply park and start walking. North Cascades National Park has no shuttle or timed entry Credit: Canva Images North Cascades National Park in Washington state charges no entrance fee and requires no timed entry reservation, despite being one of the most rugged mountain landscapes in the contiguous U.S. The park sits less than three hours from Seattle by car, yet it consistently ranks among the least visited national parks in the country. That is largely because its interior offers little in the way of paved roads or easy trails. State Route 20, known as the North Cascades Highway, is the main route through the park and one of the most scenic drives in Washington state. It winds past jagged granite peaks, turquoise glacial lakes, and dense old growth forest. The highway typically closes for winter due to snow and avalanche danger, reopening in spring, so visitors planning a drive-through trip should check road status before setting out. Diablo Lake Overlook is the easiest way to take in the park's defining feature, a lake colored an intense turquoise by fine glacial sediment called rock flour. The overlook requires nothing more than a short walk from a roadside parking area, no permit and no reservation needed. The park contains more glaciers than any other national park in the lower 48 states, feeding rivers and lakes throughout the range. Longer hikes, including the popular Cascade Pass and Sahale Arm routes, climb into that glaciated high country. They require only a standard trailhead parking pass, not a permit, for day use. Overnight backcountry camping does require a free permit, available at the Wilderness Information Center. North Cascades receives only a small share of the hikers who visit nearby Mount Rainier or Olympic National Park each year. As a result, trailhead parking lots rarely reach capacity outside of holiday weekends. Even popular viewpoints like Diablo Lake Overlook stay walkable without the crowds that gather at more famous turnouts in other Washington state parks. Black Canyon of the Gunnison draws a fraction of Colorado's park traffic Credit: Michael Kirsh / Unsplash Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park in western Colorado requires no permit to drive either rim or hike the maintained trails along the canyon edge. It receives a fraction of the visitors that Rocky Mountain National Park sees each year, despite similarly dramatic scenery. The canyon reaches depths of more than 2,000 feet in places, with walls so steep and narrow that sunlight rarely reaches the floor. In parts of the canyon, direct light touches the bottom for less than an hour a day, which is how the park got its name. The South Rim Road offers the easiest way to see the canyon, with a series of overlooks reachable by car and short walks from parking areas. None of these overlooks require a reservation or timed entry ticket. The Painted Wall, Colorado's tallest sheer cliff face at roughly 2,250 feet, is visible from one of these South Rim overlooks. It needs no advance planning beyond driving to the pullout. The North Rim, reached by a longer unpaved road, sees even fewer visitors than the South Rim. It offers a quieter set of overlooks with views back across the canyon toward the South Rim cliffs. The road connecting the two rims does not cross the canyon directly, so visiting both sides in one trip requires driving around. That discourages casual same-day visits and helps keep both rims uncrowded. Reaching the Gunnison River at the bottom of the canyon is a different matter. The inner canyon descent requires a free wilderness permit, obtained at the visitor center. The terrain includes loose rock, poison ivy, and route-finding challenges that the park wants hikers to be prepared for in advance. For visitors who stay on the rim trails and overlooks, Black Canyon of the Gunnison remains one of the more accessible dramatic landscapes in Colorado. It requires none of the timed entry reservations needed at Rocky Mountain National Park a few hours to the northeast. It also avoids the crowded trailhead parking that defines peak season at many other Colorado mountain destinations. Voyageurs National Park trades car lines for open water Credit: Canva Images Voyageurs National Park in northern Minnesota charges no entrance fee and requires no vehicle reservation, in part because most of the park cannot be reached by car at all. The park sits along the U.S.-Canada border and is built around four large lakes: Rainy Lake, Kabetogama Lake, Namakan Lake, and Sand Point Lake. Narrower channels once used by French-Canadian fur traders known as voyageurs connect the lakes, and the park takes its name from them. Three visitor centers, at Rainy Lake, Kabetogama Lake, and Ash River, are reachable by car and open to any visitor without a reservation. From those access points, most exploration happens by motorboat, canoe, or kayak, since roughly 40 percent of the park's surface area is water. Houseboat rentals, available from outfitters near the park, let visitors sleep out on the lakes themselves rather than returning to shore each night. Canoeists looking for a quieter route than the busier main lakes can follow a multi-day route across the Kabetogama Peninsula that links four smaller interior lakes by short portages. A campsite is reserved on each lake for paddlers holding camping permits. The park stages canoes at some of these interior lakes for permit holders, reducing the need to portage a canoe the entire route. Voyageurs also earned an International Dark Sky Park designation, and the northern lights are visible from the park on clear nights during periods of strong solar activity. The park's latitude puts it closer to the aurora oval than nearly any other park in the contiguous U.S. Because most visitors never get past the main lakes near the visitor centers, the interior chain of smaller lakes stays quiet even during the park's busiest summer weeks. No timed entry ticket or shuttle reservation stands between a paddler and the water, only the logistics of arranging a boat. That keeps total visitor numbers well below those of car-accessible parks with comparable scenery. Wind Cave National Park charges nothing to see bison above ground Credit: Stephanie LeBlanc / Unsplash Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota charges no entrance fee to drive through, hike its trails, or view the bison and elk herds that roam its mixed grass prairie. That holds even though it sits within a short drive of the Black Hills' busiest attractions, including Mount Rushmore and Custer State Park. Only the guided cave tours below ground carry a separate ticket price. Established in 1903, Wind Cave is one of the oldest national parks in the country and protects more than 143 miles of mapped passages beneath its surface. That makes it one of the densest cave systems known anywhere in the world relative to the size of the hill above it. The cave is known for boxwork, a honeycomb-like mineral formation made of thin calcite fins that project from the cave walls and ceilings. Wind Cave holds a greater abundance of boxwork than almost any other cave on Earth. Cave tours range from a standard walking tour suitable for most visitors to more strenuous candlelight and wild cave tours that involve crawling through tight passages using only a headlamp. Tickets for the standard tours are often available the same day, especially outside of peak summer weekends. That is a contrast to the advance lottery systems required for popular hikes at busier national parks. Above ground, the prairie surrounding the cave supports one of the country's few genetically pure bison herds. Elk, pronghorn, and prairie dog towns are also visible from the park's main roads. Several hiking trails cross this open grassland without requiring any permit, and pull-offs along the park road frequently offer close, unhurried views of grazing bison from a vehicle. Wind Cave sits in the shadow of more famous Black Hills destinations. As a result, it absorbs only a portion of the traffic that clogs roads near Mount Rushmore during peak summer months. Its own trails and cave tours stay far less crowded despite being a short drive from some of the region's most visited sites. Guadalupe Mountains National Park holds Texas' highest peak without the lines Credit: Canva Images Guadalupe Mountains National Park in West Texas protects Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas at 8,751 feet, and requires no permit or reservation to hike to its summit. The round trip hike covers roughly 8.4 miles and climbs more than 3,000 feet, making it a genuine mountain hike rather than a short overlook walk. It remains open, though, to any hiker who simply shows up and signs in at the trailhead. The park sits along a remnant of an ancient fossil reef formed hundreds of millions of years ago, when the region lay beneath a shallow tropical sea. That geologic history left behind sheer limestone cliffs and canyons that stand in sharp contrast to the flat desert scrub surrounding the park. The contrast is most visible at El Capitan, a limestone cliff face rising abruptly from the desert floor beside the park's main highway. McKittrick Canyon, a separate trailhead within the park, draws visitors each fall for one of the more reliable displays of autumn foliage in the desert Southwest. Bigtooth maple trees turn shades of orange and red inside a canyon that otherwise looks like classic Chihuahuan Desert terrain. The canyon trail requires no permit, though the park does close the gate to the parking area at set hours to manage the number of cars. Guadalupe Mountains receives only a small fraction of the visitors that pass through better known Texas destinations like Big Bend National Park. That is in part because it sits far from any major city and offers few services inside the park itself. Backcountry camping requires a free permit obtained at the visitor center. Day hikes across the park's more than 80 miles of trails need nothing beyond a trailhead sign-in sheet. That leaves popular routes like Guadalupe Peak and McKittrick Canyon largely free of the congestion found at more famous mountain parks. Lassen Volcanic National Park never adopted a timed entry system Credit: Royce Fonseca / Unsplash Lassen Volcanic National Park in Northern California has no timed entry reservation, no shuttle requirement, and no permit lottery for its main attractions. That holds true even as reservation systems have spread to more famous parks across the West. The park charges a standard entrance fee but otherwise operates the way most national parks did a generation ago: pay at the gate, park at a trailhead, and start hiking. Lassen is one of the few places on Earth where all four types of volcanoes exist within a single park: shield, cinder cone, composite, and plug dome. Lassen Peak itself, a plug dome volcano, last erupted between 1914 and 1917. The hike to its summit remains one of the more strenuous day hikes in the park, climbing roughly 2,000 feet over about five miles round trip without requiring any permit. Bumpass Hell, the park's largest hydrothermal area, offers a boardwalk trail through boiling mud pots, steaming fumaroles, and pools tinted by dissolved minerals. The features are similar in character to those found at Yellowstone. It is reachable without a park-wide reservation system or the crowds that gather at Yellowstone's most famous thermal basins. The boardwalk protects both visitors and the fragile ground around the features, and the trail requires no advance booking. Snow lingers at Lassen's higher elevations well into summer some years, since much of the park sits above 6,000 feet. That shortens the visitor season compared with lower elevation parks. It also helps keep midsummer crowds smaller than the numbers might otherwise suggest for a park within driving distance of Sacramento and Redding, California. Because Lassen receives a fraction of the visitors that travel to Yosemite or Yellowstone each year, popular trailheads like Bumpass Hell and Lassen Peak rarely reach capacity. Campgrounds inside the park often have same-day or next-day availability outside of the busiest summer holiday weekends, a rare thing at comparably scenic Western parks. New River Gorge is the newest and easiest national park to enter Credit: Canva Images New River Gorge National Park and Preserve in West Virginia charges no entrance fee and requires no reservation. It only became a national park in December 2020, making it the newest addition to the National Park System's list of full national parks. Despite the recent designation, the park protects land that has drawn climbers, rafters, and hikers for decades along one of the oldest rivers in North America. The park's centerpiece is the New River Gorge Bridge, a steel arch bridge that rises 876 feet above the river below. That makes it one of the highest vehicular bridges in the United States. Canyon Rim Visitor Center, perched near the bridge, offers a free overlook and a short boardwalk trail with views down into the gorge. Both are open to any visitor without a ticket or timed entry slot. Whitewater rafting is the activity most associated with the park. Outfitters based in nearby Fayetteville, West Virginia, run guided trips ranging from calmer upper gorge floats suitable for families to more demanding lower gorge rapids for experienced paddlers. None of these trips require a park permit, only a booking directly with a rafting company, since the park itself does not operate or ticket the rafting. Rock climbers know the New River Gorge for its sandstone cliffs, which offer more than 1,400 established climbing routes across a range of difficulty levels. That makes it one of the more significant climbing destinations in the eastern U.S. Access to most crags requires only a short hike from a roadside pull-off, with no permit needed for day climbing. New River Gorge only recently gained national park status, so it still receives a fraction of the attention paid to older, more established parks. Its entrance requirements, though, are simpler than almost anywhere else in the system. There is no gate to fight through, no fee booth backup, and no reservation to plan around. There is only a bridge, a river, and a gorge that visitors can walk right into.

item.title: The 9 best places around the world to see Yayoi Kusama's art permanently
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.17
The 9 best places around the world to see Yayoi Kusama's art permanently From a 100-meter sculpture at London's Liverpool Street to a Hawaiian shopping mall, nine places where Yayoi Kusama's art lives on permanently A commuter stepping off a train at London’s Liverpool Street Station rarely expects to walk past a 100-meter sculpture on the way to the ticket barriers, yet that is exactly where one of Yayoi Kusama’s largest works has quietly stood since 2024. Most people encounter her art the way they encounter most famous artists, through a traveling exhibition that arrives, draws a crowd, and eventually packs up and moves on to the next city. A handful of her pieces broke that pattern entirely, settling into permanent homes in train stations, shopping malls, and museums built specifically around her work. Anyone hoping to see one of these pieces doesn’t need to catch a temporary show or hope a retrospective comes to their city, since these installations simply wait, year after year, for whoever happens to show up. Kusama died in Tokyo on August 14, 2026, at the age of 97, closing out a career spanning seven decades that turned polka dots, pumpkins, and mirrored rooms into some of the most recognizable images in contemporary art. Her death makes the handful of permanent installations scattered across the world more significant than they were even a few months ago, since these sites now represent fixed, lasting access to work that will never again expand through new commissions. Some of these locations reward spontaneous visits, while others demand serious advance planning, since tickets for her most popular rooms tend to sell out within minutes of release. A traveler hoping to see several of these pieces on a single trip needs to research each site’s specific access rules well before booking flights, since a museum that welcomes walk-ins in one city might require a reservation secured months earlier in another. The 9 places below appear in Time Out and cover permanent installations of Kusama’s work across four continents, from a London train station to a Hawaiian shopping mall. Each entry focuses on a single site and what makes the specific piece housed there worth the trip. 1. London reflects Kusama’s largest sculpture Infinite Accumulation has greeted travelers outside the Elizabeth Line entrance at Liverpool Street Station since 2024, tucked between coffee shops and departure boards where few visitors expect major public art. The sculpture stretches 100 meters of connected, reflective steel spheres rising 10 meters into the air, making it both Kusama’s largest permanent sculpture anywhere in the world and her only permanent public artwork in the United Kingdom. Crossrail commissioned the piece as part of its public art program, a rare case of major infrastructure spending going toward a genuinely significant work of contemporary sculpture instead of decorative filler. The steel spheres catch and warp the City skyline as commuters weave beneath them on their way to and from the platforms, turning what would otherwise be an unremarkable station entrance into an accidental hall of mirrors that most people walk through without planning to stop. This accidental quality gives the piece a different character than Kusama’s more contained, ticketed installations elsewhere on this list. Nobody needs to book a slot or wait in line to experience Infinite Accumulation, since it exists in the middle of one of London’s busiest transit hubs, open to anyone passing through at any hour. The sculpture’s scale means even a rushed commuter catches at least a glimpse of the distorted skyline reflected across its spheres, whether or not they stop long enough to take it in properly. Liverpool Street Station handles enormous daily foot traffic, so Infinite Accumulation likely reaches more casual, unintentional viewers than any other work on this list, turning thousands of ordinary commutes into brief, unplanned encounters with major contemporary art.
