A tourist visiting London specifically for its museums might never think to look for a Kusama piece at a train station, yet this sculpture arguably reaches more eyes in a single week than a ticketed gallery installation manages in a month, simply by virtue of standing in everyone’s path. 2. Naoshima guards two of Kusama’s giant pumpkins Yue-Ting Lin / Unsplash The yellow-and-black spotted pumpkin on Naoshima’s pier ranks among the most photographed of all Kusama’s works, having sat at the edge of the island since 1994 and become inseparable from the island’s identity as Japan’s dedicated art destination. A typhoon swept the original pumpkin out to sea in 2021, damaging it badly enough that restoration wasn’t an option, but a faithful, storm-reinforced replacement took its place in 2022, built specifically to withstand the kind of weather that destroyed its predecessor. Down at Miyanoura Port, where ferries bring visitors onto the island, a second and considerably cheekier sibling waits. Installed in 2006 and standing 4 meters tall, the Red Pumpkin lets visitors climb directly inside through openings cut into its dots, turning a static sculpture into something closer to a small, walkable room. It glows after dark, which means it tends to be both the first thing arriving visitors see and the last thing departing visitors glimpse on their way back to the mainland. This pairing gives Naoshima a rare distinction among the sites on this list, since most locations feature only a single major Kusama work. Visitors get both the more famous, photographed yellow pumpkin on its quiet pier and the more playful, climbable red pumpkin at the port, two very different experiences of the same recurring motif within a short walk of each other. Naoshima’s relationship with Kusama runs deeper than either pumpkin alone, since the island has built its entire tourism identity around contemporary art installations, making the pumpkins less a standalone attraction than the most photographed piece within a much larger open-air museum spread across the island itself. Visitors who come specifically for the pumpkins often find themselves staying far longer than planned once they discover how much other art the island holds, turning what was meant as a quick photo stop into a multi-day art pilgrimage that few visitors anticipate when they first book the ferry. 3. Niigata blooms with Kusama’s favorite flower A gigantic dotted flower has stood outside Matsudai Station in the Echigo-Tsumari Art Field since 2003, one of more than 800 permanent works scattered across this stretch of rural Japan. Kusama herself named this particular sculpture as her favorite among all the open-air pieces she created over her career, a striking claim from an artist who produced a genuinely enormous number of them across seven decades of work. Few artists leave behind such a clear, specific answer when asked to single out one favorite from a body of work this large. Tsumari in Bloom stands apart from the triennale’s temporary installations in one key respect, since the wider Echigo-Tsumari Art Field rotates many of its pieces in and out for each edition of the festival while this particular flower stays on permanent display year-round. This permanence means a visitor doesn’t need to time a trip around the triennale’s exact festival dates to see it, unlike many other works scattered through the same rice terraces, some of which appear only during the few months the festival runs. The rural setting itself shapes how the sculpture reads differently than Kusama’s more urban installations elsewhere on this list. Surrounded by rice terraces instead of city streets or shopping malls, the flower’s oversized scale and bright dots create a jarring, almost surreal contrast against the quiet agricultural landscape, the kind of visual collision that a gallery setting could never quite replicate. Farmers tending the surrounding fields go about their work within sight of a sculpture that would look entirely at home in a major international museum. Kusama’s own preference for this piece adds a layer of meaning that few other works on this list can claim, since most of her sculptures exist as commissions built for specific institutions instead of pieces she pointed to herself as a personal favorite among everything she made. This personal endorsement gives Tsumari in Bloom weight beyond its physical scale, turning a visit into something closer to seeing the artist’s own choice rather than simply another stop on a list. 4. Tokyo tests fans with timed museum tickets Credit: Yayoi Kusama Museum The Yayoi Kusama Museum functions as a five-story shrine built entirely around her own work, housed inside a striking white building in Shinjuku since 2017. The museum runs two rotating exhibitions each year and includes her well-known installation The Princess with the Pea, giving repeat visitors a genuine reason to return since the collection on display changes on a regular schedule instead of staying fixed year-round. Few artists get an entire dedicated museum built around their work while still living, which makes this site distinct from every other stop on this list. Actually getting inside counts as its own small ordeal, separate from the art itself. Tickets go on sale two months before each visit date, released on the first of the month, and routinely sell out within minutes. Entry runs on a strict 90-minute slot system, and the museum sells no tickets at the door, which rules out the kind of spontaneous, same-day visit that works for several other sites on this list. Visitors who miss the release window entirely sometimes wait months for another chance. This ticketing system makes the Yayoi Kusama Museum the planner’s stop on this list, not the wanderer’s. Visitors hoping to see it need to build their entire Tokyo itinerary around a ticket release date months in advance, a level of preparation closer to booking a popular restaurant reservation than showing up at a typical museum. This level of demand shows how central Tokyo remains to any serious exploration of her legacy, despite the difficulty of actually getting through the door. The museum’s strict access rules ultimately protect an intensely personal, curated experience of Kusama’s work, built by the artist around her own vision rather than shaped by a larger institution’s broader collection or competing curatorial priorities. The scarcity built into the ticketing system, frustrating as it can feel, mirrors the same intensity and control that defined her approach to the art itself. 5. Matsumoto celebrates its hometown artist in dots Credit: Kamikochi Official Site Kusama was born in Matsumoto in 1929, and the city’s museum now holds a permanent collection of her work, giving visitors a chance to see her art in the specific place that shaped her earliest years. Outside the building, a giant sculpture called The Visionary Flowers, created in 2002, greets visitors before they even reach the entrance, setting the tone for what waits inside. Standing in the shadow of the same mountains that surrounded Kusama as a child adds context no other museum on this list can offer. The Kusama treatment extends well past the gallery walls once visitors step through the door. Vending machines, benches, and even the restrooms throughout the museum have received the same polka-dot makeover that defines her artwork, turning ordinary functional spaces into small extensions of the exhibition itself. Visitors who time their trip well might also catch the dotted Boisterous Polka Dot bus running between the train station and the museum, a detail that folds the artist’s signature style into the town’s everyday transit infrastructure. Even a short ride on public transit becomes part of the overall experience here. Matsumoto offers a distinctly quieter, more personal alternative to Tokyo’s crowds and strict ticketing rules, since the hometown museum draws a smaller, more dedicated crowd of visitors specifically interested in seeing where Kusama’s story actually began. The contrast between this intimate setting and the Tokyo museum’s high-demand, timed-entry system gives visitors two very different ways to encounter the same artist’s legacy: one built around scarcity and demand, the other around a slower, more reflective pace. A visit to Matsumoto works best paired with genuine curiosity about Kusama’s biography rather than a checklist approach to seeing her most famous pieces, since the real draw lies in the connection between the artist and the place she came from, not in any single standout artwork. Visitors leave with a stronger sense of where her vision originated than any other stop on this list provides. 6. Honolulu hides a bronze pumpkin among koi ponds Credit: Ala Moana Center A six-foot bronze pumpkin weighing 1,200 pounds has sat among the koi ponds at Ala Moana Center since 2016, installed overnight by a team working after closing hours to have it ready before the next morning’s shoppers arrived. The sculpture marked Kusama’s first permanent installation in Hawaii, placing major contemporary art in one of the least expected settings on this entire list, a busy shopping mall instead of a museum or dedicated art space. Shoppers heading to a department store or a food court find themselves walking directly past a genuine piece of art history without any advance warning. The choice of subject matter carries genuine personal weight rather than serving as a random decorative choice. Pumpkins sustained Kusama’s family through food scarcity during the Second World War, giving the vegetable a personal significance that runs through much of her broader body of work well beyond this single Honolulu piece. Placing that particular symbol among a mall’s koi ponds adds an unexpected layer of meaning to what could otherwise read as a simple decorative sculpture, connecting a moment of wartime hardship to a distinctly modern setting built around leisure and shopping. Ala Moana Center’s setting makes this installation unusually accessible compared to several other sites on this list. Shoppers encounter the pumpkin without needing to plan a museum visit or book a ticket in advance, since it sits in a space thousands of people pass through daily for entirely unrelated reasons, much like the London sculpture at Liverpool Street Station. This accessibility comes with a trade-off, though, since a shopping mall offers none of the quiet, contemplative atmosphere that a dedicated gallery space provides. The pumpkin’s presence in a shopping mall ultimately speaks to how far Kusama’s work traveled beyond the traditional art world during her lifetime, reaching audiences who might never have set foot inside a gallery but still encounter one of her most personally significant motifs on an ordinary shopping trip. 7. Los Angeles multiplies light into infinity Credit: The Broad The Broad holds two of Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms in its permanent collection, giving Los Angeles a rare distinction among the cities on this list with more than one mirror room to visit in a single museum. Step inside either one and the mirrored walls take a handful of lights or hanging shapes and multiply them endlessly, creating the disorienting sense that the room extends forever in every direction with no visible boundary. Few installations anywhere manage to make a space feel genuinely infinite using nothing more than glass, light, and careful geometry. Infinity Mirrored Room, The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away, completed in 2013, requires an advance reservation, while Longing for Eternity, from 2017 and located on the third floor, usually operates as a walk-in experience, though it can close without warning depending on capacity and staffing. This split between a bookable room and a walk-in room gives visitors two different ways to plan around the museum’s Kusama holdings, depending on how far ahead they’re organizing their trip. A visitor with a flexible schedule might get lucky with the walk-in room, while someone locked into a tight itinerary should secure the reservation-only room well in advance. Demand for these rooms reached genuinely extreme levels during The Broad’s dedicated 2017 Kusama survey, which pulled a ticket queue of roughly 150,000 people over the course of the exhibition. This number gives a clear sense of just how significant the appetite for her work became in Los Angeles specifically, well beyond what a typical museum exhibition draws even for a celebrated artist. Museum staff at the time described lines that stretched for city blocks, a scale of public interest more typical of a major concert than a contemporary art installation. The permanence of these two rooms means that demand never fully disappeared once the special exhibition ended, since both installations remain part of The Broad’s standing collection instead of existing only for the duration of a single ticketed show. Los Angeles now offers a lasting version of the frenzy that first drew those enormous 2017 crowds, minus the wait that stretched around the building back then. 8. Sydney lights a garden of oversized blooms Credit: Art Gallery NSW The Art Gallery of New South Wales commissioned Flowers that Bloom in the Cosmos specifically for its Naala Badu building, which opened in December 2022, and the piece dominates its setting from the moment visitors step outside. Oversized spotted blooms fill the terrace overlooking Woolloomooloo Bay, lit up continuously day and night, giving the installation a completely different presence depending on whether a visitor arrives at noon or after sunset. Few Kusama installations anywhere pair her signature motifs with a harbor view this dramatic. Kusama saw herself and everyone else as a single dot connected to countless others, part of one vast, spotted universe extending far beyond any individual person or object. This particular sculpture reads as one of the most literal physical expressions of that worldview she ever produced, translating an abstract philosophical idea directly into a garden of oversized, illuminated flowers that visitors can walk straight through. Standing among the blooms puts a visitor physically inside the same metaphor Kusama spent decades describing in interviews and writing. The terrace setting matters as much as the sculpture itself, since the harbor views behind Woolloomooloo Bay give the flowers a backdrop that changes constantly with the weather and time of day. A sunset visit transforms the piece entirely compared to a midday viewing, with the illuminated blooms taking on a different character as the sky shifts from blue to orange to genuine darkness. Photographers in particular tend to return at multiple times of day just to capture how differently the same sculpture reads under changing light. Few of Kusama’s permanent installations sit so openly exposed to a city skyline and harbor view, giving Sydney’s piece a sense of scale and context that some of her more enclosed, gallery-bound works elsewhere on this list simply can’t replicate. The open terrace setting turns a single sculpture into an entire outdoor experience instead of a contained room a visitor steps briefly into and out of again. 9. Canberra shrinks visitors inside a mirrored room Credit: National Gallery of Australia The National Gallery of Australia has owned The Spirits of the Pumpkins Descended into the Heavens since 2018, one of Kusama’s mirror rooms built around her recurring pumpkin motif rather than the abstract lights and shapes found in some of her other infinity rooms. Visitors peer into a small mirrored chamber crowded with illuminated, spotted pumpkins through a single peephole, and the reflections stretch what is actually a modestly sized space into something that appears to extend infinitely in every direction. The effect works because the room stays small enough to build cheaply while still delivering a sense of true infinity. This single-peephole design sets this installation apart from the walk-in mirror rooms at The Broad in Los Angeles. Rather than stepping inside the space, visitors experience the illusion through one small viewing point, creating a more intimate, almost voyeuristic relationship between viewer and artwork than a room built for full physical entry. Only one person can typically look through the peephole at a time, turning what might be a shared group experience elsewhere into something closer to a solitary moment. The work tours periodically to partner institutions instead of staying fixed in Canberra year-round, with recent stints at the Art Gallery of South Australia and the Western Plains Cultural Centre pulling it away from its home base for extended periods. Visitors hoping to see it should check the National Gallery of Australia’s website for its current location before planning a trip, since arriving in Canberra offers no guarantee the piece will actually be on-site. This uncertainty separates this installation from every other fixed location described elsewhere on this list. This touring arrangement makes The Spirits of the Pumpkins Descended into the Heavens the least predictable stop on this entire list, rewarding visitors who do their homework in advance far more than those who simply show up expecting to find it waiting in its usual home. A quick check of the museum’s website before booking flights can save an entire trip from ending in disappointment.

item.title: The 5 most walkable cities in Europe in 2026, ranked
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.13
The 5 most walkable cities in Europe in 2026, ranked From Edinburgh's historic hills to Helsinki's ice-safe winter pavements, the most walkable cities in Europe according to the people who live there A city reveals a different personality on foot than it ever does through a car window or a bus route mapped out in advance. Streets that look identical from behind glass turn out to hide a bakery worth circling back for, a museum too small to appear on any major tour, or a bar filled with music that pulls a walker in off the sidewalk. None of that happens on a fixed schedule. It happens because someone decided to wander instead of plan, and the city rewarded that decision with something a car or a train could never have delivered. Cities that make this kind of accidental discovery easy tend to earn a loyalty from visitors that a well-run transit system alone rarely inspires. Not every city makes that kind of wandering easy, though, and the difference often comes down to details a visitor would never think to ask about in advance. Wide, unbroken pavements matter as much as scenic views. A compact city center matters as much as a famous skyline. Even winter weather plays a role, since a city that keeps pedestrians safe from ice and snow holds onto its walkability in January in a way that a merely pretty city in July never has to prove. The cities that rank highest for walking tend to get all these details right at once, instead of excelling at just one. The 5 cities below appear in Time Out, covering the top-ranked entries from Time Out’s 2026 survey of more than 24,000 city dwellers across Europe, which asked locals to rate their own city’s walkability as good or amazing. The publication counted only the highest-scoring city in each country, and the entries below cover the five top-scoring cities from that ranking, from the historic hills of Scotland to the winter streets of Finland. 1. Edinburgh rewards uphill wandering Joss Broward / Unsplash Edinburgh topped Time Out’s 2026 walkability survey with a score of 93 percent, the highest of any European city in the ranking, based on how locals rated their own streets for walking. Footpaths link castle views, hidden closes, and the rocky summit of Arthur’s Seat into a single connected network, giving a walker access to the city’s most dramatic scenery without ever needing to plan a route around traffic. The relationship between Edinburgh’s Old Town and New Town shapes much of that walkability. The medieval Old Town winds uphill in narrow closes and steep lanes that predate any modern traffic planning, while the Georgian New Town spreads out below in a more orderly grid built centuries later. Both halves of the city sit close enough together that a walker can move between medieval alleyways and Georgian crescents inside a single afternoon, absorbing two entirely different eras of urban design without a single bus ride between them. Those hidden closes deserve particular attention from any visitor exploring on foot. Narrow enough to miss from a moving car, these historic alleyways branch off Edinburgh’s main streets and lead to courtyards, viewpoints, and quiet corners that a driver would never notice passing by. Discovering one unprompted, simply by choosing to turn down an unfamiliar lane, captures exactly the kind of reward that a high walkability score is meant to measure. Arthur’s Seat adds a genuine physical challenge to all that charm, an extinct volcano rising above the city that turns a casual stroll into something closer to a hike. The climb rewards effort with a panoramic view over the entire city and the Firth of Forth beyond it, and the elevation change throughout Edinburgh more broadly means a walking tour here works the legs in a way that a flatter city never would. This mix of dramatic scenery, historic density, and genuine elevation likely explains why Edinburgh edged out every other city in the survey. 2. Copenhagen flows along wide open promenades Febiyan / Unsplash Copenhagen scored 90 percent in the same survey, placing second among Europe’s most walkable cities despite a reputation built almost entirely around bicycles. Locals and visitors alike associate the Danish capital more with cyclists than pedestrians, an association so strong that many travelers arrive assuming the city favors two wheels over two feet, packing walking shoes as an afterthought behind a rental bike reservation. This assumption undersells how well Copenhagen actually works for walking. Wide pavements run throughout the city, paired with waterside promenades that flow into each other without the abrupt dead ends or narrow pinch points that interrupt walkability in many other European capitals. The urban design behind those pavements appears intentional, not incidental, suggesting that planners built pedestrian comfort into the city’s layout as deliberately as they built out its famous cycling infrastructure. This intentional design shows up most clearly in how effortless getting around the city center actually feels. A walker moving between neighborhoods rarely has to backtrack or search for a route around an obstacle, since the promenades and pavements connect in a way that keeps momentum going instead of forcing constant course corrections. Cyclists may still dominate Copenhagen’s popular image, but the city’s second-place score suggests its planners cared just as much about the experience of the people moving on foot beside them as they did about the cyclists sharing the same streets. Copenhagen’s high ranking ultimately complicates the usual assumption that a bike-first city can’t also be a walker’s city. The two systems appear to have developed alongside each other instead of in competition, giving Copenhagen a rare distinction among major European capitals. The city stands out as genuinely excellent for both cyclists and pedestrians at once, with neither mode of transport winning out over the other, a balance that fewer cities manage than the survey results might suggest. Visitors who show up expecting a city built purely for bikes tend to leave having spent just as much time happily on foot. 3. Oslo blends forest trails with the city center Marleen Mulder-Wieske / Unsplash Oslo placed third in the survey with a score of 89 percent, a result the city earns by proving that nature and urban life can share the same walkable footprint. Compact, clean, and calm, the Norwegian capital packs cutting-edge museums, waterfront saunas, and genuine forest trails into a single walkable network, all reachable without ever needing a car. Few capital cities anywhere in Europe manage to hold that much natural variety inside their own city limits. This range of experience within walking distance sets Oslo apart from cities that excel at just one type of walk. A morning spent moving between contemporary museums gives way, within the same city limits, to an afternoon at a waterfront sauna and an evening spent on a forest trail, three completely different environments connected without a single transit transfer. Few European capitals compress that much variety into a distance a pair of legs can comfortably cover in one day, let alone make that variety feel effortless instead of exhausting. Oslo’s compactness does much of the practical work behind that range. A smaller city center means the distance between a museum and a sauna, or between a sauna and a forest trailhead, stays short enough to walk without exhaustion setting in halfway through. This physical closeness turns what would be a multi-destination day trip in a larger city into a single continuous walk in Oslo, threading together experiences that elsewhere would require separate outings, each with its own transit connection and planning. The calmness locals describe likely reflects that same compactness as much as anything else. A city small enough to cross comfortably on foot naturally avoids the sprawl and traffic congestion that make many capitals feel frantic, and Oslo’s third-place score suggests that trade-off, choosing density and walkability over sheer size, works entirely in its favor. Visitors who arrive expecting a typical sprawling European capital tend to leave surprised at how much fits inside such a small, calm footprint. 4. Stockholm and Paris cross bridges built for wandering Catalina Johnson / Unsplash Stockholm and Paris tied for fourth place in the survey, each scoring 88 percent, and both cities earn that ranking through a shared relationship with water that shapes how locals move through them on foot. Bridges in both cities function as more than crossings, doubling as viewpoints that reward a walker who pauses mid-span instead of hurrying straight across. This instinct to pause instead of passing straight through may be the clearest sign of genuine walkability either city offers. Stockholm’s version of that experience centers on Gamla Stan, the city’s old town, where narrow medieval streets sit across the water from the modern city and connect to it by bridges that offer sweeping views over the surrounding archipelago. Built across a cluster of islands, Stockholm essentially forces a walker to cross water regularly just to move between neighborhoods, turning what could be a minor inconvenience into one of the city’s defining charms. Few cities manage to make a geographic constraint feel this much like a deliberate design choice. Paris earns its identical score through a different but comparably scenic relationship with elevation and water. Montmartre rises above the rest of the city as a hillside neighborhood full of winding streets, and a walk up through it delivers the kind of scenic reward that matches anything Stockholm’s bridges offer, just achieved through height instead of water crossings. The Seine itself, meanwhile, plays a role closer to Stockholm’s canals, with bridges that offer postcard views across the city and give Parisian walkers the same excuse to pause mid-crossing that Stockholm’s bridges provide. Both cities share one more quality beyond scenery. Small discoveries reveal themselves only on foot in each place, and coffee shops tucked into corners in both Stockholm and Paris go unnoticed by anyone moving through by car or Metro. This shared reward for aimless, unhurried walking likely explains how two cities with such different layouts, one built across islands and the other around a hill, ended up tied at an identical score in the same survey. 5. Helsinki lifts pedestrians above winter streets Tapio Haaja / Unsplash Helsinki rounded out the top five with a score of 85 percent, and the Finnish capital earns particular credit for staying walkable through conditions that defeat many other cities entirely. Locals describe Helsinki as a phenomenal walking destination even in winter, a season that typically empties sidewalks elsewhere in northern Europe and forces pedestrians back into cars or public transit. Surviving that seasonal test matters more for a genuine walkability score than any single summer afternoon ever could. Much of that winter resilience comes down to deliberate infrastructure choices, not luck with the climate. Many streets throughout Helsinki feature elevated pavements that separate pedestrians from vehicle traffic and, just as importantly, from the ice and slush that collect at street level during the coldest months. This small design choice keeps walking a viable option in Helsinki during exactly the season when most cities quietly abandon their pedestrians to the weather, treating winter as an afterthought instead of a season worth designing around. Helsinki’s compactness reinforces that winter-ready infrastructure. City landmarks sit close to one another throughout the center, meaning a walker never has to commit to a long, exposed trek between destinations even when temperatures drop well below comfortable. Short distances between attractions matter more in a cold climate than in a mild one, since every extra minute spent outdoors in genuinely cold weather carries a cost that a similar walk in a warmer city simply doesn’t. Helsinki’s fifth-place finish makes a strong case that surveys shouldn’t judge walkability only on ideal-weather days. A city that keeps its score this high through a genuine Nordic winter has solved a harder problem than any of the cities ranked above it, even if that achievement shows up as a slightly lower number in a survey taken across an entire year, one that never separates out a single easy summer month for special credit. A city built to handle its worst season well deserves at least as much recognition as one that only ever gets tested in June.

item.title: John Ternus is officially taking over as Apple CEO, with AI as his biggest test
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.10
John Ternus is set to become Apple $AAPL's chief executive officer on Tuesday, stepping into the role with an immediate product launch cycle and a company under pressure to close the gap with rivals in artificial intelligence. Ternus takes over for Tim Cook as Apple prepares a foldable iPhone launch and a rebuilt Siri powered by Google's Gemini AI technology Tim Cook, who led Apple for 15 years, moves to executive chairman on the same date. Cook told employees he would continue managing Apple's relationships with President Donald Trump and the Chinese government, and that he is available to assist Ternus on any tasks his successor requires, according to Bloomberg. Art Levinson, the current board chair, becomes lead independent director on Sept. 1, Apple said. Ternus, 51, joined Apple in 2001 and rose to senior vice president of hardware engineering in 2021. His first major public test as CEO comes on Sept. 9, when Apple hosts a product launch event at its Cupertino, California campus that is expected to feature the company's first foldable iPhone, new Apple Watches, and the debut of a rebuilt Siri voice assistant powered by large language models, Apple said. Apple's AI position is the most consequential issue Ternus inherits. The company faced mounting criticism over the delayed overhaul of Siri and its pace in generative AI, leading to a leadership shake-up in the AI division and a decision to rebuild Siri using Google $GOOGL's Gemini technology as its foundation. A full-scale deployment of the new Siri is set for September. Early reviews have been positive, Bloomberg reported. Ternus is also responsible for a broader set of hardware products he guided during his time as Apple's hardware chief, among them AirPods equipped with environment-sensing cameras, smart glasses, a home security system, a display mounted on a robotic arm, and a wearable pendant. A number of those products have been pushed back because Apple's AI software was not ready to support them. On his final earnings call as CEO, Cook described Apple's ability to process AI workloads directly on devices as a strategic advantage over cloud-dependent competitors, and said the company sees "enormous opportunities" ahead in AI. For supply chain and financial challenges — domains where Cook built his reputation — Ternus is anticipated to lean on Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan and Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh rather than managing those issues directly. Apple is contending with a persistent shortage of memory and storage chips that the company has cited as a driver of recent price increases, a problem it does not expect to resolve before next year. item.title: Stock futures fall after U.S. strikes Iran, ending month-long lull
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.10
Stock futures edged lower on Monday after the United States struck Iranian rocket launchers over the weekend, ending a roughly month-long pause in hostilities and pushing oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude topped $90 a barrel after the U.S. attacked Iranian rocket launchers on Sunday, the first confirmed strike in about a month U.S. Central Command acknowledged Sunday that American forces had hit a pair of rocket launchers located on Iran's Larak Island, according to CNBC. It was the first publicly acknowledged U.S. attack on Iranian positions since late July. Iranian state media reported that Tehran responded by attacking U.S. bases in Jordan, according to CNBC. The renewed confrontation sent oil prices sharply higher. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was trading at $86.25 a barrel, a gain of 3.4%, while Brent crude futures added 3.6% to reach $91.24 a barrel. Despite the early pressure, U.S. indexes remain on track to close August in positive territory. The Dow has gained 2.1% so far in August, which would make it five monthly wins in a row. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were each poised to snap a losing streak, logging their first monthly gains since May at roughly 3% and 4%, respectively. Earlier in the month, both the S&P 500 and the Dow notched record closes. Technology stocks led the month's gains. Within the S&P 500, technology shares were up nearly 6% for the month; Nvidia $NVDA surged more than 8%, and Microsoft $MSFT and Micron $MU Technology posted gains of 11% and 13%, respectively. August was not without turbulence. Rising inflation fears pushed Treasury yields to multiyear highs, and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh cautioned on Friday that, even though this summer's inflation data came in better than anticipated, it has not convinced him that the broader trend is improving. In a research note cited by CNBC, Barclays economist Jonathan Millar said Warsh's hawkish tone makes a quarter-point hike at the September meeting the most probable outcome, with the bank's baseline scenario penciling in a second increase in December. Asian equity markets were a mixed picture: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 slipped 0.14%, Seoul's Kospi added 0.46%, and mainland China's CSI 300 edged up 0.35%, while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.18%. In Europe, the broad Stoxx 600 index hovered fractionally below the unchanged mark, with London sidelined by a public holiday. Investors will get a clearer read on the economy later this week. Economists surveyed ahead of Friday's report anticipate that August payrolls grew by 50,000 after employers shed 23,000 jobs in July, according to The Wall Street Journal. Reports on activity in the manufacturing and services sectors are also scheduled for release this week. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Wall Street is heading into September with stocks near records — and reasons for caution
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.89
Wall Street is entering September with the S&P 500 close to record territory but facing a cluster of risk signals that analysts say warrant attention, even if the seasonal case for alarm is less clear-cut than commonly presented. The S&P 500 is within 2% of its all-time high, but the VIX, Treasury yields, and historical patterns are drawing investor attention The S&P 500 has stayed within 2% of its record high above 7,800 throughout August. The index has gained 12.72% year to date, with the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite up 14.23% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 10.72%. September has a well-known reputation as the worst month of the year for stocks. But Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, argued that the current setup may temper those concerns. When August finishes positive and the year's gain falls between 10% and 17.5% — conditions that match 2026 — September has averaged a 1.0% gain going back to World War II, according to Benzinga. Ryan Detrick also noted that in such conditions, the last four months of the year have finished higher in 10 of 11 instances, with an average gain of 5.6%. Still, Ryan Detrick cautioned that midterm-election-year dynamics can bring turbulence in August and September. He identified 7,610 — the S&P 500's June 2 peak — as a key support level to watch, according to Benzinga. CNBC's Mike Santoli flagged a separate set of market signals that he said warrant vigilance independent of the calendar. The CBOE Volatility Index has dropped under 15 — a reading Santoli called "eerie complacency" — which he found notable because seasonal patterns typically push volatility higher around this point on the calendar. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above 4.7% after Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh used his Jackson Hole appearance Friday to convey that the committee views short-term rate increases as the appropriate response to persistent inflation — and that one could come soon, according to CNBC. Pricing in fed-funds futures put the probability of a September hike at roughly 50% in the wake of Warsh's address, according to CNBC. Santoli argued that such evenly split odds, arriving weeks before a policy meeting, tend to keep investors from taking on additional risk. Sentiment data also leans cautious. John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors characterized the latest sentiment reading as broadly unchanged but tilted in a worrying direction, with traditional surveys like Investors Intelligence registering too many bulls and real-time market data pointing to elevated complacency. item.title: Steel and materials stocks are whipsawing as the U.S.-Canada trade war heats up
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.75
Steel and aluminum stocks surged and then retreated last week as the escalating trade war between the United States and Canada sent investors scrambling to reprice exposure to North American metals supply chains. The VanEck Steel ETF and State Street Materials Select Sector SPDR swung sharply last week as U.S.-Canada tariff tensions escalated SLX gained 1.6% on Monday, Aug. 25, following the breakdown of U.S.-Canada trade talks, and the State Street $STT Materials Select Sector SPDR (XLB) reached a new intraday record that session, topping the peak it had set in February. Shares of Nucor, Steel Dynamics, Cleveland-Cliffs, and Century Aluminum all climbed. The gains proved short-lived, however: by Friday's close, XLB had slipped into the red for the week and SLX was essentially unchanged, according to CNBC. Through Aug. 28, Morningstar data show SLX has gained more than 28% on the year and XLB more than 18%. The swing reflects the complexity of a trade war between two countries whose metals industries are deeply intertwined. Dan Luttner, who serves as managing partner of the supply chain consulting firm NEOS by Argon & Company, characterized the initial stock move to CNBC as a repricing reflex rather than a durable signal. "The stock pop is a headline reflex, honestly — mills reprice to replacement cost the second a 50% wall goes up, so of course Nucor and Cleveland-Cliffs jumped," Luttner said. "But that's not the interesting question. The interesting question is who controls their feedstock inside the wall versus who's still exposed to it?" Luttner noted that both Nucor and Cleveland-Cliffs use electric arc furnace technology whose inputs have no dependence on Canadian ore or slab, positioning them to capture tariff-driven pricing benefits without the same exposure. Cleveland-Cliffs stock is nonetheless in negative territory for 2026 because of balance sheet stress. Century Aluminum is a more complicated case: because domestic primary aluminum production is thin, the raw inputs that sustain it — alumina and semi-finished material — largely still flow across the Canadian border, undermining the protection the tariffs were meant to provide. Atsi Sheth, chief credit officer at Moody's $MCO Ratings, said uncertainty will persist. "Expect much more of this uncertainty for some time to come," Sheth said. She added that U.S. steel companies hold a modest edge over their Canadian counterparts because the U.S. market is larger, but said the auto sector has no clear winner given how deeply integrated cross-border production is. Scott Beaulier, a University of Wyoming economics professor who also serves as dean of the College of Business, urged caution against drawing firm conclusions from early stock moves. "I'd be cautious about treating an initial pop in metals stocks as evidence of a durable economy-wide gain," Beaulier said, noting that new aluminum smelting capacity takes years rather than months to build. Canada announced counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of American goods last Tuesday, matching a 50% U.S. tariff on Canadian exports that took effect the prior Saturday. Scheduled to kick in on Sept. 8, the Canadian measures apply to more than 700 categories of American goods, with duty rates of 15%, 25%, or 50% falling on products ranging from dairy and seafood to appliances and steel. Canada suspended trade talks after saying Washington proposed terms it deemed unacceptable. President Donald Trump has separately threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian autos, trucks, and steel to 50% on Jan. 1, 2027. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Honda and Nissan are striking a car software deal after their failed merger
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.45
Honda $HMC Motor Co. and Nissan Motor Co. signed a joint development agreement on Monday to standardize core electronic control units and software for their next-generation software-defined vehicles, the companies said. The two Japanese automakers will jointly develop electronic control units and software for vehicles planned for release starting in fiscal 2029 Under the deal, the two automakers will work together to establish common specifications for multiple core ECUs within the electrical and electronic architecture of next-generation vehicles, along with the in-vehicle operating system, key parts of the middleware, and vehicle control software, the companies said. The jointly developed architecture is planned for use in both companies' vehicles beginning in fiscal year 2029. Software-defined vehicles rely on software rather than mechanical hardware to deliver and update their capabilities and features, according to the Associated Press. The agreement follows a merger attempt between the two companies that did not go through, according to the Wall Street Journal. Nissan and Honda began talks in 2024 to work together on electric vehicles and automotive intelligence technology. The companies said they identified the software domain as a priority for collaboration given the speed of technological change and the need to improve research and development efficiency. By standardizing these underlying technologies, the two automakers aim to cut development costs and achieve greater economies of scale, the companies said. Honda and Nissan each operate in the shadow of Toyota $TM Motor Corp., Japan's dominant automaker, and the collaboration may give both companies a stronger footing against their larger rival, according to the Associated Press. On the other side of the globe, European manufacturers Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Stellantis $STLA have joined forces on software so their vehicles can run on a unified operating system. The two companies also said they intend to look beyond software, with plans to pursue joint work on goals such as achieving carbon neutrality and making their vehicles safer on the road. item.title: Nvidia is investing $3.5 billion in Taiwan's MediaTek to deepen AI chip partnership
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.19
Nvidia $NVDA announced on Monday that it is investing $3.5 billion in MediaTek through convertible bonds, deepening a partnership with the Taiwanese chipmaker that spans AI data center infrastructure, consumer PCs, and automotive platforms. Nvidia will buy convertible bonds in the Taiwanese chipmaker as the two companies broaden collaboration across data centers, PCs, and automotive As part of the expanded agreement, MediaTek will adopt Nvidia's NVLink Fusion platform, which is designed to help hyperscalers, cloud providers, and AI model developers build custom accelerator chips that connect into Nvidia's rack-scale data center systems, the companies said. The deal also extends their existing collaboration on Nvidia RTX Spark and DGX Spark chips for consumer and enterprise PCs, as well as AI-powered automotive platforms built around MediaTek's Dimensity Auto line. "AI is transforming every computing platform — from the world's largest AI factories to the PC and the car," Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. "Together, we're building platforms that bring NVIDIA accelerated computing to new markets and give customers the freedom to create differentiated AI systems at enormous scale." MediaTek vice chairman and CEO Rick Tsai said in a statement that Nvidia's investment "strengthens a collaboration that spans cloud AI infrastructure, local AI computing and automotive in the era of physical AI." Nvidia sees the deal as a way to anchor its interconnect technology and hardware architecture within AI data center build-outs at a moment when many of its biggest customers are pursuing their own custom silicon, according to Bloomberg. MediaTek is competing with Broadcom $AVGO and Marvell Technology for business helping data center operators design custom silicon. The NVLink Fusion platform gives customers a foundation for building custom accelerator chips — combining NVLink connectivity, high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, and rack-scale integration — so they can focus engineering resources on differentiated compute rather than surrounding infrastructure, the companies said. Nvidia has been investing in companies across the AI supply chain, including power infrastructure developer Lancium and chip designer Marvell Technology. The deal echoes terms Nvidia recently secured with Amazon $AMZN, which signed on to incorporate 2 million Nvidia components into its infrastructure and agreed to run Nvidia's connection technology in tandem with chips it develops internally, according to Bloomberg. item.title: Aon is buying rival USI Insurance Services from KKR in a $17 billion deal
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.11
Aon $AON agreed to acquire USI Insurance Services from KKR and other shareholders for $17 billion in cash, the company said Monday, extending its push into the U.S. middle-market insurance segment following its $13 billion purchase of NFP in 2024. The all-cash deal, expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, would make USI CEO Mike Sicard president of Aon USI ranks as the tenth largest U.S. insurance broker, generating approximately $3 billion in annual revenue and employing more than 10,500 people across close to 200 offices nationwide. The Valhalla, New York-based firm offers property and casualty, employee benefits, personal risk, and retirement services to mid-sized businesses. Aon said the acquisition would strengthen its foothold in the U.S. middle-market segment — a space it values at more than $40 billion — while also broadening its reach into the excess and surplus, or E&S, insurance segment, which accounts for 26% of U.S. commercial property and casualty premiums and has been among the industry's fastest-growing lines. "USI will substantially enhance our middle-market footprint and expand access for our firm in the E&S segment," Aon CEO Greg Case said in a statement. Following the close of the transaction, USI Chairman and CEO Mike Sicard will become president of Aon and global CEO of its middle-market business, reporting to Case. "Our firms share strong, one-firm cultures with a deep commitment to working together to bring the best of our capabilities to clients," Sicard said in a statement. Aon expects to fund the acquisition entirely through new debt and said it anticipates remaining investment-grade rated. The company said it does not plan to repurchase shares in the near term as it prioritizes paying down debt. The deal is expected to add to Aon's adjusted earnings per share in 2028 and is projected to generate $395 million in annual run-rate net adjusted EBITDA from revenue and cost synergies across the combined middle-market platform, the company said. For KKR, the sale represents a significant exit. The private equity firm originally took USI private alongside Canadian pension fund Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec in a $4.3 billion transaction in 2014, according to CNBC. KKR reported that the exit delivered approximately six times its return on a 2017 investment and a 3.4 times return on capital across the full life of its USI position. On the advisory side, BofA Securities and Citi worked with Aon, while KKR turned to Goldman Sachs $GS, Insurance Advisory Partners, and Morgan Stanley $MS, according to CNBC. item.title: Eli Lilly is buying a biotech startup for nearly $3 billion to expand into autoimmune diseases
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.06
Eli Lilly $LLY agreed on Monday to acquire Merida Biosciences for up to $2.875 billion in cash, adding a biotechnology platform designed to eliminate the antibodies that cause autoimmune and allergic diseases. The deal adds a pipeline targeting the antibodies behind Graves' disease, thyroid eye disease, food allergy, and other conditions The deal includes an upfront cash payment and contingent milestone payments, the company said. It is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Merida is developing biologics engineered to target and degrade disease-causing antibodies without broadly suppressing the immune system — an approach the company says differs from many existing therapies. Its lead drug candidate, MER511, is in Phase 1 development for Graves' disease and thyroid eye disease, two conditions driven by autoantibodies that activate the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor. Graves' disease affects roughly 3 million people in the U.S., and 25 to 40 percent of those patients go on to develop thyroid eye disease, which can cause pain, disfigurement, and vision loss, the company said. No approved treatments currently target the autoantibodies behind either condition. Initial Phase 1 data for MER511 showed reductions in the relevant autoantibodies, with what the company described as a favorable early safety profile. Merida's pipeline also includes MER769, a preclinical program targeting the antibody that triggers food allergy, asthma, and chronic spontaneous urticaria, along with earlier-stage work in kidney diseases such as membranous nephropathy. "We're building our pipeline around therapies that meaningfully change the course of disease, not just its downstream effects," said Francisco Ramírez-Valle, senior vice president of Lilly immunology research and early clinical development, in a statement. "We see potential to apply this precision approach across a broad range of antibody-driven diseases." Adam Townsend, chief executive officer of Merida, said in a statement that the company was founded to treat autoimmune and allergic diseases by targeting the antibodies driving them rather than suppressing the immune system broadly. "Joining Lilly gives our science the resources and commitment to realize its potential for patients with immune-mediated conditions," he said. The acquisition continues a stretch of deal-making for Indianapolis-based Lilly, which has been flush with cash from its weight-loss drug business. Last month the company struck a deal to buy mental-health-focused AtaiBeckley for an initial $2.8 billion, and in late May it reached agreements to purchase three vaccine developers in transactions worth up to nearly $4 billion combined, according to the Wall Street Journal. Merida got off the ground last year after raising $121 million in a Series A round that Bain Capital Life Sciences, BVF Partners, and Third Rock Ventures jointly led, according to the Wall Street Journal. Ropes & Gray LLP is acting as legal counsel to Lilly. Centerview Partners LLC is acting as financial advisor to Merida, with Goodwin Procter LLP serving as its legal counsel. item.title: U.S. is planning weekly Iran sanctions against banks, Bessent tells G20
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.02
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Sunday that the Treasury Department plans to roll out new secondary sanctions targeting Iran on a weekly basis, beginning with financial institutions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters the effort will escalate to cutting institutions off from the dollar-based financial system "You're going to see a lot more of these every week," Bessent told Reuters. "We're starting with the banks, and we're telling the banks it's not okay to have Iranian money and to aid the regime." Bessent made the remarks ahead of a Group of 20 finance leaders meeting, where he said he intends to press G20 finance ministers and central bank governors to sever economic ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions — penalties that can cut foreign banks and companies off from the U.S. financial system. "There can be no leakage," he said. "You're either with us or you're with the Iranians." The comments came after Treasury imposed penalties last Friday on the United Arab Emirates branches of Egypt's Banque Misr over alleged financial links to Iran. Bessent said a possible next step would be cutting an institution off entirely from the dollar-based financial system. The Treasury Department launched the sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, last week, expanding the categories of Iran-related activity that can trigger secondary sanctions and immediately designating nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels across multiple jurisdictions. Treasury also issued new sectoral sanctions determinations covering digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping. Among the entities sanctioned at the campaign's launch were a number of China- and Hong Kong-based companies and individuals, including Hong Kong-based Sweet Ocean Industrial Limited and several China-based individuals identified as Li Na, Tian Jianbai, and Zhang Limei. Bessent said Sunday that he does not share the view held by some critics that the sanctions campaign is doomed unless Chinese companies are directly subjected to secondary penalties. He argued that China's ability to keep buying Iranian oil has been sharply limited by the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, and that the stockpile of Iranian oil sitting in tankers continues to shrink, concluding: "Problem solved." The U.S.-Iran conflict, now in its sixth month, has strained the global economy. The World Bank cut its global growth forecast for 2026 to 2.5%, calling the slowdown the worst hit to the global economy since the COVID-19 pandemic, as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz pushed energy prices higher. item.title: OpenAI's ChatGPT advertising business posted $1 billion in annualized revenue
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.90
OpenAI announced Monday that its ChatGPT advertising operation has crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate, a figure the company is holding up as validation of its business diversification strategy ahead of an anticipated IPO. The roughly 200-day-old ad business is now available in more than 40 countries, with self-serve access expanding Monday The ad business, which the company said is roughly 200 days old, sits alongside revenue streams including enterprise contracts, consumer subscriptions, and usage-based APIs. ChatGPT ads have launched in more than 40 countries, with OpenAI opening up its self-serve ad platform on Monday to marketers in India, Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. Ads appear for users on OpenAI's free tier and its Go subscription plan. OpenAI said the ads carry labels, are kept separate from how ChatGPT generates answers, and are invisible to advertisers in the sense that those buyers cannot see what users discuss privately. "Our next phase of growth will bring ChatGPT Ads to more markets and introduce additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities," OpenAI said in a release. "We will also explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT." OpenAI began testing ads within ChatGPT in the U.S. in February. Rival Anthropic took notice, centering its first Super Bowl campaign on OpenAI's entry into advertising, according to CNBC. OpenAI is targeting $2.5 billion in advertising revenue for the current year and is tracking toward annualized revenue exceeding $40 billion, roughly twice its run rate at the end of 2025. The company launched ads in India last week, one of ChatGPT's largest markets by weekly active users, with 50 brands participating at rollout and partnerships with agencies WPP and Omnicom. A self-serve ad manager for Indian marketers is set to open Sept. 4, with a daily minimum budget of ₹725 ($7.60). OpenAI's broader advertising strategy has evolved since the February U.S. launch. The company introduced cost-per-click pricing earlier this year, adding a billing model that charges only when a user clicks an ad, alongside its original cost-per-thousand-impressions structure. The company also removed a $50,000 minimum spending requirement when it opened its self-serve Ads Manager to all U.S. businesses. OpenAI reported $6.7 billion in revenue for the second quarter of 2026, up from $5.7 billion the quarter before. The company posted a net loss of $38.5 billion in 2025 on $13.07 billion in revenue and is working toward a planned 2027 IPO. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Gemini won an arbitration over its collapsed crypto lending program
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.75
Gemini Space Station won an arbitration ruling earlier this month finding the crypto exchange did not mislead users or bear responsibility for the collapse of its Earn lending program, according to CNBC. An arbitrator ruled earlier this month that Gemini did not mislead users or fail in its due diligence with lending partner Genesis Global Capital The Aug. 12 ruling dismissed a claim filed in late 2024 by an Earn user who sought damages tied to emotional distress. The ruling concluded that the record contained nothing showing Gemini had deceived customers or skimped on its vetting of Genesis Global Capital, the firm's chief lending partner. "In the instant case, Claimant offered no evidence of an actual or perceived threat to his physical safety," the ruling said, according to CNBC. Rather than faulting Gemini, arbitrators trained their fire on Genesis and its parent Digital Currency Group, run by Barry Silbert, whom they accused of perpetrating a fraud so sweeping that it eluded the firm's own auditors and multiple regulatory bodies right up until Gemini uncovered it. Barry Silbert and DCG did not respond to a request for comment. Earn, which debuted in 2021, promised customers interest as high as 7.4% per year on the digital assets they deposited. Genesis served as the conduit through which Gemini placed those holdings with institutional borrowers. The structure unraveled in November 2022 when Genesis, squeezed by a sector-wide liquidity crisis, stopped processing new loans and redemptions, leaving Gemini with no choice but to suspend withdrawals for its roughly 300,000 Earn customers. Genesis filed for bankruptcy in January 2023, according to Cryptobriefing. The bankruptcy resolution eventually returned all crypto owed to Earn users. Of that total, 97% went out to customers in May 2024, with the final 3% following in June; in both cases, assets were returned in kind rather than being converted to their 2022 dollar values, according to Cryptobriefing. Gemini said that amounted to $1 billion more than when Genesis halted withdrawals. Gemini's legal troubles stemming from Earn were not limited to this arbitration. The New York attorney general sued the company over the program, settling for $50 million in 2024 and barring Gemini from operating crypto-lending programs in the state. As of earlier this month, more than a dozen arbitration disputes brought by Earn customers remained ongoing. Gemini Space Station, co-founded by Tyler Winklevoss and Cameron Winklevoss, went public in September 2025 and has faced a turbulent period since, including headcount reductions and a shareholder lawsuit alleging it misled investors about its prospects around the time of its IPO. item.title: Kalshi handed George Santos its first-ever lifetime ban over prediction market manipulation
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.46
Kalshi banned former Republican Rep. George Santos from its platform for life on Monday and imposed a $71,356 penalty, marking the first lifetime ban the prediction market company has issued, according to a Kalshi spokeswoman. The company also imposed a $71,356 penalty on the former congressman, who settled related CFTC charges in July The ban stems from a Commodity Futures Trading Commission case in which the regulator claimed Santos pocketed more than $17,000 through wagers on his own attendance at President Trump's State of the Union address, all while posting misleading content about his intentions on social media. According to the CFTC, Santos took out contracts predicting his own absence from the address when bad weather put his trip to Washington in doubt, then cashed those contracts out at a profit while simultaneously publishing posts that gave followers the impression he intended to show up. Santos agreed in July to pay more than $35,000 to settle the CFTC's claims. Santos’s attorney, Joseph Murray, said when the settlement was announced that Santos had agreed to pay solely to sidestep the expense of prolonged litigation, and that the decision carried no implication of guilt. The Wall Street Journal reported that Murray had not returned requests for comment on the permanent suspension. Kalshi cited Santos's failure to engage with its internal review as the reason for the lifetime exclusion. Separately, the CFTC imposed its own three-year trading ban on Santos across all platforms, though its settlement documentation acknowledged that he had been cooperative with federal investigators. Santos can appeal Kalshi's decision to the CFTC. Santos, a former New York lawmaker, was expelled from Congress in 2023. In 2024, he entered a guilty plea on federal wire fraud and identity theft charges, receiving a sentence of just over seven years in prison — later commuted by President Trump. The Santos case is part of a broader pattern of scrutiny over insider trading on prediction markets. Kalshi has positioned itself as the more tightly regulated U.S. alternative amid suspicious trades on platforms like Polymarket, running more than 200 insider trading investigations and banning war markets outright. On Friday, the CFTC announced that Gabriel Perez, a White House teleprompter operator, would pay a $65,000 civil penalty and surrender more than $107,000 in winnings from trades made using information gathered in his role. Kalshi suspended Perez for three years, and the CFTC imposed a matching trading ban. Federal authorities are also preparing charges against a U.S. servicemember suspected of placing bets on Polymarket tied to military operations that earned more than $1 million, according to the Wall Street Journal. item.title: FDA updated Lundberg Family Farms' white jasmine rice recall, expanding scope to 13 states
item.description:

The FDA updated the April recall to specify which states received the more than 27,000 packages of potentially contaminated rice The update covers more than 27,000 packages of White Jasmine Rice sold in 2-lb. bags that may be contaminated with foreign materials, according to the FDA. The affected lot codes are 260201MA, with a best-by date of Feb. 1, 2027, and 260202MA, with a best-by date of Feb. 2, 2027. The UPC on the product is 073416-040281. According to People, the affected rice reached consumers across California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, North Carolina, New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin. Stores known to stock the product include Wegmans, Walmart $WMT, Target $TGT, Whole Foods, and Giant. The FDA placed the recall in its Class II category, which applies when a product poses limited health risk — either that any consequences would be temporary or medically reversible, or that the chance of serious harm is unlikely. In an Aug. 29 statement provided to People, a Lundberg Family Farms spokesperson confirmed the product had already been pulled from shelves before the update was issued. "The incident was isolated to a single production run, and no illnesses were reported from consumption of the affected product," the spokesperson said. According to People, Wegmans first initiated a voluntary recall on April 4, but that earlier announcement did not include information about which states had received the product. item.title: McDonald's launches Texas-only meal with collectible artist-designed cups
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.20
McDonald's $MCD is offering an exclusive Texas Meal ahead of the nationwide return of Spicy Chicken McNuggets and Mighty Hot Sauce, which go on sale at participating restaurants across the country on Sept. 1, the company said. According to the company, the Texas Meal bundles a 10-piece Spicy Chicken McNuggets or classic Chicken McNuggets with medium fries and a medium drink, all packaged in a custom Texas-themed bag. Seven collectible cups created by Texas-based artist Avery Orendorf are available to customers who ask for one at the time of purchase. Each cup represents a different region of the state: Houston, San Antonio, Austin/Central Texas, West Texas, East Texas, Dallas/Fort Worth, and the Rio Grande Valley/South Texas. The collectible cups are available only in Texas and are not part of the national rollout. Spicy Chicken McNuggets use the classic McNugget base with a tempura coating that incorporates aged cayenne and chili peppers, the company said. Mighty Hot Sauce, which McDonald's has described as its spiciest dipping sauce, draws heat from red pepper, chilis, and garlic, with a touch of sweetness. The nuggets will be available in four sizes — 6, 10, 20, or 40 pieces — according to Allrecipes. Once live, orders can be placed in-store, via McDelivery, or through the app for pickup, the company said. McDonald's first introduced Spicy Chicken McNuggets in September 2020 and brought them back in 2021, after which the nuggets appeared periodically as a regional item, most recently in 2024. Mighty Hot Sauce has been off menus since 2021, making this its first reappearance in roughly five years. The company said some franchise locations may offer the items before the official Sept. 1 launch date. The return of both items is part of McDonald's broader effort to drive traffic through limited-time offerings. The chain posted U.S. same-store sales growth of 0.8% in the second quarter, a slowdown from the 2.5% gain in the same period a year earlier, as domestic guest counts declined. Earlier in 2026, the company launched the Big Arch burger, which it said contributed to a 3.9% domestic same-store sales gain in the first quarter. McDonald's also introduced Caramel Apple $AAPL Pie coffees on Aug. 17 as part of its fall seasonal lineup, the company said. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Kalshi is partnering with brokerage Alpaca to bring prediction markets to a global audience
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.99
Alpaca reaches 14 million brokerage accounts across more than 300 financial institutions worldwide, giving Kalshi a path to international expansion Individuals and businesses that use Alpaca's brokerage infrastructure will be able to trade Kalshi's event contracts without leaving the platform, leveraging the same technology stack they already rely on for other assets. The company serves more than 300 financial institution partners and has a global footprint spanning 14 million brokerage accounts, according to CNBC. Kalshi vice president of business development Max Crowley said Alpaca's global reach made it an appealing partner. Having Alpaca's technology in place will allow brokerages in other countries to build on top of it, making it faster to get Kalshi's prediction markets live in new markets once local regulatory approval is in place. "They're a trusted brand, they're technology forward, their customers love working with them," Crowley told CNBC. "It's going to take us a lot of time to build the business globally, but this technical partnership enables that." Alpaca pursued the deal after seeing demand from its users for access to event contracts. Tony Lee, Alpaca's chief brokerage officer, said the company's goal is to make financial services accessible to as many people worldwide as possible. "Our mission is really to open up financial services to as many people around the world as possible, and you really have to go where the customer demand is," Lee said. Alpaca earlier this month completed its registration with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, qualifying it as a U.S.-licensed futures commission merchant — a designation for brokerages that handle orders on derivatives contracts. The company's application programming interface, which lets developers create their own trading software, draws 83,000 monthly users. Yoshi Yokokawa, co-founder and CEO of Alpaca, conceded that international growth will be a gradual process, while arguing that the untapped global audience of prospective traders could ultimately prove transformative for prediction markets as an asset class. The Alpaca deal is the latest in a string of expansion moves for Kalshi. In June, the company partnered with Canadian financial firm Wealthsimple to bring its markets to Canada. Kalshi has also been moving beyond prediction markets into traditional derivatives, filing with the CFTC to launch perpetual futures contracts tied to U.S. equity indexes and copper. In May, the company raised a $1 billion Series F round at a $22 billion valuation, with annualized trading volume climbing from $52 billion to $178 billion over the preceding six months. CNBC holds a minority stake in Kalshi and has a customer acquisition arrangement with the company. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: OpenAI is cutting off AI model access to Cursor after SpaceX acquisition
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.95
OpenAI announced it is ending developer access to its AI models via Cursor, the AI coding tool now owned by SpaceX, setting a termination date of Nov. 12, 2026 for existing access and saying it will not provide future models to the service. OpenAI cited past contract violations by Elon Musk's companies as the reason for ending the agreement, with a cutoff set for Nov. 12 OpenAI explained its decision by saying it has no assurance that SpaceX will abide by its terms of service, pointing to its "experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts." The company also highlighted Musk's courtroom admission, during cross-examination in the lawsuit, that xAI had trained its models on OpenAI's output — a technique known as distillation. OpenAI added that it faces heightened responsibility to guarantee its forthcoming model, Astra, operates in accordance with its policies. In an X $TWTR post, Cursor co-founder and CEO Michael Truell disclosed that OpenAI models account for roughly 5% of the platform's user traffic, adding that his team is in talks with OpenAI to find a resolution. "Cursor was one of the very first users of OpenAI, we've worked closely with their team for years, and we've trusted their platform to be neutral infrastructure for our business," Truell wrote, according to CNBC. Musk responded on X, dismissing OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman and repeating his claim that they "stole an open source nonprofit," according to CNBC. Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown wrote on X that his company would "continue to increase compute to support Claude models in Cursor" and said it was eager to see what lies ahead for Cursor under SpaceX's ownership. The post sparked backlash on X, with Replit CEO Amjad Masad calling out Anthropic's own record of cutting off Windsurf from its Claude models the previous June. SpaceX completed its $60 billion all-stock acquisition of Anysphere, Inc., Cursor's parent company, on Aug. 14, according to financial filings. The deal came after Cursor had rebuffed two separate acquisition approaches from OpenAI, with the startup's leadership having prioritized remaining independent. The relationship between SpaceX and Cursor had been deepening before the acquisition closed. SpaceXAI and Cursor jointly trained Grok 4.5, a coding-focused AI model launched in July, using tens of thousands of Nvidia $NVDA GB300 GPUs. SpaceX had earlier folded xAI, Musk's AI venture, into its operations. The dispute is part of a broader conflict between Musk and OpenAI. Musk co-founded the company as a nonprofit in 2015 and left its board in 2018. He sued OpenAI in 2024 over its transition to a for-profit structure, but a jury ruled against him this past May, according to Engadget. Musk has vowed to appeal. item.title: Manhattan's luxury rental prices are surging as wealthy buyers opt to rent instead
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 2.10
The average price for top-tier Manhattan rentals jumped 35% over the past year, to $17,464 a month, as high-end buyers sit out the sales market That figure — drawn from the Real Deal Report by Jonathan Miller, Street Matrix's director of markets — marked a 35% jump over the past year, bringing the average luxury rental price to $17,464 a month. Across the broader market, the median Manhattan rent hit a record $5,000 a month in July, and the average climbed to $6,306 — a 15% gain from a year earlier. The surge at the high end has created a market for rentals that would have once been considered extraordinary. Compared with 2025, the count of apartments commanding more than $50,000 a month has more than doubled so far this year, and those exceeding $100,000 a month have increased sevenfold, according to CNBC. Laura Klein of Bespoke Real Estate, who recently brokered a penthouse rental in Chelsea for $177,000 a month, said the trend is being driven by a shortage of available properties to purchase. Her current portfolio includes a $175,000-a-month Tribeca unit and a $95,000-a-month Upper East Side property. She said these ultra-high-end listings never appear publicly and move exclusively through a tight circle of brokers. "The $100,000-a-month number is almost normal now," Klein said. "These are renters who want turnkey, unique, trophy properties." Brokers also pointed to New York City's new pied-à-terre tax as a factor pushing wealthy would-be buyers into the rental market. The surcharge applies to second homes worth $5 million or more, as well as co-ops and condominiums at the $1 million threshold when not used as a primary residence. Pam Liebman, president and CEO of The Corcoran Group, said: "The sharp increase in rentals following the pied-à-terre tax announcement suggests that some prospective purchasers may already be choosing flexibility over ownership." The tax's rollout has faced legal challenges. A Staten Island judge issued a temporary restraining order pausing enforcement of the surcharge after three homeowners sued, arguing their primary residences were incorrectly flagged. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration filed a motion to appeal, triggering an automatic stay of the lower court's order. A hearing in the case was scheduled for today. Klein described the owners as motivated by demand rather than financial need. "They say to me, 'If the number is right, I'll rent,'" she said. "These are properties that if they were on the market would be listed for tens of millions" of dollars. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Polymarket military bets expose security risks as soldier case reaches court
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 4.98
More than 150 cryptocurrency wallets betting on military events through Polymarket behaved in ways researchers associate with possible insider trading. Now a separate federal prosecution involving a U.S. Army master sergeant is giving those concerns a real-world legal test. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective, or ACDC, identified 152 wallets making unusually successful longshot bets in military and defence markets. Together, the wallets won about $8 million. Its August report, Classifying Insider Trading Risk: Analyzing the Longshot Betting Ecosystem on Polymarket, examined 78,496 longshot bets from 12,355 wallets on markets settled through May 5, 2026. The research does not show that those 152 wallets belonged to military personnel, government officials or anyone else holding classified information. Instead, ACDC created a statistical profile for accounts whose behaviour resembles previously reported cases of suspected insider trading. Researchers call those accounts “Orcas.” They tend to focus on relatively few subjects, win unusually often when betting on outcomes the market considers unlikely and sometimes appear shortly before the event being predicted. ACDC put wallets with longshot success rates above 75%, concentrated activity and limited market breadth among its most suspicious accounts. Suspicious military bets appeared on Polymarket before larger traders moved in Of 1,432 wallets making longshot military bets, researchers classified 152 as Orcas. Another 482 were high-volume “Whales,” while 166 appeared to be automated Bots. The Orcas put roughly $2 million into military longshots and made an average profit of about $52,514 per wallet. ACDC cautioned that proving whether any individual trader actually possessed inside information would require investigative powers beyond the study. What happened after those bets appeared may be just as important. Around major military events, winning Orca wagers generally arrived before Whales and Bots moved into the same markets. “In both cases, longshot bets by Orcas preceded longshot bets by Whales and Bots,” the researchers found in their analysis of military-market activity. It raises the possibility that sophisticated traders were watching public blockchain transactions, spotting unusual bets and following them with larger positions.
